title: Rater models: many-facet Rasch and beyond
text:
For instructors

Source: new material, not in EDUC 252. Ben added the lesson on 09-25 while reviewing the G theory lesson, as the answer to its problem 6.
Timing: about 60 minutes for the core ideas and widgets; the real-data section works as a 30-minute lab (the hierarchical rater model takes one to two minutes in local R, so start it first).
Software: the many-facet model runs in the browser with TAM. The hierarchical rater model runs only in the downloadable code (sirt::rm.sdt), and the page shows its output from the render. A fixed-effects many-facet fit to the essay table’s 315 teachers takes over a minute in local R; the lesson uses random effects in lme4 there instead.
Held back: rater × criterion interactions (differential rater functioning) and rater-specific discrimination are in the problems and Going further; drift is shown by widget and cited, not fitted, since neither table has rating dates; automated scoring, and QWK against PRMSE for judging engines, are left to AI and psychometrics and the readings.
Solutions: held back in solutions/rater-models.qmd (not published). Problem 6 is open.

title: Models for polytomous responses
text:
What this is for
Every model so far has been for dichotomous responses: right or wrong, scored 0 or 1. Much of what respondents give us isn’t like that. A Likert rating runs from strongly disagree to strongly agree, a problem earns partial credit for a correct method with a wrong answer, and a symptom item asks how often, from never to always. We could collapse them to 0 and 1, but Information, precision, and short forms showed that an item measures well near its difficulty, and five ordered categories have four boundaries, so four places to be informative; collapsing keeps one. This lesson builds the standard models for ordered categories, each splitting a response into binary questions answered by a model we already know. It fits four to seven PROMIS pain items and asks what the choice among them changes, and what collapsing would cost. The short answers: not much, and most of the information above the middle of the scale.

title: Models for polytomous responses
Models for polytomous responses
text:
Core ideas

Ordered categories
A response is polytomous when it can fall in more than two categories. The models here need the categories to be mutually exclusive and ordered, each step up meaning more of what is measured: a rating from strongly disagree to strongly agree, a frequency from never to always, or partial credit on a problem (0 for nothing, 1 for a correct setup, 2 for a correct method, 3 for a correct answer). We score the categories \(0, 1, \dots, K\), so an item has \(K\) steps; Ostini and Nering (2006) survey the models. More categories carry more information but take more parameters, and when a person scores the response, the rater becomes a source of error (Many sources of error: generalizability theory).


Three ways to split a response
How can models for 0/1 responses handle four categories? Split the response into binary questions, each with its own curve. Tutz (2022) builds a taxonomy of ordinal models on this view. Three standard splits give three families: cumulative, sequential and adjacent-category (Tutz, 1990, 1997; Mellenbergh, 1995).

Cumulative splits ask “is \(x\) at least \(k\)?” for each \(k\). The graded response model (GRM; Samejima, 1969) gives each a 2PL with the item’s slope: \[\Pr(x \ge k) = \frac{\exp\big(a(\theta - b_k)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a(\theta - b_k)\big)}, \qquad \Pr(x = k) = \Pr(x \ge k) - \Pr(x \ge k + 1).\] \(b_k\) is the \(\theta\) at which half of respondents reach category \(k\) or above. The boundaries must be ordered, \(b_1 < b_2 < \dots\), or some probabilities would be negative.
Adjacent-category splits ask “is \(x\) equal to \(k\) rather than \(k-1\)?”, among responses in one of the two. The generalized partial credit model (GPCM; Muraki, 1992) gives each a 2PL, \(\Pr(x = k \mid x \in \{k-1, k\}) = \text{logit}^{-1}\big(a(\theta - b_k)\big)\), which works out to \[\Pr(x = k) \propto \exp\Big(\sum_{v=1}^{k} a(\theta - b_v)\Big).\] \(b_k\), the step difficulty, is the \(\theta\) at which categories \(k-1\) and \(k\) are equally likely. With \(a = 1\) for every item this is the partial credit model (PCM; Masters, 1982).
Sequential splits ask “having reached category \(k - 1\), does the respondent go on to \(k\)?” The sequential model (Tutz, 1990) gives each step a 2PL, \(\Pr(x \ge k \mid x \ge k-1) = \text{logit}^{-1}\big(a(\theta - b_k)\big)\), and the respondent stops at the first step failed. It suits a problem solved in stages.

In Thissen and Steinberg’s (1986) terms, the GRM is a difference model and the partial credit family divide-by-total models (the \(\propto\) hides a division by the sum over categories).






If you’ve done Factor analysis II: an ordinal factor model, a continuous latent response cut at thresholds, is the GRM with a normal ogive in place of the logistic. Each threshold becomes a boundary \(b_k\).




Try it: three ways to split a response
Pick a response on a 0–3 item and a set of splits. Each row is one binary question; the cells say how each category answers it. The outlined column is the chosen response.


Code
viewof sp_x = Inputs.radio([0, 1, 2, 3], {value: 2, label: "Response x"})
viewof sp_model = Inputs.radio(["Cumulative (GRM)", "Adjacent categories (PCM, GPCM)", "Sequential"], {value: "Cumulative (GRM)", label: "Splits"})


















Code
sp_role = (k, c) => sp_model.startsWith("Cum") ? (c >= k ? "1" : "0") :
  sp_model.startsWith("Adj") ? (c === k ? "1" : c === k - 1 ? "0" : "not used") :
  (c >= k ? "1" : c === k - 1 ? "0" : "not used")
sp_q = k => sp_model.startsWith("Cum") ? `Is x ≥ ${k}?` : sp_model.startsWith("Adj") ? `x = ${k} rather than ${k - 1}?` : `Given x ≥ ${k - 1}, is x ≥ ${k}?`
sp_cells = [1, 2, 3].flatMap(k => [0, 1, 2, 3].map(c => ({split: sp_q(k), cat: `x = ${c}`, role: sp_role(k, c), mine: c === sp_x})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 200, marginLeft: 190, padding: 0.06,
  x: {label: null, domain: [0, 1, 2, 3].map(c => `x = ${c}`), axis: "top"}, y: {label: null, domain: [1, 2, 3].map(sp_q)},
  color: {domain: ["1", "0", "not used"], range: [palette.main, palette.light, palette.white], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(sp_cells, {x: "cat", y: "split", fill: "role", stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.text(sp_cells, {x: "cat", y: "split", text: d => d.role === "not used" ? "–" : d.role, fill: d => d.role === "1" ? palette.white : palette.ink, fontSize: 14}),
    Plot.cell(sp_cells.filter(d => d.mine), {x: "cat", y: "split", fill: null, stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 3})
  ]
})
































Code
md`A response of ${sp_x} answers ${[1, 2, 3].filter(k => sp_role(k, sp_x) !== "not used").length} of the three questions: ${[1, 2, 3].filter(k => sp_role(k, sp_x) !== "not used").map(k => `"${sp_q(k)}" ${sp_role(k, sp_x) === "1" ? "yes" : "no"}`).join("; ")}.`







Same response, three sets of binary data, three models.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A respondent answers 1 on a 0–3 item. Under the sequential model, what does that response say about step 3 (going from 2 to 3)?",
  options: [
    {text: "Nothing: the respondent never reached it", correct: true, why: "The sequential model passes steps in order and stops at the first failure. This respondent passed step 1 and failed step 2, so step 3 was never attempted."},
    {text: "That the respondent failed it", correct: false, why: "That is the cumulative reading ($x \\ge 3$? no). The sequential model only records a failure at the step where the respondent stopped."},
    {text: "That the respondent passed it", correct: false, why: "Passing step 3 would mean reaching category 3."}
  ]
})










Category curves and the expected score
Plotting \(\Pr(x = k)\) against \(\theta\) for each category gives the category response functions (CRFs). The expected score curve, \(E(x \mid \theta) = \sum_k k \Pr(x = k \mid \theta)\), plays the part of the ICC, on the response scale.

Try it: category curves and the expected score


Code
viewof cr_model = Inputs.radio(["GRM", "GPCM", "Sequential"], {value: "GPCM", label: "Model"})
viewof cr_a = Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: 1.5, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a"})
viewof cr_b1 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: -1.5, step: 0.1, label: "b1"})
viewof cr_b2 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "b2"})
viewof cr_b3 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "b3"})







































Code
cr_bs = [cr_b1, cr_b2, cr_b3]
cr_th = grid(-4, 4, 321)
cr_cols = [palette.light, palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink]
cr_rows = cr_th.flatMap(t => catProbs(cr_model, t, cr_a, cr_bs).map((p, k) => ({theta: t, p, cat: `x = ${k}`})))
cr_legend = Plot.legend({color: {domain: ["x = 0", "x = 1", "x = 2", "x = 3"], range: cr_cols}})
cr_crf = Plot.plot({
  width: 420, height: 260, marginLeft: 45, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(x = k)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {domain: ["x = 0", "x = 1", "x = 2", "x = 3"], range: cr_cols},
  marks: [Plot.ruleX(cr_model === "GRM" ? [...cr_bs].sort((u, v) => u - v) : cr_bs, {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
          Plot.line(cr_rows, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "cat", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})
cr_erf = Plot.plot({
  width: 420, height: 260, marginLeft: 45, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Expected score", domain: [0, 3]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0, 1, 2, 3], {stroke: palette.rule}),
          Plot.line(cr_th.map(t => ({theta: t, e: expectedScore(catProbs(cr_model, t, cr_a, cr_bs))})), {x: "theta", y: "e", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})
htl.html`<div>${cr_legend}<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; align-items: flex-end;">${cr_crf}${cr_erf}</div></div>`




























































Code
cr_never = [1, 2].filter(k => !everModal(cr_model, cr_a, cr_bs, k, cr_th))
md`${cr_model === "GRM" && (cr_b1 > cr_b2 || cr_b2 > cr_b3) ? "The GRM needs ordered boundaries, so the widget has sorted them. " : ""}Expected score at θ = 0: **${expectedScore(catProbs(cr_model, 0, cr_a, cr_bs)).toFixed(2)}**. ${cr_never.length ? `Category ${cr_never.join(" and ")} is never the most likely response, anywhere on the scale.` : "Every category is the most likely response somewhere on the scale."} The dashed lines mark the b parameters.`
















At the defaults each category has its turn as the most likely response; under the GPCM the dashed lines sit where neighbouring curves cross. The same \(b\) values mean different things in each model: the expected score at \(\theta = 0\) is 1.50 under the GRM and GPCM, 1.40 under the sequential model.
Now, under the GPCM, set \(b_1 = 0.5\) and \(b_2 = -0.5\). The steps are disordered, and category 1 is never the most likely response. The GRM can’t do this: it reorders the same values, and category 1 becomes most likely between them. What do disordered steps say? Not that the categories are out of order, since the expected score still rises with \(\theta\), but that a middle category is seldom chosen. What to do about it depends on an assumption. Andrich (2013) takes the categories to be designed so that each should be most likely somewhere, and reads disordered steps as a reason to revisit them. Adams, Wu and Wilson (2012) take the steps as describing category frequencies, which a small middle category explains without any problem in the ordering. The pain data below have three such items.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A GPCM item on a 0–3 scale has step difficulties $b_1 = 0.2$, $b_2 = -0.4$, $b_3 = 1.1$. What follows?",
  options: [
    {text: "Category 1 is never the most likely response", correct: true, why: "With $b_2 < b_1$, category 2 overtakes category 1 before category 1 has overtaken category 0, so category 1 never tops both its neighbours. Try it in the widget."},
    {text: "Respondents higher on θ tend to give lower scores", correct: false, why: "The expected score still rises with θ whatever the steps. Disordered steps are about how likely one category is, not about the order of the categories."},
    {text: "The model cannot be fitted", correct: false, why: "The GPCM fits such items without difficulty; only the GRM needs its boundaries in order."}
  ]
})










The partial credit model is a Rasch model






Recall from The Rasch model: under the Rasch model the sum score \(r\) is sufficient for \(\theta\), so respondents with the same sum score get the same estimate, and conditioning on \(r\) removes \(\theta\) altogether. From the 1PL to the 4PL showed the 2PL weighting items by their slopes instead.



Does sufficiency survive more than two categories? Under the PCM, take two adjacent categories: the log odds of \(k\) against \(k - 1\) is \(\theta - b_k\). Each adjacent pair is a Rasch item.

Try it: adjacent categories on the log-odds scale
The item has \(b = -1.5, 0, 1.5\). Each line is the log odds of one category against the one below it.


Code
viewof ad_model = Inputs.radio(["PCM", "GPCM", "GRM"], {value: "PCM", label: "Model"})
viewof ad_a = Inputs.range([0.5, 3], {value: 1.5, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a (GPCM, GRM)"})


















Code
ad_bs = [-1.5, 0, 1.5]
ad_slope = (k, t) => (adjacentLogit(ad_model, t + 0.01, ad_a, ad_bs, k) - adjacentLogit(ad_model, t - 0.01, ad_a, ad_bs, k)) / 0.02
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Log odds, k against k − 1", domain: [-8, 8]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["1 vs 0", "2 vs 1", "3 vs 2"], range: [palette.light, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
          Plot.line(grid(-4, 4, 161).flatMap(t => [1, 2, 3].map(k => ({theta: t, lo: adjacentLogit(ad_model, t, ad_a, ad_bs, k), pair: `${k} vs ${k - 1}`}))).filter(d => Math.abs(d.lo) < 8),
            {x: "theta", y: "lo", stroke: "pair", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})

























Code
md`Slopes of the three lines at θ = −2: **${[1, 2, 3].map(k => ad_slope(k, -2).toFixed(2)).join(", ")}**; at θ = 2: **${[1, 2, 3].map(k => ad_slope(k, 2).toFixed(2)).join(", ")}**.`







Under the PCM the lines are straight and parallel, with slope 1: three Rasch items, crossing zero at their steps. Under the GPCM the slope is \(a\). Under the GRM they bend (with \(a = 1.5\), the first line’s slope is 1.43 at \(\theta = -2\) and 0.07 at \(\theta = 2\)): built on cumulative splits, its adjacent comparisons aren’t logistic.
Because every adjacent comparison in the PCM is a Rasch item, the Rasch algebra goes through: \(\theta\) meets the responses only through the sum of the category scores, \(r = \sum_i x_i\), so \(r\) is sufficient (the Go deeper callout below factors the likelihood), and conditional maximum likelihood works as before. Under the GPCM the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) takes \(r\)’s place, as under the 2PL; the GRM has no such statistic. The rating scale model (Andrich, 1978) restricts the PCM further, giving every item the same pattern of steps; problem 2 tries it.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two respondents answer the same three 0–4 items. A answers 4, 0, 0; B answers 1, 2, 1. Under the partial credit model, how do their estimates of θ compare?",
  options: [
    {text: "They are equal", correct: true, why: "Both sum scores are 4, and under the PCM the sum of the category scores is sufficient for θ."},
    {text: "B's is higher: B's responses are more consistent", correct: false, why: "Consistency bears on how well the model fits B's pattern (person fit), not on the estimate. Only the sum score enters it."},
    {text: "It depends on the items' step difficulties", correct: false, why: "The step difficulties enter the likelihood only in a term that doesn't involve θ. Under the GRM your answer would be right."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: the PCM’s sum score, and what the other models lack





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) items with categories \(0, \dots, K_i\); the PCM holds for every item; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the step difficulties \(b_{iv}\) are known.
One item. Write \(\beta_{ik} = \sum_{v=1}^{k} b_{iv}\) (with \(\beta_{i0} = 0\); these are sums of step difficulties, not regression coefficients). The PCM is \[\Pr(x_i = k \mid \theta) = \frac{\exp(k\theta - \beta_{ik})}{D_i(\theta)}, \qquad D_i(\theta) = \sum_{h=0}^{K_i} \exp(h\theta - \beta_{ih}).\] Dividing two neighbouring categories gives \(\Pr(x_i = k)/\Pr(x_i = k-1) = \exp(\theta - b_{ik})\): the Rasch model for the adjacent pair.
The pattern. Multiply over items: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \frac{\exp(r\theta)\,\exp\big(-\sum_i \beta_{i x_i}\big)}{\prod_i D_i(\theta)}, \qquad r = \sum_i x_i.\] As in The Rasch model, the data meet \(\theta\) only in \(\exp(r\theta)\), so \(r\) is sufficient. Summing over the patterns with the same \(r\) and dividing gives \(\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r) = \exp(-\sum_i \beta_{i x_i}) / \sum_{\mathbf{y}:\,\sum y_i = r} \exp(-\sum_i \beta_{i y_i})\), with no \(\theta\) in it: conditional maximum likelihood for the steps (Masters, 1982). The same cancellation with two items gives specific objectivity for comparisons between items.
The GPCM. With slopes, \(k\theta\) becomes \(a_i k\theta\), and \(\theta\) meets the data in \(\exp(\theta\sum_i a_i x_i)\): the weighted score is sufficient, but its weights are item parameters, as in the 2PL.
The GRM. \(\Pr(x_i = k)\) is a difference of two logistic curves, which doesn’t factor into a term in \(\theta\) times a term in the data. The likelihood depends on which categories were chosen, not only on a weighted sum of them, so no statistic simpler than the pattern is sufficient. van der Ark (2001) compares what the sum score does and doesn’t guarantee under each family.






Information, and what collapsing costs






Recall from Information, precision, and short forms: a 2PL item’s information is \(a^2 P(1 - P)\), the variance of its score term, largest at \(\theta = b\). Test information is the sum over items, and the conditional SEM is \(1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}\).



What is the information in a polytomous item? The same curvature argument gives \[I(\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{K} \frac{\big(\partial \Pr(x = k)/\partial\theta\big)^2}{\Pr(x = k)}\] (Samejima, 1969), which for a 0/1 item is \(a^2P(1-P)\); for the GPCM it is \(a^2\) times the variance of the response given \(\theta\). An item with well-spaced categories is informative across the range its boundaries cover. Under the GRM, collapsing is easy to compare: the item “is \(x \ge k\)?” is a 2PL with slope \(a\) and difficulty \(b_k\), informative around that one boundary.

Try it: what collapsing costs
A GRM item scored 0–3. Compare its information with the item collapsed to 0/1 at one of its boundaries. The shading is where respondents are (a standard normal).


Code
viewof co_a = Inputs.range([0.5, 3], {value: 2, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a"})
viewof co_b1 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: -1, step: 0.1, label: "b1"})
viewof co_b2 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "b2"})
viewof co_b3 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "b3"})
viewof co_cut = Inputs.radio(["x ≥ 1", "x ≥ 2", "x ≥ 3"], {value: "x ≥ 1", label: "Collapse at"})







































Code
co_bs = [co_b1, co_b2, co_b3].sort((u, v) => u - v)
co_k = Number(co_cut.slice(-1))
co_bin = t => { const p = 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-co_a * (t - co_bs[co_k - 1]))); return co_a * co_a * p * (1 - p); }
co_th = grid(-4, 4, 321)
co_top = Math.max(...co_th.map(t => polyInfo("GRM", t, co_a, co_bs)), 0.3)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 290, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Item information", domain: [0, co_top * 1.1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Four categories", `Collapsed at ${co_cut}`], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(co_th.map(t => ({theta: t, d: dnorm(t) / dnorm(0) * co_top * 0.5})), {x: "theta", y: "d", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.4}),
    Plot.line(co_th.flatMap(t => [{theta: t, I: polyInfo("GRM", t, co_a, co_bs), item: "Four categories"},
                                 {theta: t, I: co_bin(t), item: `Collapsed at ${co_cut}`}]), {x: "theta", y: "I", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})














































Code
md`Information at θ = −1, 0.5 and 2: four categories **${[-1, 0.5, 2].map(t => polyInfo("GRM", t, co_a, co_bs).toFixed(2)).join(", ")}**; collapsed at ${co_cut}, **${[-1, 0.5, 2].map(t => co_bin(t).toFixed(2)).join(", ")}**.`







At the defaults the full item gives about 1 from \(\theta = -1\) to 2 (1.04, 1.09, 1.04). Collapsed at \(x \ge 1\) it keeps 1.00 at \(\theta = -1\) and has 0.01 at \(\theta = 2\). Each cut does well near its own boundary only, and no cut beats the full item anywhere; the second Go deeper callout proves that merging categories can’t add information. MacCallum, Zhang, Preacher and Rucker (2002) make the parallel case for continuous variables. Collapsing is a reasonable choice when a category is nearly empty, or when the only decision sits at one boundary.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A GRM item scored 0–4 has boundaries $b = -1, 0, 1, 2$ and slope 2. You collapse it to 'any symptom' ($x \\ge 1$). For whom is the loss of information largest?",
  options: [
    {text: "Respondents near θ = 2", correct: true, why: "The collapsed item is a 2PL at $b = -1$, informative only near −1. At θ = 2 the full item still has boundaries nearby; the collapsed one has none."},
    {text: "Respondents near θ = −1", correct: false, why: "That is where the collapsed item's one boundary sits, so it keeps most of the information there."},
    {text: "Everyone loses the same amount", correct: false, why: "Information is a curve, and each boundary contributes near its own location. Dropping boundaries costs most where they were."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: information for a polytomous item, and why merging categories loses it





Assumptions: one item with categories \(0, \dots, K\); \(P_k(\theta) = \Pr(x = k \mid \theta)\) is differentiable and positive; item parameters known.
Information. The log likelihood of one response is \(\log P_x(\theta)\). Its derivative is \(P_x'/P_x\), which has mean \(\sum_k P_k' = 0\) (the \(P_k\) sum to 1). Fisher information is its variance: \[I(\theta) = \sum_k P_k \left(\frac{P_k'}{P_k}\right)^2 = \sum_k \frac{(P_k')^2}{P_k}.\] With \(K = 1\) and \(P_1 = \text{logit}^{-1}(a(\theta - b))\), \(P_1' = aP_1(1-P_1)\) and \(P_0' = -P_1'\), and this is \(a^2P_1(1-P_1)\).
The GPCM. Here \(\log P_k = ak\theta - (\text{a term without } \theta) - \log D(\theta)\), so \(P_k'/P_k = a\big(k - E(x \mid \theta)\big)\), and \[I(\theta) = a^2 \sum_k P_k \big(k - E(x \mid \theta)\big)^2 = a^2\,\text{Var}(x \mid \theta).\]
Merging loses information. Merge categories \(j\) and \(k\) into one. Their joint contribution to \(I\) becomes \((P_j' + P_k')^2/(P_j + P_k)\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \[(P_j' + P_k')^2 = \left(\sqrt{P_j}\,\frac{P_j'}{\sqrt{P_j}} + \sqrt{P_k}\,\frac{P_k'}{\sqrt{P_k}}\right)^2 \le (P_j + P_k)\left(\frac{(P_j')^2}{P_j} + \frac{(P_k')^2}{P_k}\right),\] so the merged term is never larger than the two separate terms, and equals them only where \(P_j'/P_j = P_k'/P_k\), where the two categories respond to \(\theta\) identically. Collapsing to 0/1 is a sequence of such merges.



The choice among these models is a small decision; the choice to keep the categories is a large one.

title: Models for polytomous responses
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates 1,000 respondents answering six 0–3 items from the PCM, fits the PCM and the GRM, and compares both with the truth. Then it collapses every item at \(x \ge 2\), fits a 2PL, and compares test information. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load. mirt fits the PCM with the itemtype "Rasch", which for polytomous items fixes every slope at 1 and estimates the SD of \(\theta\).
With the seed as written, the PCM recovers every step within 0.15, including item 6’s disordered pair (0.5 and −0.5, estimated 0.54 and −0.65), and AIC prefers it to the GRM (14,443 against 14,470). In the plot of item 6, the GRM still gives category 1 a curve of about the right height, with outer curves a little steeper than the truth. Collapsing costs information everywhere, least in the middle (4.09 against 4.79 at \(\theta = 0\)) and most in the tails (0.56 against 1.60 at \(\theta = -2\)). Try np <- 200, steps far apart such as c(-2.5, 0, 2.5), or a collapse at resp >= 1.

title: Models for polytomous responses
text:
With real data

Pain interference
Our main example is promis1wave1_pain, from the first wave of testing of the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS), which tested item banks for health outcomes on adults from the US general population and clinical groups (Cella et al., 2010; data at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/0NGAKG). Its job is to be a polytomous scale on which most respondents report little. We use seven of the 56 candidate items for the pain-interference bank (Amtmann et al., 2010). They ask, for the past seven days, how much pain interfered with enjoying social activities, and how often it caused anxiety, led to avoiding social activities or long trips, made simple tasks hard, or prevented walking a mile or standing for an hour. HealthMeasures, which distributes PROMIS, doesn’t permit republishing the items, so we summarize them. Responses run from 1 (never, or not at all) to 5 (always, or very much): higher means more interference, and no item needs reversing. We recode them 0–4. Download the code to run every chunk yourself.


Code
library(mirt)
set.seed(8)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with a
# CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
pain_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.promis1wave1_pain/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(pain_url)
c(respondents = length(unique(df$id)), items = length(unique(df$item)))


respondents       items 
      15961         168 


Code
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
# The bank was given in blocks, so each respondent answered only some items. Seven
# interference items (PAININ36-PAININ42) were often given together. Responses run
# from 1 (never, or not at all) to 5 (always, or very much): higher = more
# interference, so no item needs reversing. We recode to 0-4.
items <- paste0("PAININ", 36:42)
pain <- as.data.frame(wide[complete.cases(wide[, items]), items]) - 1
nrow(pain)                                    # respondents who answered all seven


[1] 1908


Code
round(prop.table(table(unlist(pain))), 2)     # share of responses in each category



   0    1    2    3    4 
0.55 0.16 0.14 0.09 0.06 


Code
mean(rowSums(pain) == 0)                      # share who chose 0 on every item


[1] 0.3066038


The table’s 168 items (interference, behaviour and quality) were given in overlapping blocks, so each of the 15,961 respondents answered some of them; 1,908 answered all seven of ours. (In the behaviour and quality sections, some six-option items share one code between their two lowest options, per the IRW’s item-text notes; the interference items keep their five categories.) Of all responses, 55% are 0, and 31% of respondents chose 0 on every item.


Code
# Four models. mirt's "Rasch" itemtype is the partial credit model when items have
# more than two categories; it fixes every slope at 1 and estimates the SD of theta.
models <- c(PCM = "Rasch", GPCM = "gpcm", GRM = "graded", sequential = "sequential")
fits <- lapply(models, function(m) mirt(pain, 1, itemtype = m, verbose = FALSE))
t(sapply(fits, function(f) c(parameters = extract.mirt(f, "nest"),
                             logLik = round(extract.mirt(f, "logLik")),
                             AIC = round(extract.mirt(f, "AIC")),
                             BIC = round(extract.mirt(f, "BIC")))))


           parameters logLik   AIC   BIC
PCM                29 -12194 24445 24607
GPCM               35 -12045 24160 24355
GRM                35 -11961 23992 24186
sequential         35 -12043 24155 24349


Code
# GRM slopes and category boundaries. mirt writes the GRM as P(x >= k) =
# logistic(a * theta + d_k); IRTpars = TRUE converts to our b_k = -d_k / a.
round(coef(fits$GRM, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items, 2)


            a    b1   b2   b3   b4
PAININ36 4.41  0.04 0.67 1.21 1.83
PAININ37 2.71  0.13 0.83 1.61 2.50
PAININ38 5.17  0.26 0.68 1.28 2.08
PAININ39 4.40 -0.11 0.46 1.18 2.01
PAININ40 3.37  0.08 0.40 0.74 1.15
PAININ41 2.81  0.73 1.13 1.60 2.42
PAININ42 3.00  0.12 0.47 0.87 1.37


AIC (Akaike, 1974) and BIC (Schwarz, 1978) agree: the GRM fits best (AIC 23,992), then the sequential model and the GPCM (24,155 and 24,160), then the PCM (24,445), with six fewer parameters. PROMIS calibrated its banks with the GRM (Cella et al., 2010). The slopes, 2.71 to 5.17, are steep beside the RMET’s 0.19 to 1.13 (From the 1PL to the 4PL), and every boundary lies between \(-0.11\) and 2.50, above the middle of the scale.






If you’ve done Model fit and out-of-sample prediction: AIC and BIC say which model is preferred, not how much better it predicts new responses. Whether the choice among these models ever matters much across the IRW is a question the IMV could answer.





Code
predict({
  q: "The GRM beats the GPCM by 168 AIC points. How closely will the four models' scores for the 1,908 respondents agree?",
  choices: ["Correlations near 0.8", "Correlations near 0.9", "Correlations of 0.99 or above"],
  answer: "Correlations of 0.99 or above",
  reveal: "0.994 to 0.999. Four models with nearly the same number of parameters, fitted to the same seven items, order the respondents almost identically. Check the output below."
})









Code
# Each respondent's expected a posteriori (EAP) score under each model.
theta <- sapply(fits, function(f) fscores(f, method = "EAP")[, 1])
round(cor(theta), 3)

PCM        1.000 0.996 0.994      0.995
GPCM       0.996 1.000 0.998      0.999
GRM        0.994 0.998 1.000      0.997
sequential 0.995 0.999 0.997      1.000


The scores correlate from 0.994 to 0.999. The category curves for one item show why:


Code
# Category response functions for one item under three models. (The PCM is left out:
# it estimates the SD of theta rather than fixing it at 1, so its theta is on a
# different scale.)
th <- matrix(seq(-2, 4, length.out = 241))
item <- "PAININ40"
cols <- c(GPCM = "#c2410c", GRM = "#2780e3", sequential = "black")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = range(th), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Pain interference θ",
     ylab = "Probability of each category", las = 1)
for (m in names(cols)) {
  p <- probtrace(extract.item(fits[[m]], which(items == item)), th)
  matlines(th, p, lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols[m])
}
legend("right", names(cols), col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")









Code
par(op)


For PAININ40 (walking a mile) the GRM, GPCM and sequential curves follow each other closely: different parameters, much the same probabilities.


Code
# GPCM step difficulties: b_k is where categories k - 1 and k are equally likely.
# When b_2 < b_1, category 1 ("rarely", or "a little bit") is never the most

gpcm_b <- coef(fits$GPCM, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
round(gpcm_b, 2)

# Is category 1 ever the most likely response, anywhere on the scale? Under the
# GPCM and under the GRM, which cannot have disordered boundaries:
th_all <- matrix(seq(-4, 5, length.out = 901))
sapply(c("GPCM", "GRM"), function(m) sapply(setNames(seq_along(items), items), function(i)
  any(apply(probtrace(extract.item(fits[[m]], i), th_all), 1, which.max) == 2)))

PAININ37  TRUE  TRUE
PAININ38  TRUE  TRUE
PAININ39  TRUE  TRUE
PAININ40 FALSE FALSE
PAININ41 FALSE FALSE

Three items have disordered GPCM steps (\(b_2 < b_1\)): PAININ40, 41 and 42 (walking a mile, avoiding long trips, standing for an hour). For all three, category 1 (rarely) is never the most likely response, under the GPCM and equally under the GRM, whose boundaries can’t be disordered. The proportions say why: 10% to 12% chose category 1 on these items, against 15% to 22% on the other four, while PAININ40 and 42 have the most responses in the top category (16% and 12%). Whether that calls for rewording, or is how people experience these activities, is a question for the item writers; the model raises it without settling it.


Code
# Under the PCM the sum score is sufficient: equal sum scores, equal estimates.
# Under the GRM they can differ. Largest spread of EAP scores within a sum score:
r <- rowSums(pain)
sapply(c("PCM", "GRM"), function(m) round(max(tapply(theta[, m], r, function(v) diff(range(v)))), 2))


 PCM  GRM 
0.00 0.91 


Sufficiency, in data: under the PCM, equal sum scores get equal estimates (largest spread 0.00); under the GRM they spread by up to 0.91.
So which model would I fit to these items? The PCM offers a sufficient sum score and asks for equal slopes in return. The GRM and GPCM let slopes vary, which these items need (2.71 to 5.17), and the GRM fits best by AIC and BIC. Yet all four give scores that correlate at 0.994 or above. I’d fit the GRM and report its scores, and not spend long choosing between it and the GPCM. I’d spend the time on the next question: what would we lose by not using the categories at all?


Code

# dichotomized at "any interference" (x >= 1). Each fit sets the SD of theta in

par(op)


Collapsed to “any interference”, the seven items give about the same information near \(\theta = 0\) (23.5 against the GRM’s 22.8; each fit sets its own scale, so a small difference means little), where every collapsed item has its one boundary. Above that little is left: 4.4 against 27.4 at \(\theta = 1\), and 0.2 against 21.7 at \(\theta = 2\), among the respondents a pain measure most needs to tell apart. Below the middle neither helps: 49% of respondents have GRM scores below 0, the 31% who reported no interference share one score, \(-1.10\), and information at \(\theta = -1\) is 1.5 under either model. The categories carry the information above the floor; no model recovers what the floor hides.


Attitudes to science
For contrast, science_ltm: seven statements about science and technology put to 392 respondents in Great Britain in the 1992 Euro-Barometer 38.1 (Reif & Melich, 1995; European Commission, 2012), as distributed in the ltm package (Rizopoulos, 2006). Each statement was rated in four categories, from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Its job is to show a short scale, in a small sample, whose responses bunch in the middle rather than at a floor. Four statements favour science (it makes life more comfortable, work more interesting and the future brighter, and its benefits outweigh its harms); three are worded against it (research doesn’t matter for the environment, new technology or industry), all summarized from the ltm documentation.






Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: items worded against the construct have to be reverse-keyed before they are combined, and the data don’t always say which ones they are. For a rating scale, reversing maps category \(k\) to \(K - k\): the whole order of the categories flips, not just a 0 and a 1.





Code
sci_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.science_ltm/rows?format=csv"
ds <- read.csv(sci_url)
sci <- as.data.frame(tapply(ds$resp, list(ds$id, ds$item), function(x) x[1]))
c(respondents = nrow(sci), complete = sum(complete.cases(sci)))


respondents    complete

# agree for every item:

# development). Read with those labels, 85% of respondents would agree with it:
round(prop.table(table(sci$Industry)), 2)

0.03 0.12 0.44 0.41 


The resp_raw labels, from the ltm package, say 4 means strongly agree for every item. Read that way, 85% of respondents agreed that research does not matter to industrial development, while majorities agreed with every statement favouring science. The IRW’s item-text check compared each item’s distribution with the 1992 codebook’s figures for Great Britain: for the three statements worded against science, 4 is strongly disagree. The data arrive already reverse-keyed, every item running toward a favourable view of science; only the labels weren’t updated. Could the correlations have told us?

If you’ve done Factor analysis I: polychoric correlations estimate the correlation between the continuous responses that ordered categories are assumed to coarsen, which suits Likert items better than Pearson correlations do.



One \(\theta\) for all seven would describe two things at once; several dimensions are the subject of Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT. We fit the four statements favouring science.

From 49% (Benefit) to 68% (Comfort) of responses are in the third category, agree to some extent. The four models fit about equally well: AIC runs from 3,250 (GRM) to 3,265 (PCM), BIC from 3,313 to 3,321, the PCM second by BIC with three fewer parameters. title: Models for polytomous responses
text:
Problems

The PCM’s adjacent categories. Starting from \(\Pr(x = k) \propto \exp\big(\sum_{v \le k}(\theta - b_v)\big)\), show that \(\Pr(x = k \mid x \in \{k - 1, k\})\) is a Rasch curve with difficulty \(b_k\). Then show that the sum score is sufficient for \(\theta\) under the PCM, and find the statistic that is sufficient under the GPCM.
The rating scale model. Fit the rating scale model (itemtype = "rsm") and the PCM to the four science_ltm items worded in favour of science. What does the rating scale model assume about the items’ steps, and how many parameters does that save here? Compare AIC and BIC, and look at the PCM’s steps: do the data support the assumption? (PS8#1)
Which scores? For the pain items, compare each respondent’s GRM and GPCM scores. How large is the largest difference, and for whom? Would the choice of model change anyone’s score by more than its standard error? Would you report scores from the GRM or the GPCM, and why?
How many categories? You are writing a new frequency item for a symptom survey. Would you offer three, five or seven categories? Say what you would check in pilot data before deciding (empty categories, disordered steps, information where your respondents are), and how you would check each in mirt.
A PCM item the GRM can’t describe. Using the simulation, find step difficulties for a PCM item that the GRM describes poorly. Measure “poorly” by the largest difference between the true and the GRM’s fitted category curves, and by AIC. What kind of steps do it, and would you expect to meet them in real data? (PS8#2)
Challenge (open): the floor. Almost a third of the pain respondents chose 0 on every item, and share one score. Is a floor like that a problem for the model, for the population, or for neither? What would you change (the items, the sample, the model) to learn more about respondents at the floor, and what would each change cost? I don’t have a general answer.

title: Models for polytomous responses
text:
Going further

Ostini, R., & Nering, M. L. (2006). Polytomous item response theory models. Sage. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781412985413. A short book on the whole family, with the models’ assumptions side by side.
Samejima, F. (1969). Estimation of latent ability using a response pattern of graded scores. Psychometrika, 34(S1), 1–97. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03372160. The graded response model, and information for graded items.
Masters, G. N. (1982). A Rasch model for partial credit scoring. Psychometrika, 47(2), 149–174. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02296272. The partial credit model.
Muraki, E. (1992). A generalized partial credit model: Application of an EM algorithm. Applied Psychological Measurement, 16(2), 159–176. https://doi.org/10.1177/014662169201600206. The partial credit model with slopes.
Andrich, D. (1978). A rating formulation for ordered response categories. Psychometrika, 43(4), 561–573. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293814. The rating scale model (problem 2).
Tutz, G. (1990). Sequential item response models with an ordered response. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 43(1), 39–55. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8317.1990.tb00925.x. The sequential model, which IRTree models generalizes.
Tutz, G. (1997). Sequential models for ordered responses. In W. J. van der Linden & R. K. Hambleton (Eds.), Handbook of modern item response theory (pp. 139–152). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-2691-6_8. The sequential model as an item response model.
Tutz, G. (2020). On the structure of ordered latent trait models. Journal of Mathematical Psychology, 96, 102346. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2020.102346. How ordered latent trait models are built, and how they relate.
Tutz, G. (2022). Ordinal regression: A review and a taxonomy of models. WIREs Computational Statistics, 14(2), e1545. https://doi.org/10.1002/wics.1545. Ordinal models as compositions of binary models: the taxonomy behind this lesson’s three splits.
Thissen, D., & Steinberg, L. (1986). A taxonomy of item response models. Psychometrika, 51(4), 567–577. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02295596. Difference and divide-by-total models.
Mellenbergh, G. J. (1995). Conceptual notes on models for discrete polytomous item responses. Applied Psychological Measurement, 19(1), 91–100. https://doi.org/10.1177/014662169501900110. Cumulative, adjacent-category and sequential splits.
van der Ark, L. A. (2001). Relationships and properties of polytomous item response theory models. Applied Psychological Measurement, 25(3), 273–282. https://doi.org/10.1177/01466210122032073. What each family guarantees about the sum score.
Andrich, D. (2013). An expanded derivation of the threshold structure of the polytomous Rasch model that dispels any “threshold disorder controversy”. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 73(1), 78–124. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164412450877. Disordered steps as evidence about the categories.
Adams, R. J., Wu, M. L., & Wilson, M. (2012). The Rasch rating model and the disordered threshold controversy. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 72(4), 547–573. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164411432166. Disordered steps as a consequence of small categories.
MacCallum, R. C., Zhang, S., Preacher, K. J., & Rucker, D. D. (2002). On the practice of dichotomization of quantitative variables. Psychological Methods, 7(1), 19–40. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.7.1.19. What dichotomizing costs, for continuous variables.
Amtmann, D., Cook, K. F., Jensen, M. P., Chen, W.-H., Choi, S., Revicki, D., Cella, D., Rothrock, N., Keefe, F., Callahan, L., & Lai, J.-S. (2010). Development of a PROMIS item bank to measure pain interference. Pain, 150(1), 173–182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pain.2010.04.025. How the pain-interference bank went from 56 candidate items to 41.
Cella, D., Riley, W., Stone, A., Rothrock, N., Reeve, B., Yount, S., et al. (2010). The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) developed and tested its first wave of adult self-reported health outcome item banks: 2005–2008. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 63(11), 1179–1194. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2010.04.011. The source of the pain data, and PROMIS’s calibration with the GRM.
Reif, K., & Melich, A. (1995). Euro-barometer 38.1: Consumer protection and perceptions of science and technology, November 1992. ICPSR. https://doi.org/10.3886/ICPSR06045. The source of the attitudes-to-science data.
Rizopoulos, D. (2006). ltm: An R package for latent variable modeling and item response theory analyses. Journal of Statistical Software, 17(5). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v017.i05. The package that distributes the science data.
Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory package for the R environment. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(6). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06. The package used throughout, with every model here as an itemtype.

title: Models for polytomous responses
text:
For instructors

Source: EDUC 252 classes 8 (slides c8, 3–30) and 9 (slides c9, 1–11), problem set 8 (#1–#3), and the code in ben-domingue/252: c8/basic_polytomous_analysis.R, c9/polyexample.R, ps8/ratingscale.R, ps8/polytomous_estimates.R, ps8/polydif.R.
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 60 minutes; the two analyses work as a 30-minute lab. The real-data code takes under a minute in local R.
Changed from 252: PS8#1’s ffm_CSN has no tokenless CSV, so the rating scale model moves to science_ltm (problem 2). The pain analysis uses seven interference items that 1,908 respondents all answered, rather than the ten most-answered items across the interference, behaviour and quality sections, so that one \(\theta\) is plausible and every item has its five categories as asked. science_ltm’s seven items form two nearly uncorrelated clusters, so the lesson fits the four worded in favour of science.
Held back: splitting a response into a tree (IRTree models); nominal responses (Nominal response and multiple-choice models); ideal-point responses (Unfolding models); polytomous items in banks and adaptive tests (Item banks and adaptive testing); several dimensions (Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT). Ordinal DIF (PS8#3) is a problem on the CES-D in Differential item functioning, which doesn’t depend on this lesson. Item-level fit statistics for polytomous models aren’t covered.
Item text: PROMIS items are summarized, not quoted (HealthMeasures’ terms). The Euro-Barometer statements are summarized from the ltm documentation; the questionnaire’s licence isn’t confirmed.

Code
import {p2pl, grid, rng, logisticFit, normalQuantiles, palette} from "./widgets/irt.js"
import {sampleRange, fitItem, binned, slopeSpread, selectionCorrelations} from "./widgets/parameter-invariance.js"
import {quiz, predict} from "./widgets/quiz.js"

title: Parameter invariance
text:
What this is for
An item’s difficulty is supposed to belong to the item, not to whoever happened to answer it. That is the promise behind calibrating items once and using them for years, and behind the specific objectivity of The Rasch model. Does it hold? It depends on how you check. On the Multiracial Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, item estimates from random halves of the sample agree almost perfectly, and estimates from women and from men nearly as well. Split the same respondents into high and low scorers on the test itself, and the 2PL’s estimates collapse: slopes near zero, difficulties unrelated. The items haven’t changed. The split has. This lesson separates what the model promises from what estimates can deliver, and shows why one way of splitting a sample undoes the check it was meant to perform.

title: Parameter invariance
Parameter invariance
text:
Core ideas

Invariance belongs to the model
What does it mean for an item’s parameters to be the same in two groups? Think of a regression line. If \(y\) depends linearly on \(x\) in a population, a sample drawn only from small values of \(x\) and a sample drawn only from large ones estimate the same line, though each sees only part of it. An item characteristic curve is a regression of the response on \(\theta\), so the same holds: if the 2PL is true in a population, the same \(a\) and \(b\) govern responses in every subgroup of it, whatever its range of ability (Lord, 1980; Rupp & Zumbo, 2006).
Baker (2001, ch. 3, pp. 51–55) illustrates this with two groups of respondents, one with abilities from −3 to −1 and one from +1 to +3. Fitting the item’s curve to each group separately gives \(b = -0.39\) and \(a = 1.27\) both times: one group sees the lower tail, the other the upper tail, and both tails belong to one curve. The widget repeats the exercise. As in Baker’s illustration, the abilities are known, so each fit is a logistic regression on \(\theta\).

Try it: two groups, one curve


Code
viewof bk_c1 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: -2, step: 0.1, label: "Group 1: centre of its ability range"})
viewof bk_c2 = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "Group 2: centre of its ability range"})
viewof bk_n = Inputs.range([100, 5000], {value: 1000, step: 100, label: "Respondents per group"})
viewof bk_noise = Inputs.toggle({label: "Sampling error (off = Baker's idealized proportions)", value: true})
































Code
bk_a = 1.27
bk_b = -0.39
bk_fit = (c, r) => {
  if (!bk_noise) {
    const th = grid(c - 1, c + 1, 21), f = logisticFit(th, th.map(t => p2pl(t, bk_b, bk_a)), th.map(() => 1));
    return {pts: th.map(t => ({theta: t, p: p2pl(t, bk_b, bk_a)})), fit: {a: f.b1, b: -f.b0 / f.b1}};
  }
  const s = sampleRange(r, bk_n, c - 1, c + 1, bk_a, bk_b);
  return {pts: binned(s.theta, s.y), fit: fitItem(s.theta, s.y)};
}
bk_groups = { const r = rng(7); return [bk_fit(bk_c1, r), bk_fit(bk_c2, r)]; }
bk_g1 = bk_groups[0]
bk_g2 = bk_groups[1]
bk_curve = (g, name) => g.fit ? grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, p: p2pl(t, g.fit.b, g.fit.a), curve: name})) : []
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Group 1 fit", "Group 2 fit"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, p: p2pl(t, bk_b, bk_a)})), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.line([...bk_curve(bk_g1, "Group 1 fit"), ...bk_curve(bk_g2, "Group 2 fit")], {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(bk_g1.pts, {x: "theta", y: "p", fill: palette.main, r: 3}),
    Plot.dot(bk_g2.pts, {x: "theta", y: "p", fill: palette.contrast, r: 3})
  ]
})




























































Code
bk_txt = g => g.fit ? `a = ${g.fit.a.toFixed(2)}, b = ${g.fit.b.toFixed(2)}` : "no estimate (every response the same)"
md`True item (dashed): a = 1.27, b = −0.39. Group 1: ${bk_txt(bk_g1)}. Group 2: ${bk_txt(bk_g2)}.`
















With sampling error off, both groups recover the true curve exactly, wherever you put them: that is Baker’s figure. Turn sampling error on and the estimates wobble, most for a group far from the item. At the defaults, group 2 sits where nearly everyone answers correctly, and its proportions say little about the curve’s shape. Add respondents and both fits close in on the dashed line. Invariance is a statement about the curve; estimates only approach it.
Compare the classical difficulty, the proportion correct. At the defaults it is about 0.15 in group 1 and above 0.9 in group 2 (read the points). Baker makes the same contrast: the proportion correct describes an item in a group, while \(b\) describes the item.


Code
quiz({
  q: "An item is answered correctly by 30% of one school's students and 80% of another's. Can we conclude that its IRT parameters differ between the schools?",
  options: [
    {text: "Yes: the item behaves differently in the two schools", correct: false, why: "Not from this. The proportion correct depends on the students' abilities as well as on the item, so a stronger school gets a higher proportion from the same curve."},
    {text: "No: the proportions could come from one curve and two different ability distributions", correct: true, why: "If the model holds, the same $a$ and $b$ produce different proportions correct in groups of different ability. That is the point of Baker's two groups."},
    {text: "Yes, unless both schools have more than 1,000 students", correct: false, why: "Sample size affects how precisely we estimate each proportion, not whether a difference in proportions reflects the item or the students."}
  ]
})










Estimates live on local scales






Recall from The Rasch model: only \(\theta - b\) is identified, so the scale has no origin, and mirt sets one by fixing the mean ability at 0. From the 1PL to the 4PL added the unit: the 2PL sees only \(a(\theta - b)\), so mirt fixes the SD of ability at 1.



Baker’s groups share a scale because their abilities are known. In practice they aren’t, and each group’s fit sets the origin and unit by that group. Suppose group \(g\)’s abilities have mean \(\mu_g\) and SD \(\sigma_g\) on the population’s scale. The fit reports \(\theta^* = (\theta - \mu_g)/\sigma_g\), and to keep every \(a(\theta - b)\) unchanged it must report \[a^* = a\,\sigma_g, \qquad b^* = \frac{b - \mu_g}{\sigma_g}.\] A stronger group makes every item look easier by the same amount, and a more homogeneous group makes every slope look flatter. Under the Rasch model the slopes are fixed at 1, so only the shift remains. Nothing about the items has changed; the numbers are on local scales. Putting them on one scale is linking (Stocking & Lord, 1983; Kolen & Brennan, 2014).

Try it: two local scales


Code
viewof ls_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Group B's mean ability, relative to group A"})
viewof ls_sd = Inputs.range([0.4, 2], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Group B's SD of ability, relative to group A"})
viewof ls_link = Inputs.toggle({label: "Link B to A (mean–sigma)", value: false})

























Code
ls_b = normalQuantiles(15, 0, 1)
ls_est = { const r = rng(40); return ls_b.map(b => ({A: b + 0.08 * r.norm(), B: (b - ls_mu) / ls_sd + 0.08 * r.norm()})); }
ls_mean = v => v.reduce((u, w) => u + w, 0) / v.length
ls_sdv = v => { const m = ls_mean(v); return Math.sqrt(v.reduce((u, w) => u + (w - m) ** 2, 0) / (v.length - 1)); }
ls_Aconst = ls_sdv(ls_est.map(d => d.A)) / ls_sdv(ls_est.map(d => d.B))
ls_Bconst = ls_mean(ls_est.map(d => d.A)) - ls_Aconst * ls_mean(ls_est.map(d => d.B))
ls_pts = ls_est.map(d => ({A: d.A, B: ls_link ? ls_Aconst * d.B + ls_Bconst : d.B}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 520, height: 420, x: {label: "Difficulty estimated in group A", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: ls_link ? "Group B's estimate, linked to A's scale" : "Difficulty estimated in group B", domain: [-5, 5]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[-5, -5], [5, 5]], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.dot(ls_pts, {x: "A", y: "B", fill: ls_link ? palette.main : palette.contrast, r: 5})
  ]
})




























































Code
md`${ls_link ? `Linked: B's estimates are multiplied by ${ls_Aconst.toFixed(2)} and shifted by ${ls_Bconst.toFixed(2)}, and the points fall on the identity line (dashed) up to estimation error.` : `Unlinked: the points lie near a line with slope ${(1 / ls_sd).toFixed(2)} (one over B's relative SD) and intercept ${(-ls_mu / ls_sd).toFixed(2)}, not on the identity line (dashed).`}`







Before linking, the fifteen items lie on a straight line, just not the identity line: its intercept comes from the difference in means and its slope from the ratio of SDs. With B’s mean at 0 and SD at 1 the line is the identity. Link, and the points fall on it whatever the sliders say. A straight line in this plot is what invariance predicts. What it doesn’t predict is an item off the line.






If you’ve done Linking and equating: these are the mean–sigma constants that lesson used on TIMSS booklets, and its Stocking–Lord method does the same job through the characteristic curves.









NoteGo deeper: the linear indeterminacy of 2PL estimates across groups





Assumptions: the 2PL holds in a population with item parameters \(a_i, b_i\); group \(g\)’s abilities are normal with mean \(\mu_g\) and SD \(\sigma_g\) on the population’s scale; the software fixes each group’s mean at 0 and SD at 1.
One group. Write \(\theta = \mu_g + \sigma_g\theta^*\), so that \(\theta^*\) has mean 0 and SD 1 in group \(g\). Then \[a_i(\theta - b_i) = a_i(\mu_g + \sigma_g\theta^* - b_i) = a_i\sigma_g\Big(\theta^* - \frac{b_i - \mu_g}{\sigma_g}\Big),\] so the group’s responses follow a 2PL in \(\theta^*\) with \(a_i^* = a_i\sigma_g\) and \(b_i^* = (b_i - \mu_g)/\sigma_g\).
Two groups. Eliminate \(b_i\) using \(b_i = \mu_1 + \sigma_1 b_{i1}^*\): \[b_{i2}^* = \frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}\,b_{i1}^* + \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\sigma_2}, \qquad a_{i2}^* = \frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\,a_{i1}^*.\] Every item obeys the same \(A = \sigma_1/\sigma_2\) and \(B = (\mu_1 - \mu_2)/\sigma_2\): difficulties map by \(b_2 = A b_1 + B\) and slopes by \(a_2 = a_1/A\), the linking relation of Linking and equating. Because \(A\) and \(B\) are common to all items, two sets of estimates carry a test of invariance: after the best common \(A\) and \(B\), the items should agree up to estimation error. An item that doesn’t is functioning differently in the two groups (Differential item functioning).
What bends it. The normal shape enters only through the software’s assumption: a group selected on \(\theta\) has a truncated distribution, which bends the estimates slightly. A group selected on the responses themselves breaks a deeper assumption, taken up two sections below.





Code
quiz({
  q: "Two groups' 2PL difficulty estimates satisfy $b_B \\approx 0.5\\,b_A - 1$ for every item. What is the most likely explanation?",
  options: [
    {text: "Every item works differently in the two groups", correct: false, why: "A common linear relation for all items is what invariance predicts when the groups differ in ability. Differential functioning would put individual items off the line."},
    {text: "Group B is stronger and more spread out than group A", correct: true, why: "The slope is $\\sigma_A/\\sigma_B = 0.5$, so B's SD is twice A's, and the negative intercept says B's mean is higher: items look easier to B. Linking removes both."},
    {text: "Group B's estimates didn't converge", correct: false, why: "Non-convergence wouldn't produce a clean linear relation across every item."}
  ]
})










Narrow groups give imprecise estimates
Baker’s groups were two logits wide. What if a group covers only a sliver of the scale? The slope is how fast the curve rises, and a group that spans a narrow range sees little rise to measure.

Try it: how wide a range?


Code
viewof rr_w = Inputs.range([0.25, 6], {value: 4, step: 0.25, label: "Width of the ability range sampled"})
viewof rr_c = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Centre of the range"})


















Code
rr = slopeSpread(11, 200, 300, rr_c - rr_w / 2, rr_c + rr_w / 2, 1.27, -0.39)
rr_sd = (() => { const v = rr.slopes, m = v.reduce((u, w) => u + w, 0) / v.length; return Math.sqrt(v.reduce((u, w) => u + (w - m) ** 2, 0) / (v.length - 1)); })()
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Estimated slope a (true 1.27), 200 samples of 300 respondents", domain: [-1, 4]}, y: {label: "Samples"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(rr.slopes.filter(a => a > -1 && a < 4), Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: grid(-1, 4, 51), fill: palette.main})),
    Plot.ruleX([1.27], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})

























Code
md`SD of the slope estimates: **${rr_sd.toFixed(2)}**. ${(100 * rr.slopes.filter(a => Math.abs(a - 1.27) < 0.25).length / 200).toFixed(0)}% of samples land within 0.25 of the truth${rr.failed ? `; ${rr.failed} gave no estimate at all` : ""}.`







At a width of 4 the estimates cluster around 1.27, with an SD of 0.15. Narrow the range to 1 and the SD triples; at 0.5 some samples give a slope below zero. Move the centre away from \(b = -0.39\) and the spread grows again, since a group far from the item sees only a flat stretch of curve. The item is the same in every setting; what shrinks is the information about it. A restricted group mostly costs precision.






If you’ve done Information, precision, and short forms: there, an item told us most about respondents near its difficulty. Turn it around and a respondent tells us most about an item near their ability: to pin down a slope, we need respondents on both sides of \(b\).






Splitting on the sum score selects on the outcome
A narrow range of \(\theta\) costs precision. Selecting on the responses does something else. Suppose we split respondents into high and low scorers on the test we are calibrating. Within the high half the sum score can’t be low, so a respondent who missed one item must have made it up on others: among respondents with similar sum scores, answering one item correctly makes answering another less likely. Selection has introduced a dependence between items that has nothing to do with \(\theta\), so local independence no longer holds within the group. The sum score is a common effect of every item, and selecting on a common effect induces dependence between its causes, a problem known well beyond psychometrics (Elwert & Winship, 2014). A 2PL fit reads the items’ correlations as evidence of a common \(\theta\), and in a selected half those correlations are close to zero.

Try it: what selection does to the correlations


Code
viewof sel_k = Inputs.range([4, 40], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Number of items"})
viewof sel_a = Inputs.range([0.3, 2.5], {value: 0.6, step: 0.1, label: "Slope of every item"})


















Code
sel = selectionCorrelations(3, 2000, sel_k, sel_a)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 230, marginLeft: 180, x: {label: "Mean correlation between pairs of items (2,000 simulated respondents)", domain: [-0.25, 0.5]},
  y: {label: null, domain: sel.map(d => d.group)},
  color: {domain: ["none", "ability", "sum score"], range: [palette.ink, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: palette.rule}), Plot.dot(sel, {x: "r", y: "group", fill: "split", r: 6})]
})


















Code
md`Everyone: **${sel[0].r.toFixed(3)}**. Upper half split on true ability: **${sel[1].r.toFixed(3)}**. Upper half split on the sum score: **${sel[3].r.toFixed(3)}**.`













Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: reliability is a property of scores in a population, the share of observed-score variance that is true-score variance.



Splitting on true ability lowers the correlations, because each half has a narrower range of \(\theta\) (the previous section). Splitting on the sum score lowers them further, to about zero at the defaults. With four or five items it pushes them well below zero, since a fixed sum spread over a few items forces a trade-off between them. Raise the slope and every correlation rises, but the sum-score halves stay below the ability halves at every setting.
What about the Rasch model? There the sum score is sufficient, and conditional maximum likelihood estimates the difficulties from the responses given the sum score. Selecting respondents by that sum score leaves the conditional likelihood unchanged.






Recall from The Rasch model: specific objectivity asks that comparisons between items not depend on which respondents are used. Conditioning on the sum score removes \(\theta\), so under the Rasch model the conditional ML difficulties from high and low scorers should agree, and Andersen (1973) turned that comparison into a likelihood-ratio test.



So the split that distorts a 2PL calibration is the one Andersen’s test is built on. The difference lies in what each fit conditions on. The 2PL’s marginal likelihood assumes the responses are independent given \(\theta\), and selection on the sum score undoes that. The Rasch conditional likelihood takes the sum score as given, so the selection has nothing left to undo.


Code
quiz({
  q: "You split respondents at the median of their sum score on 20 items and fit a 2PL to the same 20 items in the top half. Most slopes come out near 0. What is the most likely explanation?",
  options: [
    {text: "Among strong respondents, the items don't measure the construct", correct: false, why: "It could happen, but it isn't needed. Selecting on the sum score by itself pushes the items' correlations toward zero, and the 2PL reads that as flat curves."},
    {text: "The selection removed the correlations the 2PL relies on", correct: true, why: "Within a band of sum scores, a correct answer on one item makes others less likely. The items look unrelated, so the slopes shrink toward 0."},
    {text: "The top half is too small to estimate slopes", correct: false, why: "Half of a large sample is still large. Small samples make slopes noisy, not systematically near zero."}
  ]
})










When invariance fails for real
Estimation error, local scales and selection all make estimates differ when the items don’t. What is left after linking, in groups formed without selecting on the responses, is a difference in the items themselves. An item that is relatively harder for one group than another at the same \(\theta\) shows differential item functioning (Holland & Wainer, 1993), the subject of Differential item functioning. One limit is worth stating now. A shift common to every item can’t be told apart from a difference between the groups’ abilities, so invariance is checked item against item, never for the test as a whole.

title: Parameter invariance
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates one population answering 20 items from a 2PL, then splits the respondents three ways: at random, on their true ability, and on their sum score. It fits the 2PL separately in each half and compares the estimates with the true parameters re-expressed on that half’s scale (\(a\sigma_g\) and \((b - \mu_g)/\sigma_g\), from the Go deeper callout). It runs in your browser; the first run takes a minute or more: 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, then six fits.
With the seed as written, the random halves recover the slopes well (correlations of 0.94 and 0.91 with the truth). Halves split on true ability recover them less precisely (0.46 and 0.63) but at about the right level: median slopes of 0.65 and 0.56, against 0.56 and 0.58 on each half’s own scale. Halves split on the sum score get them too small: medians of 0.38 and 0.32, against 0.64 and 0.67. The last lines show why. The mean correlation between items is 0.149 in everyone, 0.052 in the upper half by ability and 0.019 in the upper half by sum score.
Try ni <- 5, and the sum-score halves get worse, as the widget suggested. Try np <- 10000 in your own R session: the ability halves close in on the truth, while the sum-score halves stay too flat, because more data doesn’t undo selection.

title: Parameter invariance
text:
With real data
Our main example is wilmer-mrmet-normative-data-set-2022, the normative sample for the Multiracial Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (MRMET; Kim et al., 2024). Like the RMET of From the 1PL to the 4PL, each item shows the eye region of a face and offers four words for the mental state it shows; the MRMET uses racially inclusive faces and answer choices that aren’t gendered. Its job here is to be a large sample with background variables, which we can split several ways to see which splits the item estimates survive. A response is 1 when the respondent chose the correct word. Download the code to run every chunk yourself.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
mrmet_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v24_0.wilmer-mrmet-normative-data-set-2022/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(mrmet_url)
# resp is 1 when the respondent chose the correct word; resp_raw is the word chosen
# ("none" when no word was chosen, scored 0). The table is marked longitudinal because
# respondents took the test on different dates, but each took it once:

mean_r <- function(d) { R <- cor(d); mean(R[upper.tri(R)]) }

All 9,295 respondents answered all 37 items. The IRW marks the table as longitudinal because respondents were tested on different dates, but each has one date. The items run from 30% to 92% correct, and they correlate weakly with one another: 0.065 on average, close to what the selection widget’s 20 items with slopes of 0.6 produce and less than half the simulation’s 0.149. Weak correlations leave a restricted sample less to work with.
We fit the Rasch model and the 2PL in each half of four splits: random halves; women and men (the 419 respondents who reported genderqueer are left out of this split only, a group too small for its own 2PL calibration); high and low scorers on these 37 items; and, for the 18 even-numbered items, high and low scorers on the 19 odd-numbered ones.

Code
# Fit the Rasch model and the 2PL separately in two groups, and compare each item's
# estimates across the groups. IRTpars = TRUE converts mirt's intercept d to our
# difficulty, b = -d/a (for the Rasch model, b = -d).
fit_pars <- function(d, type) {
  coef(mirt(d, 1, itemtype = type, verbose = FALSE), simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items[, c("a", "b")]
}
compare <- function(d, g, split, groups) {
  r1 <- fit_pars(d[g, ], "Rasch"); r2 <- fit_pars(d[!g, ], "Rasch")
  t1 <- fit_pars(d[g, ], "2PL");   t2 <- fit_pars(d[!g, ], "2PL")
  list(split = split, groups = groups, n = c(sum(g), sum(!g)), rasch = list(r1, r2), twopl = list(t1, t2),
       summary = data.frame(split = split, n1 = sum(g), n2 = sum(!g),
                            rasch_b_r = cor(r1[, "b"], r2[, "b"]),
                            rasch_shift = mean(r1[, "b"] - r2[, "b"]),
                            twopl_b_r = cor(t1[, "b"], t2[, "b"]),
                            twopl_a_r = cor(t1[, "a"], t2[, "a"]),
                            median_a_1 = median(t1[, "a"]), median_a_2 = median(t2[, "a"]),
                            mean_r_1 = mean_r(d[g, ]), mean_r_2 = mean_r(d[!g, ])))
}
set.seed(40)
random <- compare(resp, sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), nrow(resp), replace = TRUE), "random halves", c("half 1", "half 2"))
mf <- person$cov_gender %in% c("female", "male")
gender <- compare(resp[mf, ], person$cov_gender[mf] == "female", "women vs. men", c("women", "men"))
score  <- compare(resp, r > median(r), "high vs. low sum score", c("high", "low"))
odd <- seq(1, ncol(resp), by = 2); even <- seq(2, ncol(resp), by = 2)
r_odd <- rowSums(resp[, odd])
oddsplit <- compare(resp[, even], r_odd > median(r_odd), "even items, split on odd-item score",
                    c("high on odd items", "low on odd items"))
comps <- list(random, gender, score, oddsplit)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(comps, `[[`, "summary"))
print(format(res, digits = 2), row.names = FALSE)

Code
par(op)


Read the table a row at a time.

Random halves. Rasch difficulties correlate 1.00, 2PL difficulties 0.99 and 2PL slopes 0.97. This is the baseline: two samples from one population, differing only by estimation error.
Women and men. Rasch difficulties correlate 0.99, with a shift of −0.24: on the women’s scale every item is about a quarter of a logit easier, which the model reads as women scoring higher on average, not as items that differ. The 2PL slopes agree less well (0.92), but slopes are the noisier parameter even between random halves (0.97).
High and low scorers. The Rasch difficulties still correlate 0.96, shifted by 1.18 logits, the difference between the groups’ means. The 2PL collapses: its difficulties correlate −0.05, and the median slope is −0.04 in the high half and 0.19 in the low half. The mean correlation between items is −0.003 in the high half, as the selection widget predicted.
Even items, split on the odd items. Selecting on other items avoids the common-effect problem, but the halves are narrower in ability, since the odd-item score tracks \(\theta\). The 2PL difficulties correlate 0.77 and the slopes 0.76, better than the sum-score split and worse than random halves: the cost of a restricted range.



Code
# In the high and low halves by sum score, the 2PL slopes:
round(rbind(high = quantile(score$twopl[[1]][, "a"], c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1)),
            low  = quantile(score$twopl[[2]][, "a"], c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1))), 2)


        0%   25%   50%  75% 100%
high -0.68 -0.15 -0.04 0.41 0.75
low  -0.43  0.01  0.19 0.43 1.18


Code
# The same items in everyone, for comparison:
full_2pl <- fit_pars(resp, "2PL")
round(quantile(full_2pl[, "a"], c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1)), 2)


  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
0.21 0.42 0.60 0.92 1.19 


Among high scorers the 2PL slopes run from −0.68 to 0.75; in the full sample the same items run from 0.21 to 1.19, median 0.60. A negative slope says that stronger respondents are less likely to answer correctly, and selection produced it here from items that all rise with ability in the full sample. With slopes near zero, \(b = -d/a\) divides by almost nothing, which is why some difficulties fall off the plot, as Y15’s did in From the 1PL to the 4PL.
What does the Rasch model’s 0.96 on that split mean? Under conditional ML the split is Andersen’s test, and legitimate:


Code
# Conditional maximum likelihood (psychotools::raschmodel) conditions on the sum
# score, so selecting respondents by that same sum score leaves its likelihood intact.
# Splitting there is Andersen's (1973) test of the Rasch model.
library(psychotools)
cml <- function(d) { m <- raschmodel(d); list(b = itempar(m), ll = logLik(m)) }
hi <- cml(resp[r > median(r), ]); lo <- cml(resp[r <= median(r), ]); all <- cml(resp)
round(cor(hi$b, lo$b), 3)


[1] 0.963


Code
# Andersen's likelihood-ratio statistic, on (items - 1) degrees of freedom:
c(LR = round(2 * (as.numeric(hi$ll) + as.numeric(lo$ll) - as.numeric(all$ll))), df = ncol(resp) - 1)


  LR   df 
1588   36 


Code
# Which items move between the halves? Compare with each item's 2PL slope in everyone.
moved <- (hi$b - mean(hi$b)) - (lo$b - mean(lo$b))
round(cor(moved, full_2pl[, "a"]), 2)


[1] -0.98


The conditional ML difficulties from the two halves correlate 0.963, and the likelihood-ratio statistic is 1,588 on 36 degrees of freedom, far beyond what the Rasch model allows. Which items move? The shift in each item’s difficulty between the halves correlates −0.98 with its 2PL slope in the full sample. Items that discriminate well look relatively easier to high scorers and harder to low scorers, which is what crossing curves do. Specific objectivity fails here in the way From the 1PL to the 4PL anticipated: the MRMET’s items differ in slope.
So how would I split a sample to check invariance? The assumptions first. A 2PL fit in each group assumes the responses are independent given \(\theta\) within the group; the Rasch model fitted by conditional ML needs that only given the sum score. A split on the sum score of the calibrated items keeps the second and breaks the first. My choice is random halves for a baseline, then a background variable (gender, age, country) or a score on other items. I wouldn’t split a 2PL calibration on the sum score of the items being calibrated. If the model is Rasch and the estimator is conditional ML, that split is Andersen’s test, and I’d use it.

title: Parameter invariance
text:
Problems

Asymptotes and the Rasch model. Using the Go deeper callout, show that a 3PL’s lower asymptote \(c\) is the same on every group’s scale. Then show that under the Rasch model, where mirt fixes the slopes at 1 and estimates the SD of \(\theta\), two groups’ difficulties differ only by a shift. Where does the group’s SD go?
Linking women and men. Link the men’s MRMET 2PL difficulties to the women’s scale by mean–sigma. How close do the items get? Which item is furthest off after linking, and what is its slope?
Age. Split the MRMET respondents into those under 25 and those over 40, and repeat the comparison. After removing the Rasch shift, which items differ most? Are the difficulties invariant, and how would you tell a real difference from estimation error?
A colleague’s split. A colleague checks a new test’s calibration by fitting the 2PL separately to the top and bottom thirds of scorers, finds slopes near zero in both, and concludes that the items don’t measure anything. What would you tell them, and what would you run instead?
Calibrating for a new population. A test calibrated on adults will be used with 12- to 15-year-olds. You can collect data from 1,500 respondents. Whom would you sample, and why? What would you compare before trusting the adult parameters?
Challenge: fewer parameters, more invariance? On every split, the Rasch difficulties agree better than the 2PL’s. Is that a property of the MRMET’s items, or of estimating one parameter per item instead of two? Wright (1997) makes the case for measurement whose item comparisons don’t depend on the sample. Design a simulation that could tell the two apart. This one is open: I don’t know of a general answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.
