title: Nominal response and multiple-choice models
text:
What this is for
Score a multiple-choice item 0/1 and two respondents who both got it wrong look the same, though one chose the answer a nearly-right reader would choose and the other the answer nobody who read the question would. Guessing and priors asked what to do about the floor of an item’s curve; this lesson asks what the wrong answers say. It gives every option its own curve (Bock’s nominal response model), reads those curves, adds a “don’t know” state (Thissen and Steinberg’s multiple-choice model), and fits the models to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test and a medical residency exam. The short answers: the wrong answers add information about the respondents who miss items, and they point to the handful of items where the keyed answer behaves like a wrong one. On a multiple-choice test I’d keep the option chosen and read its curves before scoring anything 0/1.

title: Nominal response and multiple-choice models
Nominal response and multiple-choice models
text:
Core ideas

Every option gets a curve






Recall from Models for polytomous responses: the partial credit family are divide-by-total models (Thissen & Steinberg, 1986). Each category gets an exponential, and its probability is its share of the total. The GPCM has \(\Pr(x = k) \propto \exp\big(\sum_{v \le k} a(\theta - b_v)\big)\), with the categories ordered in advance.



What if we can’t trust an order in advance? The options of a multiple-choice item are four answers, one of them keyed. Bock (1972) dropped the ordering and gave each option \(k\) of item \(i\) its own slope \(a_{ik}\) and intercept \(\gamma_{ik}\): \[\Pr(x_{ij} = k \mid \theta_j) = \frac{\exp(a_{ik}\theta_j + \gamma_{ik})}{\sum_{h} \exp(a_{ih}\theta_j + \gamma_{ih})}.\] Only differences between options matter, so one option is fixed at \(a = \gamma = 0\) as a reference. With two options this is the 2PL, with slope \(a_{i1} - a_{i0}\). Thissen, Cai and Bock (2010) describe the model’s parameterizations and uses. We write \(\gamma\) for the intercept because \(c\) is the lower asymptote; mirt calls it d.
What do the slopes do? The log odds of option \(k\) against option \(h\) is \((a_k - a_h)\theta + (\gamma_k - \gamma_h)\), a straight line in \(\theta\). So the option with the largest slope wins at the top of the scale, the one with the smallest wins at the bottom, and an option whose slope is in between can be the most likely only in the middle, and only if its intercept is large enough. The model, not the scorer, orders the options along \(\theta\).

Try it: option curves
A four-option item. The key’s slope is 1 and its intercept 0; set the three distractors.


Code
viewof oc_aB = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -1, step: 0.1, label: "B: slope"})
viewof oc_gB = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -0.5, step: 0.1, label: "B: intercept"})
viewof oc_aC = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "C: slope"})
viewof oc_gC = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "C: intercept"})
viewof oc_aD = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -0.5, step: 0.1, label: "D: slope"})
viewof oc_gD = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -1, step: 0.1, label: "D: intercept"})














































Code

oc_cols = [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink, palette.guide]
oc_a = [1, oc_aB, oc_aC, oc_aD]
oc_g = [0, oc_gB, oc_gC, oc_gD]
oc_th = grid(-4, 4, 161)
oc_rows = oc_th.flatMap(t => nominalProbs(t, oc_a, oc_g).map((p, k) => ({theta: t, p, option: oc_names[k]})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(option chosen)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: oc_names, range: oc_cols},
  marks: [Plot.line(oc_rows, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "option", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})





















































Code
oc_peak = k => oc_th.reduce((best, t) => nominalProbs(t, oc_a, oc_g)[k] > nominalProbs(best, oc_a, oc_g)[k] ? t : best, oc_th[0])
oc_order = [0, 1, 2, 3].sort((u, v) => oc_a[u] - oc_a[v]).map(k => oc_names[k])
oc_ties = [[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]].filter(([u, v]) => Math.abs(oc_a[u] - oc_a[v]) < 1e-9).map(([u, v]) => `${oc_names[u]} and ${oc_names[v]}`)
md`From the bottom of the scale to the top, the slopes order the options **${oc_order.join(", ")}**. ${[1, 2, 3].map(k => `${oc_names[k]} peaks at θ = ${oc_peak(k).toFixed(1)}`).join("; ")} (−4 or 4 means it keeps falling or rising). ${oc_ties.length ? `${oc_ties.join("; ")} have the same slope: their odds against each other don't change with θ, so which of them was chosen says nothing about θ.` : ""} ${oc_a.slice(1).some(v => v > 1) ? "A distractor with a slope above the key's overtakes it at the top of the scale." : ""}`






























At the defaults B, with the smallest slope, takes over at the bottom; C, with a slope between B’s and the key’s, peaks near \(\theta = 0\) at about 0.46; and the key leads from \(\theta = 0.5\) up. Give D a slope of 1.5 and it overtakes the key at the top.


Code
quiz({
  q: "In a nominal model, option C has slope $a_C = 0.4$, between the key's $1.2$ and the other two distractors' $-0.8$ and $-0.5$. Which statement must be true?",
  options: [
    {text: "C is not the most likely option at the very top or the very bottom of the scale", correct: true, why: "At the top the largest slope (the key) wins; at the bottom the smallest (−0.8) wins. C can be most likely only in between, and only if its intercept is large enough."},
    {text: "C is the most likely option somewhere in the middle", correct: false, why: "Only if its intercept is large enough. With a small intercept, C sits under the other curves everywhere (try C's intercept at −2 in the widget)."},
    {text: "C's curve rises with θ, because its slope is positive", correct: false, why: "What matters is how C's slope compares with the others'. At the top, the key's larger slope drives C's probability back toward 0, so C's curve rises and then falls."}
  ]
})










Reading option curves
What do the curves say about an item? Thissen, Steinberg and Fitzpatrick (1989) treat the distractors as part of the item and read their curves as evidence about it. Four shapes recur:

the key rises;
a distractor that falls draws the respondents lowest on \(\theta\);
a distractor that peaks in the middle draws respondents who know part of the answer;
a distractor that rises at the top is chosen more by stronger respondents: a second defensible answer, or a sign that the key should be checked.

A distractor almost nobody chooses has a flat, low curve. Gierl, Bulut, Guo and Zhang (2017) review how distractors are written, analysed and used.






If you’ve done From construct map to items: building an instrument: a distractor nobody would choose adds only reading time, and distractors built from specific errors earn their place (Haladyna, Downing & Rodriguez, 2002). Option curves are how the data check that rule. And in Validity as causation, children who missed a word on a vocabulary task chose the semantically related picture (47% of wrong answers) more often than the unrelated one (22%).




Try it: which is the key?
These are the fitted option curves for one item of the residency exam in With real data, labelled as the exam printed them. Which option is keyed?

Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {label: "P(option chosen)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: wk_names, range: [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink, palette.guide]},

    {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "option", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})
































Code
md`${wk_pick === null ? "Pick an option to see the answer." :
  wk_pick === "A" ? "**Yes, A is keyed.** Nothing in the curves says so: A peaks near θ = −1 and then declines, while C rises across the whole range." :
  wk_pick === "C" ? "**C is what the curves suggest, but the key is A.** C is the option stronger respondents choose; the keyed option, A, peaks near θ = −1 and declines." :
  `**No, the key is A.** ${wk_pick === "D" ? "D falls: it draws the weakest respondents." : "B stays low everywhere."} A peaks near θ = −1; C, not the key, rises with θ.`}`







We return to this item below.



Distractors carry information, mostly at low θ






Recall from Models for polytomous responses: an item’s information is \(I(\theta) = \sum_k (P_k')^2/P_k\), which is \(a^2 P(1-P)\) for a 0/1 item. Merging two categories never adds information, and loses none only where the two respond to \(\theta\) identically. Information, precision, and short forms added it up over items.



For the nominal model the formula gives something simple: an item’s information is the variance of its option slopes, weighted by how likely each option is at \(\theta\), \[I(\theta) = \sum_k P_k(\theta)\,\big(a_k - \bar a(\theta)\big)^2, \qquad \bar a(\theta) = \sum_k P_k(\theta)\,a_k.\] Scoring 0/1 merges the three distractors into one category. What does that cost? Split the variance into a part between “key” and “not key” and a part among the distractors: \[I(\theta) = \underbrace{P(1 - P)\,(a_{\text{key}} - \bar a_D)^2}_{\text{scored 0/1}} \;+\; (1 - P)\,\text{Var}_D(a \mid \theta),\] where \(P\) is the key’s probability, and \(\bar a_D\) and \(\text{Var}_D\) are the mean and variance of the slopes among the distractors, weighted by how often each is chosen at \(\theta\). The first term is the information in the 0/1 score; the second is what the distractors add. It is weighted by \(1 - P\), the chance of choosing a distractor at all, so it matters below the item’s difficulty and fades above it. The Go deeper callout derives both lines.

The item from the option-curves widget: move its sliders and this plot follows.

Plot.plot({

    Plot.line(in_th.flatMap(t => [{theta: t, I: nominalInfo(t, oc_a, oc_g), s: "All four options (nominal)"},
                                  {theta: t, I: keyedInfo(t, oc_a, oc_g, 0), s: "Scored 0/1"}]), {x: "theta", y: "I", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})


















Code
md`Information at θ = −2, 0 and 2: all four options **${[-2, 0, 2].map(t => nominalInfo(t, oc_a, oc_g).toFixed(2)).join(", ")}**; scored 0/1, **${[-2, 0, 2].map(t => keyedInfo(t, oc_a, oc_g, 0).toFixed(2)).join(", ")}**. The key is chosen with probability ${[-2, 0, 2].map(t => nominalProbs(t, oc_a, oc_g)[0].toFixed(2)).join(", ")}.`







At the defaults the options give 0.22 at \(\theta = -2\), where the 0/1 score gives 0.05, and 0.20 against 0.19 at \(\theta = 2\), where 80% choose the key. Give all three distractors the same slope and the two curves coincide: distractors that don’t differ in slope carry nothing beyond the 0/1 score.

  q: "An easy item: 90% of respondents choose the key. Its distractors have very different slopes. Where does keeping the options add most information?",
  options: [
    {text: "Among respondents well below the item's difficulty", correct: true, why: "The distractors' term is weighted by $1 - P$, the chance of choosing a distractor. On an easy item that is large only for the weakest respondents."},
    {text: "Among the strongest respondents, since they are the majority", correct: false, why: "Nearly all of them choose the key, so which distractor they would have chosen hardly ever shows. The extra term is weighted by $1 - P$, near 0 for them."},
    {text: "Evenly across the scale", correct: false, why: "Information is a curve. The distractors' share of it tracks how often distractors are chosen, which changes with θ."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: why distractor information sits below the item’s difficulty





Assumptions: one item with options \(k = 1, \dots, K\) following Bock’s nominal model with known \(a_k\) and \(\gamma_k\); one option is keyed, with probability \(P = P_{\text{key}}\).
Nominal information. \(\log P_k = a_k\theta + \gamma_k - \log \sum_h \exp(a_h\theta + \gamma_h)\), so \(\partial \log P_k/\partial\theta = a_k - \bar a(\theta)\). Fisher information is the variance of this score over the options, \(I(\theta) = \sum_k P_k(a_k - \bar a)^2 = \text{Var}(a \mid \theta)\), as for the GPCM in Models for polytomous responses, where the slopes are \(a \cdot k\).
The decomposition. Let \(D\) be the set of distractors, with total probability \(1 - P\), mean slope \(\bar a_D = \sum_{k \in D} P_k a_k / (1 - P)\) and variance \(\text{Var}_D = \sum_{k \in D} P_k (a_k - \bar a_D)^2/(1 - P)\). The law of total variance, conditioning on “key or not”, gives \[\text{Var}(a \mid \theta) = P(1 - P)(a_{\text{key}} - \bar a_D)^2 + (1 - P)\,\text{Var}_D.\]
The first term is the 0/1 information. \(P' = P(a_{\text{key}} - \bar a)\) and \(\bar a = P a_{\text{key}} + (1 - P)\bar a_D\), so \(P' = P(1 - P)(a_{\text{key}} - \bar a_D)\), and \((P')^2/\big(P(1 - P)\big) = P(1 - P)(a_{\text{key}} - \bar a_D)^2\): the information in the item scored 0/1, from the polytomous formula with two categories.
Where the second term lives. \(\text{Var}_D\) is at most a quarter of the squared range of the distractors’ slopes, so \((1 - P)\text{Var}_D\) goes to 0 as \(P \to 1\), above the item’s difficulty. Below it, \(1 - P\) is near 1 and the distractors add their spread of slopes. The term is zero only when the distractors chosen at \(\theta\) share one slope, the equality case of the merging argument in Models for polytomous responses. On an easy test that puts the distractors’ information with the respondents the 0/1 scores measure least precisely.






Guessing, again: the multiple-choice model






Recall from Guessing and priors: fixing the lower asymptote at \(1/k\) assumes that a respondent who doesn’t know the answer picks at random. On a two-button reading task, some items fell below chance, because not knowing pushed respondents toward one answer.



What does the nominal model say about a respondent who knows nothing? As \(\theta\) falls, the option with the smallest slope takes over, so the weakest respondents all choose one distractor rather than spreading over the options. Thissen and Steinberg (1984) add a latent “don’t know” category, 0, with its own slope and intercept, and share its respondents among the options in proportions \(\delta_k\) that sum to 1: \[\Pr(x = k \mid \theta) = \frac{\exp(a_k\theta + \gamma_k) + \delta_k\exp(a_0\theta + \gamma_0)}{\sum_{h=0}^{K} \exp(a_h\theta + \gamma_h)}.\] With \(a_0\) the smallest slope, “don’t know” takes over at the bottom, and every option’s probability heads for its \(\delta_k\). The key’s floor is \(\delta_{\text{key}}\), estimated rather than assumed to be \(1/k\), and each distractor gets a floor too. Guessing here is a state a respondent is in, with its own account of which options guessers choose.

Try it: a “don’t know” category
A four-option item under the multiple-choice model. Choose the share of “don’t know” respondents who pick the key, and how unevenly the rest spread over the three distractors.

Code

mc_g = [0.5, 0, 0, -0.5]
mc_rest = 1 - mc_dk
mc_d = [mc_dk, mc_rest * (1 / 3 + (2 / 3) * mc_skew), mc_rest * (1 / 3) * (1 - mc_skew), mc_rest * (1 / 3) * (1 - mc_skew)]

mc_th = grid(-4, 3, 141)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "θ", domain: [-4, 3]}, y: {label: "P(option chosen)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: mc_names, range: [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink, palette.guide]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0.25], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(mc_th.flatMap(t => mcProbs(t, mc_a, mc_g, -2.5, -1, mc_d).map((p, k) => ({theta: t, p, option: mc_names[k]}))),
      {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "option", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})





















































Code
mc_key = mc_th.map(t => mcProbs(t, mc_a, mc_g, -2.5, -1, mc_d)[0])
mc_min = Math.min(...mc_key)
md`At θ = −4 the options are chosen with probabilities **${mcProbs(-4, mc_a, mc_g, -2.5, -1, mc_d).map(p => p.toFixed(2)).join(", ")}** (key, B, C, D), close to the don't-know shares. The key's curve reaches its lowest point, ${mc_min.toFixed(2)}, at θ = ${mc_th[mc_key.indexOf(mc_min)].toFixed(1)}. The dashed line is 1/4, where a 3PL with c fixed at chance would put the key's floor.`























At the defaults every curve starts at 0.25. The key’s curve then dips to 0.19 near \(\theta = -1\) before it rises: respondents just above “don’t know” are drawn to distractor B, and choose the key less often than guessers do. A 3PL curve can’t dip. Lower the key’s share to 0.1 and its floor falls below chance, like the items below chance in Guessing and priors.
The multiple-choice model isn’t in mirt. mirt does fit the nested logit model of Suh and Bolt (2010), which splits a response in two: whether the respondent chose the key, from a 2PL (or a 3PL, with a floor), and, if not, which distractor, from a nominal model. The key’s curve is then a 2PL, rising everywhere, and the distractors add their information below it. The nested logit suits scores that should stay on a 2PL or 3PL scale; Bock’s model suits a first look at items, since it assumes nothing about the key; the multiple-choice model suits tests on which many respondents sit near chance.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under Thissen and Steinberg's multiple-choice model, what is the probability of choosing the key for a respondent far below every item?",
  options: [
    {text: "$\\delta_{\\text{key}}$, the share of don't-knows who choose it, which is estimated", correct: true, why: "At the bottom the don't-know category takes over, and its respondents are spread over the options in proportions $\\delta_k$. Nothing forces $\\delta_{\\text{key}} = 1/4$."},
    {text: "$1/4$ on a four-option item", correct: false, why: "That is the assumption behind a floor fixed at chance. The multiple-choice model estimates the share, and it can be above or below 1/4."},
    {text: "0, because the option with the smallest slope takes over", correct: false, why: "That is Bock's nominal model. The don't-know category is what the multiple-choice model adds to change this."}
  ]
})










Nominal and ordinal are two ends of one range
Bock’s model assumes no order. Give option \(k\) the slope \(a \cdot k\) and it becomes the GPCM, with the categories ordered in advance (problem 1; Thissen & Steinberg, 1986). Between the two ends, the fitted slopes of a nominal model say how ordered the categories are: a Likert item whose slopes come out in the order of its categories behaves as ordinal, and one whose neighbouring categories share a slope is using fewer categories than it offers. Nalbandyan, Gilbert, Franco and Domingue (2026) use nominal fits this way to ask how ordered the categories of rating scales are. The order of categories, like the order of options, is something the data can check.

title: Nominal response and multiple-choice models
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates 1,000 respondents answering 20 four-option items from the nominal model. On each item two distractors fall with \(\theta\), one is flat (it draws respondents with partial knowledge), and the key rises. It fits the 2PL to the 0/1 scores and the nominal model to the options chosen, and compares both with the true \(\theta\), overall and in the bottom and top thirds. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load.
With the seed as written, the nominal model recovers \(\theta\) a little better overall (correlations of 0.946 against 0.929) and more clearly in the bottom third (0.778 against 0.677), while in the top third the RMSEs are close (0.331 against 0.346). Set partial <- -1, so that every distractor falls alike, and the advantage vanishes (0.670 against 0.664 in the bottom third). Try np <- 300 to see how noisy the option slopes become.

title: Nominal response and multiple-choice models
text:
With real data

The RMET’s wrong words






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL: the data say little about \(c\) when few respondents sit near chance. On the RMET, 84 of 17,680 respondents (0.48%) answered 9 or fewer of the 36 items correctly, and the 3PL’s median lower asymptote was 0.01 although chance is 0.25.



Our main example is wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022, the normative sample of the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test released by Kim et al. (2024), used again on purpose: From the 1PL to the 4PL scored it 0/1, and here we ask which wrong word each respondent chose. Each item shows a photograph of the eyes of a face and offers four words for what the person is thinking or feeling (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001); the IRW has the word chosen, not the photographs. For item 14 they are accusing (keyed), irritated, disappointed and depressed, the four listed for that item in Baron-Cohen et al.’s Appendix A (2001, p. 248). Its job is to show what the distractors add on an easy test with almost nobody near chance. Download the code to run every chunk yourself; it needs mirt (Chalmers, 2012).


Code
library(mirt)
# The same pinned version as in the 1PL-to-4PL lesson. resp is 1 when the respondent
# chose the correct word; resp_raw is the word they chose.
rmet_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v22_0.wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(rmet_url)
df$item_n <- as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", df$item))
items <- sort(unique(df$item_n))
ids <- sort(unique(df$id))
# The keyed word for each item is the one scored 1.
key <- tapply(df$resp_raw[df$resp == 1], df$item_n[df$resp == 1], unique)
# Order each item's four words with the key last: mirt's nominal model fixes the
# scoring of the first and last categories, and putting the key last points theta
# the right way.
words <- lapply(items, function(i) {
  w <- sort(unique(df$resp_raw[df$item_n == i]))
  c(setdiff(w, key[[as.character(i)]]), key[[as.character(i)]])
})
names(words) <- paste0("item_", items)
# Two wide matrices: the option chosen (1-4, key = 4) and the 0/1 score.
opt <- x01 <- matrix(NA, length(ids), length(items), dimnames = list(NULL, names(words)))
for (j in seq_along(items)) {
  d <- df[df$item_n == items[j], ]
  r <- match(d$id, ids)
  opt[r, j] <- match(d$resp_raw, words[[j]])
  x01[r, j] <- d$resp
}
c(respondents = nrow(opt), items = ncol(opt), missing = sum(is.na(opt)))

      17680          36           0

All 17,680 respondents chose a word on every item. The key comes last in each item’s words, which sets the direction of \(\theta\) in mirt’s nominal model.

The nominal model’s \(\theta\) correlates 0.96 with the number correct. Of the 108 distractors, 70 fall across the whole range from \(\theta = -3\) to 3, 38 peak inside it, and none rises to the top. Item 14’s irritated is the typical peak: it draws 20% at \(\theta = -3\), peaks near \(-2.2\) and falls to 2% at \(\theta = 3\), while depressed and disappointed draw 31% each at the bottom and almost nobody at the top. Item 25 is the exception. Its keyed word is interested, and incredulous draws 17% at \(\theta = -3\), 22% at 0 and 23% at 3, peaking at 2.35. Among the ablest respondents, almost a quarter read that face as incredulous.

Do the respondents near chance choose at random?

# Respondents at or below chance (9 of 36) in the full sample: which words did they
# choose? If they picked at random, each of the four would draw a quarter.
low <- rowSums(x01) <= 9
share <- function(rows) {
  t(sapply(seq_along(words), function(j) {
    tab <- tabulate(opt[rows, j], 4) / sum(rows)
    c(key = tab[4], top_distractor = max(tab[1:3]), bottom_distractor = min(tab[1:3]))
  }))
}

wrong_top <- sapply(seq_along(words), function(j) {
  w <- opt[x01[, j] == 0, j]

Not quite. For the 84 respondents at or below chance, the median item’s key draws 20% of them, its most popular distractor 33% and its least popular 18%, where random choice would give 25% each. Among all wrong answers, the most popular distractor takes a median of 54% (37% to 71% across items), against a third if wrong answers were random. The low lower asymptotes of From the 1PL to the 4PL don’t mean that nobody guesses. They mean that almost nobody sits near chance, and that those who miss an item seldom miss it at random.

# The nested logit model (Suh & Bolt, 2010): a 2PL for the key and, among wrong
# answers, a nominal model for which distractor. mirt needs the key (here, 4).
fit_nrm <- mirt(rmet_opt, 1, itemtype = "2PLNRM", key = rep(4, ncol(rmet_opt)), verbose = FALSE)
sapply(list(nominal = fit_nom, nested_logit = fit_nrm),
       function(f) round(c(parameters = extract.mirt(f, "nest"), AIC = extract.mirt(f, "AIC"),
                           BIC = extract.mirt(f, "BIC"))))

A residency exam
For contrast, borges_brazil_residency_2024_pbt: 100 four-option items (A–D) from the paper-based version of a medical residency exam at a hospital in Brazil, taken by 1,994 applicants (Borges et al., 2024; the data are released under CC0). Its job is to show a harder test, on which a few keyed answers behave unlike the rest. The text column holds the option marked, and we take the key from resp.


Code
# resp is 1 for the keyed option; text is the option marked (A-D). A few responses
# are "_" or "X" (no single option recorded), scored 0 in resp.
borges_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v60_0.borges_brazil_residency_2024_pbt/rows?format=csv"
bz <- read.csv(borges_url)
blank <- !bz$text %in% c("A", "B", "C", "D")

Ten distractors rise by at least 0.2 from \(\theta = -3\) to 3, and the four items with negative item-rest correlations (21, 32, 78 and 95) are all among them. Item 21 is the widget’s item. Its key, A, was marked by 841 applicants and C by 798; C’s curve climbs from 0.03 to 0.73 while A’s peaks and falls. The 0/1 analysis shows a slightly negative item-rest correlation; the option curves say which answer the strongest applicants chose instead. Whether C is a defensible second answer, or the key needs checking, is a question for the exam’s authors, who know the item; the data can raise it but not settle it. These are four items out of 100.
So what would I do with a multiple-choice test? Keep the option chosen, fit the nominal model, and read the option curves before scoring anything 0/1. On the RMET they show that wrong answers are rarely random and add information where the 0/1 scores have least; on the residency exam they turn four items with low slopes into four questions about specific options. For reported scores I’d still usually fit a 2PL, or the nested logit if the low end matters, because the gain from the distractors sits with the weakest respondents.

title: Nominal response and multiple-choice models
text:
Problems

The GPCM inside the nominal model. Show that Bock’s nominal model with option slopes \(a_k = a \cdot k\) (\(k = 0, \dots, K\)) and suitably chosen intercepts is the GPCM, and find the intercepts in terms of the step difficulties \(b_v\). What does it mean if a fitted nominal model’s slopes are not in the order of the categories?
Real data with a twist: are Likert categories ordered? Fit the nominal model to the ten five-category items of bfi_goldberg_1992_conscientiousness (reverse-key first). Are the estimated slopes in the order of the categories? Where two neighbouring categories share a slope, what would merging them cost?
Judgment. On RMET item 25, incredulous draws almost a quarter of the ablest respondents. You maintain the test. Would you rewrite the item, keep it, or give credit for incredulous? What evidence would change your mind?
Design. You are writing four-option items on which each distractor diagnoses a different misconception. What would the option curves look like if the design worked, and how would you check it in pilot data?
Real data: paper and computer. The same hospital’s computer-based exam is borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt (120 items; the option is in resp_raw). Fit the nominal model and repeat this lesson’s analysis. Do rising distractors show up there too, and do the two tests’ distractors add information in the same place?
Challenge (open): credit for a good wrong answer. The nominal model can give a respondent who chose a partial-knowledge distractor a higher \(\theta\) than one who chose a falling distractor. Should a reported score do that? Think about what the test promises, about blanks (dropped here), and about distractors that behave differently across groups (Suh & Bolt, 2011). I don’t know of a general answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: Missing responses: omitted, not reached, and ignorable
text:
What this is for
A fourth grader answers the first eight questions on a reading passage, leaves the ninth blank, answers the tenth and eleventh, and writes nothing after that. What should the blank on item 9 count for, and the four at the end? Most analyses in this course have left gaps missing, a choice that rests on why a response is missing. This lesson separates responses that are omitted (seen and skipped) from those not reached (never got to), recovers the two from the order of the items in an IRW table that doesn’t record them, and asks, in PIRLS 2023 reading data, which kind carries information about ability. It picks up from Estimating abilities, because the EAP’s pull toward the mean is part of what a missing response does to a score.

title: Missing responses: omitted, not reached, and ignorable
Missing responses: omitted, not reached, and ignorable
text:
Core ideas

Why a response is missing is part of the data






Recall from Item response data and the IRW: a missing response is an absent row in a long table, and it becomes an empty cell when the table is reshaped. Skipped at random, missing by booklet design and stopped early leave different patterns of gaps, and the table alone doesn’t say which produced a given gap.



Write \(m_{ij} = 1\) when respondent \(j\)’s response to item \(i\) is missing, so that every cell carries a pair \((x_{ij}, m_{ij})\), with \(x_{ij}\) unseen when \(m_{ij} = 1\). Rubin (1976) sorted the ways the \(m_{ij}\) can arise into three kinds (Little & Rubin, 2019; Schafer & Graham, 2002):

Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness has nothing to do with the respondent or the item, as when a page is lost in the post.
Missing at random (MAR): it depends only on what we observe. A booklet design, an adaptive test (the next item depends on the answers so far) and a stopping rule on the first half of a test are MAR.
Missing not at random (MNAR): it depends on something unobserved, such as the response itself (“skip it if I’d get it wrong”) or \(\theta\) (weaker readers skip more).

The labels describe the process that produced the gaps, not the gaps (Seaman, Galati, Jackson & Carlin, 2013, state them with care). The design and the source’s missing codes say which kind we have; the long table rarely does.

Try it: three mechanisms
2,000 simulated respondents answer twelve Rasch items (\(b\) from −2 to 2). Choose how responses go missing; the grid shows 30 of them, sorted by true \(\theta\).


Code
viewof mm_mech = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Skipped at random (MCAR)", "MCAR"], ["Stopping rule after item 6 (MAR)", "MAR"], ["Lower θ skips more (MNAR)", "MNAR-theta"], ["Skip if it would be wrong (MNAR)", "MNAR-own"]]), {value: "MCAR", label: "Mechanism"})
viewof mm_share = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.4], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Target share missing"})


















Code
mm = simMissing(mm_mech, mm_share)
mm_rows = Array.from({length: 30}, (_, j) => j * Math.floor(mm.theta.length / 30))
  .sort((a, c) => mm.theta[a] - mm.theta[c])
mm_cells = mm_rows.flatMap((j, r) => mm.b.map((_, i) => ({row: r + 1, item: i + 1,
  state: mm.M[j][i] ? "Missing" : (mm.X[j][i] ? "Right" : "Wrong")})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 520, height: 420, padding: 0.05,
  x: {label: "Item (easiest to hardest)", tickFormat: d => d}, y: {label: "Respondent (lowest θ at top)", ticks: []},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Right", "Wrong", "Missing"], range: [palette.main, palette.light, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.cell(mm_cells, {x: "item", y: "row", fill: "state"})]
})
































Code
mm_mean = a => a.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0) / a.length
mm_obs = mm.X.flatMap((x, j) => x.filter((_, i) => !mm.M[j][i]))
mm_gap = mm.theta.filter((_, j) => mm.M[j].some(Boolean))
mm_nogap = mm.theta.filter((_, j) => !mm.M[j].some(Boolean))
md`Missing: **${(100 * mm_mean(mm.M.flat().map(Number))).toFixed(0)}%** of cells. Proportion correct among the observed responses: **${mm_mean(mm_obs).toFixed(2)}**, against **${mm_mean(mm.X.flat()).toFixed(2)}** with nothing missing. Mean true θ of respondents with at least one gap: **${mm_gap.length ? mm_mean(mm_gap).toFixed(2) : "none"}**; without a gap: **${mm_nogap.length ? mm_mean(mm_nogap).toFixed(2) : "none"}**.`





































Under MCAR the observed responses are a fair sample: 0.50 correct, as in the complete data. Under the other three the observed proportion correct rises (to 0.61, 0.55 and 0.63 at the default share), because the missing responses would more likely have been wrong. On this summary the stopping rule looks no better than the two MNAR mechanisms; what separates them is what a model can do about it.


Code
quiz({
  q: "An online test shows each respondent a random 20 of 60 items, and records which 20. Which mechanism describes the 40 unseen items?",
  options: [
    {text: "Missing completely at random", correct: true, why: "Which items go unseen is decided by a random draw that has nothing to do with the respondent or their answers. (Because the draw is recorded, it is also MAR; MCAR is the stronger statement.)"},
    {text: "Missing not at random, because respondents differ in which items they saw", correct: false, why: "MNAR means the missingness depends on something unobserved, such as the response or $\\theta$. Here it depends on a random draw only."},
    {text: "It can't be classified without fitting a model", correct: false, why: "The mechanism is a fact about how the data were collected, and here the design says it: a random draw. Fitting a model can't establish the mechanism."}
  ]
})










Ignorable: when the likelihood can leave the gaps alone
Why does the mechanism matter for a fitted model? Rubin (1976) showed that if the gaps are MAR, and the parameters of the missingness process are distinct from the model’s, the likelihood of the observed responses alone gives the right answer: the process is ignorable (Mislevy & Wu, 1996, and Mislevy, 2017, work this out for item response models). The marginal likelihood that mirt maximizes (Bock & Aitkin, 1981; Chalmers, 2012) is that likelihood: an empty cell contributes nothing. So booklet designs and adaptive tests are ignorable, although an adaptive test’s gaps depend on ability through the answers already given. The Go deeper callout writes out the argument.
Deleting incomplete respondents (listwise deletion) is also unbiased under MCAR, at the cost of the data it discards; in a booklet design it discards everyone (in the TIMSS 2007 data checked below, no student saw every item). Finch (2008) compares treatments of missing responses for item parameters.






If you’ve done Confirmatory factor analysis: lavaan’s missing = "ml" (full-information ML) is the same idea for factor models (Enders & Bandalos, 2001). If you’ve done Estimating item parameters: EM treats \(\theta\) itself as missing data.









NoteGo deeper: why MAR gaps drop out of the likelihood, and when they don’t





Assumptions: responses \(x\) follow an item response model with item parameters \(\beta\) and a population distribution \(g(\theta)\); the indicators \(m\) follow a model with parameters \(\phi\); write \(x = (x_{\text{obs}}, x_{\text{mis}})\). (Here \(\beta\) collects every item parameter, not regression coefficients.)
The factorization. The observed data are \((x_{\text{obs}}, m)\), and their probability averages over what we didn’t see: \[p(x_{\text{obs}}, m \mid \beta, \phi) = \int\!\!\int p(x_{\text{obs}}, x_{\text{mis}} \mid \theta, \beta)\, p(m \mid x_{\text{obs}}, x_{\text{mis}}, \theta, \phi)\, g(\theta)\, dx_{\text{mis}}\, d\theta.\] Under MAR, \(p(m \mid x_{\text{obs}}, x_{\text{mis}}, \theta, \phi) = p(m \mid x_{\text{obs}}, \phi)\): the gaps depend only on what we observe. That factor then leaves both integrals, and \[p(x_{\text{obs}}, m \mid \beta, \phi) = p(m \mid x_{\text{obs}}, \phi) \int p(x_{\text{obs}} \mid \theta, \beta)\, g(\theta)\, d\theta.\] If \(\phi\) and \(\beta\) are distinct (no restriction ties them), the first factor is a constant as far as \(\beta\) is concerned, and maximizing the second, the marginal likelihood of the observed responses, is all we need.
Where it breaks. If the gaps depend on \(\theta\), as when lower-ability respondents skip more, then \(p(m \mid \cdot)\) contains \(\theta\) and can’t leave the integral over it. For the marginal likelihood this is MNAR, although no single response is hidden from the mechanism. It becomes ignorable again if we add a second latent variable \(\xi\) for the propensity to respond, correlated with \(\theta\): given \((\theta, \xi)\), the gaps depend on nothing unobserved. That is the premise of the propensity models in this lesson (Holman & Glas, 2005). Gaps that depend on the unseen response itself (“skip it if wrong”) remain MNAR even then.
Why it is load-bearing. Concurrent calibration across booklets (Linking and equating), adaptive testing (Item banks and adaptive testing) and a skip node in a tree (IRTrees) all rest on this factorization.





Omitted: wrong, missing, or something in between?
A student who reads an item and leaves it blank has omitted it. The two simple treatments are each an assumption: scoring it wrong assumes the student would have got it wrong, and leaving it missing assumes the omit says nothing about \(\theta\). Lord (1974) argued that the first is not justified when estimating abilities or item parameters, and gave a method that uses what omits reveal. Treatments are compared in simulation by De Ayala, Plake and Impara (2001) and reviewed for large-scale assessments by Robitzsch (2021).






Recall from Estimating abilities: the EAP is pulled toward the prior mean, most where the likelihood is flattest, which includes short tests; and a respondent who gets every item right has no maximum-likelihood estimate.



Leaving an omit missing shortens the respondent’s test, so both apply. A respondent who answers only the items they know can have a perfect pattern on those items, and no MLE; their EAP is pulled toward the population mean, which moves a below-average respondent up.

Try it: one respondent, omits scored two ways
Ten Rasch items (\(b\) from −2 to 2, easiest first), normal(0, 1) prior. Tick the items right and the items omitted (an omit overrides a “correct” tick); the rest are wrong.


Code
og_b = Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => -2 + 4 * i / 9)
og_labels = og_b.map((_, i) => `${i + 1}`)
viewof og_right = Inputs.checkbox(og_labels, {label: "Correct on item", value: ["1", "2", "3"]})
viewof og_omit = Inputs.checkbox(og_labels, {label: "Omitted item", value: ["6", "7", "8", "9", "10"]})
































Code
og_x = og_labels.map(l => og_right.includes(l) ? 1 : 0)
og_om = og_labels.map(l => og_omit.includes(l))
og_w = posteriorGaps(og_x, og_om, og_b, "wrong")
og_m = posteriorGaps(og_x, og_om, og_b, "missing")
og_pm = Math.max(...og_w.post, ...og_m.post)
og_data = og_w.nodes.flatMap((t, q) => [
  {theta: t, y: og_w.post[q] / og_pm, curve: "Posterior, omits wrong"},
  {theta: t, y: og_m.post[q] / og_pm, curve: "Posterior, omits missing"}])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: "Posterior (scaled)", domain: [0, 1.05]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Posterior, omits wrong", "Posterior, omits missing"], range: [palette.contrast, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(og_data, {x: "theta", y: "y", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([og_w.eap], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([og_m.eap], {stroke: palette.main, strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
})





















































Code
og_fmt = v => Number.isFinite(v) ? v.toFixed(2) : (Number.isNaN(v) ? "none (no responses)" : (v > 0 ? "+∞ (no maximum)" : "−∞ (no maximum)"))
md`Omits scored wrong (all 10 items count): EAP **${og_w.eap.toFixed(2)}** (posterior SD ${og_w.psd.toFixed(2)}), MLE ${og_fmt(og_w.mle)}. Omits left missing (${og_m.nCounted} items count): EAP **${og_m.eap.toFixed(2)}** (posterior SD ${og_m.psd.toFixed(2)}), MLE ${og_fmt(og_m.mle)}. Dashed lines mark the EAPs.`
















With three right, two wrong and five omitted, the EAP is −0.73 when the omits are wrong and −0.31 when they are missing. Tick items 4 and 5 as omitted too: left missing, the three answered items are all right, the MLE is \(+\infty\), and the EAP rises to 0.45, though the respondent answered only the three easiest items. The posterior SD grows as items drop out.


Code
quiz({
  q: "On a test where lower-ability respondents omit more, you leave every omit missing and score by EAP. On average, what happens to the heavy omitters' estimates?",
  options: [
    {text: "They come out too high", correct: true, why: "Each omit shortens the respondent's test, so the EAP leans on the prior mean more; heavy omitters sit below that mean, so they move up. Leaving omits missing also sets aside the information that omitting goes with lower ability."},
    {text: "They come out too low, because fewer answers means fewer right", correct: false, why: "Left missing, an omit is neither right nor wrong. The estimate rests on the answered items, and the EAP moves toward the prior mean, which for below-average respondents is up."},
    {text: "Nothing changes on average; the EAP is unbiased under MAR", correct: false, why: "If omitting depends on $\\theta$, the gaps are not MAR for the marginal likelihood, and the EAP's shrinkage adds its own pull toward the mean."}
  ]
})










Modelling the propensity to respond
If omitting goes with ability, can a model use it? The latent-ignorability models add a second latent variable, the response propensity \(\xi_j\), which drives the indicators \(m_{ij}\) and correlates with \(\theta_j\) (Holman & Glas, 2005; Rose, von Davier & Xu, 2010). Given both, the gaps are ignorable, and the correlation carries what omitting says about \(\theta\). The model of Mislevy and Wu (1996) also lets an omit depend on the response the student would have given; scoring omits wrong and latent ignorability are special cases of it (Rose, von Davier & Nagengast, 2017). Each rests on an assumption about unseen responses that the data can’t check directly. On the German National Educational Panel Study’s competence tests, the model-based treatments and leaving the gaps missing gave similar results, and scoring omits wrong different ones (Pohl, Gräfe & Rose, 2014; Köhler, Pohl & Carstensen, 2015).






If you’ve done IRTrees: a first node “answered?” is a propensity model (Debeer, Janssen & De Boeck, 2017). There, simulated heavy skippers came out 0.24 too low with skips wrong, 0.41 too high with skips missing, and 0.02 off with the skip node.




Try it: the propensity dial
400 simulated respondents answer 16 Rasch items and omit about a fifth; their propensity to respond correlates with \(\theta\) at the value you choose. Each is scored by EAP three ways, with the true parameters known. The bars show the average error (\(\hat\theta - \theta\)) for the quarter who omit most.


Code
viewof pd_rho = Inputs.range([0, 0.8], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Correlation of propensity and θ"})









Code
pd = propensityStudy(pd_rho)
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 220, marginLeft: 150, x: {label: "Average error for heavy omitters (EAP − θ)", domain: [-1.2, 0.8]},
  y: {label: null, domain: ["Omits scored wrong", "Omits left missing", "Propensity model"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.barX(pd, {y: "scoring", x: "heavyError", fill: palette.main})
  ]
})


















Code
md`At a correlation of **${pd_rho.toFixed(1)}**, heavy omitters' average error: omits wrong **${pd[0].heavyError.toFixed(2)}**, omits missing **${pd[1].heavyError.toFixed(2)}**, propensity model **${pd[2].heavyError.toFixed(2)}**. Root mean squared error for everyone, in the same order: ${pd.map(d => d.rmse.toFixed(2)).join(", ")}.`







At a correlation of 0, leaving omits missing is right on average (−0.02), the propensity model agrees, and scoring them wrong puts heavy omitters about a logit too low. As the correlation rises, the “missing” estimates drift up (0.24 at 0.5, 0.42 at 0.8), while the propensity model stays within 0.04 of zero. Scoring wrong stays furthest off, since these respondents omit without regard to whether they’d be right.



Not reached: time, not knowledge
A not-reached item sits at the end of a timed part the respondent never finished, and it says something about speed, which may or may not go with ability. The IEA, which runs TIMSS and PIRLS, defines it by position: within a part of the booklet, an unanswered item is not reached if the item before it is also unanswered and no later item in the part is answered (Foy, Galia & Li, 2008, §11.3.3). So the first blank of a trailing run counts as omitted, and a run of one is an omit. TIMSS 2007 treated not-reached items as not administered when it estimated item parameters, and as wrong when it scored students (the same section).
Why treat them differently for items? Scored wrong, an item late in a timed test looks harder than it is. In TIMSS 2003 the same item looked harder when it came late in a booklet than when it came early (the same report, §11.3.1), and Oshima (1994) showed the effect in simulation. Speeded respondents can also be modelled as a latent class (Bolt, Cohen & Wollack, 2002) or with a propensity for speed (Glas & Pimentel, 2008); van der Linden (2018) treats speededness in full.
The IEA rule needs only the order in which items were presented and where each timed part ends. The IRW keeps the gaps, so where the order is known the rule works on a table that records no codes at all.

Try it: read the order
The PIRLS 2023 learners from the main table below, in item order: 150 of the 1,894 are plotted, sorted by their last answer, and the counts use everyone. Choose a rule for the gaps.


Code
viewof ro_rule = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Every gap omitted", "omit"], ["Every trailing gap not reached", "trailing"], ["IEA rule (first trailing gap omitted)", "iea"]]), {value: "iea", label: "Rule"})









Code
ro_ans = p23_ans.map(s => s.split("").map(c => c === "1"))
ro_src = p23_src.map(s => s.split(""))
ro_last = ro_ans.map(a => a.lastIndexOf(true))
ro_order = ro_ans.map((_, j) => j).sort((a, c) => ro_last[a] - ro_last[c] || a - c)
ro_show = Array.from({length: 150}, (_, r) => ro_order[Math.floor(r * ro_order.length / 150)])
ro_cls = ro_ans.map(a => classifyGaps(a, ro_rule))
ro_cells = ro_show.flatMap((j, r) => ro_cls[j].map((c, i) => ({row: r + 1, item: i + 1, state: c === "answered" ? "Answered" : c === "omitted" ? "Omitted" : "Not reached"})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 520, height: 460, padding: 0,
  x: {label: "Item, in the order printed", tickFormat: d => d}, y: {label: "Learner (sorted by last answer)", ticks: []},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Answered", "Omitted", "Not reached"], range: [palette.rule, palette.contrast, palette.main]},
  marks: [Plot.cell(ro_cells, {x: "item", y: "row", fill: "state"})]
})




























































Code
ro_flat = ro_cls.flat()
ro_srcf = ro_src.flat()
ro_nr = ro_flat.filter(c => c === "not reached").length
ro_om = ro_flat.filter(c => c === "omitted").length
ro_coded = ro_flat.map((c, q) => [c, ro_srcf[q]]).filter(([, s]) => s === "n" || s === "o")
ro_agree = ro_coded.filter(([c, s]) => (c === "not reached") === (s === "n")).length
md`Under this rule: **${ro_nr.toLocaleString()}** not reached and **${ro_om.toLocaleString()}** omitted. Agreement with the source's own codes on the ${ro_coded.length.toLocaleString()} cells it codes 6 (not reached) or 9 (omitted): **${(100 * ro_agree / ro_coded.length).toFixed(1)}%**.`



















































Learners lower down the plot stop earlier. Calling every gap an omit agrees with the source on 43.5% of the coded cells; calling the whole trailing run not reached, 89.5% (it misses wherever a learner’s first trailing blank was a skip); the IEA rule, 100%.


Code
quiz({
  q: "In one timed part of ten items, a respondent answers items 1–6, leaves 7 blank, answers 8, and leaves 9 and 10 blank. Under the IEA rule, how are items 7, 9 and 10 coded?",
  options: [
    {text: "7 omitted, 9 omitted, 10 not reached", correct: true, why: "Item 7 has a later answer, so it is an omit. Items 9 and 10 form the trailing run; its first item counts as omitted and the rest as not reached."},
    {text: "7 omitted, 9 and 10 not reached", correct: false, why: "That calls the whole trailing run not reached. The IEA rule needs the item *before* a blank to be blank too, so the first blank of the run is an omit."},
    {text: "All three omitted, since the respondent reached item 8", correct: false, why: "Reaching item 8 makes item 7 an omit, but nothing after item 8 is answered, so item 10 meets the definition of not reached."}
  ]
})

title: Missing responses: omitted, not reached, and ignorable
text:
Simulate
What does each treatment do when we know the truth? The code below simulates Rasch responses (1,000 respondents, 20 items), deletes some by four mechanisms like those in the first widget, and fits the Rasch model with the gaps missing and with them scored wrong. It reports the average and worst error in \(b\), and the average error in the EAP for the tenth of respondents with the most gaps. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while mirt loads.
With the seed as written, leaving the gaps missing recovers \(b\) within 0.07 on average under MCAR, the stopping rule and the \(\theta\)-driven skips, and misses by −0.57 when respondents skip what they’d get wrong. Scoring the gaps wrong is right only in that last case, and pushes \(b\) up by half a logit under MCAR. For the heavy skippers under \(\theta\)-driven skipping, the EAPs come out 0.43 too high with the gaps missing and 0.46 too low with them wrong, though \(b\) is nearly right. Try the skip correlation at −0.3 or 0 (the -0.6 in the line that makes xi), or n <- 5000 locally.

title: Missing responses: omitted, not reached, and ignorable
text:
With real data
Our main example is mthimkhulu_2023_pirls_reading: 1,894 South African fourth graders’ responses to the fifteen questions on “Octopuses”, a released informational passage from PIRLS 2023, shared by the University of Pretoria (Mthimkhulu, Roux & Mihai, 2023; CC BY 4.0). Its job is to be a fixed-order test on which a quarter of the responses are missing. Constructed-response items were scored by PIRLS raters (0–1, 0–2 or 0–3) and the four multiple-choice items against the key, so higher is better throughout. The IRW script drops the source’s missing codes, so a missing response is an absent row. Download the code to run every chunk yourself; every choice about missing data is marked in its comments.


Code
library(mirt)
p23_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_4:v9_0.mthimkhulu_2023_pirls_reading/rows?format=csv"
p23 <- read.csv(p23_url)
# One released passage, "Octopuses": items RP51Z01 to RP51Z15, numbered in the order
# they are printed. Constructed-response items are scored 0-1, 0-2 or 0-3 by PIRLS
# raters; the four multiple-choice items are scored 1 = the keyed option.
items <- sprintf("RP51Z%02d", 1:15)
ids <- sort(unique(p23$id))
Y <- matrix(NA, length(ids), 15, dimnames = list(ids, items))
Y[cbind(match(p23$id, ids), match(p23$item, items))] <- p23$resp
# Missing-data choice: a learner-item pair with no row in the table is a missing
# response. The IRW processing script drops rows whose source code is 6 (not
# reached) or 9 (omitted or invalid), so the table doesn't say which is which.
# Learners who answered nothing on this passage have no rows, so they aren't here.
c(learners = nrow(Y), items = ncol(Y), share_missing = round(mean(is.na(Y)), 3),
  no_gap = round(mean(rowSums(is.na(Y)) == 0), 2))


     learners         items share_missing        no_gap 
     1894.000        15.000         0.252         0.360 


Code
table(booklet = tapply(p23$cov_booklet, p23$id, `[`, 1))   # two booklets carry the passage


booklet
 12  17 
950 944 


A quarter of the cells are empty, and 36% of learners have no gap. Is a gap an omit or a sign of running out of time? We treat the passage as one timed part and apply the IEA rule in item order.


Code
# The IEA's rule, applied within one timed part: an unanswered item is not reached if
# the item before it is also unanswered and nothing after it is answered. So the
# first item of a trailing run of gaps counts as omitted, and a run of one is an omit.
classify <- function(miss) {           # miss: TRUE/FALSE per item, in the order given
  last <- max(c(0, which(!miss)))      # position of the last answered item
  nr <- seq_along(miss) > last + 1     # after the last answer, and after the first gap
  ifelse(!miss, "answered", ifelse(nr, "not reached", "omitted"))
}
# Missing-data choice: the whole passage is treated as one timed part, in item order.
code <- t(apply(is.na(Y), 1, classify))
dimnames(code) <- dimnames(Y)
table(code)


code
   answered not reached     omitted 
      21254        4043        3113 


Code
round(rbind(not_reached = colMeans(code == "not reached"),
            omitted = colMeans(code == "omitted")), 2)


            RP51Z01 RP51Z02 RP51Z03 RP51Z04 RP51Z05 RP51Z06 RP51Z07 RP51Z08
not_reached    0.00    0.00    0.01    0.03    0.05    0.08    0.10    0.12
omitted        0.07    0.13    0.19    0.17    0.11    0.10    0.09    0.17
            RP51Z09 RP51Z10 RP51Z11 RP51Z12 RP51Z13 RP51Z14 RP51Z15
not_reached    0.15    0.17    0.23    0.26    0.28    0.30    0.35
omitted        0.06    0.14    0.08    0.09    0.13    0.08    0.05


Code
nr <- rowSums(code == "not reached"); om <- rowSums(code == "omitted")
c(any_not_reached = round(mean(nr > 0), 2), five_or_more = sum(nr >= 5))


any_not_reached    five_or_more 
           0.35          427.00 


The rule finds 4,043 not-reached cells and 3,113 omits. Not reached climbs along the passage from 0 on the first two items to 35% on the last; omits stay between 5% and 19%. A third of learners (35%) have at least one not-reached item, and 427 have five or more.
The source file keeps the codes, so we can check the rule. It also carries each learner’s first plausible value, PIRLS’s reading score from the whole booklet: an ability measure from outside these fifteen items.


Code
# A check against the source file (CC BY 4.0), which keeps codes 6 and 9. It also
# carries the learners' first plausible value, PIRLS's own reading score from the
# whole booklet (two passages), which we use as an ability measure from outside the
# 15 items. Needs the haven package.
sav <- tempfile(fileext = ".sav")
download.file("https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/43586289", sav, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
src <- haven::read_sav(sav, user_na = TRUE)   # user_na = TRUE keeps codes 6 and 9
src <- src[match(ids, as.numeric(src$IDSTUD)), ]
raw <- sapply(items, function(v) as.numeric(unclass(src[[v]])))
source_code <- ifelse(raw %in% 6, "6 not reached", ifelse(raw %in% 9, "9 omitted",
                 ifelse(is.na(raw), "blank in source", "answered")))
table(source = source_code, rule = code)


                 rule
source            answered not reached omitted
  6 not reached          0        4032       0
  9 omitted              0           0    3107
  answered           21254           0       0
  blank in source        0          11       6


Code
pv1 <- as.numeric(src$ASRREA01)


The rule reproduces the source’s codes on every cell: 4,032 of 4,032 not reached and 3,107 of 3,107 omitted. The 17 cells blank in the source, with neither code, come out as 11 not reached and 6 omitted. With the item order, the IRW table holds everything the codes would have told us.


Code
predict({
  q: "In PIRLS 2023 South Africa, which tracks reading ability (the first plausible value) more closely: how many items a learner omits, or how many they don't reach?",
  choices: ["Omitted items", "Not-reached items", "Both about equally", "Neither"],
  answer: "Omitted items",
  reveal: "Omitted items: the correlation is −0.16, against −0.02 for not-reached items. By fifth of reading ability, omits fall from 13% of the passage in the lowest fifth to 7% in the highest; not-reached items don't fall steadily (11%, 15%, 17%, 18%, 11%). Check the output below."
})









Code
# Does omitting or not reaching go with reading ability?
round(c(omitted = cor(om, pv1), not_reached = cor(nr, pv1)), 2)


    omitted not_reached 
      -0.16       -0.02 


Code
fifth <- cut(pv1, quantile(pv1, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = 1:5)
round(rbind(omitted = tapply(om / 15, fifth, mean),
            not_reached = tapply(nr / 15, fifth, mean)), 3)   # share of the 15 items


                1     2     3     4     5
omitted     0.131 0.124 0.117 0.105 0.071
not_reached 0.113 0.147 0.167 0.177 0.107


Omits track ability and not-reached items hardly do: −0.16 against −0.02. The lowest fifth omits 13.1% of the items and the highest 7.1%, while not reached rises from 11.3% to 17.7% across the first four fifths and falls back to 10.7% in the top one. Skipping leans toward the bottom of the ability range; running out of time sits in its middle.
What do the treatments do? We fit the partial credit model (Masters, 1982) with every gap wrong, every gap missing, and a split by the rule (rule in the code): omits 0, and not-reached items missing, as TIMSS calibrates them.


Code
# Three ways to score the same gaps, each fitted with the partial credit (Rasch)
# model. mirt's "Rasch" item type gives the partial credit model for items with more
# than two categories.
Y_wrong <- Y;   Y_wrong[is.na(Y)] <- 0              # every gap scored 0
Y_missing <- Y                                      # every gap left missing
Y_rule <- Y;    Y_rule[code == "omitted"] <- 0      # omits 0, not reached missing
fits <- lapply(list(wrong = Y_wrong, missing = Y_missing, rule = Y_rule),
               function(Z) mirt(as.data.frame(Z), 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE))
# An item's location: the mean of its step difficulties (b for a 0/1 item).
loc <- function(f) {
  cf <- coef(f, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
  rowMeans(cf[, grep("^b", colnames(cf)), drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
}
b <- sapply(fits, loc)
round(c(last5 = mean(b[11:15, "wrong"] - b[11:15, "rule"]),
        first5 = mean(b[1:5, "wrong"] - b[1:5, "rule"])), 2)


 last5 first5 
  0.40   0.06 


Code
# EAP abilities under each scoring, standardized within each scoring.
th <- scale(sapply(fits, function(f) fscores(f, method = "EAP")[, 1]))
rbind(nr5 = colMeans(th[nr >= 5, ]), om4 = colMeans(th[om >= 4, ])) |> round(2)


    wrong missing  rule
nr5 -0.51   -0.10 -0.20
om4 -0.49   -0.31 -0.56


Code
c(n_nr5 = sum(nr >= 5), n_om4 = sum(om >= 4))


n_nr5 n_om4 
  427   322 


With every gap wrong, the last five items sit 0.40 logits higher on average than under the split, and the first five only 0.06 higher: the late items absorb the time limit. The 427 learners with five or more not-reached items average −0.51 SD with every gap wrong, −0.10 with every gap missing and −0.20 under the split. For the 322 learners with four or more omits, the last two change places: −0.31 with gaps missing, −0.56 under the split.
A propensity model gives the omits a second latent variable; not-reached items stay missing on both the item and its indicator.


Code
# A response-propensity model: a second latent variable (xi) drives whether a reached
# item is answered, and correlates with theta. Missing-data choice: an omit is a 0 on
# its indicator; a not-reached item is missing on both the item and its indicator.
answered <- ifelse(code == "not reached", NA, ifelse(code == "omitted", 0, 1))
colnames(answered) <- paste0("ans_", 1:15)
two <- mirt.model("theta = 1-15\n xi = 16-30\n COV = theta*xi")
fit_prop <- mirt(data.frame(Y_missing, answered), two, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
S <- coef(fit_prop, simplify = TRUE)$cov
round(c(cor_theta_xi = S[1, 2] / sqrt(S[1, 1] * S[2, 2])), 2)


cor_theta_xi 
         0.3 


Code
th_prop <- scale(fscores(fit_prop, method = "EAP")[, 1])
round(c(om4_propensity = mean(th_prop[om >= 4])), 2)


om4_propensity 
         -0.46 


The propensity to answer a reached item correlates 0.30 with reading ability, and the heavy omitters’ mean estimate is −0.46 SD: between leaving their omits missing (−0.31) and scoring them 0 (−0.56), nearer the second.

A contrast: when the codes were merged
Our contrast table is pirlsmissing_sirt, one PIRLS 2011 booklet (the PIRLS Reader) taken by fourth graders in Austria, Germany, France and the Netherlands, released with the sirt package (Robitzsch, 2022). Its job is to show the rule where the source had already merged omitted and not reached into one code. Responses are 1 when correct; each passage is taken to be its own timed part, still to be checked against the PIRLS 2011 design.


Code
# Contrast: PIRLS 2011, one booklet (the PIRLS Reader), four countries. The source
# had already merged omitted and not reached into one code, which the IRW keeps as
# rows with an empty resp.
p11 <- read.csv("https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v64_0.pirlsmissing_sirt/rows?format=csv")
# Missing-data choice: R31G08CZ and R31G13CZ combine the lettered parts of their
# question, so we drop them and keep the parts.
p11 <- p11[!grepl("CZ$", p11$item), ]
items11 <- sort(unique(p11$item)); ids11 <- sort(unique(p11$id))
X <- matrix(NA, length(ids11), length(items11), dimnames = list(ids11, items11))
X[cbind(match(p11$id, ids11), match(p11$item, items11))] <- p11$resp
country <- p11$country[match(ids11, p11$id)]
# Missing-data choice: each passage (G, then P) is its own timed part, items in
# number order.
code11 <- X; code11[] <- NA
for (part in list(grep("^R31G", items11), grep("^R31P", items11)))
  code11[, part] <- t(apply(is.na(X[, part]), 1, classify))
round(prop.table(table(code11)), 3)


code11
   answered not reached     omitted 
      0.915       0.013       0.072 


Code
pc <- rowSums(X, na.rm = TRUE) / rowSums(!is.na(X))   # proportion correct on answered items
round(c(omitted = cor(rowSums(code11 == "omitted"), pc),
        not_reached = cor(rowSums(code11 == "not reached"), pc)), 2)


    omitted not_reached 
      -0.26       -0.14 


Code
# The same Netherlands-France comparison under three scorings (Rasch, pooled, no
# weights: a check on the scoring, not an estimate of either country's performance).
X_wrong <- X; X_wrong[is.na(X)] <- 0
X_rule <- X;  X_rule[code11 == "omitted"] <- 0
gap <- sapply(list(wrong = X_wrong, missing = X, rule = X_rule), function(Z) {
  s <- fscores(mirt(as.data.frame(Z), 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE))[, 1]
  s <- s / sd(s)
  mean(s[country == "NLD"]) - mean(s[country == "FRA"])
})
round(gap, 2)


  wrong missing    rule 
   0.46    0.28    0.43 


The rule splits the missing cells into 7.2% omitted and 1.3% not reached. Here both kinds go with the proportion correct on the answered items (−0.26 and −0.14), unlike PIRLS 2023. The Netherlands–France difference is 0.46 SD with every gap wrong, 0.28 with every gap missing and 0.43 under the split. Without the student weights, these show how far a comparison moves with the scoring, not either country’s performance.


A twist: a table that has already decided
In borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt, 3,223 applicants to medical residency at a Brazilian hospital took a 120-item computer-based exam (Borges et al., 2024; CC0). Its job is to show a table in which the gaps have already been scored. The source marks some responses “X” (on a computer-based test most likely an item with no option chosen, though the deposit doesn’t say); the IRW script scores an X as 0 and leaves resp_raw empty, so those rows can still be found.


Code
# Twist: a table that has already scored its gaps. In the source, "X" marks an item
# with no chosen option; the IRW script scores it 0 and blanks resp_raw.
bz <- read.csv("https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v64_0.borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt/rows?format=csv")

table(cut(n_x, c(-1, 0, 2, 9, 120), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3-9", "10+")))

round(tapply(p_right, cut(n_x, c(-1, 0, 2, 120), labels = c("0", "1-2", "3+")), mean), 2)

NoteA check on the rule: TIMSS 2007, two timed parts





The exact match in PIRLS 2023 comes from one passage in one part. Does the rule hold where a booklet has two timed parts? TIMSS 2007 grade 8 data from Russia, released with sirt, keep the IEA codes. Each booklet holds four blocks in two parts (Ruddock, O’Sullivan, Arora & Erberber, 2008, Exhibit 2.13), and the code recovers each student’s booklet from the blocks they saw.


Code
# Sanity check on the rule: TIMSS 2007 grade 8, Russia (sirt::data.timss07.G8.RUS),
# where the IEA codes are kept (6/96 not reached, 9/99 omitted, blank = not given).
library(sirt)
data(data.timss07.G8.RUS)
Tr <- data.timss07.G8.RUS
it <- as.character(Tr$iteminfo$item)
R <- as.matrix(Tr$raw[, it])
tcode <- matrix(ifelse(is.na(R), NA, ifelse(R %in% c(9, 99), "omitted",
                ifelse(R %in% c(6, 96), "not reached", "answered"))), nrow(R))
# Items given to the same students form a block (a mathematics block and the science
# block with the same number go together); the file lists blocks in order M01..M14.
# A few items are blank for a few students, so a block is keyed on the first ten
# students who saw the item.
seen <- !is.na(R)
key <- apply(seen, 2, function(z) paste(head(which(z), 10), collapse = ","))
grp <- match(key, unique(key[colSums(seen) > 0]))
grp[colSums(seen) == 0] <- NA                     # items no student in Russia saw
max(grp, na.rm = TRUE)                            # 14 blocks


[1] 14


Code
given <- colSums(seen) > 0
c(students = nrow(R), items_given = sum(given),
  saw_every_item = sum(rowSums(seen[, given]) == sum(given)))   # a booklet design


      students    items_given saw_every_item 
          4472            437              0 


Code
subj <- substr(it, 1, 1)
# Booklet k holds blocks k and k+1 (booklet 14 holds 14 and 1). Odd booklets give
# mathematics in part 1 and science in part 2; even booklets the reverse.
rule_all <- truth_all <- whole_all <- nobreak_all <- nobreak_truth <- character()
for (j in which(rowSums(seen) > 0)) {
  bl <- sort(unique(grp[seen[j, ]]))
  k <- if (identical(bl, c(1L, 14L))) 14 else min(bl)
  k2 <- if (k == 14) 1 else k + 1
  blk <- function(s, g) which(grp == g & subj == s)
  first <- if (k %% 2 == 1) "M" else "S"; second <- setdiff(c("M", "S"), first)
  parts <- list(c(blk(first, k), blk(first, k2)), c(blk(second, k), blk(second, k2)))
  # Missing-data choice: an item left blank for this student (not given) is dropped
  # from the sequence.
  parts <- lapply(parts, function(p) p[!is.na(tcode[j, p])])
  for (p in parts) {
    miss <- tcode[j, p] != "answered"
    if (!any(miss)) next
    last <- max(c(0, which(!miss)))
    rule_all <- c(rule_all, classify(miss)[miss])
    whole_all <- c(whole_all, ifelse(seq_along(miss) > last, "not reached", "omitted")[miss])
    truth_all <- c(truth_all, tcode[j, p][miss])
  }
  both <- unlist(parts); miss <- tcode[j, both] != "answered"   # ignore the break
  if (any(miss)) {
    nobreak_all <- c(nobreak_all, classify(miss)[miss])
    nobreak_truth <- c(nobreak_truth, tcode[j, both][miss])
  }
}
table(IEA_code = truth_all, rule = rule_all)


             rule
IEA_code      not reached omitted
  not reached        3804       7
  omitted             123   26399


Code
# Agreement with the IEA codes, and the share of not-reached cells found, for the
# rule and for two simplifications: every trailing gap not reached, and no break
# between the parts.
agree <- function(pred, truth) c(agree = mean(pred == truth),
  not_reached_found = mean(pred[truth == "not reached"] == "not reached"))
round(rbind(rule = agree(rule_all, truth_all), whole_run = agree(whole_all, truth_all),
            no_part_break = agree(nobreak_all, nobreak_truth)), 3)


              agree not_reached_found
rule          0.996             0.998
whole_run     0.933             1.000
no_part_break 0.923             0.389


No student saw every item, as a booklet design intends. With the parts known, the rule agrees with the IEA codes on 99.6% of missing cells. Calling every trailing gap not reached gets 93.3%, and ignoring the break between parts finds only 39% of the not-reached cells. So the rule needs both the order and the part boundaries.





Which treatment to report
Each treatment is an assumption. Leaving omits missing assumes they say nothing about \(\theta\); scoring them 0, that the respondent would have got them wrong; a propensity model, that the correlation between answering and ability carries what omitting reveals. Treating not-reached items as not administered assumes the student would have answered them like those who reached them; scoring them wrong counts running out of time as part of the performance.
In the case that omissions are rare and unrelated to ability, leaving them missing under marginal maximum likelihood may be sufficient for some purposes. Where omission tracks ability, as it does in PIRLS 2023 South Africa, neither simple rule is neutral, and reporting \(\theta\) under both, with a response-propensity model as a check, may be sufficient for some purposes. For not-reached items, the TIMSS rule (missing when calibrating, wrong when scoring) keeps what an item is apart from what a respondent did; it is one defensible choice among several.

title: Missing responses: omitted, not reached, and ignorable
text:
Problems

The factorization. For a Rasch test, show that under MAR with distinct \(\phi\), \(m\) drops out of the likelihood for the item parameters. Then show where the argument breaks when omitting depends on \(\theta\) and the likelihood is marginal over \(\theta\).
Undo the scoring. In borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt, set resp to missing where resp_raw is empty and fit a Rasch model both ways. Whose estimates move, and how far? Are the X’s of the 18 applicants with ten or more at the end of the exam, or scattered?
Which comparison to report. In PIRLS 2011, the Netherlands–France difference is 0.46, 0.28 or 0.43 SD, depending on the scoring. Which would you report in a comparison of the two countries, and what else would you want to see first?
Formats. In PIRLS 2023, compare the omission rates of the four multiple-choice and eleven constructed-response items. The source’s code 9 means “omitted or invalid”. What might explain the difference, and what does each scoring do to a comparison of formats?
Design a record. For a low-stakes online test with a 20-minute limit, what would you record (timestamps, the order each respondent saw, a “skip” button) so that omitted and not-reached items can be told apart without an order rule?
Challenge (open): what an omit would have been. Whether an omitted item would have been answered correctly is never observed. What assumption lets the Mislevy–Wu model estimate it, and could any design check that assumption? As far as I know, this is not settled.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.
