title: Measurement invariance: comparing groups with multigroup CFA
text:
What this is for
In a Dutch community sample, women report a little more anxiety than men on the DASS-21 (0.16 SD, as we’ll see). Is that a difference in anxiety, or a difference in how the items work for women and men? The scores alone can’t say. Factor analysis II fitted a factor model to one sample. This lesson fits it to two groups at once and asks, one constraint at a time, whether the same model holds in both: measurement invariance. Where it holds, the groups’ factor means can be compared. Where an item breaks it, we find the item and decide what to do about it. We start with a scale where invariance holds, the DASS-21 across women and men, and then turn to one where a single item doesn’t: crying on the CES-D.

title: Measurement invariance: comparing groups with multigroup CFA
Measurement invariance: comparing groups with multigroup CFA
text:
Core ideas

One model, two groups






Recall from Factor analysis II: a confirmatory model fixes most loadings at zero before seeing the data, and it is identified once each factor’s scale is set, by fixing one loading or the factor’s variance. Nested models are compared by a (scaled) difference in χ².



A multigroup CFA fits the model in several groups at once, with any parameter free in each group or held equal across them (Jöreskog, 1971). With intercepts, the model for item \(i\) in group \(g\) is \(x_i = \nu_{ig} + \lambda_{ig}\eta + \varepsilon_i\). Measurement invariance means that responses depend on the factor and not on the group (Meredith, 1993). It is tested in steps, each adding constraints to the one before (Vandenberg & Lance, 2000; Millsap, 2011; Putnick & Bornstein, 2016):

configural: the same items load on the same factors in every group, every parameter free;
metric: the loadings \(\lambda_i\) are equal, so a unit of the factor means the same in each group;
scalar: the intercepts \(\nu_i\) (for ordered items, the thresholds) are equal too, so respondents at the same factor level have the same expected response.

Meredith adds a fourth step, strict invariance, with equal unique variances as well.
Why these comparisons at these steps? A factor has no unit and no origin of its own. In the configural model each group’s factor is scaled separately, so nothing links them. Once the loadings are equal, the items carry one unit across groups, and group B’s factor variance, and its correlations and regressions, can be estimated relative to group A’s. Once the intercepts are equal too, the items carry one origin, and group B’s factor mean can be estimated relative to A’s; lavaan frees it at that step. Comparing correlations or regressions needs metric invariance; comparing means needs scalar.
In item response language, an unequal loading is non-uniform differential item functioning and an unequal intercept is uniform DIF; Differential item functioning takes up the same question item by item, matching on an observed score instead of a factor.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A study compares women and men on the correlation between depression and anxiety factors, and on the mean of the anxiety factor. Which level of invariance does each comparison need?",
  options: [
    {text: "Metric for the correlation, scalar for the mean", correct: true, why: "Equal loadings give the factors one unit in both groups, which is what variances, covariances and correlations need. A mean also needs one origin, which the equal intercepts supply."},
    {text: "Scalar for both", correct: false, why: "Scalar invariance would do, but the correlation doesn't need the intercepts: it involves no means. Metric is enough."},
    {text: "Configural for the correlation, metric for the mean", correct: false, why: "In the configural model each group's factors are scaled separately, so nothing ties group B's unit to group A's; and a mean needs a common origin, which only equal intercepts give."}
  ]
})









What an unequal intercept does

Try it: one item that works differently
Four items measure one factor in groups A and B (loadings 0.7, intercepts 0, factor SD 1). Item 4 can behave differently in group B.


Code
viewof inv_k = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "True factor mean, B minus A (SDs)"})
viewof inv_nu = Inputs.range([-0.5, 0.5], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Item 4's intercept, B minus A"})
viewof inv_l = Inputs.range([-0.4, 0.4], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Item 4's loading, B minus A"})

























Code
inv = {
  const sdA = Math.sqrt((4 * 0.7) ** 2 + 4 * (1 - 0.49));
  return {gap: (inv_nu + (3 * 0.7 + 0.7 + inv_l) * inv_k) / sdA, fair: (4 * 0.7 * inv_k) / sdA,
          level: Math.abs(inv_l) > 1e-9 ? "metric invariance fails (non-uniform DIF), and so does scalar" :
                 Math.abs(inv_nu) > 1e-9 ? "metric invariance holds, but scalar fails (uniform DIF)" : "scalar invariance holds"};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 290, x: {label: "Factor η", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {label: "Expected response to item 4"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Group A", "Group B"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: palette.main, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}), Plot.ruleX([inv_k], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
          Plot.line(grid(-3, 3, 61).flatMap(e => [{e, y: 0.7 * e, g: "Group A"}, {e, y: inv_nu + (0.7 + inv_l) * e, g: "Group B"}]),
            {x: "e", y: "y", stroke: "g", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})


















Code
md`Here ${inv.level}. Sum-score gap, B minus A: **${inv.gap.toFixed(2)}** SDs of group A's sum score; if item 4 were invariant it would be **${inv.fair.toFixed(2)}**. (Dashed lines: each group's factor mean.)`







With both item-4 controls at 0 the lines coincide, and the sum-score gap (0.45 SD) is the latent 0.5 SD shrunk by unreliability. Set the true gap to 0 and item 4’s intercept to 0.3: the sum scores differ by 0.10 SD between groups that don’t differ at all. A loading difference makes the lines cross, so the item favours one group at low factor levels and the other at high ones.
What does the factor model make of the same item? If we impose scalar invariance anyway, the model has to explain item 4’s higher mean in group B with the one thing it has left free, group B’s factor mean. The shift is spread over every item, and the factor mean absorbs part of it. The remedy is partial invariance (Byrne, Shavelson & Muthén, 1989): free the offending item’s intercept and keep the others equal, so that the comparison of means rests on the items that do work alike.


Try it: what the scalar constraint does to the factor mean
Now \(k\) items load 0.7 in both groups, and the last item’s intercept is higher in group B by the amount you set. The widget computes the large-sample answer: group B’s estimated factor mean under full and under partial scalar invariance, and how often the test of the scalar step (on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom) would catch the shifted item.


Code
viewof ss_k = Inputs.range([4, 12], {value: 4, step: 1, label: "Number of items k"})
viewof ss_d = Inputs.range([-0.5, 0.5], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Last item's intercept, B minus A"})
viewof ss_kap = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "True factor mean, B minus A (SDs)"})
viewof ss_n = Inputs.range([50, 2000], {value: 300, step: 50, label: "Respondents per group"})
































Code
ss = scalarStep({k: ss_k, kappa: ss_kap, delta: ss_d, n: ss_n})
ss_bars = [{m: "Truth", v: ss_kap}, {m: "Full scalar invariance", v: ss.kappaHat}, {m: "Partial (last item free)", v: ss.kappaPartial}]
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 150, marginLeft: 180, x: {domain: [-1.4, 1.4], label: "Group B's factor mean, minus group A's (SDs)"}, y: {label: null, domain: ss_bars.map(d => d.m)},
  marks: [Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
          Plot.dot(ss_bars, {x: "v", y: "m", r: 7, fill: d => d.m === "Full scalar invariance" ? palette.contrast : palette.main}),
          Plot.text(ss_bars, {x: "v", y: "m", text: d => d.v.toFixed(3), dy: -14})]
})

























Code
ss_pow = grid(50, 2000, 79).map(n => ({n, p: ss.powerAt(n)}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 240, x: {label: "Respondents per group"}, y: {label: "Chance the scalar step fails (5% level)", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0.05], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
          Plot.line(ss_pow, {x: "n", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.dot([{n: ss_n, p: ss.power}], {x: "n", y: "p", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})]
})


















Code
md`Full scalar model: group B's mean is off by **${(ss.kappaHat - ss_kap).toFixed(3)}** SD. Expected χ² difference at the scalar step **${(ss.ncp + ss.df).toFixed(1)}** on ${ss.df} df (5% critical value ${ss.crit.toFixed(1)}); chance it fails: **${ss.power.toFixed(2)}**. (Dashed line: 5%, the chance with no shifted item.)`







At the start, the groups don’t differ, yet the scalar model puts group B 0.107 SD above A. With equal loadings the error is the shift divided by \(k\lambda\) (problem 1), here \(0.3/(4 \times 0.7)\). The partial model recovers the truth. With 300 respondents per group, the scalar step fails 97% of the time; halve the shift and the error halves while the chance of catching it falls to 44%. Raise \(k\) to 12 and the error falls to 0.036: more invariant items dilute one shifted one. Move the true mean: the error stays the same size, whatever the groups’ real difference.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Eight items load 0.7 in both groups. One item's intercept is 0.4 higher in group B, and a scalar model puts group B's factor mean 0.2 SD above group A's. Roughly what would a partial model, with that intercept free, give?",
  options: [
    {text: "About 0.13", correct: true, why: "The error is the shift over $k\\lambda$: $0.4/(8 \\times 0.7) \\approx 0.07$. Take it off: $0.2 - 0.07 \\approx 0.13$."},
    {text: "About −0.2", correct: false, why: "Freeing one intercept removes that item's shift from the comparison; it doesn't reverse the difference. The item accounts for only about 0.07 of it."},
    {text: "About 0.2: one item out of eight can't matter", correct: false, why: "It can, a little: the scalar model spreads the item's 0.4 over the factor mean, about $0.4/(8 \\times 0.7) \\approx 0.07$ SD."}
  ]
})










Testing the steps
Each step is nested in the one before, so a χ² difference tests it, scaled when the estimator is robust (Satorra & Bentler, 2001). As with any χ² test, a large enough sample rejects a step for differences too small to matter. So changes in fit indices are read alongside: Cheung and Rensvold (2002) proposed treating a drop in CFI of more than 0.01 as a failed step, and Chen (2007) paired it with changes in RMSEA and SRMR; Putnick and Bornstein (2016) survey how these criteria are used and questioned.
When a step fails, which constraint is responsible? A score test (lavTestScore() in lavaan) says, for each equality constraint, how much the χ² would fall if that constraint alone were released. The largest is the first suspect. But a scalar model with many items holds dozens of constraints, and a few small \(p\)-values turn up by chance.

Try it: how many flags by chance?


Code
viewof fl_m = Inputs.range([1, 60], {value: 39, step: 1, label: "Equality constraints tested"})
viewof fl_a = Inputs.select([0.05, 0.01, 0.001], {value: 0.01, label: "Level α for each test"})


















Code
fl = Array.from({length: 60}, (_, i) => ({m: i + 1, p: 1 - (1 - fl_a) ** (i + 1)}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 240, x: {label: "Constraints tested"}, y: {label: "Chance at least one p < α", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [Plot.line(fl, {x: "m", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.dot([fl[fl_m - 1]], {x: "m", y: "p", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})]
})


















Code
md`If every one of ${fl_m} constraints were true and the tests were independent, at least one would fall below ${fl_a} with probability **${fl[fl_m - 1].p.toFixed(2)}**. A Bonferroni threshold would be ${fl_a} / ${fl_m} = **${(fl_a / fl_m).toPrecision(2)}**.`







At 39 constraints and α = 0.01, a flag turns up by chance about a third of the time (0.32); at α = 0.05, 86% of the time. Score tests on one model aren’t independent, so these are rough guides, but they set the baseline for reading the largest test.



Choosing an estimator for multigroup fits






Recall from Factor analysis II: choose the estimator from the data. ML for continuous, roughly normal items; MLR for skewed items or five or more categories used fairly evenly; WLSMV, on thresholds and polychorics, for fewer than five categories or responses piled at one end; FIML, or the graded model, when responses are missing.



In a multigroup fit the guide applies group by group, and three things change. With ordered items each group gets its own thresholds, so every category of every item needs responses in each group; a category that is nearly empty in one group is a problem even when it isn’t in the pooled data (Rutkowski, Svetina & Liaw, 2019, who also show that collapsing categories changes fit). Which parameters must be fixed at each step to keep ordinal models identified and nested is subtler than with continuous items (Wu & Estabrook, 2016). And the difference tests behave differently across estimators: in simulations by Sass, Schmitt and Marsh (2014), their Type I error rates varied across ML, MLR and WLSMV, and changes in fit indices under WLSMV needed caution in misspecified models. With missing ordinal responses, WLSMV with pairwise deletion was the one method in the simulations of Chen, Wu, Garnier-Villarreal, Kite and Jia (2020) whose difference tests did not reasonably control their Type I error rate; the full-information ordinal models recovered loadings best.
So a reasonable plan with sparse categories is MLR for the ladder, items as numbers, with an ordinal fit as the check, on collapsed categories if need be.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A four-category item has 40 responses in its top category among men and none among women. You want to test scalar invariance with WLSMV. What happens?",
  options: [
    {text: "Nothing changes: WLSMV handles skewed items", correct: false, why: "Skew is fine; an empty category isn't. With ordered items each group gets thresholds, and no top-category threshold can be estimated for women, so the two groups' thresholds can't even be set equal as they stand."},
    {text: "The top threshold can't be estimated for women, so you collapse the top two categories (in both groups), or treat the items as numbers", correct: true, why: "Collapsing keeps the ordinal model but changes the item, and it can change fit (Rutkowski et al., 2019); MLR sidesteps thresholds altogether. Either way, say which you did."},
    {text: "Use MLR with FIML, because the missing category is missing data", correct: false, why: "No response is missing: every woman answered the item. An empty category is a fact about the responses, not a missing value."}
  ]
})

title: Measurement invariance: comparing groups with multigroup CFA
text:
Simulate
The code simulates 500 respondents in each of two groups answering six items that measure one factor, with group B’s factor mean 0.3 SD higher and item 6’s intercept 0.4 higher. It climbs the ladder with lavaan, runs the score tests on the scalar model, frees the item with the largest one, and compares group B’s estimated factor mean with the truth. The first run installs lavaan, which takes a little while; after that, each run takes a few seconds.
With the seed as written, configural to metric passes (\(p = 0.31\)) and the scalar step fails (Δχ² = 42.3 on 5 df); item 6’s intercept has by far the largest score test (40.5); and group B’s mean comes out at 0.377 under full scalar invariance and 0.319 with item 6 free (truth 0.3). Set shift <- 0 and the scalar step should pass; set n <- 150 and see how often the test still finds item 6 across a few seeds.

title: Measurement invariance: comparing groups with multigroup CFA
text:
With real data

The DASS-21: women and men
Our main example returns to neurodegenerative_huizinga_2019_dass, the Dutch DASS-21 answered by a community sample recruited by Huizinga et al. (2020), with the three-factor model of Factor analysis II (Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995). Its job is to show the ladder where it holds. Download the code to run every chunk.


Code
library(lavaan)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
dass_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.neurodegenerative_huizinga_2019_dass/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(dass_url)
df$resp <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df$resp))   # missing responses arrive as text
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
dass <- as.data.frame(wide[, paste0("DASS.", 1:21)])
names(dass) <- paste0("d", 1:21)
dass$sex <- df$cov_sex[match(rownames(dass), df$id)]

            "anx =~", paste(anx, collapse = " + "), "\n",
            "str =~", paste(stress, collapse = " + "))


The table’s cov_sex codes are unlabelled in the processing script. The paper reports 785 women among its 1,461 participants (its Table 1), and code 2 holds exactly 785 of the table’s 1,461 respondents, so we read 2 as women: a match of counts, not a codebook.
Which estimator? For the single-group structure the guide pointed to WLSMV: four categories, piled at zero. Group by group, the top category is thin.

Every item’s top category holds between 1 and 12 responses in each group, and five items (four among men, one among women) hold a single one. Thresholds resting on one response per group are fragile, so we climb the ladder with MLR, items as numbers, and fit WLSMV as the check.

# Configural: same pattern in both groups. Metric: loadings equal. Scalar: loadings

Equal loadings cost almost nothing (a scaled Δχ² of 13.5 on 18 df, \(p = 0.76\)), and neither do equal intercepts (24.6 on 18 df, \(p = 0.14\)). Robust CFI is 0.931 or 0.932 at every step, far inside the 0.01 criterion. The configural fit is modest, but the question at each step is whether the constraints make it worse, and they don’t.


Code
# Which equality constraint strains most? One score test per constraint.
score_tests <- function(fit) {
  st <- lavTestScore(fit)$uni
  pt <- parTable(fit)
  st$constraint <- sapply(st$lhs, function(l) with(pt[pt$plabel == l, ], paste(lhs, op, rhs)))
  st[order(-st$X2.scaled), c("constraint", "X2.scaled", "df", "p.value.scaled")]
}

# Group 2's factor means under scalar invariance, in units of group 1's factor SD.
latent_means <- function(fit, factors) {
  pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
  mu2 <- pe[pe$op == "~1" & pe$lhs %in% factors & pe$group == 2, c("lhs", "est", "se")]
  sd1 <- sqrt(diag(lavInspect(fit, "est")[[1]]$psi))
  data.frame(factor = mu2$lhs, mean_diff = round(mu2$est, 3), se = round(mu2$se, 3),
             in_group1_SDs = round(mu2$est / sd1[mu2$lhs], 2))
}

# The same ladder with the items as ordered categories (WLSMV): the thresholds play
# the intercepts' part. (lavaan may warn about the parameters' covariance matrix:
# some top categories hold one response in a group.)
cfg_o <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", ordered = TRUE)
met_o <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", ordered = TRUE, group.equal = "loadings")
sca_o <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", ordered = TRUE,
             group.equal = c("loadings", "thresholds", "intercepts"))

round(rbind(configural = fitMeasures(cfg_o, idx_o), metric = fitMeasures(met_o, idx_o),
            scalar = fitMeasures(sca_o, idx_o)), 3)

# Are these three models nested? Count what each one frees beyond the loadings and
# thresholds: the default scalar model frees 21 scale factors and 3 factor means
# that the default metric model fixes, so it is not the metric model plus constraints.
sapply(list(configural = cfg_o, metric = met_o, scalar = sca_o), function(f) {
  pt <- parTable(f)
  c(free_scale_factors = sum(pt$op == "~*~" & pt$free > 0),
    free_factor_means = sum(pt$op == "~1" & pt$lhs %in% c("dep", "anx", "str") & pt$free > 0))
})

free_factor_means           0      0      3


As ordered categories, every step fits well (CFI 0.978 to 0.987, RMSEA at most 0.050). We read only the indices. lavaan’s default ordinal scalar model frees 21 scale factors and 3 factor means that its metric model fixes, so the two aren’t nested and their difference isn’t a test of the thresholds alone (problem 5). The DASS-21 passes.


The CES-D: where one item breaks
Our failure case is alexandrowicz_2018_cesd: the 20-item CES-D (Radloff, 1977), answered 0 to 3 by a sample of Austrian adults (Alexandrowicz, Jahn & Wancata, 2018). Its job is to show the ladder failing and what to do next.

So what should a report say? One view drops the crying item, so that the scale is invariant as it stands. Another keeps it and frees its parameters, so that the comparison rests on the other 19 items while the item still counts toward each respondent’s score. A third ignores the failure because it is one item in twenty. The first changes the instrument, and its scores no longer match published norms; the third lets one item push the comparison, by 0.03 SD here; the second needs enough invariant items to carry the comparison. When enough items hold, freeing the item and reporting the comparison both ways, with the item and the reason named, may be sufficient for some purposes: a reader can see how much rests on the one item. Here the two give 0.21 and 0.18 SD, and the conclusion doesn’t change.

title: Measurement invariance: comparing groups with multigroup CFA
text:
Problems

The size of the error. Four items with equal loadings \(\lambda\) and unique variances \(\psi\) measure one factor in two groups, with item 4’s intercept higher by \(\delta\) in group B. (a) Show that the gap between the groups’ expected sum scores is \(4\lambda\kappa + \delta\), and express it in SDs of group A’s sum score, as the first widget does. (b) With \(k\) items, show that the scalar model’s population estimate of group B’s mean is \(\kappa + \delta/(k\lambda)\). (Hint: with the covariances fitted exactly, the scalar model’s mean part is a generalized least-squares regression of the item mean differences on \(\lambda\).)
A different grouping. Split the CES-D respondents at the median of cov_age and climb the ladder with the same two-factor model. Does the crying item stand out again? Which constraints do, and what would you do about them?
Significant but small. A scale is compared across two groups of 10,000 respondents each. The scalar step gives a scaled Δχ² of 180 on 20 df (\(p < .001\)) and a drop in CFI of 0.003. Is the scale invariant enough to compare means? What would you look at before deciding, and what would you report?
Design. You want to compare DASS-21 scores across the education levels in cov_education. Which level of invariance do you need to compare means, and which to compare the depression–anxiety correlation? Check the group sizes first: which estimator would you use, and what would you do if one item’s intercept failed in one group?
Nested or not? Using the code’s ordinal DASS fits, list what each of the three models fixes and frees (thresholds, scale factors, factor means and variances). Why is the default metric-to-scalar difference not a test of equal thresholds? Build a nested sequence as Wu and Estabrook (2016) propose (the semTools function measEq.syntax() writes the syntax), test it, and compare the verdict with the MLR ladder.
Challenge (open). With thirty countries, Asparouhov and Muthén (2014) note, the scalar model tends to fit poorly and to throw up many large modification indices. They propose alignment, which estimates the countries’ factor means without requiring exact invariance. What does alignment assume in place of invariance, and how would you decide whether the means it gives are trustworthy enough to rank the countries? I don’t know of a settled answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
text:
What this is for
Every lesson since The Rasch model has leaned on a promise: mirt estimates the item parameters first, and everything else follows. Where do they come from? To estimate an item we’d like to know the respondents’ abilities, and to estimate abilities we need the items. Neither is observed. This lesson takes three ways out: estimate everything at once (joint maximum likelihood), condition the abilities away (conditional maximum likelihood, for the Rasch model), or integrate them out against a distribution (marginal maximum likelihood, fit by the EM algorithm). On a short test they give different answers: on eleven true-or-false science statements, the joint estimates come out stretched by 10%, as theory predicts for eleven items.

title: Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
text:
Core ideas
The widgets in this lesson are rebuilt from an interactive walkthrough of EM for the 2PL that I (Ben Domingue) wrote for teaching, in the course’s notation: item \(i\), respondent \(j\), quadrature node \(q\).

θ is the missing data






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: with a predictor we can see, such as Elo, each chess problem was a logistic regression, fit by maximizing \(\sum [y \log p + (1 - y)\log(1 - p)]\). glm() does it with a version of Newton’s method, and this lesson was promised as the place that opens up the machinery.



Suppose we knew every respondent’s \(\theta\). Then each item would be exactly that: a logistic regression of the item’s responses on \(\theta\), with slope \(a_i\) and intercept \(-a_i b_i\), fit one item at a time (Baker & Kim, 2004). What we have instead is a matrix of 0s and 1s with no \(\theta\) column. The model is symmetric in people and items, \(\theta_j - b_i\), but the data are not: a few items and many respondents.

Try it: θ known, then hidden
Four hundred simulated respondents answer five 2PL items. Choose an item; the solid curve is the logistic regression fit to \((\theta, x)\), the dashed curve the truth.


Code
ie_quad = quadrature()
ie_sim = simulate2pl(400, demoA, demoB)
ie_pats = tabulate(ie_sim.X)
viewof k1_item = Inputs.radio([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], {value: 3, label: "Item", format: i => `Item ${i}`})
viewof k1_hide = Inputs.toggle({label: "Hide θ (what we actually observe)", value: false})







































Code
k1_i = k1_item - 1
k1_x = ie_sim.X.map(x => x[k1_i])
k1_fit = logisticFit(ie_sim.theta, k1_x)
k1_a = k1_fit.b1
k1_b = -k1_fit.b0 / k1_fit.b1
k1_hide ?
  Inputs.table(ie_sim.X.slice(0, 10).map((x, j) => ({respondent: j + 1, "θ": "?", ...Object.fromEntries(x.map((v, i) => [`item ${i + 1}`, v])), "sum score": x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0)})), {layout: "auto"}) :
  Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ (known)", domain: [-3.5, 3.5]}, y: {label: "Response, and P(correct)", domain: [-0.1, 1.1]},
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(ie_sim.theta.map((t, j) => ({t, y: k1_x[j] + ((j * 37) % 11 - 5) * 0.01})), {x: "t", y: "y", r: 2.5, fill: palette.light}),
      Plot.line(grid(-3.5, 3.5).map(t => ({t, p: logistic(demoA[k1_i] * (t - demoB[k1_i]))})), {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "5,3", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.line(grid(-3.5, 3.5).map(t => ({t, p: logistic(k1_a * (t - k1_b))})), {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5})
    ]
  })














































Code
md`${k1_hide ? "This is all the data contain: which items each respondent got right. The θ column is empty, so there is nothing to put on the horizontal axis." : `Item ${k1_item}: fitted a = **${k1_a.toFixed(2)}**, b = **${k1_b.toFixed(2)}**; true a = ${demoA[k1_i]}, b = ${demoB[k1_i]}.`}`







With \(\theta\) in hand the fit lands close to the truth (item 3: \(a\) = 1.53 against 1.6, \(b\) = 0.32 against 0.2), and it’s ordinary logistic regression. Hide \(\theta\) and the problem is circular: the items need \(\theta\), and \(\theta\) needs the items. Each method below breaks the circle differently.


Code
quiz({
  q: "If every respondent's $\\theta$ were known, how would you estimate one item's slope and difficulty under the 2PL?",
  options: [
    {text: "A logistic regression of that item's responses on $\\theta$, one item at a time", correct: true, why: "With $\\theta$ observed it is a predictor like Elo: the slope is $a_i$ and the intercept $-a_i b_i$. Items don't interact, so each is its own regression."},
    {text: "A logistic regression of the sum score on $\\theta$", correct: false, why: "The sum score isn't binary, and it mixes every item together. Each item's own 0/1 responses are the outcome."},
    {text: "It can't be done without also estimating the other items", correct: false, why: "That is the situation when $\\theta$ is unknown. With $\\theta$ known, the items separate."}
  ]
})










Joint maximum likelihood, and why it stretches
The first idea is to treat every \(\theta_j\) as one more parameter and alternate: abilities with the items held fixed, then items with the abilities held fixed, and repeat. That is joint maximum likelihood (JML), and each half is a problem we’ve already solved.






Recall from Estimating abilities, its Go deeper callout: a respondent who answers every item correctly (or none) has no finite maximum-likelihood estimate, so joint maximum likelihood has to set such respondents aside before it starts.



What goes wrong? Each new respondent brings more data about the items, but also a new parameter, estimated from the same handful of items however large the sample. Neyman and Scott (1948) showed that when such incidental parameters grow with the sample, maximum likelihood estimates of the structural ones (here, the items) need not converge to the truth. For the Rasch model the JML difficulties are spread out by a factor of about \(I/(I-1)\), where \(I\) is the number of items, and multiplying them by \((I-1)/I\) removes most of it (Wright & Douglas, 1977). Why spread out? Each \(\hat\theta_j\) comes from only \(I\) responses, so the estimates are more spread out than the abilities (in Estimating abilities, an SD of 1.26 against a true 1), and difficulties fit to them follow.

Try it: the JML stretch
Simulated Rasch data with difficulties evenly spaced from −2 to 2. The dots are the JML difficulties; the dashed line is the truth, the solid line \(I/(I-1)\) times the truth.


Code
viewof js_I = Inputs.range([2, 40], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Items (I)"})
viewof js_N = Inputs.range([250, 5000], {value: 1000, step: 250, label: "Respondents"})


















Code
js_b = Array.from({length: js_I}, (_, i) => -2 + 4 * i / (js_I - 1))
js_fit = jmlRasch(simulateRasch(js_N, js_b))
js_slope = slopeThroughOrigin(js_b, js_fit.b)
js_top = Math.max(2.6, 1.05 * Math.max(...js_fit.b.map(Math.abs)))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "True difficulty", domain: [-2.4, 2.4]}, y: {label: "JML difficulty", domain: [-js_top, js_top]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[-2.4, -2.4], [2.4, 2.4]], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "5,3"}),
    Plot.line([[-2.4, -2.4 * js_I / (js_I - 1)], [2.4, 2.4 * js_I / (js_I - 1)]], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 1.5, clip: true}),
    Plot.dot(js_b.map((b, i) => ({b, est: js_fit.b[i]})), {x: "b", y: "est", r: 5, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})







































Code
md`${js_I} items, ${js_N} respondents (${js_fit.dropped} set aside with a zero or perfect score). The JML difficulties are **${js_slope.toFixed(2)}** times the truth; I/(I − 1) = ${(js_I / (js_I - 1)).toFixed(2)}.`







With 5 items and 1,000 respondents the JML difficulties are 1.34 times the truth, and with 5,000 respondents still 1.34: more respondents don’t cure it. More items do: 1.13 at 10 items (against \(I/(I-1)\) = 1.11) and 1.04 at 40. With 3 or 4 widely spread items the stretch exceeds \(I/(I-1)\), an approximation; the Go deeper callout below finds the exact factor for two. Joint estimates do settle down when items and respondents grow together (Haberman, 1977), so JML with its correction is a reasonable choice for long tests.






Recall from The Rasch model, its Go deeper callout: under the Rasch model the sum score is sufficient, and conditioning on it removes \(\theta\) from the likelihood. Maximizing what’s left is conditional maximum likelihood (CML), whose difficulty estimates converge to the truth as respondents are added (Andersen, 1970).



So CML never estimates a \(\theta\) at all, and it assumes nothing about how abilities are distributed. It is a reasonable choice whenever the Rasch model is the model; it doesn’t extend to the 2PL, whose sufficient statistic, the weighted score, depends on the slopes being estimated (From the 1PL to the 4PL).






NoteGo deeper: with two items, JML exactly doubles the difference





Assumptions: the Rasch model; two items with difficulties \(b_1 < b_2\); responses from many respondents. Write \(\delta = b_2 - b_1\).
Respondents who got both items or neither right have no finite \(\hat\theta\) and are set aside. Each of the \(n\) who remain got exactly one right, so their score equation is \(P_1(\hat\theta_j) + P_2(\hat\theta_j) = 1\). By the symmetry of the logistic curve the solution is the midpoint, \(\hat\theta_j = (b_1 + b_2)/2\), the same for everyone. Let \(n_1\) of them get item 1 right. Item 1’s score equation says its expected number correct equals \(n_1\): \[n \cdot \text{logit}^{-1}\Big(\tfrac{b_1 + b_2}{2} - b_1\Big) = n_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\delta_{\text{JML}} = 2\,\text{logit}\Big(\frac{n_1}{n}\Big).\] CML uses the same respondents (the others carry no information about \(\delta\) once we condition on the score). By the Rasch lesson’s two-item result, \(\Pr(x_1 = 1 \mid x_1 + x_2 = 1) = 1/(1 + e^{b_1 - b_2}) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\delta)\), which does not involve \(\theta\), so \[\hat\delta_{\text{CML}} = \text{logit}\Big(\frac{n_1}{n}\Big).\] CML is consistent, so \(\hat\delta_{\text{CML}} \to \delta\) as \(n\) grows, and \(\hat\delta_{\text{JML}} = 2\hat\delta_{\text{CML}} \to 2\delta\): a stretch of exactly \(2 = I/(I-1)\). More respondents make the JML estimate more precise, around the wrong value. Set the widget to two items to see it.





Code
quiz({
  q: "A 6-item Rasch test is calibrated by JML on 500 respondents, and the difficulties look stretched. A colleague proposes collecting 5,000 more respondents. What happens to the stretch?",
  options: [
    {text: "It stays at about $6/5 = 1.2$", correct: true, why: "Each new respondent brings a new $\\theta$ estimated from the same six items, so the stretch doesn't shrink with the sample. More respondents make the estimates more precise around the stretched values."},
    {text: "It shrinks toward 1, as maximum likelihood estimates do with more data", correct: false, why: "That holds when the number of parameters stays fixed. Here every respondent adds one (the incidental-parameter problem), so the usual large-sample argument doesn't apply."},
    {text: "It gets worse, because more respondents are set aside with perfect scores", correct: false, why: "The share set aside stays about the same. The stretch comes from estimating each $\\theta$ from six responses, not from who is dropped."}
  ]
})










Marginal maximum likelihood: integrate θ out






Recall from Estimating abilities: the EAP estimate evaluates likelihood × prior at a grid of nodes \(t_1, \dots, t_Q\) and averages, with no closed-form integral needed. That lesson left the nodes and weights for this one.



The third idea treats abilities as draws from a distribution \(g(\theta)\), normal with mean 0 by default in mirt. A respondent’s pattern then has a probability that involves only the items: average its likelihood over \(g\). On the grid of nodes, with prior weights \(w_q\) that sum to 1, the marginal log likelihood is \[\ell(\text{items}) = \sum_j \log \sum_{q=1}^{Q} L(\mathbf{x}_j \mid t_q)\, w_q .\] Maximizing it is marginal maximum likelihood (MML; Bock & Aitkin, 1981). The number of parameters no longer grows with the sample, so the incidental-parameter problem is gone. The price is \(g\), taken up at the end of this section.
How do we climb this surface? Directly, by Newton–Raphson over all the item parameters at once (Bock & Lieberman, 1970), or by the EM algorithm (Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977), mirt’s default. Both reach the same top.
EM’s idea is easiest to see with two coins (Do & Batzoglou, 2008). Sets of ten tosses come from one of two biased coins, but we aren’t told which. If we knew, each bias would be a proportion of heads. So guess the biases; for each set, work out how probable each coin is; split the set’s heads and tails between the coins in those proportions; re-estimate each bias from its expected heads and tosses; repeat. Item estimation is the same problem with \(Q\) “coins”, the nodes, and one set of tosses per respondent.
The two ways of climbing differ in how they treat each respondent’s posterior weights, \[W_{jq} = \frac{L(\mathbf{x}_j \mid t_q)\, w_q}{\sum_{q'} L(\mathbf{x}_j \mid t_{q'})\, w_{q'}},\] the probability that respondent \(j\) sits at node \(q\), given their responses and the current items. Every \(W_{jq}\) depends on every item. In direct MML the weights move whenever any item parameter moves, tying the items together. EM computes the weights once per cycle and holds them fixed while it updates the items.

Try it: the ripple and the fix
The five items from the first widget, at their MML estimates, where every gradient is zero. Move item 1’s difficulty. The heat map shows posterior weights for six patterns; the table gives each item’s gradient with respect to \(b_i\) with the weights recomputed (direct MML) and held from the start of the cycle (EM).


Code
ie_mle = cyclesToConverge(ie_pats, ie_quad, 1e-9)
viewof rf_shift = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Move item 1's b by"})


















Code
rf_b = ie_mle.b.map((v, i) => (i === 0 ? v + rf_shift : v))
rf_e0 = eStep(ie_pats, ie_mle.a, ie_mle.b, ie_quad)
rf_e1 = eStep(ie_pats, ie_mle.a, rf_b, ie_quad)
rf_show = ["00000", "10000", "11000", "11100", "11110", "11111"]
rf_cells = rf_show.flatMap(k => {
  const W = posterior(k.split("").map(Number), ie_mle.a, rf_b, ie_quad).W;
  return ie_quad.nodes.map((t, q) => ({pattern: k, t: t.toFixed(1), W: W[q]}));
})
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 230, marginLeft: 60, x: {label: "Node t_q", domain: ie_quad.nodes.map(t => t.toFixed(1))}, y: {label: null, domain: rf_show},
  color: {type: "linear", range: [palette.white, palette.main], label: "W", legend: true},
  marks: [Plot.cell(rf_cells, {x: "t", y: "pattern", fill: "W", inset: 0.5})]
})














































Code
rf_g1 = gradB(rf_e1.r, rf_e1.f, ie_mle.a, rf_b, ie_quad)
rf_g0 = gradB(rf_e0.r, rf_e0.f, ie_mle.a, rf_b, ie_quad)
Inputs.table(rf_g1.map((g, i) => ({item: `Item ${i + 1}${i === 0 ? " (moved)" : ""}`, "b": rf_b[i].toFixed(2),
  "gradient, weights recomputed (MML)": g.toFixed(2), "gradient, weights held (EM)": rf_g0[i].toFixed(2)})), {layout: "auto"})























With item 1 moved by 0.5, items 2 to 5, which haven’t moved, now have gradients from 3.1 to 8.0 under direct MML: their best values depend on item 1’s. Under EM their gradients stay at zero. Neither is a mistake. Direct MML sees the true slope of the surface and must move all the items together; EM climbs a simpler surface on which the items are separate, and pays with more cycles.



The E step and the M step
E step. With the current item parameters, compute every respondent’s posterior weights \(W_{jq}\), then add them up two ways: \[f_q = \sum_j W_{jq}, \qquad r_{iq} = \sum_j W_{jq}\, x_{ij}.\] \(f_q\) is the expected number of respondents at node \(q\); \(r_{iq}\) is the expected number of them who got item \(i\) right. No respondent is assigned to one node: each is spread across all of them, in proportion to how well each node explains their responses.

Try it: from one pattern to the expected counts
Choose a response pattern (with its count among the 400) and an item. The bars are the pattern’s posterior weights, the dashed line the prior. Below, the proportion \(r_{iq}/f_q\) at each node (dot size is \(f_q\)), with the item’s current curve.


Code
viewof es_key = Inputs.select(ie_pats.map(p => p.key), {value: "11000", label: "Pattern", format: k => `${k} (${ie_pats.find(p => p.key === k).n})`})
viewof es_item = Inputs.radio([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], {value: 4, label: "Item", format: i => `Item ${i}`})


















Code

Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 200, x: {label: "Node t_q", domain: [-3.8, 3.8]}, y: {label: "Posterior weight W", domain: [0, Math.max(0.3, ...es_W) * 1.05]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(ie_quad.nodes.map((t, q) => ({t, W: es_W[q]})), {x1: d => d.t - 0.2, x2: d => d.t + 0.2, y: "W", fill: palette.main}),

es_pts = ie_quad.nodes.map((t, q) => ({t, f: rf_e0.f[q], p: rf_e0.r[es_i][q] / rf_e0.f[q]}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 250, x: {label: "Node t_q", domain: [-3.8, 3.8]}, y: {label: "r / f at each node", domain: [0, 1]},
  r: {range: [1, 14]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(grid(-3.8, 3.8).map(t => ({t, p: logistic(ie_mle.a[es_i] * (t - ie_mle.b[es_i]))})), {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(es_pts.filter(d => d.f > 0.05), {x: "t", y: "p", r: "f", fill: palette.main, fillOpacity: 0.8})
  ]
})

























Code
es_n = ie_pats.find(p => p.key === es_key).n
es_top = es_W.indexOf(Math.max(...es_W))
md`Pattern ${es_key} puts its largest weight, ${es_W[es_top].toFixed(2)}, on the node at θ = ${ie_quad.nodes[es_top].toFixed(1)}, so its ${es_n} respondents add ${(es_n * es_W[es_top]).toFixed(1)} to f there${es_key[es_i] === "1" ? ` and the same to r for item ${es_item}, which they got right` : `, and nothing to r for item ${es_item}, which they got wrong`}. Summed over nodes, f comes to **${rf_e0.f.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0).toFixed(1)}** (every respondent, counted once) and r for item ${es_item} to **${rf_e0.r[es_i].reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0).toFixed(1)}**, the number who got it right.`























The pattern 11000 (right on the two easiest items) spreads from about −1.5 to 1, peaking at 0. However the weights are spread, each respondent adds exactly 1 to the total of \(f\), and \(r_{iq}\) adds up to the number who got item \(i\) right.
M step. Now hold \(r_{iq}\) and \(f_q\) fixed and maximize, for each item separately, \[\ell_i = \sum_{q=1}^{Q}\Big[\, r_{iq} \log P_i(t_q) + (f_q - r_{iq}) \log\big(1 - P_i(t_q)\big) \Big].\] This is the logistic regression from the first widget, with \(Q\) nodes carrying fractional counts in place of respondents: \(f_q\) trials and \(r_{iq}\) successes at \(\theta = t_q\) (Harwell, Baker & Zwarts, 1988). In the plot above, it fits the curve to the dots, weighted by their size. No item’s \(\ell_i\) involves another item’s parameters, so the M step is \(I\) small, separate regressions. The next E step recomputes the weights, and the cycle repeats; no cycle lowers the marginal log likelihood (Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977).

em_pats = em_set === "As simulated" ? ie_pats : tabulate(simulate2pl(400, em_A, demoB).X)
em_hist = runEM(em_pats, ie_quad, Math.min(em_n, 300))

em_conv = cyclesToConverge(em_pats, ie_quad, 1e-3)
Plot.plot({

  fx: {label: null, tickFormat: i => `Item ${i}`},

    Plot.line([1, 2, 3, 4, 5].flatMap(i => grid(-3, 3, 61).map(t => ({i, t, p: logistic(em_now.a[i - 1] * (t - em_now.b[i - 1]))}))), {fx: "i", x: "t", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5})

Plot.plot({

Code
md`After **${em_now.cycle}** cycle${em_now.cycle === 1 ? "" : "s"}${em_n > 300 ? " (the widget stops at 300)" : ""}: marginal log likelihood ${em_now.ll.toFixed(2)}${em_now.cycle > 0 ? `, a gain of ${(em_now.ll - em_hist[em_hist.length - 2].ll).toFixed(4)} on the last cycle` : ""}. With these items EM needs **${em_conv.cycles}** cycles before a cycle gains less than 0.001.`







The first cycle does most of the work: from the flat start, one E step and one M step put every difficulty within about 0.2 of where it ends up, and the log likelihood jumps from −1,357 to −1,124. After that each cycle gains less than the one before, and at 11 cycles the gain drops below 0.001. The slopes move last. Switch to the weaker items. Their posteriors are flatter, since five weak items say little about where a respondent sits, and each cycle moves the parameters less: EM now needs 22 cycles. Every cycle goes up, but EM is not fast when the items carry little information (Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977). The recovery plot shows the other half of the story: five items and 400 respondents recover difficulties better than slopes.


Code
quiz({
  q: "In the M step, why can each item be estimated on its own?",
  options: [
    {text: "Because $r_{iq}$ and $f_q$ are held fixed, and item $i$'s objective involves only its own parameters", correct: true, why: "Once the posterior weights are frozen, $\\ell_i = \\sum_q [r_{iq}\\log P_i + (f_q - r_{iq})\\log(1 - P_i)]$ contains no other item's $a$ or $b$."},
    {text: "Because the items are locally independent, so their parameters never depend on each other", correct: false, why: "Local independence holds given $\\theta$, but with $\\theta$ unknown the items are tied together through the posterior weights, as the ripple widget showed. EM separates them by freezing the weights for one cycle."},
    {text: "Because each respondent is assigned to the node where their posterior is highest", correct: false, why: "No respondent is assigned to one node: each is spread over every node by their weights $W_{jq}$."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: one EM cycle for the Rasch model, by hand





Assumptions: the Rasch model, \(P_i(t) = \text{logit}^{-1}(t - b_i)\); abilities drawn from a known distribution with weights \(w_q\) at nodes \(t_q\); every respondent answers all \(I\) items. Write \(\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}\).
E step. For respondent \(j\) with sum score \(r_j\), the likelihood at node \(q\) factorizes as in the Rasch lesson’s Go deeper callout: \(L(\mathbf{x}_j \mid t_q) = e^{r_j t_q}\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_{ij}} / \prod_i (1 + e^{t_q - b_i})\). The factor \(\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_{ij}}\) doesn’t depend on \(q\), so it cancels from \(W_{jq}\): \[W_{jq} = \frac{e^{r_j t_q}\, w_q \big/ \prod_i (1 + e^{t_q - b_i})}{\sum_{q'} e^{r_j t_{q'}}\, w_{q'} \big/ \prod_i (1 + e^{t_{q'} - b_i})}.\] Under the Rasch model the posterior weights depend on the pattern only through the sum score, so the E step needs \(I + 1\) rows of weights, one per score, not one per pattern. With \(N_s\) respondents at score \(s\), \(n_{is}\) of them right on item \(i\), and \(W_{sq}\) the weights for score \(s\), \[f_q = \sum_{s} N_s W_{sq}, \qquad r_{iq} = \sum_s n_{is} W_{sq}.\]
M step. For item \(i\), the derivative of \(\ell_i\) with respect to \(b_i\) is \(-\sum_q (r_{iq} - f_q P_{iq})\), and the second derivative is \(-\sum_q f_q P_{iq}(1 - P_{iq})\). One Newton step is \[b_i \leftarrow b_i - \frac{\sum_q \big(r_{iq} - f_q P_{iq}\big)}{\sum_q f_q P_{iq}\big(1 - P_{iq}\big)}.\] At the solution \(\sum_q f_q P_{iq} = \sum_q r_{iq}\), the number of respondents who got item \(i\) right: the expected number correct matches the observed, the score equation of The likelihood and logistic regression, with the expectation now taken over the posterior. If the SD of \(\theta\) is estimated too (as mirt does for the Rasch model), it gets an M step of its own, from the spread of the nodes weighted by \(f_q\).
Why it climbs. The marginal log likelihood equals the expected complete-data log likelihood under the weights, minus a term that the current weights themselves maximize. Raising the first term with the weights held fixed can’t lower the total (Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977).






The price: a distribution for θ
Marginal ML gets rid of the incidental parameters by assuming a distribution for \(\theta\). What if it’s wrong? The posterior weights depend on the prior weights \(w_q\), so a wrong prior can bend the item estimates; Seong (1990) found that a prior matched to the true distribution improved item estimates in large samples. One check needs no outside information: estimate the weights \(w_q\) along with the items, as an empirical histogram updated from the \(f_q\) (Bock & Aitkin, 1981; Mislevy, 1984), or a spline-smoothed version (Woods & Thissen, 2006). If the items barely move, the prior wasn’t doing much harm.

title: Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates Rasch responses for 5, 10 and 40 items (1,000 respondents, difficulties from −2 to 2) and estimates the difficulties by JML (written out in the code) and by mirt’s MML. Then it draws abilities from a skewed distribution (a standardized chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom: nobody below −1, a long tail above) and fits a 2PL with every true slope 1.5, with the normal prior and with an empirical histogram. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, and the fits about another minute.
With the seed as written, JML stretches the difficulties by 1.39 with 5 items (against \(I/(I-1)\) = 1.25), 1.13 with 10 (1.11) and 1.03 with 40 (1.03), while MML stays within 0.04 of 1. In the second part the normal prior bends the 2PL: the slopes, all 1.5 in truth, run from 0.76 for the easiest item to 2.56 for the hardest, and the easiest item’s difficulty is off by 1.57. The histogram brings the slopes back to between 1.33 and 2.04 and the largest difficulty error to 0.36. Set np to 5000 in your own R session: the JML stretch doesn’t budge.

title: Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
text:
With real data
Our example is enders_2022_science_literacy: eleven statements about science that 2,054 US adults marked true or false, in a national survey on conspiracy beliefs and vaccine hesitancy (Enders, Uscinski, Klofstad & Stoler, 2022). The statements (that the center of the Earth is very hot, for instance, or that lasers work by focusing sound waves) are listed with their answers in the article’s S1 file. Its job here is to be a short test, where JML and the marginal method part company. Download the code; it needs mirt (Chalmers, 2012).


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with a
# CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
sl_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_6:v3_5.enders_2022_science_literacy/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(sl_url)
"wave" %in% names(df)   # no wave column: one administration


[1] FALSE

wide <- wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))]

c(respondents = nrow(wide), complete = sum(complete.cases(wide)))

There is one administration, and 2,040 of the 2,054 respondents answered all eleven statements; we use them.

R <- cor(X)
block <- function(g, h) {

  c(mean = round(mean(v), 2), negative = sum(v < 0), of = length(v))

The correlations turn up something about the coding. Within the six true statements and within the five false ones (S1 file), correlations average 0.08 and 0.14, and 1 of 25 is negative; between the groups, 24 of 30 are negative. A respondent who knows more science should get both kinds right, so in the table a 1 must record a “true” answer, not a correct one (the table is built from the survey’s raw export). Recoding the five false statements makes 1 a correct answer (higher = more knowledge), and every item-rest correlation turns positive, from 0.05 to 0.24: low, against a median of 0.49 for the reading test in Classical test theory and reliability. Nobody scores 0 or 1, and 145 respondents get all eleven right.


Code
# Marginal ML by EM: mirt fixes the mean of a normal theta distribution at 0 and
# estimates its SD. Its d is an easiness, so b = -d.
m <- mirt(as.data.frame(X), 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
b_mml <- -coef(m, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
c(EM_cycles = extract.mirt(m, "iterations"),
  sd_theta = round(sqrt(coef(m)$GroupPars[, "COV_11"]), 2))


EM_cycles  sd_theta 
    37.00      0.64 


mirt needed 37 EM cycles, and the SD of ability is 0.64, small next to the 1.22 of the chess problems in The Rasch model: the statements don’t spread these respondents far apart.


Code
# Joint ML by hand: alternate a Newton step for every theta (items fixed) with one for
# every b (abilities fixed), with the b's summing to 0. Respondents with a perfect
# score have no finite theta and are set aside first (nobody here scores 0).
jml <- function(X, tol = 1e-8, maxit = 500) {
  X <- X[rowSums(X) > 0 & rowSums(X) < ncol(X), ]
  r <- rowSums(X); s <- colSums(X)
  b <- -qlogis(colMeans(X)); b <- b - mean(b)
  th <- qlogis(r / ncol(X))
  for (it in 1:maxit) {
    P  <- plogis(outer(th, b, "-"))
    th <- th + (r - rowSums(P)) / rowSums(P * (1 - P))
    P  <- plogis(outer(th, b, "-"))
    step <- -(s - colSums(P)) / colSums(P * (1 - P))
    b <- b + step; b <- b - mean(b)
    if (max(abs(step)) < tol) break
  }
  list(b = b, kept = nrow(X), cycles = it)
}
J <- jml(X)
c(kept = J$kept, set_aside = nrow(X) - J$kept, cycles = J$cycles)


     kept set_aside    cycles 
     1895       145         7 


JML sets the 145 perfect scorers aside and converges in 7 rounds on the other 1,895.


Code
# Conditional ML by hand. Given the sum score r, a pattern's probability is
# prod(eps^x) / gamma_r(eps), with eps = exp(-b) and gamma_r the elementary symmetric
# function of order r (the Rasch lesson's Go deeper callout); theta has cancelled.
esf <- function(eps) {           # gamma_0, ..., gamma_I, one item at a time
  g <- 1
  for (e in eps) g <- c(g, 0) + c(0, g * e)
  g
}
cml_negll <- function(b_free) {
  b <- c(b_free, -sum(b_free))   # difficulties sum to 0
  -(sum(X %*% (-b)) - sum(log(esf(exp(-b))[r + 1])))
}
fit <- optim(rep(0, I - 1), cml_negll, method = "BFGS",
             control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000))
b_cml <- c(fit$par, -sum(fit$par))

The JML difficulties are 1.09 times the MML ones and 1.10 times the CML ones: \(11/10\). The largest gap is 0.14, for statement 7, the hardest (lasers). Multiplied by \(10/11\), the JML difficulties come within 0.02 of MML everywhere. CML and MML, which condition \(\theta\) away and integrate it out, agree to within 0.01 (a slope of 1.005).






Recall from The Rasch model: only \(\theta - b\) is identified, so software fixes an origin. mirt sets the mean ability to 0, while our JML and CML make the difficulties sum to 0; the comparisons above put all three on that second origin.



Last, the marginal model’s prior. Is the normal distribution doing any harm here?


Code
# The price of marginal ML is a distribution for theta. Refit with the distribution
# estimated as a histogram over the quadrature nodes instead of assumed normal.
m_eh <- mirt(as.data.frame(X), 1, itemtype = "Rasch", dentype = "EH", verbose = FALSE)
b_eh <- -coef(m_eh, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
w <- extract.mirt(m_eh, "Prior")[[1]]; t <- m_eh@Model$Theta[, 1]
mu <- sum(w * t)
round(c(histogram_mean = mu, histogram_sd = sqrt(sum(w * (t - mu)^2)),
        skewness = sum(w * (t - mu)^3) / sum(w * (t - mu)^2)^1.5), 2)


histogram_mean   histogram_sd       skewness 
         -0.08           0.78           1.56 


Code
# Difficulties on the same origin (summing to 0): how far does the prior move them?
round(max(abs((b_eh - mean(b_eh)) - b_m)), 3)


[1] 0.008


Code
plot(t, w, type = "h", lwd = 3, col = "#2780e3", xlab = "Ability (quadrature node)",
     ylab = "Estimated share of respondents", xlim = c(-3, 3))
lines(t, dnorm(t, 0, sqrt(coef(m)$GroupPars[, "COV_11"])) * diff(t[1:2]), lty = 2)









The estimated histogram (bars) is not normal: its skewness is 1.56, with a long right tail where the perfect scorers sit, and its SD is 0.78 against the normal fit’s 0.64 (dashed). Yet the difficulties move by at most 0.008. That is a reassuring null: with one common slope, the Rasch difficulties are set largely by each statement’s proportion correct, and the prior has little room to bend them. The Simulate section showed a case where it does, a 2PL with skewed abilities; problem 3 tries the 2PL here.
So which estimate would I trust for item parameters? First the assumptions. JML assumes nothing about the distribution of \(\theta\) but estimates one \(\theta\) per respondent, and pays with a stretch that more respondents don’t fix. CML assumes nothing about the distribution either, but needs the sum score to be sufficient, which means the Rasch model. MML works for any model and has no incidental parameters, but assumes a distribution for \(\theta\), which can be checked. For a short test, and for any model beyond the Rasch model, I use marginal ML by EM and check the prior by refitting with an empirical histogram. I’d use JML only with its \((I-1)/I\) correction, and only when the items number in the dozens, where the stretch is a few percent before the correction. When the Rasch model is the model, CML is the check I’d add; here it agrees with MML to 0.01.

title: Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
text:
Problems

The joint likelihood. Here is a Rasch joint log likelihood with a deliberate mistake: \(\ell = \sum_j \sum_i \big[x_{ij}(\theta_j - b_i) - \log\big(1 + e^{\theta_j + b_i}\big)\big]\). Find it, correct it, and derive \(\partial \ell/\partial \theta_j\) and \(\partial \ell/\partial b_i\). Show that setting them to zero gives “expected equals observed” for each respondent’s score and each item’s total, and explain why the equation for a respondent with a perfect score has no solution. (252, slides c5)
Two coins. Write the two-coin EM in R: five sets of ten tosses with 5, 9, 8, 4 and 7 heads, starting from biases 0.6 and 0.5 (Do & Batzoglou, 2008). Then simulate data of your own. How sensitive are the estimates to the starting values, to how far apart the true biases are, and to the number of sets and of tosses per set? What happens if you start both coins at the same bias? (c5/EM-coins.R, c5/EM-example.R)
The 2PL, twice. Fit a 2PL to the recoded science-literacy data with the default normal prior and with dentype = "EH", and put the two on the same scale (the Simulate code shows how). Do the slopes move more than the Rasch difficulties did? Which statements move most, and does that match the pattern in the simulation?
The M step is a regression. Show that the expected complete-data log likelihood, \(\sum_j \sum_q W_{jq} \log\big[L(\mathbf{x}_j \mid t_q)\,w_q\big]\), equals \(\sum_i \sum_q \big[r_{iq} \log P_i(t_q) + (f_q - r_{iq})\log(1 - P_i(t_q))\big]\) plus terms that don’t involve the item parameters. Which of those other terms would you maximize to estimate the prior weights \(w_q\) as well, and what is the answer?
When is JML enough? Rasch analyses of long tests are sometimes run by JML with the \((I-1)/I\) correction. Using the stretch widget and the simulation, decide how many items you’d want before you’d accept corrected JML difficulties without comparing them with CML or MML. What else would make you more or less comfortable: the spread of the difficulties, missing responses, the number of perfect scores?
Challenge (open): how wrong can the prior be? The 252 slides ask how sensitive marginal ML is to the assumed distribution of \(\theta\), and answer that they don’t know. Start from Seong (1990) and Woods & Thissen (2006), and find what has been learned since. Then design a study across the IRW: which tables would you refit with an empirical histogram, and what would count as the prior “mattering”? I don’t know the answer. (PS5#1)







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: Estimating item parameters: JML and EM
text:
Going further

Baker, F. B., & Kim, S.-H. (2004). Item response theory: Parameter estimation techniques (2nd ed.). Marcel Dekker. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781482276725. JML, CML and MML by EM, worked through step by step.
Bock, R. D., & Aitkin, M. (1981). Marginal maximum likelihood estimation of item parameters: Application of an EM algorithm. Psychometrika, 46(4), 443–459. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02293801. The E step and M step this lesson follows, and the empirical histogram.
Harwell, M. R., Baker, F. B., & Zwarts, M. (1988). Item parameter estimation via marginal maximum likelihood and an EM algorithm: A didactic. Journal of Educational Statistics, 13(3), 243–271. https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986013003243. Bock and Aitkin’s algorithm written out in full.
Bock, R. D., & Lieberman, M. (1970). Fitting a response model for n dichotomously scored items. Psychometrika, 35(2), 179–197. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02291262. Marginal ML maximized directly, by Newton–Raphson.
Dempster, A. P., Laird, N. M., & Rubin, D. B. (1977). Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 39(1), 1–22. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1977.tb01600.x. EM in general, and why each cycle climbs.
Do, C. B., & Batzoglou, S. (2008). What is the expectation maximization algorithm? Nature Biotechnology, 26(8), 897–899. https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt1406. The two coins.
Neyman, J., & Scott, E. L. (1948). Consistent estimates based on partially consistent observations. Econometrica, 16(1), 1–32. https://doi.org/10.2307/1914288. The incidental-parameter problem.
Wright, B. D., & Douglas, G. A. (1977). Best procedures for sample-free item analysis. Applied Psychological Measurement, 1(2), 281–295. https://doi.org/10.1177/014662167700100216. The bias of JML for the Rasch model, and a correction.
Andersen, E. B. (1970). Asymptotic properties of conditional maximum-likelihood estimators. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 32(2), 283–301. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1970.tb00842.x. Why CML is consistent.
Haberman, S. J. (1977). Maximum likelihood estimates in exponential response models. The Annals of Statistics, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176343941. Joint estimates as both items and respondents grow, with the Rasch model as the example.
Mislevy, R. J. (1984). Estimating latent distributions. Psychometrika, 49(3), 359–381. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02306026. The ability distribution estimated from the responses, including a non-parametric version.
Seong, T.-J. (1990). Sensitivity of marginal maximum likelihood estimation of item and ability parameters to the characteristics of the prior ability distributions. Applied Psychological Measurement, 14(3), 299–311. https://doi.org/10.1177/014662169001400307. What a mismatched prior does, by simulation.
Woods, C. M., & Thissen, D. (2006). Item response theory with estimation of the latent population distribution using spline-based densities. Psychometrika, 71(2), 281–301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-004-1175-8. A smooth alternative to the empirical histogram.
Enders, A. M., Uscinski, J., Klofstad, C., & Stoler, J. (2022). On the relationship between conspiracy theory beliefs, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy. PLOS ONE, 17(10), e0276082. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0276082. The source of the science-literacy data; the S1 file lists the statements and their answers.
Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory package for the R environment. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(6). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06. EM, and the empirical histogram (dentype = "EH").
Glas, C. A. W. (2017). Maximum-likelihood estimation. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 2. Statistical tools (pp. 197–217). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/b19166-11. A handbook chapter on maximum-likelihood estimation for item response models.
Aitkin, M. (2017). Expectation maximization algorithm and extensions. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 2. Statistical tools (pp. 217–236). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/b19166-12. A handbook chapter on the EM algorithm and its extensions.
Haberman, S. J. (2017). Models with nuisance and incidental parameters. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 2. Statistical tools (pp. 151–170). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/b19166-9. A handbook chapter on estimation when a model has nuisance or incidental parameters, such as person parameters.
Junker, B. W., Patz, R. J., & VanHoudnos, N. M. (2017). Markov chain Monte Carlo for item response models. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 2. Statistical tools (pp. 271–312). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/b19166-15. A handbook chapter on Markov chain Monte Carlo for item response models.

For instructors

Source: EDUC 252 class 5 (slides c5, 33–63), problem set 5 (#1), and the code in ben-domingue/252: c5/EM-coins.R, c5/EM-example.R. The widgets are rebuilt from Ben Domingue’s interactive EM walkthrough (em_irt.html, not published), in the course’s notation and colours.
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 60 minutes; the science-literacy analysis works as a 25-minute lab. Every fit takes a few seconds in local R.
Changed from 252: the slides make JML’s inconsistency a quotation from Baker and Kim; here the stretch widget, the two-item Go deeper and the real data show it, and CML is added as a third estimator. The coins are a paragraph and a problem. The real data are new, and their keying had to be fixed first (five false statements recoded).
Held back: priors on item parameters (Guessing and priors); many-item, sparse designs in which each respondent sees some items (Linking and equating, Item banks and adaptive testing); a prior that depends on covariates, and crossed random effects as another estimator (Explanatory item response models); standard errors for item parameters.
Solutions: held back in solutions/item-estimation.qmd (not published).

title: Item response data and the IRW
text:
What this is for
Every analysis in this course starts from a record of which respondent gave which response to which item. Before fitting a model, we should know how it is stored, what is missing, what rides along, and what a few simple numbers say. Item response data have their surprises (an item scored the opposite way from its neighbours, a respondent who appears hundreds of times, a missing response that was never asked for), and they are far cheaper to find now than after a model has been fit. This lesson introduces the data, the Item Response Warehouse (IRW) that supplies them, and a first look at three IRW tables: yes/no answers on verbal aggression, a five-point Big Five inventory, and thousands of timed perceptual judgements.

title: Item response data and the IRW
Item response data and the IRW
Item response data and the IRW
text:
Simulate
The code builds a long table (each respondent with a propensity to say yes, each item with its own popularity), deletes 5% of rows, reshapes, and takes the first look, in base R.
With the seed as written, item means run from 0.23 to 0.80 and the median item-rest correlation is 0.28. Set spread <- 0, so every respondent has the same propensity: the means barely move, but the correlations collapse (median 0.03), since nothing about a respondent carries over between items. With spread <- 2 the median rises to 0.54. Positive item-rest correlations are the first sign that items measure something in common.

title: Item response data and the IRW
text:
With real data
verbagg is the main example, with 0/1 responses; manolika_2021_mini_ipip is the contrast for Likert responses and keying; rr98_accuracy is the contrast for response times and trials. The code is base R (download it).


Code
# Every IRW table has a landing page, itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/,
# with a "Download CSV" link that needs no account. The link names the version
# of the data (e.g. v59_0), so reading it off the page gets the current release.
irw_csv_url <- function(table) {
  page <- readLines(paste0("https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/", tolower(table), "/"),
                    warn = FALSE)
  hit <- regmatches(page, regexpr('https://redivis\\.com/api/v1/tables/[^"]+format=csv', page))
  hit[[1]]
}
irw_csv <- function(table) read.csv(irw_csv_url(table))

# Long (one row per response) to wide (one row per respondent, one column per
# item). A respondent-item pair with no row becomes an empty (NA) cell.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(colnames(wide))])
}
# Correlation of each item with the sum of the *other* items.
item_rest <- function(resp) {
  tot <- rowSums(resp)
  sapply(names(resp), function(i) cor(resp[[i]], tot - resp[[i]], use = "complete.obs"))
}



Verbal aggression: 0/1 responses
The verbal aggression data, from De Boeck and Wilson (2004) and distributed with the lme4 R package (Bates et al., 2015), come from 316 Belgian psychology students (per the psychotools documentation). Each item pairs one of four frustrating situations (two where someone else is to blame, such as a bus that fails to stop; two where you are) with a reaction (cursing, scolding, shouting), in two modes: would you want to, and would you do it? S2WantCurse is situation 2, want, curse. Keying: 1 means the reaction was reported.

        Intellect.IPIP_15R         Intellect.IPIP_20R 
                      0.38                       0.48 


Every within-trait correlation is positive (0.18 to 0.59), as is every within-trait item-rest correlation. The ten R items arrive already reverse-scored: higher means more of the trait on all 20, and IPIP_17R’s 4.5 means most respondents disagreed. (The IRW’s item-text notes agree, and record that respondents answered a Greek translation.) Keying: higher means more Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism (not emotional stability) or Intellect.
How should an analyst decide which way items run? One route trusts the documentation, the scoring key and codebook; the other reads the direction off the data, from signs like these. My rule: before summing a scale, I find out from the documentation which way each item should run, and then I check it in the data, because neither is enough alone. Here the codebook would have had us reverse ten items twice; Classical test theory and reliability meets an item the data can’t settle.

round(apply(sums, 2, function(s) c(mean = mean(s), sd = sd(s))), 1)

title: Item response data and the IRW
text:
Problems

Item-total against item-rest. For \(k\) items with equal variances and pairwise correlation \(\rho\), derive the item-total and item-rest correlations. How much does including the item inflate the correlation when \(k = 5\)? When \(k = 40\)? Check on verbagg.
Response time and difficulty (PS1#3a). In rr98_accuracy (or another timed table; with a Redivis account, irw::irw_filter(var = "rt", n_categories = 2, density = NULL) lists them), compute each item’s median response time for correct and incorrect responses, and its proportion correct. Are harder items slower? What complicates the inference?
Long or wide? Give two situations where wide format is the better store, and two things long format makes easy.
Your own data. A 12-item Likert questionnaire, four items reverse-worded, is answered before and after an intervention by two randomized groups, with each respondent’s age. Give the IRW-format columns and three example rows, and say how you would record which items are reverse-worded and whether they have been reversed.
A first look of your own (PS1#3c). Pick an IRW table, compute the four descriptives, and write a paragraph on what they show, ending with a question they can’t answer.
Challenge: wording and endorsement (PS1#3b). Using the Mini-IPIP’s item text (IPIP scoring key), relate a feature of the wording (length, negation) to the item means, as stored and with the reverse-scoring undone. With 20 items, what could this show, and what not? The IRW vignette on item language and difficulty asks a similar question across many tests.
