title: Measurement invariance under treatment and life events
text:
What this is for
A fractions program for struggling fifth graders raises its students’ test scores by more than a standard deviation. Did it raise every item, or a handful? Differential item functioning ended on a vocabulary trial in which one word, expedition, carried over a quarter of the raw effect. This lesson takes that finding further. Experience, whether a program, the loss of a spouse or a second sitting of the same test, can change how a measure works, and a randomized trial is the one setting where we can separate that change from a change in the respondents. We read treatment as a grouping variable, use the pretest as a placebo, fit a model that gives every item its own treatment effect, and ask what the spread of those effects does to the average effect we report.

title: Measurement invariance under treatment and life events
Measurement invariance under treatment and life events
text:
Core ideas

When experience changes the measure
After a spouse dies, older adults in the Health and Retirement Study report more depressive symptoms on an eight-item, yes/no version of the CES-D (Radloff, 1977), and the rise fades within about a year (Domingue, Duncan, Harrati & Belsky, 2021). The items don’t share the rise equally: loneliness and sadness carry most of it (the preprint, Domingue et al., 2019, Supplemental Figures S7–S8). Is that more depression, or depression measured differently? A widow who now reports feeling lonely may be no more depressed, in the sense the other items capture, than a year earlier; the loneliness item is also answering a question about her circumstances. The IRW has no item-level data from this study, so the result stays a cited figure.
The possibility has names. Golembiewski, Billingsley and Yeager (1976) distinguished three kinds of change. Alpha change is a change in level on an instrument that stays the same; beta change, a change in the scale respondents use to answer; gamma change, a redefinition of the construct itself (Livingston et al., 2022, give a short account). In health research, Sprangers and Schwartz (1999) call the last two response shift: a change in what a self-evaluation means, from new internal standards, new values or a new conception of the construct. Each is a failure of invariance across occasions. Gamma change is a change in the factor structure; beta change, unequal loadings or intercepts (Jabrayilov, Emons, de Jong & Sijtsma, 2017; Oort, 2005; Widaman, Ferrer & Conger, 2010).






Recall from Fairness in testing: impact is a difference in the attribute itself; bias is a difference in scores that comes from something else. Invariance is always relative to the other items: a shift shared by every item looks like impact.



Swap “group” for “occasion” and the fairness lesson carries over: a change in level is impact across time, and an item whose meaning shifts is DIF across time. A program, a bereavement and a second sitting are all experiences between two measurements, and each can change the measure along with the person.






If you’ve done Measurement invariance: longitudinal invariance is the multigroup ladder (configural, metric, scalar) with occasions in place of groups. Generalizability theory treats the occasion as a facet, a source of error to average over; here it is a condition that may change what is measured. Factor analysis I used BFI-2 data in which students were randomly assigned a response format, the same design with the format as the treatment. And What does a score mean? computed a reliable change index, which assumes the scale measures the same thing at both waves (Jacobson & Truax, 1991).





Code
quiz({
  q: "After a mindfulness course, participants' scores on a stress scale fall. Nearly all of the fall is on one item, about feeling unable to control what matters in one's life. What is the most careful reading?",
  options: [
    {text: "Stress fell, or the course changed how participants read that item; the item-level pattern is a reason to check before reporting a general fall in stress", correct: true, why: "A change concentrated in one item is what beta or gamma change would produce. It is also what a real but narrow change in stress would produce. The pattern calls for a check, not a verdict."},
    {text: "Stress fell: the total went down and the scale is reliable", correct: false, why: "Reliability at each occasion says nothing about whether the items mean the same thing at both. The item-level pattern is exactly what invariance across occasions asks about."},
    {text: "The item is biased and should be dropped", correct: false, why: "A flag isn't a verdict. A sense of control may be precisely what the course teaches, in which case the item is carrying the effect, not distorting it."}
  ]
})









Treatment as the grouping, and the pretest as a placebo






Recall from Differential item functioning: in a randomized trial, treatment assignment is a grouping too. Among children with the same total, the vocabulary item expedition was far easier for treated children, and DIF by treatment is variation in the treatment effect from item to item.



After a bereavement we can’t separate change in the person from change in the measure, since who is bereaved isn’t random. A randomized trial removes the problem. At the pretest, treated and control respondents come from the same population, so there is no impact and, since the program hasn’t happened yet, no reason for any item to work differently. Any treatment DIF found then is a false positive, and the pretest becomes a placebo test for the whole analysis, from the handling of waves to the matching score. At the posttest the arms differ only by assignment, so an item that works differently for treated respondents does so because of the treatment (Gilbert, Kim & Miratrix, 2023; Ahmed et al., 2025).
What the treatment causes is still relative. If the program raised every item by the same amount, the matched comparison would find nothing: that is impact, the average effect. Treatment DIF is each item’s departure from the average.

Try it: the pretest as a placebo
A simulated trial: respondents in each arm answer the same Rasch items twice. At the pretest nobody has been treated. At the posttest everyone has grown by 0.5 logits, treated respondents by a further 0.5 on average, and each item’s effect departs from that average with the spread you set. Each dot is an item’s Mantel–Haenszel delta by treatment (positive: easier for treated respondents with the same total), orange when \(p < .05\).


Code
viewof pl_n = Inputs.range([50, 500], {value: 200, step: 50, label: "Respondents per arm"})
viewof pl_items = Inputs.range([10, 60], {value: 30, step: 5, label: "Items"})
viewof pl_sz = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of item effects (logits)"})
viewof pl_seed = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Sample"})
































Code
pl = placeboTrial({seed: pl_seed, nPer: pl_n, nItems: pl_items, beta1: 0.5, sigmaZeta: pl_sz})
{
  const rows = [...pl.pre.map(d => ({...d, wave: "pretest"})), ...pl.post.map(d => ({...d, wave: "posttest"}))];
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Item", tickFormat: d => d + 1, ticks: []}, y: {label: "MH delta by treatment"},
    fx: {label: null, domain: ["pretest", "posttest"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
      Plot.ruleY([-1, 1], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "item", y: "delta", fx: "wave", r: 4, fill: d => (d.p < 0.05 ? palette.contrast : palette.main)})
    ]
  });
}


















Code
md`Pretest: **${pl.pre.filter(d => d.p < 0.05).length}** of ${pl_items} items significant at .05 (chance alone would give about ${(0.05 * pl_items).toFixed(1)}). Posttest: **${pl.post.filter(d => d.p < 0.05).length}** of ${pl_items}.`







Step through the samples: the pretest flags hover around what chance allows, while the posttest, with the spread at 0.5, flags about a third of the items. Now set the spread to 0. Every item moves by the same amount and the posttest looks like the pretest again: a treatment that lifts all items equally shows up as impact, not DIF.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A trial's pretest has 40 items. Checked for treatment DIF at $\\alpha = .05$, 11 are flagged. What does that suggest?",
  options: [
    {text: "Something outside the program: about 2 flags are expected, so check randomization, the data (are the waves what you think?) and the matching score", correct: true, why: "Before treatment the arms come from the same population and no item can respond to a program that hasn't happened. Eleven flags, against about 2 expected, point to a problem in the design or the analysis."},
    {text: "The program works on those 11 items", correct: false, why: "At the pretest the program hasn't happened yet. Whatever produced the flags, it wasn't the treatment."},
    {text: "Nothing unusual; with 40 items some DIF is expected", correct: false, why: "Some is: about $40 \\times .05 = 2$. Eleven is well beyond that, which is what makes the pretest useful as a placebo."}
  ]
})










A treatment effect for every item
Rather than test items one at a time, we can model the variation. The IL-HTE model (Gilbert, Kim & Miratrix, 2023; Gilbert, Himmelsbach, Soland, Joshi & Domingue, 2025) is the Rasch model with persons and items both random (De Boeck & Wilson, 2004) and a random item slope on treatment, \(T_j\): \[\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) &= \theta_j - b_i + \zeta_i T_j,\\
\theta_j &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_j + \varepsilon_j, \qquad \varepsilon_j \sim N(0, \sigma_\theta^2),\\
\begin{pmatrix} b_i \\ \zeta_i \end{pmatrix} &\sim N\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_b^2 & \rho\sigma_b\sigma_\zeta \\ \rho\sigma_b\sigma_\zeta & \sigma_\zeta^2 \end{pmatrix}\right).
\end{aligned}\] \(\beta_1\) is the average effect on \(\theta\); item \(i\)’s effect is \(\beta_1 + \zeta_i\). \(\sigma_\zeta\) is the spread of item effects around the average. At zero every item moves by \(\beta_1\), which is what a Rasch model fitted to both arms assumes: treatment changes \(\theta\) and nothing else. \(\rho\) says whether harder items (positive) or easier items (negative) move more. Dividing \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma_\zeta\) by \(\sigma_\theta\) puts them in standard deviations of ability.
It is a generalized linear mixed model, so lme4 fits it (Bates, Mächler, Bolker & Walker, 2015; De Boeck et al., 2011):
glmer(resp ~ treat + (1 | id) + (treat | item), data, family = binomial)
lme4’s item intercept is an easiness, \(-b_i\), so the correlation it prints is \(-\rho\). Is \(\sigma_\zeta\) zero? Compare this model with one that has (1 | item) by a likelihood ratio. A variance can’t be negative, so the null value sits on the boundary of the parameter space, and halving the \(\chi^2\) \(p\)-value is the usual correction (Self & Liang, 1987).

Try it: item effects around an average
Twenty items with difficulties spread around the average respondent. Set the average effect \(\beta_1\), the spread \(\sigma_\zeta\) and the correlation \(\rho\) between difficulty and effect. The five items that respond most are orange.


Code
viewof ie_b1 = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Average effect β₁ (logits)"})
viewof ie_sz = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of item effects (logits)"})
viewof ie_rho = Inputs.range([-0.9, 0.9], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Correlation ρ (difficulty, effect)"})

























Code
ie = {
  const {b, zeta} = itemEffects({nItems: 20, sigmaZeta: ie_sz, rho: ie_rho});
  const eff = zeta.map(z => ie_b1 + z);
  const order = eff.map((e, i) => i).sort((i, j) => eff[j] - eff[i]);
  const avg = (ix) => ix.reduce((u, i) => u + eff[i], 0) / ix.length;
  const ec = expectedCorrect(b, zeta, ie_b1);
  return {items: b.map((bi, i) => ({b: bi, effect: eff[i], top: ie_sz > 0 && order.slice(0, 5).includes(i)})),
          top: avg(order.slice(0, 5)), bottom: avg(order.slice(-5)),
          pp: 100 * ec.reduce((u, d) => u + d.treated - d.control, 0) / ec.length};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 270, x: {label: "Item difficulty b (logits)", domain: [-2.2, 2.2]},
  y: {label: "Item's treatment effect (logits)", domain: [-2, 3]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.ruleY([ie_b1], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot(ie.items, {x: "b", y: "effect", r: 5, fill: d => (d.top ? palette.contrast : palette.main)})
  ]
})


















Code
md`Average item effect over all 20 items: **${ie_b1.toFixed(2)}** logits; over the 5 that respond most, **${ie.top.toFixed(2)}**; over the 5 that respond least, **${ie.bottom.toFixed(2)}**. On the expected proportion correct over all 20 items, the effect is **${ie.pp.toFixed(1)}** percentage points.`







With \(\sigma_\zeta\) at 0 every dot sits on the dashed line, and a test built from any five items would show the same effect in logits. At the default, the five most responsive items average more than twice the overall effect and the five least about zero: two short forms of one test, one program, two conclusions. Move \(\rho\) to −0.8 and the orange dots move left, among the easy items.



What item-level effects do to the estimate
Does the spread change the average? Not by itself: the sum score, a constant-effect model and the IL-HTE model estimate much the same average, as the fractions trial below shows. It changes three other things.
Precision. The items are a sample from those that could have been written, and if they respond unequally, a different sample would give a different average. Treating the items as fixed leaves that variation out, which understates standard errors and inflates false positives (Gilbert, Kim & Miratrix, 2023). Across 15 trials, Ahmed et al. (2025) found one item driving nearly 40% of an effect, and item-level patterns that could make 31% of the significant effects null once counted as uncertainty.
Generalizability. \(\sigma_\zeta\) says how far the effect on a fresh set of items from the same domain could fall from the one observed. A claim about the construct, rather than about these items, needs it (Gilbert, Himmelsbach, et al., 2025).






Recall from Validity as an argument: an interpretation/use argument has a generalization link, from the observed score to the score over all the tasks it stands for. \(\sigma_\zeta\) is evidence on that link for an effect rather than a score.



Interactions. Trialists ask who benefits most by interacting treatment with a pretest. Suppose every respondent gains the same amount on \(\theta\), but easier items respond more. In the treated arm the items’ effective difficulties, \(b_i - \zeta_i\), are more spread out than in the control arm, the sum score rises less steeply with \(\theta\), and a sum-score regression finds a negative treatment-by-pretest interaction that no respondent has. From sum scores alone the two stories can’t be told apart; item-level data can tell them apart (Gilbert, Miratrix, Joshi & Domingue, 2025).

Try it: an interaction nobody has
Treatment adds 0.5 logits to every respondent’s \(\theta\), whatever their pretest; the 20 items’ effects have the spread and correlation you set. The curves are the expected sum score at each pretest level in each arm, computed from the model, so there is no sampling noise.


Code
viewof si_sz = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.8, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of item effects (logits)"})
viewof si_rho = Inputs.range([-0.9, 0.9], {value: -0.8, step: 0.1, label: "Correlation ρ (difficulty, effect)"})


















Code
si = spuriousInteraction({...itemEffects({nItems: 20, sigmaZeta: si_sz, rho: si_rho}), beta1: 0.5})
si0 = spuriousInteraction({...itemEffects({nItems: 20, sigmaZeta: 0, rho: 0}), beta1: 0.5})
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 270, x: {label: "Pretest (SDs)"}, y: {label: "Expected sum score (of 20)", domain: [0, 20]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["control", "treated"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(si.rows.map(d => ({...d, arm: d.T ? "treated" : "control"})), {x: "pre", y: "s", stroke: "arm", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})

























Code
md`Slope on the pretest: control **${si.control.slope.toFixed(2)}**, treated **${si.treated.slope.toFixed(2)}** points per SD. Treatment-by-pretest interaction: **${si.interaction.toFixed(2)}**; with every item moving equally it would be ${si0.interaction.toFixed(2)}.`







With every item moving equally the interaction is already slightly negative, from the sum score’s bounded range. At the default, where easier items move more, it is five times that, with no heterogeneity among respondents at all. Set \(\rho\) to +0.8 and it changes sign.






NoteGo deeper: why the interaction appears





Assumptions: the IL-HTE model above; no person-level heterogeneity (every respondent’s \(\theta\) rises by \(\beta_1\)); the outcome analysed is the sum score \(S = \sum_i x_i\).
Two tests in one. In the control arm item \(i\) has difficulty \(b_i\). In the treated arm it behaves as if its difficulty were \(b_i - \zeta_i\), on top of the shift of \(\beta_1\) in \(\theta\). The spread of effective difficulties in the treated arm is \[\text{Var}(b_i - \zeta_i) = \sigma_b^2 + \sigma_\zeta^2 - 2\rho\sigma_b\sigma_\zeta,\] which exceeds \(\sigma_b^2\) whenever \(\rho \le 0\), and can fall below it when \(\rho\) is positive and large enough.
What spread does to the sum score. The expected sum score is the test characteristic curve, \(E(S \mid \theta) = \sum_i P_i(\theta)\) with \(P_i(\theta) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\theta - b_i)\). Its slope at \(\theta\) is \(\sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)\), the test information under the Rasch model. An item near \(\theta\) contributes close to the maximum of 1/4; spreading the items out moves some of them where they contribute little. So in the middle of the ability range the treated arm’s curve is flatter when \(\rho < 0\).
The interaction. A regression of \(S\) on treatment, pretest and their product estimates the slope of \(S\) on the pretest in each arm. The pretest predicts \(\theta\) equally well in both arms, but the treated arm’s flatter curve turns a unit of \(\theta\) into fewer points, so its slope is smaller and the interaction is negative, although every respondent gained the same. Gilbert, Miratrix, Joshi and Domingue (2025) show analytically and by simulation that a sum score cannot distinguish this from a true interaction, and that a model with item-specific effects can. The bounded range of \(S\) adds a smaller effect of its own, which is why the widget’s interaction is not quite zero when \(\sigma_\zeta = 0\).





Code
quiz({
  q: "An IL-HTE model gives an average effect of 0.40 SD and $\\sigma_\\zeta$ = 0.50 SD on a 10-item outcome. A colleague plans to replicate with 10 different items written to the same blueprint. What should she expect?",
  options: [
    {text: "An average effect that could differ noticeably from 0.40, since items respond unequally and hers are a new sample", correct: true, why: "The mean of 10 new item effects varies around the true average with an SD of roughly $0.50/\\sqrt{10} \\approx 0.16$ SD, before any sampling of respondents. That is the generalizability question $\\sigma_\\zeta$ answers."},
    {text: "0.40 again, up to sampling error in respondents", correct: false, why: "That holds only if every item responds alike ($\\sigma_\\zeta = 0$). With a spread of 0.50 SD, which items she writes matters too."},
    {text: "An effect about 0.50 SD larger", correct: false, why: "$\\sigma_\\zeta$ is a spread around the average, not a shift. Her items' average effect is as likely to fall below 0.40 as above it."}
  ]
})










Bias, or what the program taught?
Is an item that moves most a biased item? It may be the item closest to what an intervention taught. For evaluating the intervention, that can be the signal: the program changed what it set out to change, and the near items show it. For a claim of general gain, it is a threat: a test made mostly of near items overstates transfer, in the sense of Barnett and Ceci’s (2002) taxonomy of near and far transfer. Whether item-level heterogeneity is bias depends on the interpretation and the use, as Validity as an argument would lead you to expect. Group-specific item parameters can also be judged by prediction: do they predict new responses better than shared ones? The InterModel Vigorish measures that (Domingue et al., 2024). Explaining which items move, with features such as alignment to the curriculum, is a job for What is an item?.

title: Measurement invariance under treatment and life events
text:
Simulate
The code simulates a trial with 800 respondents and 20 items. Treatment raises every respondent’s \(\theta\) by 0.5, whatever their pretest; the items’ departures have \(\sigma_\zeta = 0.8\) and \(\rho = -0.8\) (easier items move more). It fits a sum-score regression, a constant-effect model and the IL-HTE model, each with treatment, pretest and their product. Loading lme4 takes 10 to 20 seconds the first time the page runs code; the fits take a few seconds more.
With the seed as written, the IL-HTE model recovers \(\sigma_\zeta\) = 0.78 and \(\rho\) = −0.78, and its item effects correlate 0.99 with the true ones. The interaction, 0 in truth, is −0.08 SD in the sum-score regression and −0.10 logits in the constant-effect model; the IL-HTE model puts it at 0.04. Its standard error is about 0.06 in both models, so a single run is noisy: try other seeds. Set rho <- 0.8 and the constant-effect interaction turns positive (0.03); set sigma_zeta <- 0 and the three models agree.

title: Measurement invariance under treatment and life events
text:
With real data
Download the code; it needs lme4, and the model fits take about a minute.

A fractions trial, before and after
Our main table is gilbert_meta_20, from a randomized trial of a small-group fractions intervention for fifth graders performing well below grade level (Jayanthi et al., 2021; data at doi:10.7910/DVN/Z4WMFE), part of the trial collection of Gilbert, Himmelsbach, et al. (2025). Its job is to be a trial with a pretest, so the placebo check is real. Students who scored between the 15th and 37th percentiles on a fractions screener were randomized within teacher, and the table holds the final analytic sample of 186 (data description). Items are scored 1 for correct.

# The IRW table, from the CSV link on its landing page (pinned to one version).

f20 <- f20[!is.na(f20$resp), ]
# Waves: 0 = pretest, 1 = posttest. How many items and students in each?

                                            students = length(unique(x$id)))))

On waves: wave 0 is the pretest and wave 1 the posttest. The posttest repeats all 37 pretest items (26 from the fourth-grade Test for Understanding of Fractions, tuf4, and 11 fractions procedures) and adds 56: the fifth-grade form (tuf5), more procedures, and a block the dataset labels TransMath (trans_math). Eighteen posttest responses are missing, all from one student, who drops out of the complete-case analyses.
We match on the total score and test uniform DIF, the kind a shift in one item’s treatment effect produces, with the logistic regression of the DIF lesson (Swaminathan & Rogers, 1990). With 37 or 93 tests, we also control the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), and give the \(\Delta R^2\) categories of Jodoin and Gierl (2001).


Code
# One wide matrix per wave: a row per student, a column per item (1 = correct).
wide <- function(long, items) {
  x <- long[long$item %in% items, ]
  A <- tapply(x$resp, list(x$id, x$item), function(v) v[1])
  A <- A[complete.cases(A), items]
  list(X = A, treat = kids20$treat[match(rownames(A), kids20$id)])
}
# Logistic-regression DIF for one item, matching on the total score, as in the DIF
# lesson but for uniform DIF only, the kind a shift in one item's treatment effect
# produces: the 1-df likelihood-ratio test of M0 (total) against M1 (total and
# treatment), and the change in Nagelkerke's R^2 between them.
nagelkerke <- function(m, ll0, n) {
  cs <- 1 - exp(2 * (ll0 - as.numeric(logLik(m))) / n)
  cs / (1 - exp(2 * ll0 / n))
}
lr_item <- function(y, g, total) {
  d <- data.frame(y = y, g = g, total = total)
  ll0 <- as.numeric(logLik(glm(y ~ 1, binomial, d)))
  m0 <- glm(y ~ total, binomial, d)
  m1 <- glm(y ~ total + g, binomial, d)
  c(beta_treat = unname(coef(m1)["g"]),
    p = anova(m0, m1, test = "LRT")[2, "Pr(>Chi)"],
    dR2 = nagelkerke(m1, ll0, nrow(d)) - nagelkerke(m0, ll0, nrow(d)))
}
# Every item; p-values also after the Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate
# correction; Jodoin-Gierl categories (A below .035, B to .07, C above, and A
# whenever the test is not significant).
treatment_dif <- function(W) {
  tot <- rowSums(W$X)
  out <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(colnames(W$X), function(i) lr_item(W$X[, i], W$treat, tot))))
  out$p_BH <- p.adjust(out$p, "BH")
  out$jg <- ifelse(out$p >= 0.05 | out$dR2 < 0.035, "A", ifelse(out$dR2 < 0.07, "B", "C"))
  out
}
count_flags <- function(r) c(items = nrow(r), p_below_05 = sum(r$p < 0.05),
                             expected_by_chance = round(0.05 * nrow(r), 1),
                             after_BH = sum(r$p_BH < 0.05), B = sum(r$jg == "B"), C = sum(r$jg == "C"))


The pretest is also our sanity table: before treatment, its flags estimate the false-positive rate. It has 3 flags at .05 among 37 items, about what chance allows, and none survives the correction (the table below).

Most items that favour treated students come from the procedures and TransMath blocks; several from the understanding tests (tuf4, tuf5) go the other way, moved less than the rest of the test.
The IL-HTE model summarizes all of this in a few numbers:


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(lme4))
# The IL-HTE model (Gilbert, Kim & Miratrix, 2023), in lme4's parameterization:
#   logit P(x_ij = 1) = beta0 + beta1 T_j + theta_j + e_i + zeta_i T_j,
# with theta_j ~ N(0, s_theta^2) and (e_i, zeta_i) bivariate normal. lme4's item
# intercept e_i is an easiness, the negative of the lesson's difficulty b_i, so the
# correlation it reports has the opposite sign to rho in the lesson; we flip it.
# Following the IRW vignette, effects are standardized by s_theta from the model with
# a constant effect, and sigma_zeta is tested by a likelihood-ratio test against
# that model, halving the p-value because a variance of zero sits on the boundary
# (Self & Liang, 1987).
ilhte <- function(long) {
  m0 <- glmer(resp ~ treat + (1 | id) + (1 | item), long, family = binomial)
  m1 <- glmer(resp ~ treat + (1 | id) + (treat | item), long, family = binomial)
  s_theta <- sqrt(VarCorr(m0)$id[1])
  vc <- VarCorr(m1)$item
  lr <- as.numeric(2 * (logLik(m1) - logLik(m0)))
  list(m0 = m0, m1 = m1, s_theta = s_theta,
       summary = c(students = length(unique(long$id)), items = length(unique(long$item)),
                   effect_constant_SD = unname(fixef(m0)["treat"]) / s_theta,
                   effect_average_SD = unname(fixef(m1)["treat"]) / s_theta,
                   sigma_zeta_SD = sqrt(vc[2, 2]) / s_theta,
                   rho_difficulty = -attr(vc, "correlation")[1, 2],
                   LR = lr, p = 0.5 * pchisq(lr, 2, lower.tail = FALSE)))
}

Health knowledge in India

The average effect is 0.48 SD and \(\sigma_\zeta\) is 0.28 SD (\(p\) = 0.00019), a much smaller spread than in the fractions trial. The three items that moved most are the three about night blindness (0.68 to 0.81 logits), the subject of one of the programme’s five modules: a single film about a boy who can’t see at dusk (Supplementary Material A). The paper’s own results by topic agree: night blindness had the largest effect of the four topics, and the lowest knowledge in the control arm (Carpena, 2024, longer-term knowledge by topic). Knowing to wash hands before cooking and knowing that condoms prevent pregnancy moved least (0.17 and 0.12 logits). \(\rho\) = 0.33: harder items moved somewhat more.


Code
# Who gains most? The treatment-by-baseline interaction, with a constant effect for
# every item and with IL-HTE (std_baseline: the IRW's standardized baseline score).
mB <- glmer(resp ~ treat * std_baseline + (1 | item) + (1 | id), f37, family = binomial)
mC <- glmer(resp ~ treat * std_baseline + (treat | item) + (1 | id), f37, family = binomial)
round(rbind(constant_items = summary(mB)$coef["treat:std_baseline", 1:2],
            ilhte = summary(mC)$coef["treat:std_baseline", 1:2]), 3)


               Estimate Std. Error
constant_items    0.024      0.065
ilhte             0.020      0.066


Does IL-HTE change the answer to “who gained most?” here? Barely: the treatment-by-baseline interaction is 0.024 logits with a constant effect for every item and 0.020 with IL-HTE, both well inside their standard errors. With a spread of 0.28 SD, against 0.70 in the fractions trial, and a moderate \(\rho\), there is little for the constant-effect model to misread.
What should a trialist take from this? Two positions rest on different assumptions. If the outcome’s items are the target (the state test a program will be judged on), the average over these items is the estimand, and the sum score answers it. If the items stand for a domain (fractions, health knowledge), the effect on the domain is the estimand, and the spread of item effects is part of its uncertainty. My practice, when a trial’s outcome comes with item-level data, is to fit the IL-HTE model beside the sum-score analysis, report \(\sigma_\zeta\) next to the average effect, and use the pretest as a placebo when there is one. In the fractions trial that means reporting an effect of about 1.1 SD together with the fact that items on the same test moved by amounts more than a standard deviation apart. An average effect is a claim about items as well as people.

title: Measurement invariance under treatment and life events
text:
Problems

Raw effects and difficulty. Under the IL-HTE model with every \(\zeta_i = 0\), and \(\theta \sim N(0, 1)\) in control and \(N(\beta_1, 1)\) in the treated arm, write the effect on item \(i\)’s expected proportion correct as a function of \(b_i\). Show that it is largest for items near the average ability and small for very easy or very hard items. Why, then, can raw differences in proportion correct and item effects on the logit scale rank the items differently, and which would you use to say which items a program moved?
How much do the flagged items carry? (PS5#4). In gilbert_meta_20 at the posttest, drop the 10 items in B or C and re-estimate the effect on the sum score and on \(\theta\). How much of the effect did they carry? Now drop instead the 10 items with the smallest estimated IL-HTE effects. Which short form would a program developer prefer, and which would you report?
The interaction, with and without item slopes (PS7#1). In gilbert_meta_37, estimate the treatment-by-baseline interaction on the sum score, with a constant-effect model and with IL-HTE. From the IL-HTE fit, compute the SD of the items’ effective difficulties in each arm. Using the Go deeper, explain why the three estimates are so close here.
Bereavement. After spousal loss, the CES-D items on loneliness and sadness carry most of the rise in symptoms (Domingue et al., 2019). Set out what you would have to assume to report “depression rose”, and what you would have to assume to report “the CES-D measured something different”. Given item-level data from waves before and after the loss, which model would you fit, and what result would lead you to each report?
Near and far. You are designing the outcome measure for a vocabulary intervention that teaches 40 words. Design a test that can separate near transfer (taught words) from far transfer (untaught words of similar frequency), and say how you would model item-level effects so that the two can be compared. What would you report if the near items moved and the far items didn’t?
Challenge: evidence for or against? Suppose the items that move most in a trial are exactly those most aligned with the intervention’s content. Is item-level heterogeneity then evidence against the measure’s validity for evaluating the intervention, evidence for it, or neither? Does your answer change if the same test is also used to report students’ general proficiency? This one is open.

title: Information, precision, and short forms
text:
What this is for
How precise is a score? Classical test theory gives one answer for everyone, yet a test measures well where its items are and poorly where they aren’t, so a respondent in the middle of a well-built test and one far above it get very different precision from the same items. Item response models put this in numbers. The curvature of a respondent’s likelihood becomes information, information adds up across items, and one over its square root is a standard error that changes along the scale. This lesson builds that machinery for the Rasch model, the 2PL and the 3PL, then uses it for two jobs: seeing where a real test is precise, and choosing a few items that are precise where a decision is made.

title: Information, precision, and short forms
Information, precision, and short forms
text:
Core ideas

Information is the curvature of the likelihood






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: a sharper peak in the log likelihood means a more precise estimate. The negative of the second derivative at the peak is the Fisher information, and one over its square root is the standard error. Observations with a probability near 0 or 1 add almost nothing, because each contributes a term \(p(1-p)\).



Nothing in that argument was specific to coins. Take one respondent, hold the item parameters fixed, and treat \(\theta\) as the unknown: the observations are that respondent’s answers, and the log likelihood for \(\theta\) is a sum over items (Birnbaum, 1968; Lord, 1980). Its curvature says how sure we can be about this respondent’s \(\theta\). The general formula for that curvature, the information function, is in the Go deeper callout below; the rest of the lesson uses its special cases, one model at a time. What makes it sharper: more items, or better-placed ones?






NoteGo deeper: the information function in general





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; the item parameters are known; \(P_i(\theta) = \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\) is a smooth function of \(\theta\), with derivative \(P_i'(\theta)\); responses are locally independent given \(\theta\). No particular item model is assumed until the last step.
Definition. The log likelihood for \(\theta\) is \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_i \big[x_i \log P_i + (1 - x_i)\log(1 - P_i)\big]\), a sum because local independence makes the probability of the pattern a product. Its derivative, the score, is \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i \frac{P_i'\,(x_i - P_i)}{P_i(1 - P_i)}.\] The Fisher information for \(\theta\) is the expected negative second derivative of \(\ell\), which equals the variance of the score (Fisher, 1925): \[I(\theta) = -\,E\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta^2}\right] = \text{Var}\!\left[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta}\right].\]
One item. Each term of the score has mean 0, and \(x_i\) has variance \(P_i(1 - P_i)\), so \[I_i(\theta) = \frac{P_i'(\theta)^2}{P_i(\theta)\,\big(1 - P_i(\theta)\big)}.\] The test. Under local independence the terms are independent, so their variances add: \(I(\theta) = \sum_i I_i(\theta)\) (Birnbaum, 1968; Lord, 1980). If two items share something beyond \(\theta\) (a reading passage, say), their terms are positively correlated and the sum overstates what the pair tells us (Sireci, Thissen & Wainer, 1991, show the same problem in reliability).
The special cases. Only \(P_i'\) changes from model to model.

Rasch: \(P' = P(1 - P)\), so \(I_i = P(1-P)\), a Bernoulli variance, at most \(1/4\), at \(\theta = b\).
2PL: \(P' = aP(1 - P)\), so \(I_i = a^2P(1-P)\). The score is \(\sum_i a_i(x_i - P_i)\), the weighted score minus its expectation, and its second derivative contains no \(x_i\), so the observed curvature equals the expected information: a test has one information curve, drawn before anyone takes it.
3PL: \(P = c + (1 - c)L\) with \(L = \text{logit}^{-1}(a(\theta - b))\), so \(P' = a(P - c)(1 - P)/(1 - c)\) and \(I_i = a^2\frac{(P - c)^2}{(1 - c)^2}\frac{1 - P}{P}\). Here the observed curvature depends on the responses, and this is the expected information.

The standard error \(1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}\) is a large-sample approximation, as it was for the coin; with few items, or near the ends of the scale, it can mislead, and the simulation below shows where.




Try it: one respondent’s likelihood
A respondent with true ability \(\theta\) answers Rasch items whose difficulties are spread (SD 1) around a centre you choose. The curve is the log likelihood for \(\theta\), shifted so its peak sits at 0.


Code
viewof rl_n = Inputs.range([3, 60], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Number of items"})
viewof rl_center = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Where the items sit (mean b)"})
viewof rl_theta = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Respondent's true θ"})

























Code
rl_u = { const r = rng(36); return Array.from({length: 60}, () => r.unif()); }
rl_b = normalQuantiles(rl_n, rl_center, 1)
rl_x = rl_b.map((b, i) => rl_u[i] < p2pl(rl_theta, b) ? 1 : 0)
rl_r = rl_x.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0)
rl_mle = raschMle(rl_x, rl_b)
rl_top = Number.isFinite(rl_mle) ? raschLoglik(rl_mle, rl_x, rl_b) : Math.max(...grid(-5, 5, 201).map(t => raschLoglik(t, rl_x, rl_b)))
rl_curve = grid(-5, 5, 401).map(t => ({theta: t, ll: raschLoglik(t, rl_x, rl_b) - rl_top})).filter(d => d.ll > -6)
rl_info = Number.isFinite(rl_mle) ? testInfo(rl_mle, rl_b.map(b => ({b}))) : NaN
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Candidate θ", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: "Log likelihood (peak at 0)", domain: [-6, 0.3]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([-0.5], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([rl_theta], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.ruleX(rl_b, {x: d => d, y1: -6, y2: -5.6, stroke: palette.contrast}),
    Plot.line(rl_curve, {x: "theta", y: "ll", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    ...(Number.isFinite(rl_mle) ? [Plot.dot([{theta: rl_mle, ll: 0}], {x: "theta", y: "ll", r: 5, fill: palette.main})] : [])
  ]
})



































































Code
md`${rl_r} of ${rl_n} correct. ${Number.isFinite(rl_mle) ?
  `The maximum-likelihood estimate is **${rl_mle.toFixed(2)}** (true θ ${rl_theta.toFixed(1)}, grey line). The information there is ${rl_info.toFixed(2)}, so the standard error is 1 / √${rl_info.toFixed(2)} = **${(1 / Math.sqrt(rl_info)).toFixed(2)}**. The curve falls by one half (dashed line) about one standard error either side of the peak.` :
  `With ${rl_r === 0 ? "no item right" : "every item right"}, the likelihood keeps rising toward ${rl_r === 0 ? "−∞" : "+∞"}: there is no finite maximum, and no standard error.`} Item difficulties are the ticks along the bottom.`







At the defaults this respondent gets 3 of 10 right, and the estimate, −1.01, lands two standard errors (0.75 each) below the true 0.5. With 40 items the curve narrows: the estimate is 0.49 and the standard error 0.35, about half, as four times the items should give. Put 10 items far above the respondent (mean \(b\) = 3) and nothing is right: the curve never turns over, which is a problem for Estimating abilities.



Item information for the Rasch model, the 2PL and the 3PL
Each item adds one term to the curvature. Under the Rasch model that term is \[I_i(\theta) = P_i(\theta)\,\big(1 - P_i(\theta)\big),\] the variance of a single 0/1 response. It is largest, 1/4, where \(P_i = 1/2\), which under the Rasch model is at \(\theta = b_i\), and it fades on either side: a respondent far above or below an item almost always gives the answer we’d have predicted, and a predictable answer carries little news. The Go deeper callout above gives the general formula it comes from.
The 2PL multiplies it by the squared slope, \[I_i(\theta) = a_i^2\,P_i(\theta)\,\big(1 - P_i(\theta)\big),\] so an item with \(a = 2\) carries four times the information of a Rasch item at its peak, over a narrower band.






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL: under the 2PL the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) is sufficient for \(\theta\), so a correct answer counts in proportion to its item’s slope. The score equation was \(\partial\ell/\partial\theta = \sum_i a_i (x_i - P_i)\).



Information is where that weighting shows up in precision. Each term of the score equation is \(a_i\) times a Bernoulli residual, so its variance is \(a_i^2 P_i(1-P_i)\): the item’s weight, squared, times the Bernoulli variance. Items that count for more in the score also tell us more about \(\theta\), and an item with a slope near zero tells us almost nothing wherever it sits.
The 3PL adds a lower asymptote \(c\), and the information (the expected information; see the callout above) becomes \[I_i(\theta) = a_i^2\,\frac{\big(P_i - c_i\big)^2}{(1 - c_i)^2}\,\frac{1 - P_i}{P_i}.\] With \(c > 0\) it falls, most of all below the item’s difficulty, where a correct answer may be a guess and so says less about \(\theta\); the peak moves above \(b\) (problem 1 finds by how much). What fixing \(c\) or giving it a prior does to information at the bottom of the scale is for Guessing and priors.

Try it: an item’s information curve


Code
viewof ii_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof ii_a = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a"})
viewof ii_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "Lower asymptote c"})

























Code
ii_th = grid(-4, 4, 401)
ii_curve = ii_th.map(t => ({theta: t, p: p4pl(t, ii_b, ii_a, ii_c), info: itemInfo(t, ii_b, ii_a, ii_c), rasch: itemInfo(t, ii_b)}))
ii_peak = ii_curve.reduce((m, d) => d.info > m.info ? d : m)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 190, x: {label: null, domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([ii_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(ii_curve, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})
































Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 240, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Item information", domain: [0, Math.max(0.3, ii_peak.info * 1.1)]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["This item", "Rasch item with the same b"], range: [palette.main, palette.light]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([ii_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(ii_curve, {x: "theta", y: "rasch", stroke: () => "Rasch item with the same b", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5,3"}),
    Plot.line(ii_curve, {x: "theta", y: "info", stroke: () => "This item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([ii_peak], {x: "theta", y: "info", r: 5, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})









Code
md`Information peaks at θ = **${ii_peak.theta.toFixed(2)}** (b = ${ii_b.toFixed(1)}), at a height of **${ii_peak.info.toFixed(3)}**. A Rasch item peaks at its difficulty, at 0.25.`







Raise the slope to 2 and the peak rises to 1.000, four times the Rasch item’s, over a narrower range; at 0.5 it falls to 0.063. With \(a = 1\) and \(c = 0.25\) the peak drops to 0.155 and moves up to 0.31, and the left side sinks further than the right.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A 2PL item has $a = 2$ and $b = 1$. Where is its information largest, and how large is it?",
  options: [
    {text: "At $\\theta = 1$, where it is 1", correct: true, why: "A 2PL item's information $a^2P(1-P)$ peaks where $P = 1/2$, at $\\theta = b = 1$, and there it is $a^2/4 = 4/4 = 1$."},
    {text: "At $\\theta = 1$, where it is 0.25", correct: false, why: "0.25 is the Rasch item's peak. The slope enters squared, so $a = 2$ multiplies it by 4."},
    {text: "At $\\theta = 1$, where it is 0.5", correct: false, why: "That would be $a/4$. Information goes with $a^2$, as the weight in the score equation does when you take its variance."},
    {text: "Above $\\theta = 1$, because steep items favour stronger respondents", correct: false, why: "Without a lower asymptote the curve is symmetric about $b$, and so is its information. It is $c > 0$ that moves the peak above $b$."}
  ]
})










Information adds; precision follows
Local independence lets item information add: the test information is \[I(\theta) = \sum_i I_i(\theta),\] and the conditional standard error of measurement (CSEM) at \(\theta\) is \[SE(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{I(\theta)}}.\]






Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: the standard error of measurement, \(\sigma_E = \sigma_X\sqrt{1 - \rho_{XX'}}\), is the typical distance between a respondent’s observed and true scores, and CTT gives the same one to everyone, whatever their score.



The CSEM replaces that one number with a curve, low where many informative items sit and rising where they run out, which need not be at the extremes of the respondents. Samejima (1977) argued for this standard error, rather than reliability, as the index of how dependable a score is, and Kolen, Zeng and Hanson (1996) carry it to a reported score scale. The standard error of one respondent’s estimate evaluates the CSEM at their \(\hat\theta\): Estimating abilities picks up there.

Try it: build a test
Choose how many items, where they sit and how steep they are. The curve is the CSEM; the shading is where respondents are (a standard normal). The dashed line is the one SEM this test would get if its error variance were averaged over those respondents, CTT style.


Code
viewof bt_n = Inputs.range([5, 80], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Number of items"})
viewof bt_mean = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean difficulty"})
viewof bt_sd = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Spread of difficulties (SD)"})
viewof bt_a = Inputs.range([0.5, 2.5], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Slope a (every item)"})
































Code
bt_items = normalQuantiles(bt_n, bt_mean, bt_sd).map(b => ({b, a: bt_a}))
bt_th = grid(-4, 4, 401)
bt_se = bt_th.map(t => ({theta: t, se: 1 / Math.sqrt(testInfo(t, bt_items))}))
bt_w = bt_th.map(t => dnorm(t))
bt_one = Math.sqrt(bt_th.reduce((s, t, k) => s + bt_w[k] / testInfo(t, bt_items), 0) / bt_w.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Conditional SEM", domain: [0, 2]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(bt_th.map((t, k) => ({theta: t, d: bt_w[k] / dnorm(0) * 1.2})), {x: "theta", y: "d", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([bt_one], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "5,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX(bt_items, {x: "b", y1: 0, y2: 0.08, stroke: palette.contrast}),
    Plot.line(bt_se.filter(d => d.se <= 2), {x: "theta", y: "se", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})














































Code
md`CSEM at θ = −2: **${(1 / Math.sqrt(testInfo(-2, bt_items))).toFixed(2)}**; at θ = 0: **${(1 / Math.sqrt(testInfo(0, bt_items))).toFixed(2)}**; at θ = 2: **${(1 / Math.sqrt(testInfo(2, bt_items))).toFixed(2)}**. One SEM for everyone: ${bt_one.toFixed(2)}. Item difficulties are the ticks along the bottom.`







At the defaults the CSEM is 0.49 at the centre and 0.66 two SDs out, so the one SEM, 0.53, is too large for the middle and too small at the edges. Forty items shrink every CSEM by \(\sqrt 2\) (0.49 becomes 0.35); doubling the slope instead takes the centre to 0.29. Move the mean difficulty to 1.5 with a spread of 0.3, and the CSEM is 0.47 at \(\theta = 2\) and 1.30 at \(\theta = -2\): the test now measures well where few respondents are.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A test has information 16 at $\\theta = 0$. What is its conditional SEM there, and what would it be if you added a second, identical set of items?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.25, then about 0.18", correct: true, why: "$1/\\sqrt{16} = 0.25$. Doubling the items doubles the information to 32, and $1/\\sqrt{32} \\approx 0.18$: precision improves with the square root."},
    {text: "0.25, then 0.125", correct: false, why: "Doubling the items doubles the information, not its square root. The SEM falls by $\\sqrt 2$, not by 2."},
    {text: "0.0625, then about 0.031", correct: false, why: "That is $1/16$ and $1/32$: the error *variance*. The SEM is its square root."}
  ]
})










Targeting: a test is precise where its items are






Recall from The Rasch model: a Wright map puts respondents and item difficulties on one scale. Where they overlap, the test can tell people apart; where respondents sit beyond every item, it can’t. That lesson handed the idea on by name: precision depends on where you are on the scale.



The test information curve is the Wright map with error bars. Read against the distribution of respondents, it says for whom a test is precise, and the design question turns around: given the respondents we care about, where should the items go? Lord (1977) set out test construction this way: specify the information you need along the scale (a target information function), then add items until their sum reaches it. A test that must rank everyone wants its items spread across the population; a test that makes one pass/fail decision wants them bunched at the cut. What a CSEM means for a reported score, and for respondents near a cut score where information is low, is the subject of What does a score mean?.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A certification exam passes respondents above $\\theta = 1.5$. With 20 Rasch items to spend, which test classifies respondents near the cut most precisely?",
  options: [
    {text: "All 20 items with difficulties near 1.5", correct: true, why: "Each Rasch item's information peaks at its difficulty, so stacking the items at the cut gives the most information there. Try it in the widget above: mean difficulty 1.5, spread near 0."},
    {text: "20 items spread evenly from −2 to 2", correct: false, why: "That test measures everyone moderately well, which is what you want for ranking the whole population, but it spends most of its items where no decision is made."},
    {text: "20 items centred on the mean respondent, θ = 0", correct: false, why: "They are informative for respondents near 0, who are far below the cut and pass or fail without much doubt either way."}
  ]
})









Short forms






Recall from What is measurement?: among the things we want from a measure are that it be calibrated to its task, sometimes covering a wide range and sometimes making fine distinctions near one point, and that it give precise information quickly, with few items.



Information turns “precise quickly” into something we can compute. If a respondent will answer only five items, which five? Information at a target \(\theta\) is a sum over the chosen items, so the best five are the five most informative there, and they may be poor elsewhere. Other costs don’t show in the information curve: a short form covers less of the construct’s content, and its validity has to be checked on its own (Smith, McCarthy & Anderson, 2000). Choosing items one at a time, each the most informative at the current estimate, is adaptive testing: Item banks and adaptive testing.

Try it: pick a five-item form
Here are the 18 items of the financial-literacy test analysed below, with their 2PL slopes and difficulties. Pick five and a target \(\theta\).


Code
sf_labels = flItems.map(d => `${d.item} (a = ${d.a.toFixed(2)}, b = ${d.b.toFixed(2)})`.replaceAll("-", "−"))
viewof sf_pick = Inputs.checkbox(sf_labels, {label: "Your form", value: sf_labels.slice(0, 5)})
viewof sf_target = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: -1, step: 0.1, label: "Target θ"})

























Code
sf_sel = flItems.filter((d, i) => sf_pick.includes(sf_labels[i]))
sf_all5 = combinations(18, 5)
sf_infoT = flItems.map(d => itemInfo(sf_target, d.b, d.a))
sf_sums = sf_all5.map(k => k.reduce((s, i) => s + sf_infoT[i], 0)).sort((x, y) => x - y)
sf_best = sf_infoT.map((v, i) => ({v, i})).sort((x, y) => y.v - x.v).slice(0, 5)
sf_mine = testInfo(sf_target, sf_sel)
sf_th = grid(-4, 4, 321)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Financial literacy θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Test information"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["All 18 items", "Your form", "Best five for the target"], range: [palette.light, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([sf_target], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(sf_th.flatMap(t => [
      {theta: t, I: testInfo(t, flItems), form: "All 18 items"},
      {theta: t, I: testInfo(t, sf_sel), form: "Your form"},
      {theta: t, I: testInfo(t, sf_best.map(d => flItems[d.i])), form: "Best five for the target"}]),
      {x: "theta", y: "I", stroke: "form", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})




























































Code
md`${sf_sel.length === 5 ? "" : `*You have picked ${sf_sel.length} items; the comparison is with five-item forms.* `}At θ = ${sf_target.toFixed(1)}, your form gives information **${sf_mine.toFixed(2)}** (CSEM ${(1 / Math.sqrt(sf_mine)).toFixed(2)}), more than ${(100 * sf_sums.filter(v => v < sf_mine).length / sf_sums.length).toFixed(0)}% of all ${sf_sums.length.toLocaleString()} five-item forms. The median form gives ${sf_sums[Math.floor(sf_sums.length / 2)].toFixed(2)}; the best five (${sf_best.map(d => flItems[d.i].item).join(", ")}) give **${sf_best.reduce((s, d) => s + d.v, 0).toFixed(2)}** (CSEM ${(1 / Math.sqrt(sf_best.reduce((s, d) => s + d.v, 0))).toFixed(2)}); all 18 items give ${testInfo(sf_target, flItems).toFixed(2)}.`







The default form (the first five items) gives 1.72 at \(\theta = -1\), more than 35% of the possible forms. The best five give 4.18, more than half the full test’s 7.25. Move the target to 1.5 and the best five change completely (to FL_10, FL_5, FL_4, FL_17 and FL_11), while the whole test reaches only 1.55: there aren’t enough hard items to make this test precise for its strongest respondents.

title: Information, precision, and short forms
text:
Simulate
Does \(1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}\) describe how far estimates actually fall from the truth? The code below simulates Rasch responses from 4,000 respondents spread evenly from \(\theta = -3\) to 3, estimates each \(\theta\) by maximum likelihood with the difficulties treated as known, and compares the SD of \(\hat\theta - \theta\) within bins of true \(\theta\) with the CSEM. It is base R and runs in a second or two.
With the seed as written (20 items from \(b = -2\) to 2), the two agree closely across the middle: 0.53 and 0.52 near \(\theta = 0\), and 0.56 and 0.56 at \(\theta = 1.25\). At the ends they part. In the bins at \(\pm 2.75\), 34 and 38 respondents answered every item wrong or every item right and have no estimate at all, and the rest scatter less than the CSEM says (0.66 and 0.64 against 0.79): the respondents who would have had the largest errors are the ones who drop out. Change b to rep(1, 20), all items at one difficulty. Now 202 respondents in the lowest bin have no estimate, and the CSEM there, 1.49, is more than three times the scatter of the rest (0.42). Then try five items, seq(-2, 2, length.out = 5). The formula is a large-sample result; with few items it is a rough guide, and what to do about respondents with no finite estimate is for Estimating abilities.

title: Information, precision, and short forms
text:
With real data

A financial-literacy test
Our main example is bialowolski_2024_financial_literacy: 18 questions answered by 4,389 Polish adults (Bialowolski, 2024), about inflation, bonds, diversification, loan interest and the like. Its job is to be a test aimed near the middle of its population. A response is 1 for a correct answer and 0 otherwise, including “don’t know”, which every question offered (the deposit’s supplementary appendix lists the questions). Each question came in one of three wordings that differed in grammatical gender; the IRW table pools them, and so do we. Lusardi and Mitchell (2014) review research on financial literacy. Download the code to run every chunk yourself; it needs mirt (Chalmers, 2012).


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with a
# CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
fl_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_4:v7_0.bialowolski_2024_financial_literacy/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(fl_url)
# resp is 1 for a correct answer and 0 otherwise ("don't know" included). Every
# respondent answered every item once; there are no waves.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
}
fl <- long2wide(df)
c(respondents = nrow(fl), items = ncol(fl), complete = sum(complete.cases(fl)))


respondents       items    complete 
       4389          18        4389

round(range(colMeans(fl)), 2)   # proportion correct: the hardest and easiest items

Every respondent answered every item. The items run from hard (17% correct) to very easy (96%).


Code
# Rasch and 2PL. mirt writes the 2PL as a*theta + d; our difficulty is b = -d/a.
fl_r <- mirt(fl, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
fl_2 <- mirt(fl, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
c(BIC_Rasch = round(extract.mirt(fl_r, "BIC")), BIC_2PL = round(extract.mirt(fl_2, "BIC")))

The last column is each item’s information at its peak, \(a^2/4\): 1.18 for FL_1, 0.00 for FL_2.

# Test information is the sum of the item informations; the conditional SEM is one
# over its square root. testinfo() and iteminfo() do the sums.

The test information peaks at 7.45 near \(\theta = -0.77\), where the CSEM is 0.37, and falls to 1.01 at \(\theta = 2\) (CSEM 1.00). The two flat items add 0.003 and 0.031 to the peak, under half a percent between them. The item informations sum to the test information exactly (all.equal returns TRUE).


Code
# The single-number summary: mirt's marginal reliability of the ability estimates,
# and the one SEM it implies on a scale whose ability SD is 1.
eap <- fscores(fl_2, full.scores.SE = TRUE)
rel <- empirical_rxx(eap)
c(reliability = round(unname(rel), 2), one_sem = round(sqrt(1 - unname(rel)), 2))


reliability     one_sem

# The conditional SEM at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the respondents' estimates.

round(c(q, csem = 1 / sqrt(testinfo(fl_2, matrix(q)))), 2)

Summarised as one number, this test’s reliability is 0.81, which on a \(\theta\) scale with SD 1 implies one SEM of 0.44 for everyone. The curve says otherwise: 0.50 at the 2.5th percentile of respondents, 0.81 at the 97.5th, and 0.37 at its best. The single number averages over a curve that varies by more than a factor of two across these respondents.

     axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")

par(op)


This is the Wright map with error bars that the Rasch lesson promised: the respondents’ estimates (bars) with the CSEM (line) laid over them. The CSEM is lowest just below the middle of the respondents and rises faster to the right, because the test has few hard items: only three difficulties are above 0.5.


A short form for decisions near \(\theta = -1\)
Suppose the test were used to decide who is offered a financial-education course, with the decision made at about \(\theta = -1\) (14% of these respondents have estimates below it). Five items, chosen for that point:


Code
# A five-item short form for decisions made near theta = -1: take the five items
# with the most information there. Compare it with the full test and with every
# possible five-item form (choose(18, 5) = 8,568 of them).
target <- -1
c(share_of_respondents_below_target = round(mean(eap[, "F1"] < target), 2))


share_of_respondents_below_target 
                             0.14 


Code
item_info <- function(t) sapply(colnames(fl), function(i) iteminfo(extract.item(fl_2, i), t))
info_target <- item_info(target)
best5 <- names(sort(info_target, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
best5


[1] "FL_1"  "FL_12" "FL_14" "FL_6"  "FL_13"


Code
forms <- combn(18, 5)
all5 <- apply(forms, 2, function(k) sum(info_target[k]))
c(full_test = round(sum(info_target), 2), best_five = round(sum(info_target[best5]), 2),
  median_five = round(median(all5), 2), five_90th_percentile = round(unname(quantile(all5, 0.9)), 2))


           full_test            best_five          median_five 
                7.25                 4.18                 1.99 
five_90th_percentile 
                2.88 


Code
# What the targeted form gives up away from its target.
up <- 1.5
info_up <- item_info(up)
c(full_test = round(sum(info_up), 2), best_five = round(sum(info_up[best5]), 2),
  best_five_for_1.5 = round(sum(sort(info_up, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]), 2))


        full_test         best_five best_five_for_1.5 
             1.55              0.20              0.89 


Code
round(1 / sqrt(c(best5_at_target = sum(info_target[best5]), best5_at_1.5 = sum(info_up[best5]))), 2)


best5_at_target    best5_at_1.5 
           0.49            2.22 


The best five for \(\theta = -1\) (FL_1, FL_12, FL_14, FL_6 and FL_13) give information 4.18 there, 58% of the full test’s 7.25, from 28% of the items. The median of all 8,568 possible five-item forms gives 1.99, and the 90th percentile 2.88, so a form picked without looking at information is likely to give less than half as much. What the targeted form gives up shows at \(\theta = 1.5\): its information there is 0.20 (a CSEM of 2.22, against 0.49 at its target), and even the best five for \(\theta = 1.5\) would reach only 0.89.
So what should a practitioner do with a short form? It depends on an assumption about its use. If it serves one decision at a known point on the scale, precision elsewhere matters little, and information at that point is the right criterion. If it must rank everyone, or serve decisions no one has located yet, a form aimed at one point is a poor bet. When I know where the decisions are made, I build the short form from the items most informative there and report its CSEM at that point, not its reliability. Here, five well-chosen items give a CSEM of 0.49 at the decision point, against the full test’s 0.37; no five items, and not even all eighteen, make the test precise at \(\theta = 1.5\).


A scale aimed high
For contrast, a scale built for a different job: the Perceptual Aberration scale of the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales–Short Forms (Winterstein et al., 2011), in christensen_2018_wsssf_5831. The data are 5,831 undergraduates who completed the scales as part of mass screening at one university (Christensen et al., 2018). Its job here is to show a test whose information sits, by design, far from most of the people who took it. The items are true–false statements, and the scale measures distortions of body image and perception (Chapman, Chapman & Raulin, 1978, who developed the full scale). They are keyed so that 1 is the response scored toward schizotypy (Christensen et al., 2018, p. 2537).

The information peaks at 18.22 at \(\theta = 1.83\), a CSEM of 0.23, lower than the financial-literacy test reaches anywhere. At \(\theta = 0\) the CSEM is 0.88; at \(\theta = -1\) it is 2.27. Everyone who endorsed nothing gets the same estimate, −0.55, where the CSEM is 1.49, and only 16% of respondents have a CSEM below 0.4. For most of these students, the scale says little more than “not high”.
That is what a screening scale is for. Its items are ones few people endorse, so that endorsing several picks out the few respondents high on the trait; its precision is spent at the high end, where a screen makes its decisions. The curve that would be a problem for ranking all 5,831 students is the right shape for finding the ones to invite for a follow-up interview. Whether a test is precise is always a question of where, and for which decision.

title: Information, precision, and short forms
text:
Problems

The 3PL’s information. Starting from \(P = c + (1 - c)L\) with \(L = \text{logit}^{-1}(a(\theta - b))\) and the general formula \(I = P'^2/[P(1-P)]\), fill in the algebra that gives the 3PL item information \(a^2\frac{(P - c)^2}{(1 - c)^2}\frac{1 - P}{P}\). Then show that it peaks at \(\theta = b + \frac{1}{a}\log\frac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 8c}}{2}\), and check the answer against the widget with \(a = 1\) and \(c = 0.25\). (PS3#1)
Three items. A test has three Rasch items with \(b = -1, 0, 1.5\). Write down the test information, plot it, and find where it is largest. What is the CSEM there, and at \(\theta = 3\)? Which single item would you add to bring the CSEM at \(\theta = 3\) below 1? (PS4#1)
What can go? In the financial-literacy test, which three items could you drop with the least loss of information below \(\theta = 0\)? Define “below \(\theta = 0\)” yourself (a point, an average over a range, an average over the respondents there), and say whether your answer depends on the choice.
Design a form. Ten Rasch items have difficulties \(-2.5, -2, -1.5, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2\). Find the best five-item form for \(\theta = -1\) and its CSEM there. Then draw ten random five-item forms and compare. How often does a random form come within 10% of the best one’s information? (PS6#3)
Is it a flaw? A colleague reads the Perceptual Aberration output and says the scale is imprecise for 84% of respondents and should be revised. Write a paragraph in reply. For which uses is the colleague right, and for which not? What would you change if the scale had to rank all students, and what would that cost the screen?
Challenge (open): is the curve right? A CSEM curve is computed from the model, so it inherits the model’s assumptions (one \(\theta\), local independence, the right item curves). How would you check whether the CSEM curve for the financial-literacy test describes the real precision of its scores? Think about what you’d need: a retest, a split of the items, a second measure. I don’t know of a check that works well with one administration and no other measure.

title: Information, precision, and short forms

For instructors

Source: EDUC 252 class 3 (slides c3, 35–42) and class 4 (slide 49), problem sets 3 (#1), 4 (#1) and 6 (#3), and the code in ben-domingue/252: c4/info.R.
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 60 minutes; the two real-data analyses work as a 30-minute lab. The fits take a few seconds each in local R.
Changed from 252: 2PL and 3PL information are taught here directly, since the lesson follows From the 1PL to the 4PL. The contrast table uses one subscale of the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales (Perceptual Aberration) rather than all 60 items, because the four subscales form two nearly uncorrelated groups and one information curve assumes one \(\theta\). The general information function, with the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL cases and additivity, is one Go deeper callout at the top of Core ideas (Ben, 09-25); problem 1 fills in the 3PL algebra and finds its peak.
Held back: the standard error of an individual estimate, and respondents with perfect or zero scores (Estimating abilities); choosing items by information one at a time (Item banks and adaptive testing); error bands on reported scores and precision at cut scores (What does a score mean?); what fixing \(c\) or giving it a prior does to information at the bottom of the scale (Guessing and priors); information from polytomous items (Models for polytomous responses) and from distractors (Nominal response and multiple-choice models). Local dependence, which inflates information, is named here; the lessons that treat it (Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT, Explanatory item response models) are outside this lesson’s prerequisite chain.

title: Many sources of error: generalizability theory
text:
What this is for
Classical test theory gives a score one error term. Suppose 202 people list unusual uses for a paperclip, a garbage bag and a rope, and five raters judge how clever each list is. A respondent might have done better with other objects, and would have got a different score from other raters. Which source of error is larger decides whether to add raters or objects. Generalizability theory (G theory) asks what the score should generalize over, then splits the error into those sources and prices each one (Cronbach, Rajaratnam & Gleser, 1963). In the cleverness ratings the answer is more tasks; in teachers’ ratings of essays, more raters. Like CTT, G theory is a theory of observed scores. Item response theory, from The Rasch model on, is a latent-trait theory that models each response, and the two rest on different assumptions.

title: Many sources of error: generalizability theory
Many sources of error: generalizability theory
text:
Core ideas

One error term, many sources






Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: an observed score is \(X = T + E\), reliability is \(\sigma^2_T/(\sigma^2_T + \sigma^2_E)\), alpha estimates it from the items of one administration, and the Spearman–Brown formula says what lengthening the test does.



Where does \(E\) come from? The items behind alpha are one source; From construct map to items added another, the rater who scores a constructed response; occasions and forms are more. G theory calls each such source a facet, and each of its values (this rater, that task) a condition (Cronbach, Gleser, Nanda & Rajaratnam, 1972, a book with no DOI, linked here through Bock’s review in Science).






Recall from Constructs and construct maps: a test built from a blueprint supports a claim about a domain, and its items can be seen as a sample from a larger pool.



G theory applies that view to every facet. The tasks we used are a sample from the tasks we could have used; the raters, from the raters we would accept. Together these make up the universe of admissible observations, which the investigator, not the data, defines. A decision maker may care about only part of it (raters trained on this rubric, say); that part is the universe of generalization. A respondent’s average over it is the universe score, G theory’s counterpart of the true score, and the question of this lesson is how well an average over the few conditions we used stands in for it (Shavelson, Webb & Rowley, 1989). A facet we generalize over is random; a facet we don’t (these three objects and no others) is fixed, and what is specific to its conditions stops being error (Brennan, 2001).


Variance components
Take the cleverness design: every person \(p\) does every task \(t\), and every rater \(r\) rates every response, so all three are crossed. A rating is a sum of effects: \[X_{ptr} = \mu + \nu_p + \nu_t + \nu_r + \nu_{pt} + \nu_{pr} + \nu_{tr} + \nu_{ptr,e}.\] Each \(\nu\) is a random effect with mean zero and its own variance, and the effects are uncorrelated, so the variance of one rating splits into seven variance components, \(\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_t + \dots + \sigma^2_{ptr,e}\) (Brennan, 2001). \(\sigma^2_p\) is how much people differ, the signal; \(\sigma^2_r\), how much raters differ in severity; \(\sigma^2_{pt}\), how much people’s standing changes from task to task; \(\sigma^2_{pr}\), raters disagreeing about who is better. The last term mixes the three-way interaction with whatever else the design can’t separate from it, hence the \(e\).
Not every design is crossed. If each essay is read by its own teachers, raters are nested within essays (\(r{:}p\)), and a teacher seen with one essay can’t show both how harsh they are and how they react to that essay: \(\sigma^2_r\) and \(\sigma^2_{pr}\) merge into \(\sigma^2_{r:p}\) (Brennan, 2001).
How do we estimate them? Classically, by setting the mean squares of an analysis of variance equal to their expected values, a reasonable choice for a balanced design (Brennan, 2001) and one the essay section uses as a check. This lesson fits each term as a random intercept in a mixed model, with lme4 (Bates, Mächler, Bolker & Walker, 2015) and a long table of one row per rating:
lmer(resp ~ 1 + (1 | id) + (1 | item) + (1 | rater) +
       (1 | id:item) + (1 | id:rater) + (1 | item:rater), data = ratings)
The residual variance is \(\sigma^2_{ptr,e}\). lmer estimates the variances by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Plain maximum likelihood treats the fixed effects as known and so underestimates each variance, by more the fewer levels a facet has; REML removes that bias (Patterson & Thompson, 1971; Harville, 1977), which matters with facets of three and five levels. In a balanced design REML reproduces the ANOVA estimates whenever none is negative (Searle, Casella & McCulloch, 1992), and it also handles sparse designs like the second table’s.


Two G coefficients
Why are some components error only some of the time? It depends on the decision. For a relative decision (who ranks above whom), only the components that change a person’s standing count: those that interact with \(p\). For a score averaged over \(n_t\) tasks and \(n_r\) raters, the relative error variance is \[\sigma^2_\delta = \frac{\sigma^2_{pt}}{n_t} + \frac{\sigma^2_{pr}}{n_r} + \frac{\sigma^2_{ptr,e}}{n_t n_r}.\] For an absolute decision (is this score above 3? how clever is this list, on the rating scale?), a harsh rater or a hard task moves the score itself, so the main effects count too: \[\sigma^2_\Delta = \sigma^2_\delta + \frac{\sigma^2_t}{n_t} + \frac{\sigma^2_r}{n_r} + \frac{\sigma^2_{tr}}{n_t n_r}.\] Each coefficient sets the universe-score variance against one of them (Brennan, 2001): the generalizability coefficient \(E\rho^2 = \sigma^2_p/(\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_\delta)\) and the dependability coefficient \(\Phi = \sigma^2_p/(\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_\Delta)\). Since \(\sigma^2_\Delta \ge \sigma^2_\delta\), \(\Phi\) is never the larger. Error near a cut score is taken up in What does a score mean?.
Both have the form of reliability in Classical test theory and reliability, \(\sigma^2_T/(\sigma^2_T + \sigma^2_E)\): the “true” variance is universe-score variance, \(\sigma^2_p\), what stays with a person across the conditions we generalize over, and the error is what changes from one sample of conditions to another. Fix a facet and the split moves (the interrater section shows how).

Try it: the two coefficients side by side
Each bar is one coefficient’s denominator: the universe score plus the error it counts; the light pieces count only for Φ. The sliders start at the cleverness estimates from With real data; switch to the essays to see raters that differ in severity (there, “task” is a rating criterion).
