title: Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
text:
What this is for
What is an item? explained item difficulty with a matrix of item features and kept every respondent on one continuum. This lesson keeps the matrix and drops the continuum. Suppose respondents differ not in how much of something they have but in which skills they have: a student who can find a common denominator but can’t borrow from a whole number needs different teaching from one with the opposite gap, even if both get half the items right. Latent class analysis puts respondents in a few unobserved groups; cognitive diagnosis builds the groups from profiles of skills, with a matrix saying which skills each item needs. Constructs and construct maps asked whether a construct is a continuum or a set of classes, and summary statistics couldn’t tell. Here we fit both and see which the data prefer.

title: Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
text:
Core ideas

Latent classes






Recall from Constructs and construct maps: latent classes are unobserved groups inside each of which people are alike. Ordered classes close together gave nearly the same sum scores and item-rest correlations as a continuum, and telling them apart was left to models fit to the responses.



A latent class model says each respondent belongs to one of \(C\) classes, class \(c\) holding a share \(\pi_c\) of the population, and that within a class each item has its own probability of success, \(p_{ic}\). Given the class, responses are independent: local independence, with a class in place of \(\theta\). The probability of respondent \(j\)’s responses is a mixture over the classes, \[\Pr(\mathbf{x}_j) = \sum_{c=1}^{C} \pi_c \prod_{i} p_{ic}^{\,x_{ij}}\,(1 - p_{ic})^{1 - x_{ij}}.\] The model comes from Lazarsfeld’s latent structure analysis (Lazarsfeld & Henry, 1968); Goodman (1974) took up its estimation and when its parameters are identified. With \(I\) items it has \(C - 1\) class shares and \(C \times I\) item probabilities. It is fit by EM: from a guess at the item probabilities, compute each respondent’s posterior probability of each class, re-estimate the item probabilities with responses weighted by those posteriors, and repeat. We use the poLCA package (Linzer & Lewis, 2011).
Read the formula from the inside out. Inside class \(c\), each item contributes \(p_{ic}\) if it was answered correctly and \(1 - p_{ic}\) if not, and local independence lets us multiply those factors into the probability of the whole pattern if the respondent were in class \(c\). We don’t know the class, so each class’s product is weighted by its share \(\pi_c\) and the weighted products are added. Each term’s part of the sum is the posterior probability that the respondent is in that class, which is how EM assigns respondents.

Try it: building the probability of a response pattern
Three classes answer four items. Low and High are ordered; Uneven finds items 1 and 2 easy and items 3 and 4 hard. Choose a response pattern and the classes’ relative sizes.


Code
viewof mx_x = Inputs.checkbox(["Item 1", "Item 2", "Item 3", "Item 4"], {value: ["Item 1", "Item 2"], label: "Answered correctly"})
viewof mx_w1 = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "Relative size: Low"})
viewof mx_w2 = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Relative size: High"})
viewof mx_w3 = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "Relative size: Uneven"})
































Code
mx_pat = [1, 2, 3, 4].map(i => mx_x.includes(`Item ${i}`) ? 1 : 0)
mx = mixtureParts(mx_pat, [mx_w1, mx_w2, mx_w3].every(w => w === 0) ? [1, 1, 1] : [mx_w1, mx_w2, mx_w3])
mx_cell = "padding:0.2rem 0.6rem;border-bottom:1px solid " + palette.rule + ";text-align:right"
htl.html`<table style="font-size:0.9rem;border-collapse:collapse">
  <thead><tr><th style=${mx_cell + ";text-align:left"}>Class</th>
    ${[1, 2, 3, 4].map(i => htl.html`<th style=${mx_cell}>Item ${i} (${mx_pat[i - 1] ? "p" : "1 − p"})</th>`)}
    <th style=${mx_cell}>Product: P(pattern | class)</th><th style=${mx_cell}>× share π</th><th style=${mx_cell}>= contribution</th><th style=${mx_cell}>Posterior</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>${mx.rows.map(r => htl.html`<tr><td style=${mx_cell + ";text-align:left"}><b>${r.name}</b></td>
    ${r.factors.map(f => htl.html`<td style=${mx_cell}>${f.toFixed(2)}</td>`)}
    <td style=${mx_cell}>${r.within.toFixed(4)}</td><td style=${mx_cell}>${r.pi.toFixed(2)}</td><td style=${mx_cell}>${r.contrib.toFixed(4)}</td><td style=${mx_cell}>${r.post.toFixed(2)}</td></tr>`)}
  <tr><td style=${mx_cell + ";text-align:left"} colspan="7"><b>Sum of the contributions: Pr(pattern)</b></td><td style=${mx_cell}><b>${mx.px.toFixed(4)}</b></td><td style=${mx_cell}>1.00</td></tr></tbody></table>`
































Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 90, x: {label: "Pr(pattern), split by the class each part comes from", domain: [0, Math.max(0.3, mx.px)]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: lcClasses.map(c => c.name), range: [palette.light, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.barX(mx.rows, Plot.stackX({x: "contrib", fill: "name"})), Plot.ruleX([0])]
})







With the default pattern, items 1 and 2 right and 3 and 4 wrong, Uneven supplies most of the probability (a posterior of 0.63), though it is the smallest class. Now answer items 3 and 4 instead: the score is still 2, but the pattern is about thirty times less likely and Low takes 0.70 of the posterior. A latent class model reads which items were answered, not only how many. Setting a class’s size to 0 removes its term from the sum.






If you’ve done Estimating item parameters: the two biased coins that introduced EM were a two-class latent class model, with the ten tosses in a set as its items.



Another class always raises the log likelihood, so the number of classes is chosen by a criterion that charges for parameters, such as BIC, and by whether the classes mean anything. A latent class model is a reasonable choice when a theory says there are types, as Moffitt’s account of antisocial behaviour does, or to describe how responses hang together without assuming a continuum.






If you’ve done Model fit and out-of-sample prediction: AIC and BIC, which charge for each parameter, also compare models that aren’t nested, such as a latent class model and a 2PL.





Code
quiz({
  q: "A latent class model with four classes is fit to 28 binary items. How many parameters does it have?",
  options: [
    {text: "115", correct: true, why: "Three free class shares (the fourth is one minus the others) plus $4 \\times 28 = 112$ item probabilities."},
    {text: "112", correct: false, why: "That counts the item probabilities but forgets the class shares, $C - 1 = 3$ of them."},
    {text: "31", correct: false, why: "Each class has its own probability for *every* item, so the item parameters number $C \\times I$, not $I$."}
  ]
})










Classes or a continuum?
A latent class model has no \(\theta\). All it has is a set of classes, each a share of respondents and a row of success rates, one per item, like the rows of the table in the last widget. So the question “types or a continuum?” has to be asked of those rows. What pattern in them would a continuum leave behind?
Draw each class’s row as a line across the items, easiest to hardest: a profile. If the classes are really types, respondents who differ in which items they find hard, the profiles cross: one class beats another on some items and loses on others. If the classes are levels of one thing, each class does better than the class below it on every item, and the profiles stack without crossing.

Try it: class profiles, stacked or crossing
The widget makes classes that are levels of one thing. The top panel shows where they come from, which the latent class model never sees: a normal \(\theta\) split into equal-sized groups. The bottom panel shows what the model does see, each class’s profile on ten Rasch items, in the same colour as its group. The toggle adds a class that is a type: it finds the odd-numbered items easy and the even-numbered ones hard.


Code
viewof cc_K = Inputs.range([2, 7], {value: 4, step: 1, label: "Number of classes (levels)"})
viewof cc_skill = Inputs.toggle({label: "Add a class that differs in which items it finds hard", value: false})


















Code
cc = cutClasses(cc_K, cc_skill)
cc_names = Array.from({length: cc_K}, (_, k) => `Class ${k + 1}`)
// light blue to dark blue, one shade per class (like R's colorRampPalette)
cc_shades = d3.quantize(d3.interpolateRgb(palette.light, d3.interpolateRgb(palette.main, palette.ink)(0.5)), Math.max(cc_K, 2)).slice(0, cc_K)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 130, marginTop: 10, x: {label: "θ (where the classes came from; the model never sees it)", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {axis: null},
  color: {domain: cc_names, range: cc_shades},
  marks: [Plot.areaY(cc.density, {x: "theta", y: "d", fill: "cls", z: "cls"})]
})
































Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, color: {domain: [...cc_names, "Type"], range: [...cc_shades, palette.contrast]}, x: {label: "Item (easiest to hardest)", ticks: 10}, y: {label: "P(correct) in the class", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(cc.rows, {x: "item", y: "p", z: "cls", stroke: "cls", strokeWidth: d => d.kind === "skill" ? 3 : 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(cc.rows, {x: "item", y: "p", fill: "cls", r: 3}),
    Plot.text(cc.rows.filter(d => d.item === 10), {x: "item", y: "p", text: "cls", dx: 8, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 10})
  ], marginRight: 80
})









Code
md`Items on which a class does worse than the class below it (classes ordered by their average): **${cc.outOfOrder} of 10**.`







However many levels you choose, the profiles stack: 0 of 10 items are out of order. Add the type and its profile zigzags across the rest, putting all ten out of order. So a latent class model that finds stacked profiles has found what a continuum would give it, a continuum cut into a few levels, not evidence of types. The converse holds too: a Rasch model whose \(\theta\) takes only a few values, ordered classes by another name, gives nearly the same item estimates as the Rasch model’s conditional likelihood once it has at least \((I + 1)/2\) of them (Lindsay, Clogg & Grego, 1991). Evidence for classes as something other than a continuum has to come from crossings, classes that differ in which items they find hard.



Cognitive diagnosis: classes built from attributes






Recall from What is an item?: the LLTM wrote each item’s easiness as \(\beta_i = \sum_k q_{ik}\eta_k\), where \(q_{ik}\) is 1 if item \(i\) has feature \(k\). The matrix of \(q_{ik}\) described the items, and respondents stayed on one continuum.



Cognitive diagnosis uses such a matrix differently. Each respondent has a profile \(\boldsymbol\alpha_j = (\alpha_{j1}, \dots, \alpha_{jK})\) of binary attributes, skills they have (\(\alpha_{jk} = 1\)) or lack. \(K\) attributes give \(2^K\) profiles, and each profile is a latent class. The Q-matrix says which attributes each item requires: \(q_{ik} = 1\) if item \(i\) needs attribute \(k\). In the LLTM the matrix explained how hard an item is; here it decides which classes an item can tell apart. A cognitive diagnosis model (CDM) is therefore a restricted latent class model (Haertel, 1989): the classes are fixed in advance by the attributes, and the Q-matrix ties their item probabilities together (Rupp, Templin & Henson, 2010).
The classic example is fraction subtraction, from Kikumi Tatsuoka’s work on diagnosing students’ errors (Tatsuoka, 1983; the data as analysed by Tatsuoka, 2002). Twenty items are coded on eight attributes, giving \(2^8 = 256\) profiles. The attribute labels are those of the CDM package documentation, which takes the Q-matrix from DeCarlo (2011) and de la Torre and Douglas (2004).

Try it: the Q-matrix at work
Choose a student’s attributes. Under DINA (next section), an item is answered correctly with probability \(1 - s\) if the student has every attribute it needs, and \(g\) otherwise.


Code
viewof qm_has = Inputs.checkbox(fracAttributes, {value: fracAttributes.filter((_, k) => k !== 4), label: "Attributes the student has"})
viewof qm_g = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Guess g (all items)"})
viewof qm_s = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Slip s (all items)"})

























Code
qm_profile = fracAttributes.map(a => qm_has.includes(a) ? 1 : 0)
qm_items = dinaItems(qm_profile, qm_g, qm_s)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Item", tickFormat: d => d}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["has every attribute the item needs", "lacks at least one"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(qm_items, {x: "item", y: "p", fill: d => d.eta ? "has every attribute the item needs" : "lacks at least one", title: d => d.eta ? "" : `lacks ${d.missing}`}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})

























Code
md`This profile can do **${qm_items.filter(d => d.eta).length} of 20** items; its expected score is **${qm_items.reduce((s, d) => s + d.p, 0).toFixed(1)}**.`







The default student lacks only A5, borrowing from the whole number part; eight items need it, so 12 of 20 are within reach. Now tick A5 and untick A7, subtracting numerators: 19 items need A7, and one is left. Profiles that lack different attributes can also reach similar expected scores through different items, a difference a sum score can’t see.
A profile also describes a respondent, so it can be handed to a simulator. Zhou, Liu, Tang and Wilson (2026), a preprint, took 15 of these fraction items coded on five attributes, wrote each attribute profile as a short description of a student, and asked language models to answer as that student. Answering with no profile, the models were more accurate and more alike than the 536 students. Given profiles, their scores spread more like the students’, and the 1PL difficulties from their answers came closer to the students’ difficulties: in the strongest case, the rank correlation rose from 0.24 to about 0.9. AI and psychometrics takes up language models as simulated respondents more generally.



DINA: all or nothing
The DINA model (“deterministic inputs, noisy and gate”; Junker & Sijtsma, 2001) asks one question per item: does the respondent have every attribute it needs? Write \[\eta_{ij} = \prod_{k} \alpha_{jk}^{\,q_{ik}},\] which is 1 if they do and 0 if they lack any. Then \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1 \mid \boldsymbol\alpha_j) = (1 - s_i)^{\eta_{ij}}\, g_i^{\,1 - \eta_{ij}}.\] The slip \(s_i\) is the chance that a respondent with everything the item needs still gets it wrong; the guess \(g_i\) is the chance that one without gets it right. Each item has two parameters, because the model splits the \(2^K\) classes into two groups per item. Having some of the required attributes counts for nothing.






If you’ve done From the 1PL to the 4PL: its section on ceilings and slips pointed here. DINA’s \(1 - s\) and \(g\) are an upper and a lower asymptote, like the 4PL’s \(u\) and \(c\), with nothing in between.



Other models relax the rule. In DINO, any one required attribute is enough (Templin & Henson, 2006), which suits a symptom that several conditions can produce. G-DINA (de la Torre, 2011) gives each combination of an item’s \(K_i\) required attributes its own probability, \(2^{K_i}\) of them, and contains DINA and DINO; the log-linear CDM (Henson, Templin & Willse, 2009) is an equivalent family written as a logistic regression on the attributes and their interactions. DINA is a reasonable choice when an item is solved by a chain of steps that must all succeed, as fraction subtraction is, and when there are too few respondents for G-DINA’s extra parameters; G-DINA, when there are enough to let the data say how partial mastery counts.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under DINA, an item needs attributes A2 and A5 and has $g = 0.2$, $s = 0.1$. What is P(correct) for a student with A2, A3 and A7 but not A5?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.2", correct: true, why: "The student lacks A5, so $\\eta = 0$ and the probability is the guess, $g$. Having A2 earns nothing under DINA."},
    {text: "0.55", correct: false, why: "That is halfway between $g$ and $1 - s$, as if having one of the two attributes earned half the credit. G-DINA could say that; DINA can't."},
    {text: "0.9", correct: false, why: "That is $1 - s$, for students with *every* required attribute. A3 and A7 aren't needed by this item, so they don't make up for A5."}
  ]
})









Tying the attributes to a continuum: the higher-order model
DINA says how an item depends on a profile, but not how profiles are spread among respondents. Left free, that spread is a share \(\pi\) for every one of the \(2^K\) profiles, with nothing linking them. Do respondents who have one attribute tend to have the others? The higher-order model (de la Torre & Douglas, 2004) answers yes, through one continuous trait. Each respondent has a \(\theta_j\), normally distributed, and given \(\theta_j\) the attributes are independent, with \[\Pr(\alpha_{jk} = 1 \mid \theta_j) = \frac{\exp(\lambda(\theta_j - \delta_k))}{1 + \exp(\lambda(\theta_j - \delta_k))}.\] Each attribute has a threshold \(\delta_k\), the point on \(\theta\) where it is as likely mastered as not, and \(\lambda\) says how sharply mastery rises around it. This is a Rasch-type model with the attributes in place of the items, except that the attributes are never observed. The share of a profile is the product of these probabilities, averaged over \(\theta\), so the \(2^K - 1\) free shares become \(K\) thresholds (and \(\lambda\)). With \(\lambda\) fixed at 1, as GDINA does by default, that is one parameter per attribute.
What does an item look like against \(\theta\) now? Below the attributes’ thresholds a respondent probably lacks something the item needs and sits near the guess; above them they probably have it all and sit near \(1 - s\).

Try it: two plateaus, and a curve between them
Take one item and a respondent with a given \(\theta\). With thresholds \(\delta_k\) spread from −1 to 1, the widget computes the chance that they have every attribute the item needs, \(\prod_k \Pr(\alpha_{jk} = 1 \mid \theta_j)\) over those attributes, and mixes the plateaus in that proportion: \(\Pr(x_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_j) = g + (1 - s - g)\prod_k \Pr(\alpha_{jk} = 1 \mid \theta_j)\).


Code
viewof ho_m = Inputs.range([1, 4], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Attributes the item needs"})
viewof ho_l = Inputs.range([0.5, 4], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Attribute slope λ"})
viewof ho_g = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.2, step: 0.01, label: "Guess g"})
viewof ho_s = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Slip s"})
































Code
ho = hoCurve(ho_m, ho_l, ho_g, ho_s)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([ho_g, 1 - ho_s], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.line(ho, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})


















Code
md`At θ = 0 the chance of having all ${ho_m} required attribute${ho_m > 1 ? "s" : ""} is **${ho[120].all.toFixed(2)}**, and P(correct) is **${ho[120].p.toFixed(2)}**.`







The dashed lines are the plateaus, \(g\) and \(1 - s\), where respondents lacking an attribute and those with all of them sit. Given only \(\theta\) the attributes are uncertain, so the curve runs between. With one attribute it is a 4PL curve (see the Go deeper callout). Require more and the curve moves right and loses its symmetry, since every threshold must be passed. Raise \(\lambda\) and the curve steepens toward a step.



How many classes, which Q-matrix, and why not IRT?
Eight attributes give 256 profiles, so an unrestricted distribution over them has 255 parameters, to be estimated from 536 students in the fraction data. Two restrictions shrink that. The higher-order model above needs 8, one per attribute. An attribute hierarchy allows only profiles consistent with an order of learning, ruling out an advanced skill without its prerequisite (Templin & Bradshaw, 2014). Both move a CDM toward a continuum.

Try it: the cost of a profile


Code
viewof pc_K = Inputs.range([1, 12], {value: 8, step: 1, label: "Attributes K"})
viewof pc_n = Inputs.range([100, 5000], {value: 536, step: 1, label: "Respondents"})


















Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Attributes K"}, y: {label: "Parameters for the distribution of profiles", type: "log"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Unrestricted: 2^K - 1", "Higher-order: K"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(classCounts(12), {x: "K", y: "count", stroke: "model", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([pc_K], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})
  ]
})









Code
md`With ${pc_K} attribute${pc_K > 1 ? "s" : ""}: **${2 ** pc_K}** profiles and **${2 ** pc_K - 1}** free class share${pc_K > 1 ? "s" : ""}, against **${pc_K}** for the higher-order model. ${pc_n} respondents spread evenly would put **${(pc_n / 2 ** pc_K).toFixed(1)}** in each profile.`







At eight attributes and 536 respondents, an even spread leaves about two students per profile. Each attribute doubles the unrestricted count and adds one to the higher-order count.
The Q-matrix usually comes from content experts, and may be wrong. Empirical Q-matrix validation looks for better entries. The PVAF method (de la Torre & Chiu, 2016) asks, item by item, for the smallest set of attributes whose G-DINA success probabilities carry at least a set share (by default 95%) of the variation that the item’s full set of attributes would give. It is a reasonable way to find items whose coding deserves a second look; a suggestion is a hypothesis about the item, to be checked against what the item asks and by refitting. Is a CDM better than IRT? The models aren’t nested, so we compare them by AIC and BIC, or by predicting held-out responses (problem 3). Ma, Liu, Kanopka, Ma and Domingue (2026) did the latter, with the IMV, on 11 datasets previously analysed with CDMs, including the ECPE and the fraction data used below. When each respondent was assigned their most probable profile, the 2PL predicted held-out responses better than DINA and G-DINA in every dataset. When predictions used each respondent’s probability of mastering each attribute, a CDM did better in 6 of the 11, by small margins (an IMV under 0.02). G-DINA in particular fit the data it was estimated on much better than it predicted new responses. Why might a CDM lose on data it was built for? The IMV site has an interactive version of the simulation side: data come from DINA with correlated skills, and as the correlation rises the profiles collapse toward one dimension and the 2PL closes the gap.


Code
quiz({
  q: "On the same data, a higher-order DINA model has a much lower BIC than DINA with an unrestricted distribution of profiles. What does that suggest?",
  options: [
    {text: "Much of what distinguishes respondents' profiles lies along one continuum", correct: true, why: "The higher-order model spends one parameter per attribute because it ties the attributes to a single $\\theta$. If that fits better than hundreds of free class shares, the profiles are mostly ordered along that $\\theta$."},
    {text: "The Q-matrix is wrong", correct: false, why: "Both models use the same Q-matrix. They differ only in how respondents are spread over the profiles."},
    {text: "The attributes are unrelated to one another", correct: false, why: "The opposite: the higher-order model says every attribute depends on the same $\\theta$, so attributes go together."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: with one attribute, the higher-order DINA item is a 4PL





Assumptions: the DINA model for item \(i\), with guess \(g\) and slip \(s\); a higher-order model in which, given a continuous \(\theta\), attribute \(k\) is mastered with probability \(\text{logistic}(\lambda(\theta - \delta_k))\), independently across attributes.
Given \(\theta\), a respondent answers correctly either by having every required attribute and not slipping, or by lacking one and guessing: \[\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta) = (1 - s)\,P_{\text{all}}(\theta) + g\,\big(1 - P_{\text{all}}(\theta)\big) = g + (1 - s - g)\,P_{\text{all}}(\theta),\] where \(P_{\text{all}}(\theta) = \prod_{k:\,q_{ik}=1} \text{logistic}(\lambda(\theta - \delta_k))\) is the probability of having all of them.
With one required attribute, \(P_{\text{all}}(\theta) = \text{logistic}(\lambda(\theta - \delta))\), and \[\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta) = g + \big((1 - s) - g\big)\,\frac{\exp(\lambda(\theta - \delta))}{1 + \exp(\lambda(\theta - \delta))},\] which is the 4PL with \(c = g\), \(u = 1 - s\), slope \(a = \lambda\) and difficulty \(b = \delta\). The curve’s location and slope belong to the attribute: every item that needs only attribute \(k\) has the same slope and difficulty and differs only in its asymptotes.
With \(m \ge 2\) attributes, \(P_{\text{all}}\) is a product of logistic curves, which isn’t a logistic curve. In log-odds its lower tail has slope \(m\lambda\) and its upper tail slope \(\lambda\), so it leaves the floor abruptly and approaches the top slowly; and at the largest threshold every other factor is above 0.5 and that one equals 0.5, so its midpoint sits to the right of every \(\delta_k\). As \(\lambda\) grows, each factor becomes a step at \(\delta_k\) and the product a step at the largest threshold. So the higher-order DINA is a unidimensional IRT model whose item curves are built from the Q-matrix. DeCarlo (2011) fits a logistic version of DINA with software for latent class analysis, along the same lines.

title: Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
text:
Simulate
The code simulates 1,000 respondents answering ten items on three attributes and fits DINA with GDINA (Ma & de la Torre, 2020), then G-DINA, then DINA with one wrong Q-matrix entry. The first run takes about half a minute, most of it installing GDINA.
With the seed as written, guesses and slips come back within about 0.05 of the truth, except item 7’s slip (0.18 true, 0.27 estimated), on the item needing all three attributes. Each attribute is classified correctly for 94% to 95% of respondents, the whole profile for 84%. AIC prefers DINA (10,692) to G-DINA (10,712), as it should: DINA generated the data. Telling the model that item 4 needs only A1 (it needs A1 and A2) sends its slip from 0.19 to 0.50: respondents with A1 but not A2 now count as able, and get it wrong. The AIC rises to 10,828. Try n <- 300, or make some profiles rare in share.

title: Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
text:
With real data
cdm_ecpe has two jobs: the latent class example, fit without a Q-matrix to ask whether its classes come out ordered, and the contrast for cognitive diagnosis, a test whose attributes may be one scale in disguise. frac20 is the main example, Tatsuoka’s fraction subtraction items. Both tables carry their Q-matrix in Qmatrix__ columns. Download the code; it needs poLCA, GDINA and mirt (Chalmers, 2012).

ECPE: classes without a Q-matrix
The Examination for the Certificate of Proficiency in English (ECPE) data are 28 grammar items answered by 2,922 respondents, from a tutorial by Templin and Hoffman (2013). The Q-matrix codes three attributes: morphosyntactic, cohesive and lexical rules (CDM package documentation; George et al., 2016). Keying: 1 is correct.


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(poLCA); library(GDINA); library(mirt)})
options(digits = 7)  # R's default, in case a .Rprofile changes it
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v60_0.cdm_ecpe/rows?format=csv"
ecpe <- read.csv(url)
# One row per response; the Q-matrix travels in the Qmatrix__ columns.
wide <- reshape(ecpe[, c("id", "item", "resp")], idvar = "id", timevar = "item",
                direction = "wide")
wide <- wide[order(wide$id), ]
e_items <- paste0("E", 1:28)
Xe <- as.matrix(wide[, paste0("resp.", e_items)])
colnames(Xe) <- e_items
Qe <- unique(ecpe[, c("item", "Qmatrix__skill1", "Qmatrix__skill2", "Qmatrix__skill3")])
Qe <- as.matrix(Qe[match(e_items, Qe$item), -1])
colnames(Qe) <- c("morphosyntactic", "cohesive", "lexical")
cat(nrow(Xe), "respondents,", ncol(Xe), "items,", sum(is.na(Xe)), "missing responses\n")


2922 respondents, 28 items, 0 missing responses


Code
cat("Proportion correct: from", min(round(colMeans(Xe), 2)), "to", max(round(colMeans(Xe), 2)), "\n")


Proportion correct: from 0.43 to 0.9 


Code
# The same data ship with GDINA; check that the copies agree.
data(realdata_ECPE, package = "GDINA")
cat("Same responses as GDINA's copy:", all(Xe == as.matrix(realdata_ECPE$dat)),
    "  Same Q-matrix:", all(Qe == as.matrix(realdata_ECPE$Q)), "\n")


Same responses as GDINA's copy: TRUE   Same Q-matrix: TRUE 


Nothing is missing, and proportions correct run from 0.43 to 0.90. First, set the attributes aside and fit one to five classes:


Code
# poLCA wants categories coded 1, 2, ...; nrep = 5 starts each fit from five random
# places and keeps the best, since EM can stop on a local maximum.
d <- as.data.frame(Xe + 1)
f <- as.formula(paste("cbind(", paste(e_items, collapse = ","), ") ~ 1"))
set.seed(252)
lca <- lapply(1:5, function(k)
  poLCA(f, d, nclass = k, nrep = if (k == 1) 1 else 5, maxiter = 3000, verbose = FALSE))
rasch_e <- mirt(Xe, 1, "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
twopl_e <- mirt(Xe, 1, "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
fits <- data.frame(
  model = c(paste(1:5, "classes"), "Rasch", "2PL"),
  logLik = round(c(sapply(lca, `[[`, "llik"), extract.mirt(rasch_e, "logLik"),
                   extract.mirt(twopl_e, "logLik")), 1),
  parameters = c(sapply(lca, `[[`, "npar"), extract.mirt(rasch_e, "nest"),
                 extract.mirt(twopl_e, "nest")),
  AIC = round(c(sapply(lca, `[[`, "aic"), extract.mirt(rasch_e, "AIC"),
                extract.mirt(twopl_e, "AIC"))),
  BIC = round(c(sapply(lca, `[[`, "bic"), extract.mirt(rasch_e, "BIC"),
                extract.mirt(twopl_e, "BIC"))))
print(fits, row.names = FALSE)


     model   logLik parameters   AIC   BIC
 1 classes -45376.9         28 90810 90977
 2 classes -42972.7         57 86059 86400
 3 classes -42547.8         86 85268 85782
 4 classes -42453.2        115 85136 85824
 5 classes -42402.6        144 85093 85954
     Rasch -42729.8         29 85518 85691
       2PL -42546.7         56 85205 85540


BIC chooses three classes (85,782); AIC keeps falling through five. But the 2PL has a lower BIC (85,540) than any class model, and with 56 parameters its log likelihood (−42,546.7) matches the three-class model’s (−42,547.8) with 86. Do the class profiles stack?


Code
# Put each solution's classes in order of their average proportion correct, then
# count the items on which a higher class does worse than the class below it.
class_probs <- function(fit) {
  P <- sapply(fit$probs, function(p) p[, 2])   # classes x items: P(correct)
  o <- order(rowMeans(P))
  list(P = P[o, , drop = FALSE], share = fit$P[o])
}
for (k in 2:5) {
  cp <- class_probs(lca[[k]])
  out_of_order <- sum(apply(cp$P, 2, function(v) any(diff(v) < 0)))
  cat(sprintf("%d classes: shares %s; mean P(correct) %s; items out of order: %d\n", k,
              paste(sprintf("%.2f", cp$share), collapse = " "),
              paste(sprintf("%.2f", rowMeans(cp$P)), collapse = " "), out_of_order))
}


2 classes: shares 0.47 0.53; mean P(correct) 0.58 0.84; items out of order: 0
3 classes: shares 0.19 0.51 0.30; mean P(correct) 0.48 0.70 0.89; items out of order: 0
4 classes: shares 0.13 0.38 0.37 0.12; mean P(correct) 0.44 0.64 0.81 0.94; items out of order: 0
5 classes: shares 0.14 0.35 0.11 0.29 0.11; mean P(correct) 0.45 0.65 0.74 0.82 0.94; items out of order: 15


Up to four classes, yes, like the levels in the class-profiles widget. The five-class solution puts 15 items out of order. Where do its classes cross?


Code
# The five-class solution, with its items grouped by the attributes the ECPE's
# Q-matrix says they need (1 = needed; order: morphosyntactic, cohesive, lexical).
cp5 <- class_probs(lca[[5]])
pattern <- apply(Qe, 1, paste, collapse = "")
tab5 <- aggregate(t(cp5$P), list(Q_row = pattern), mean)
names(tab5)[-1] <- paste0("class", 1:5)
tab5$items <- as.vector(table(pattern)[tab5$Q_row])
print(cbind(tab5[, 1, drop = FALSE], round(tab5[, 2:6], 2), items = tab5$items), row.names = FALSE)


 Q_row class1 class2 class3 class4 class5 items
   001   0.47   0.74   0.81   0.88   0.95    10
   010   0.57   0.74   0.66   0.87   0.93     4
   011   0.70   0.90   0.87   0.93   0.98     1
   100   0.42   0.52   0.68   0.71   0.93     5
   101   0.30   0.50   0.71   0.77   0.95     7
   110   0.60   0.76   0.77   0.89   0.97     1


Class 3 (11% of respondents) beats class 2 on items needing morphosyntactic rules (0.68 against 0.52 on the five needing only those, 0.71 against 0.50 on the seven also needing lexical rules) and trails it on the four needing only cohesive rules (0.66 against 0.74). That is a class that differs in which items it finds hard, and the difference follows the Q-matrix, which the fit never saw. But BIC doesn’t support a fifth class (85,954 against 85,782 for three). The unrestricted classes mostly come out ordered: a continuum cut into pieces.


Fraction subtraction: DINA
These are 536 students’ responses to the 20 items (Tatsuoka, 2002); the IRW table matches the copy in GDINA. Keying: 1 is correct.


Code
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v60_0.frac20/rows?format=csv"
frac <- read.csv(url)
wide <- reshape(frac[, c("id", "item", "resp")], idvar = "id", timevar = "item",
                direction = "wide")
wide <- wide[order(wide$id), ]
f_items <- paste0("item_", 1:20)
Xf <- as.matrix(wide[, paste0("resp.", f_items)])
colnames(Xf) <- f_items
Qf <- unique(frac[, c("item", paste0("Qmatrix__", 1:8))])
Qf <- as.matrix(Qf[match(f_items, Qf$item), -1])
colnames(Qf) <- paste0("A", 1:8)
cat(nrow(Xf), "respondents,", ncol(Xf), "items,", sum(is.na(Xf)), "missing responses\n")


536 respondents, 20 items, 0 missing responses


Code
data(realdata_Tatsuoka1990, package = "GDINA")
cat("Same responses as GDINA's copy:", all(Xf == as.matrix(realdata_Tatsuoka1990$dat)),
    "  Same Q-matrix:", all(Qf == as.matrix(realdata_Tatsuoka1990$Q)), "\n")


Same responses as GDINA's copy: TRUE   Same Q-matrix: TRUE 


Code
cat("Attributes per item:", rowSums(Qf), "\n")


Attributes per item: 3 2 2 4 4 1 3 1 1 4 3 2 4 2 2 2 3 4 5 4 


Code
cat("Items needing each attribute:", colSums(Qf), "\n")


Items needing each attribute: 3 13 3 5 8 2 19 3 


Items need one to five attributes. A7 is needed by 19 items and A2 by 13; A1, A3 and A8 by three each, and A6 by two. Now DINA:


Code
dina_f <- GDINA(Xf, Qf, model = "DINA", verbose = 0)
gs <- coef(dina_f, "gs")
print(round(t(gs[, c("guessing", "slip")]), 2))


         Item 1 Item 2 Item 3 Item 4 Item 5 Item 6 Item 7 Item 8 Item 9 Item 10
guessing   0.03   0.02   0.00   0.22   0.30   0.10   0.03   0.44   0.29    0.03
slip       0.09   0.04   0.13   0.11   0.17   0.04   0.20   0.18   0.25    0.21
         Item 11 Item 12 Item 13 Item 14 Item 15 Item 16 Item 17 Item 18
guessing    0.07    0.13    0.01    0.06    0.03    0.11    0.04    0.12
slip        0.08    0.04    0.33    0.06    0.11    0.11    0.14    0.14
         Item 19 Item 20
guessing    0.02    0.01
slip        0.24    0.16


Code
cat(sprintf("Items with slip at most 0.25: %d of 20. Largest guess: %.2f (item %d)\n",
            sum(gs[, "slip"] <= 0.25), max(gs[, "guessing"]), which.max(gs[, "guessing"])))


Items with slip at most 0.25: 19 of 20. Largest guess: 0.44 (item 8)


Code
cat("Log likelihood", round(logLik(dina_f), 1), "with", npar(dina_f)$`No. of parameters`,
    "parameters\n")


Log likelihood -4402.3 with 295 parameters


Slips are at most 0.25 on 19 items; item 13’s is 0.33. Most guesses are near zero, as expected for free-response subtraction. Item 8 stands out with a guess of 0.44: it needs only A7, yet students without A7 answer it correctly 44% of the time by the model’s estimate. Perhaps it can be solved another way, or its Q row misses something. Who has which attributes?


Code
prev <- extract(dina_f, "prevalence")$all[, "Level1"]
cat("Proportion mastering each attribute:", round(prev, 2), "\n")


Proportion mastering each attribute: 0.58 0.77 0.72 0.69 0.6 0.79 0.81 0.82 


Code
att_f <- personparm(dina_f, "EAP")   # attribute mastered if its posterior probability > 0.5
n_att <- rowSums(att_f)
cat("Respondents with all eight:", sum(n_att == 8), sprintf("(%.1f%%)", 100 * mean(n_att == 8)),
    "  Distinct profiles among", nrow(att_f), "respondents:",
    length(unique(apply(att_f, 1, paste, collapse = ""))), "\n")


Respondents with all eight: 200 (37.3%)   Distinct profiles among 536 respondents: 49 


Between 58% (A1) and 82% (A8) of students master each attribute, and 200 of 536 (37.3%) are classified as having all eight. Counting an attribute as mastered when its posterior probability is above 0.5, the students fall into 49 profiles.






Recall from The Rasch model: under the Rasch model the sum score is sufficient for \(\theta\). Two respondents with the same number right get the same estimate, whichever items they got right.



DINA reads which items. Among students with the same sum score, do the profiles differ?


Code
r <- rowSums(Xf)
profile <- apply(att_f, 1, paste, collapse = "")
by_r <- data.frame(sum_score = sort(unique(r)),
                   respondents = as.vector(table(r)),
                   profiles = as.vector(tapply(profile, r, function(p) length(unique(p)))),
                   fewest_attributes = as.vector(tapply(n_att, r, min)),
                   most_attributes = as.vector(tapply(n_att, r, max)))
print(by_r[by_r$sum_score %in% c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20), ], row.names = FALSE)


 sum_score respondents profiles fewest_attributes most_attributes
         0          13        1                 0               0
         5          31       11                 2               5
        10          16       10                 5               7
        15          23        3                 7               8
        20          30        1                 8               8


Code
cat("\nThe 16 respondents with 10 correct, by profile (A1 ... A8):\n")



The 16 respondents with 10 correct, by profile (A1 ... A8):


Code
print(sort(table(profile[r == 10]), decreasing = TRUE))



01010111 11010111 01110111 00111111 01011110 01101011 01110011 10010111 
       4        3        2        1        1        1        1        1 
11101111 11110111 
       1        1 


Code
rasch_f <- mirt(Xf, 1, "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
theta_f <- fscores(rasch_f)[, 1]
cat("\nCorrelation of attributes mastered with the sum score:", round(cor(n_att, r), 2),
    "; with Rasch theta:", round(cor(n_att, theta_f), 2), "\n")



Correlation of attributes mastered with the sum score: 0.95 ; with Rasch theta: 0.93 


At a sum score of 10, 16 students fall into 10 different profiles, with five to seven attributes; at 0 and at 20 everyone shares a profile. The number of attributes mastered correlates 0.95 with the sum score and 0.93 with the Rasch \(\theta\). The count of attributes mostly says what the sum score says; the profile adds which skills lie behind it, and that addition rests on the Q-matrix. How do the models compare?


Code
gdina_f <- GDINA(Xf, Qf, model = "GDINA", verbose = 0)
ho_f <- GDINA(Xf, Qf, model = "DINA", att.dist = "higher.order", verbose = 0)
twopl_f <- mirt(Xf, 1, "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
cdm_row <- function(name, m) data.frame(model = name, logLik = round(as.numeric(logLik(m)), 1),
  parameters = npar(m)$`No. of parameters`, AIC = round(AIC(m)), BIC = round(BIC(m)))
irt_row <- function(name, m) data.frame(model = name, logLik = round(extract.mirt(m, "logLik"), 1),
  parameters = extract.mirt(m, "nest"), AIC = round(extract.mirt(m, "AIC")),
  BIC = round(extract.mirt(m, "BIC")))
print(rbind(cdm_row("DINA", dina_f), cdm_row("G-DINA", gdina_f),
            cdm_row("higher-order DINA", ho_f), irt_row("Rasch", rasch_f),
            irt_row("2PL", twopl_f)), row.names = FALSE)


             model  logLik parameters  AIC   BIC
              DINA -4402.3        295 9395 10658
            G-DINA -4265.8        445 9422 11328
 higher-order DINA -4509.6         48 9115  9321
             Rasch -4796.3         21 9635  9725
               2PL -4640.1         40 9360  9532


Code
# The higher-order model: each attribute is a Rasch-type item on one theta (slope
# fixed at 1, GDINA's default), so its profile distribution has 8 parameters, not 255.
cat("\nHigher-order DINA, attribute intercepts:", round(coef(ho_f, "lambda")[, "intercept"], 2),
    "; slopes:", unique(coef(ho_f, "lambda")[, "slope"]), "\n")



Higher-order DINA, attribute intercepts: 0.44 2.48 2.86 1.21 0.58 3.6 1.39 2.54 ; slopes: 1 


Code
# A Q-matrix with no thought behind it: redraw the entries for attributes 5 to 8 at
# random, keeping each attribute's share of items (as in 252's c7/3_cdm.R).
set.seed(10103101)
Q_random <- Qf
for (k in 5:8) Q_random[, k] <- rbinom(20, 1, mean(Qf[, k]))
dina_random <- GDINA(Xf, Q_random, model = "DINA", verbose = 0)
cat("\nDINA with attributes 5-8 of the Q-matrix redrawn at random: AIC", round(AIC(dina_random)), "\n")



DINA with attributes 5-8 of the Q-matrix redrawn at random: AIC 9769 


DINA beats the Rasch model by AIC (9,395 against 9,635) but not the 2PL (9,360), and by BIC trails both: 255 of its 295 parameters are class shares. G-DINA’s extra parameters don’t pay (AIC 9,422). The higher-order DINA wins on both criteria (AIC 9,115, BIC 9,321, 48 parameters), with all its attributes riding on one \(\theta\). The Q-matrix carries information: with attributes 5 to 8 redrawn at random, the AIC rises to 9,769. Do the data suggest a better one?


Code
# Empirical Q-matrix validation by the proportion of variance accounted for (PVAF;
# de la Torre & Chiu, 2016), starting from the DINA fit and from the G-DINA fit.
# For each suggestion, refit the same model with the suggested Q-matrix.
for (m in list(list("DINA", dina_f), list("GDINA", gdina_f))) {
  Q_sug <- extract(Qval(m[[2]], method = "PVAF", eps = 0.95), "sug.Q")
  changed <- which(rowSums(Q_sug != Qf) > 0)
  refit <- GDINA(Xf, Q_sug, model = m[[1]], verbose = 0)
  cat(sprintf("From %s: changes suggested to %d items (%s). AIC %.0f with the original Q, %.0f with the suggested one.\n",
              m[[1]], length(changed), paste(changed, collapse = ", "), AIC(m[[2]]), AIC(refit)))
}


From DINA: changes suggested to 10 items (4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20). AIC 9395 with the original Q, 9527 with the suggested one.
From GDINA: changes suggested to 8 items (1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 19). AIC 9422 with the original Q, 9340 with the suggested one.


Starting from the DINA fit, PVAF suggests changing 10 of the 20 items, and DINA refit with the suggested matrix is worse (AIC 9,527 against 9,395). Starting from G-DINA, the model the method is defined under, it suggests 8, and G-DINA with the suggested matrix improves (9,340 against 9,422). The suggestions depend on the starting model, and one is worth taking only if it survives a refit and a look at the item (problem 3).


ECPE with its Q-matrix
Back to the ECPE, now with its three attributes and eight profiles.


Code
predict({
  q: "G-DINA estimates the share of ECPE respondents in each of the eight profiles of three attributes. How many profiles does it take to hold at least 90% of respondents?",
  choices: ["Two", "Four", "Six", "All eight, roughly evenly"],
  answer: "Four",
  reveal: "Four profiles hold 0.956 of respondents: none of the three attributes (0.302), lexical rules only (0.125), lexical and cohesive (0.180), and all three (0.349). They form a chain. The output is below."
})









Code
gdina_e <- GDINA(Xe, Qe, model = "GDINA", verbose = 0)
shares <- extract(gdina_e, "posterior.prob")[1, ]
print(round(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE), 3))


  111   000   011   001   101   110   010   100 
0.349 0.302 0.180 0.125 0.016 0.014 0.012 0.002 


Code
cat("Four largest profiles together:", round(sum(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE)[1:4]), 3), "\n")


Four largest profiles together: 0.956 


Four profiles hold 95.6% of respondents, the other four under 2% each. The four form a chain: lexical rules first, then cohesive, then morphosyntactic, so knowing how many attributes a respondent has tells you which. Templin and Bradshaw (2014) used these data to test for such a hierarchy. With only the four profiles allowed:


Code
dina_e <- GDINA(Xe, Qe, model = "DINA", verbose = 0)
# G-DINA allowed only the four profiles of a chain: none, lexical, lexical + cohesive, all
chain <- matrix(c(0, 0, 0,  0, 0, 1,  0, 1, 1,  1, 1, 1), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
gdina_chain <- GDINA(Xe, Qe, model = "GDINA", att.str = chain, verbose = 0)
print(rbind(cdm_row("DINA", dina_e), cdm_row("G-DINA", gdina_e),
            cdm_row("G-DINA, four-profile chain", gdina_chain),
            irt_row("Rasch", rasch_e), irt_row("2PL", twopl_e)), row.names = FALSE)


                      model   logLik parameters   AIC   BIC
                       DINA -42841.6         63 85809 86186
                     G-DINA -42738.6         81 85639 86124
 G-DINA, four-profile chain -42751.3         68 85639 86045
                      Rasch -42729.8         29 85518 85691
                        2PL -42546.7         56 85205 85540


The chain matches the full G-DINA’s AIC (85,639) with 13 fewer parameters, so its BIC is better (86,045 against 86,124). But the Rasch model (AIC 85,518) and the 2PL (85,205) beat every CDM on both criteria. A four-step chain is an ordinal scale, and here the continuum describes the responses better. Both routes through the ECPE, classes without a Q-matrix and profiles with one, arrive at ordered groups. In the fraction data the Q-matrix adds information, but the model that uses it best ties the attributes to one continuum.
Whether a test’s attributes behave as separate skills or collapse toward one continuum, as in both datasets here, is hard to know in advance, and AIC and BIC can disagree about it. Responses the models haven’t seen are the acid test: fit a CDM and a unidimensional model, compare how well each predicts held-out responses (problem 3), and let that comparison guide the choice.

title: Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
text:
Problems

The DINA likelihood. Write the likelihood of one respondent’s responses under DINA as a latent class model over the \(2^K\) profiles. Show that with a single attribute (\(K = 1\)), DINA is a two-class latent class model whose item probabilities are \(g_i\) in one class and \(1 - s_i\) in the other. How many parameters does each model have, and are they the same model?
The Q-matrix in an LLTM. Fit resp ~ 0 + Qmatrix__1 + ... + Qmatrix__8 + (1 | id) to frac20 with glmer, as in What is an item? (PS7#2 B). Do items with the same Q row have similar Rasch difficulties? What does the LLTM assume about attributes that DINA doesn’t, and the reverse?
Held out. Hold out a random 20% of frac20 responses (set them to missing), fit the Rasch model, the 2PL, DINA and the higher-order DINA to the rest, and compute each model’s IMV over the Rasch model on the held-out responses (Model fit and out-of-sample prediction). Does the ranking agree with AIC, and with what Ma et al. (2026) found for these data? The IRW vignette Calculating IMV values has the cross-validation code. Then run the full PVAF analysis: which suggested changes make sense for the items as written? (PS7#2 D.)
Skill reports from a state test. A district wants attribute-level reports for each student from a state mathematics test built from a blueprint of content strands, not a Q-matrix. Advise them. What would you want to see before any report goes home?
Design a Q-matrix. Write a Q-matrix for eight items on three attributes in which each attribute has an item that needs it alone. Why does that matter for telling the \(2^3\) profiles apart under DINA? Try a Q-matrix without such items in the simulation.
Challenge (open). When attributes form a hierarchy, as the ECPE’s appear to, is a CDM a new kind of model or a unidimensional model with cut points? Set out what each reading predicts about data you could collect, such as items needing a later attribute but not an earlier one. What would convince you?

title: Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis
text:
Going further

Rupp, A. A., Templin, J., & Henson, R. A. (2010). Diagnostic measurement: Theory, methods, and applications. Guilford Press. https://openlibrary.org/works/OL15026394W. A book-length treatment of cognitive diagnosis models, from Q-matrices to estimation.
Ma, W., & de la Torre, J. (2020). GDINA: An R package for cognitive diagnosis modeling. Journal of Statistical Software, 93(14). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v093.i14. The package used here, with examples.
Linzer, D. A., & Lewis, J. B. (2011). poLCA: An R package for polytomous variable latent class analysis. Journal of Statistical Software, 42(10). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v042.i10. Latent class models in R, including covariates for class membership.
Lindsay, B., Clogg, C. C., & Grego, J. (1991). Semiparametric estimation in the Rasch model and related exponential response models, including a simple latent class model for item analysis. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 86(413), 96–107. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1991.10475008. Why a few ordered latent classes can stand in for the Rasch model’s continuum.

The DINA fit to the fraction data follows c7/3_cdm.R (same data and Q-matrix, and the same log likelihood, −4,402.3), including its randomly redrawn Q-matrix. Attributes are classified by posterior probability above 0.5 rather than by the most probable profile, because personparm(..., "MAP") breaks ties at random.

The held-out comparison and the full PVAF analysis are problem 3. cdm_timss07 (15 attributes) is too slow for class.

title: Estimating abilities: MLE and EAP
text:
What this is for
A respondent answers all ten items of a vocabulary test correctly. What is their ability? The likelihood, which has given us every estimate so far, says it is larger than any number you care to name. Abilities come to us only through an estimator, and the estimators disagree most for the respondents a test measures worst, at the top and the bottom. With the item parameters known, this lesson starts from maximum likelihood, shows where it has no answer, brings in a prior to get the expected a posteriori (EAP) estimate, and fits four estimators to the Wordsum vocabulary test, where 12% of respondents have no maximum-likelihood estimate at all.

title: Estimating abilities: MLE and EAP
Estimating abilities: MLE and EAP
text:
Core ideas

One respondent, one unknown






Recall from The Rasch model: mirt estimates the item parameters first, then abilities treating them as known.



This lesson is the second step. With the item parameters known, a respondent’s answers are independent Bernoulli trials whose probabilities depend on one unknown, \(\theta\): a logistic regression with the respondent’s items as the observations (Lord, 1980). For the 2PL, \[\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i} \Big[x_i \log P_i(\theta) + (1 - x_i)\log\big(1 - P_i(\theta)\big)\Big], \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\big(x_i - P_i(\theta)\big),\] and the Rasch model sets every \(a_i = 1\).






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: at the maximum the derivative of the log likelihood (the score equation) is zero, and the curvature gives the standard error. With an intercept, the score equation says the predicted number of successes equals the observed number.



Here \(\theta\) is that intercept. Under the Rasch model the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) solves \(\sum_i P_i(\hat\theta) = r\): the expected number correct equals the observed number. Software solves it by Newton–Raphson, stepping from a guess by the ratio of the derivative to the curvature (Baker & Kim, 2004).






Recall from Information, precision, and short forms: the negative curvature of the log likelihood is the test information, \(I(\theta) = \sum_i a_i^2 P_i(1 - P_i)\), and the conditional standard error of measurement is \(SE(\theta) = 1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}\). For one respondent’s estimate, evaluate it at their \(\hat\theta\).



So the standard error of the MLE is \(1/\sqrt{I(\hat\theta)}\), a large-sample approximation that holds up better in the middle of a test than at its ends.

Try it: the likelihood of a response pattern
Three Rasch items (\(b\) = −1, 0, 1.5). Choose which the respondent gets right; the bold curve is that pattern’s likelihood, the pale ones the other seven.


Code
lp_b = [-1, 0, 1.5]
lp_labels = lp_b.map((b, i) => `Item ${i + 1} (b = ${b})`.replace("-", "−"))
viewof lp_x = Inputs.checkbox(lp_labels, {label: "Correct on", value: [lp_labels[0], lp_labels[1]]})

























Code
lp_pattern = lp_labels.map(l => lp_x.includes(l) ? 1 : 0)
lp_r = lp_pattern.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0)
lp_all = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].map(m => lp_b.map((_, i) => (m >> i) & 1))
lp_th = grid(-5, 5, 301)
lp_curves = lp_all.flatMap(x => lp_th.map(t => ({theta: t, L: Math.exp(loglik(t, x, lp_b)), pat: x.join(""),
  mine: x.join("") === lp_pattern.join("")})))
lp_mle = mleR(lp_r, lp_b)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: "Likelihood", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(lp_b, {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(lp_curves.filter(d => !d.mine), {x: "theta", y: "L", z: "pat", stroke: palette.light, strokeWidth: 1.2}),
    Plot.line(lp_curves.filter(d => d.mine), {x: "theta", y: "L", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 3}),
    ...(Number.isFinite(lp_mle) ? [Plot.dot([{theta: lp_mle, L: Math.exp(loglik(lp_mle, lp_pattern, lp_b))}], {x: "theta", y: "L", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})] : [])
  ]
})





















































Code
md`Pattern **${lp_pattern.join("-")}** (sum score ${lp_r}). ${Number.isFinite(lp_mle) ?
  `The likelihood peaks at θ = **${lp_mle.toFixed(2)}**, where the information is ${(1 / seR(lp_mle, lp_b) ** 2).toFixed(2)} and the standard error 1 / √${(1 / seR(lp_mle, lp_b) ** 2).toFixed(2)} = **${seR(lp_mle, lp_b).toFixed(2)}**.` :
  `The likelihood keeps ${lp_r === 0 ? "rising as θ falls" : "rising as θ grows"}: it has no peak, so there is no maximum-likelihood estimate.`} Item difficulties are the grey lines.`







The default pattern, 1-1-0, peaks at 1.02, with a standard error of 1.37: three items locate a respondent only roughly. The other two-right patterns peak at the same place, though lower. Tick all three: the likelihood climbs toward 1 and never turns over.



Perfect patterns have no maximum
Why does the all-correct pattern never peak? Each item’s probability of a correct answer rises with \(\theta\), so their product does too. The score equation asks the expected number correct to equal the number of items, which it approaches but never reaches. The MLE is \(+\infty\), and for an all-wrong pattern \(-\infty\).






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression, its Go deeper callout: if a predictor perfectly separates successes from failures, the logistic regression MLE doesn’t exist (Albert & Anderson, 1984). It named a respondent who answers every item correctly as the item-response version.



It is the coin with ten heads in ten flips: \(\hat p = 1\), whose log odds is infinite. mirt reports \(\pm\)Inf; optimize() on \([-10, 10]\) returns the bound, a number that looks like an estimate (the simulation below shows it). One fix that needs no prior is the weighted likelihood estimate (WLE), which is finite for every pattern under the Rasch model, the 2PL and even the 3PL and 4PL (Magis & Verhelst, 2017); it has its own subsection below.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A respondent answers all three items in the widget correctly. You give them a fourth item, much harder ($b = 3$), and they get it wrong. What happens to their maximum-likelihood estimate?",
  options: [
    {text: "It becomes finite", correct: true, why: "With 3 of 4 right, the score equation $\\sum_i P_i(\\theta) = 3$ has a solution: the expected score climbs from 0 to 4 and passes 3 on the way. One wrong answer is enough for the likelihood to turn over. (Here the estimate is 2.49.)"},
    {text: "It stays at $+\\infty$, because the respondent still got every easy item right", correct: false, why: "Under the Rasch model only the sum score matters, and 3 of 4 is not a perfect score. The wrong answer makes very large values of $\\theta$ less likely, so the likelihood peaks."},
    {text: "It becomes finite, and it must be below 3, the new item's difficulty", correct: false, why: "It does become finite (2.49 here), but nothing ties it to the new item's $b$. Had all four items sat at $b = 3$, 3 of 4 would give $3 + \\log 3 \\approx 4.1$."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: why perfect patterns have no MLE, and what keeps the alternatives finite





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items under the 2PL (the Rasch model is \(a_i = 1\)), with the item parameters known and responses locally independent given \(\theta\). Write \(P_i = \text{logit}^{-1}\big(a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)\).
No maximum. If every \(x_i = 1\), the log likelihood is \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_i \log P_i(\theta)\), and \[\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} = \sum_i a_i\,\big(1 - P_i(\theta)\big) > 0 \quad\text{for every } \theta.\] The log likelihood is strictly increasing, bounded above by 0, and approaches 0 as \(\theta \to \infty\). It has a least upper bound but no maximum. The all-wrong pattern is the mirror image. This is separation in the sense of Albert and Anderson (1984): with \(\theta\) as the only parameter, a pattern with no variation is perfectly separated.
The WLE stays finite. Warm (1989) adds a term to the score equation that removes the first-order bias of the MLE. For the Rasch model it is \[\sum_i (x_i - P_i) + \frac{J(\theta)}{2I(\theta)} = 0, \qquad J(\theta) = \sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)(1 - 2P_i),\quad I(\theta) = \sum_i P_i(1 - P_i).\] For a perfect score the first term is \(\sum_i (1 - P_i)\), which falls to 0 as \(\theta\) grows, while the second tends to \(-1/2\): as every \(P_i \to 1\), \(1 - 2P_i \to -1\) and \(J \to -I\). As \(\theta\) falls, the first term tends to \(I\), the number of items, and the second to \(+1/2\). The left-hand side is positive at the bottom of the scale and negative at the top, so it has a root: the WLE is finite. Magis and Verhelst (2017) prove this for every response pattern under the one- to four-parameter logistic models.
The EAP and MAP stay finite. With a normal prior, the log posterior is \(\ell(\theta) - (\theta - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) plus a constant. The first term is bounded above by 0 and the second falls without limit, so the log posterior has a maximum (the MAP). The posterior is a bounded function times a normal density, so it has a finite mean (the EAP).
Why it matters later. Joint maximum likelihood, which estimates items and respondents together, has to set perfect patterns aside before it starts (Estimating item parameters). An adaptive test estimates \(\theta\) after one or two items, when all-correct patterns are the rule (Item banks and adaptive testing). And a reported score has to say something about everyone at the ceiling (What does a score mean?).





Bring in a prior: the EAP estimate
The likelihood lesson set aside the Bayesian reading, in which \(\theta\) gets a prior distribution, \(g(\theta)\), and the data turn it into a posterior, \[p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{L(\theta \mid \mathbf{x})\,g(\theta)}{\int L(t \mid \mathbf{x})\,g(t)\,dt}.\] For ability, the natural prior is the distribution of \(\theta\) in the respondent’s population, which mirt estimates with the items (a normal with mean 0 and an SD fixed at 1 or estimated). The expected a posteriori (EAP) estimate is the posterior mean, and its standard error is the posterior SD (Bock & Mislevy, 1982). The integral needs no closed form: evaluate likelihood × prior at nodes \(t_1, \dots, t_Q\) and average, \[\hat\theta_{\text{EAP}} = \frac{\sum_q t_q\,L(t_q)\,g(t_q)}{\sum_q L(t_q)\,g(t_q)}.\] Nothing iterates and nothing fails: a normal prior times a bounded likelihood always has a mean, even when the likelihood never peaks. The posterior’s peak is the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate, also called Bayes modal (Mislevy, 1986).

Try it: prior × likelihood = posterior
The ten Wordsum items analysed below, with their Rasch difficulties. Choose a sum score and the prior’s SD (the fitted value is 1.88); each curve is scaled to a peak of 1.


Code
viewof pp_r = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 9, step: 1, label: "Sum score (of 10)"})
viewof pp_sd = Inputs.range([0.3, 4], {value: 1.88, step: 0.01, label: "Prior SD"})


















Code
pp = posteriorR(pp_r, wsB, 0, pp_sd, grid(-7, 7, 561))
pp_ll = pp.nodes.map(t => logLikR(t, pp_r, wsB))
pp_llmax = Math.max(...pp_ll)
pp_pmax = Math.max(...pp.post)
pp_data = pp.nodes.flatMap((t, k) => [
  {theta: t, y: Math.exp(pp_ll[k] - pp_llmax), curve: "Likelihood"},
  {theta: t, y: Math.exp(-0.5 * (t / pp_sd) ** 2), curve: "Prior"},
  {theta: t, y: pp.post[k] / pp_pmax, curve: "Posterior"}])
pp_mle = mleR(pp_r, wsB)
pp_map = mapR(pp_r, wsB, 0, pp_sd)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-7, 7]}, y: {label: "Scaled to a peak of 1", domain: [0, 1.05]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Prior", "Likelihood", "Posterior"], range: [palette.guide, palette.light, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(pp_data, {x: "theta", y: "y", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    ...(Number.isFinite(pp_mle) ? [Plot.ruleX([pp_mle], {stroke: palette.light, strokeDasharray: "4,3"})] : []),
    Plot.ruleX([pp.eap], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})




























































Code
md`Sum score ${pp_r} of 10. MLE: **${Number.isFinite(pp_mle) ? pp_mle.toFixed(2) : (pp_mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞")}**${Number.isFinite(pp_mle) ? ` (SE ${seR(pp_mle, wsB).toFixed(2)}; dashed line)` : " (no peak)"}. MAP: **${pp_map.toFixed(2)}**. EAP: **${pp.eap.toFixed(2)}** (posterior SD ${pp.psd.toFixed(2)}; solid line).`







At a score of 9 the MLE is 2.55, the MAP 1.95 and the EAP 2.08: the prior pulls about half a logit toward 0. At 10 the likelihood never falls, yet the posterior has a peak (2.83) and a mean (3.05). With a prior SD of 1 the EAP for a score of 9 is 1.34; with 4 it is 2.66, just beyond the MLE, as the posterior is skewed toward the open end. At a score of 6 the EAP stays within about 0.1 of the MLE at any prior SD. That pull toward the prior mean is shrinkage, largest where the likelihood is flattest: at the ends of the scale, and on short tests.


Try it: shrinkage by score, and by test length
Estimates for every score on the Wordsum items. “Test length” repeats the ten items (40 items is four copies of each); the horizontal axis is the proportion correct.


Code
viewof sh_k = Inputs.radio(new Map([["10 items", 1], ["20 items", 2], ["40 items", 4]]), {value: 1, label: "Test length"})
viewof sh_sd = Inputs.range([0.5, 4], {value: 1.88, step: 0.01, label: "Prior SD"})


















Code
sh_b = Array.from({length: sh_k}, () => wsB).flat()
sh_n = sh_b.length
sh_rows = Array.from({length: sh_n + 1}, (_, r) => ({r, prop: r / sh_n, mle: mleR(r, sh_b), wle: wleR(r, sh_b), eap: posteriorR(r, sh_b, 0, sh_sd).eap}))
sh_long = sh_rows.flatMap(d => [
  ...(Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? [{prop: d.prop, est: d.mle, which: "MLE"}] : []),
  {prop: d.prop, est: d.wle, which: "WLE"}, {prop: d.prop, est: d.eap, which: "EAP"}])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "Proportion correct", domain: [0, 1]}, y: {label: "Estimate of θ", domain: [-6, 6]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["MLE", "WLE", "EAP"], range: [palette.light, palette.guide, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(sh_long, {x: "prop", y: "est", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(sh_long, {x: "prop", y: "est", fill: "which", r: sh_k === 1 ? 4 : 2.5})
  ]
})







































Code
sh_90 = sh_rows[Math.round(0.9 * sh_n)]
md`At 90% correct (${sh_90.r} of ${sh_n}): MLE **${sh_90.mle.toFixed(2)}**, WLE ${sh_90.wle.toFixed(2)}, EAP **${sh_90.eap.toFixed(2)}**. At 100%: no MLE, WLE ${sh_rows[sh_n].wle.toFixed(2)}, EAP ${sh_rows[sh_n].eap.toFixed(2)}.`
















The MLE at 90% correct is 2.55 whatever the length, because repeating every item multiplies both sides of the score equation by the same number. The EAP moves toward it as the test grows, from 2.08 with 10 items to 2.42 with 40, as the likelihood sharpens. The WLE, taken up below, sits nearer the MLE and gives a perfect score a finite value (3.59 with 10 items).
Shrinkage carries into anything computed from the estimates. If you’ve done Model fit and out-of-sample prediction, it is why outfit computed from mirt’s default EAP abilities averaged about 0.9 on simulated 20-item data where the model was true.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two respondents each answer 90% of their items correctly, one on a 10-item test and one on a 40-item version with four copies of each item. Both are scored by EAP with the same prior. Whose estimate is pulled further toward the prior mean?",
  options: [
    {text: "The respondent on the 10-item test", correct: true, why: "With fewer items the likelihood is flatter, so the prior carries more weight in the posterior. In the widget, the EAP at 90% correct is 2.08 with 10 items and 2.42 with 40, against an MLE of 2.55 for both."},
    {text: "The respondent on the 40-item test, since more items give the prior more to work with", correct: false, why: "The prior is the same in both cases; what changes is the likelihood. Forty items give a sharper likelihood, which outweighs the prior."},
    {text: "Neither: the same proportion correct gives the same estimate", correct: false, why: "That's true of the MLE here, whose score equation scales with the number of items. The EAP also depends on how sharp the likelihood is."}
  ]
})










MAP, EAP and plausible values
The MAP sits close to the EAP; it is found by Newton–Raphson with the prior adding a term to the score equation, and suits software that finds modes more easily than means. If the prior describes the population, the EAP has the smallest mean squared error averaged over that population, since squared error is what a posterior mean minimizes; shrinkage is the other side of that coin.
No individual estimate carries the spread of \(\theta\) itself (EAPs vary too little, MLEs too much), so variances, correlations and regressions built on them are off. Large-scale assessments such as NAEP use plausible values (Mislevy, 1991; Mislevy, Beaton, Kaplan & Sheehan, 1992): several random draws from each respondent’s posterior, under a prior that is a regression of \(\theta\) on background variables. Each set has the spread and group differences of \(\theta\); the analysis is run on each and combined as in multiple imputation. They are a tool for population quantities, not scores to report for individuals (Wu, 2005). What does a score mean? takes them up in full.


The weighted likelihood estimate
What if we want an estimate that borrows nothing from the population but exists for every pattern? Warm (1989) weights the likelihood by a function of \(\theta\) chosen to cancel the leading term of the MLE’s bias, the bias that Lord (1983) derives. This adds \(J(\theta)/2I(\theta)\) to the score equation (the Go deeper callout writes it out). The WLE has the MLE’s large-sample variance, less bias, and a finite value for every pattern (Magis & Verhelst, 2017). It is Firth’s (1993) bias reduction, which penalizes the likelihood by the Jeffreys prior and also gives finite logistic regressions under separation (Heinze & Schemper, 2002); for the Rasch model and 2PL the WLE is the peak of the likelihood times that prior, while under the 3PL the two part (Magis & Raîche, 2012).
How does it compare? Warm’s Monte Carlo studies favoured it over the MLE and Bayes modal estimates on several criteria across a wide range of abilities, and Kim and Nicewander (1993) found the WLE, MAP and EAP all close to unbiased where the test’s items are. That is the evidence: less bias than the MLE at the same variance, and finiteness, not optimality in general. The cost is the EAP’s lower error. The WLE doesn’t shrink, so in the simulation below its RMSE is 0.77 against the EAP’s 0.61, and its SD 1.28 against a true 1. It suits estimates that must not depend on a population prior, as when respondents come from different populations.


Sufficiency, revisited






Recall from The Rasch model: under the Rasch model the sum score \(r\) is sufficient for \(\theta\). The likelihood factorizes into \(e^{r\theta}\), times a term free of \(\theta\), over a term free of the pattern.



Every estimator here uses the responses only through the likelihood, so under the Rasch model every one depends on them only through \(r\): the score equations contain the data only as \(r\), and in the posterior the pattern’s own factor cancels. Ten Wordsum items give eleven possible EAPs, which is how the widgets above could list every estimate.






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL: under the 2PL the likelihood depends on the pattern only through the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\), which is therefore sufficient; the score equation is \(\sum_i a_i (x_i - P_i) = 0\).



So respondents with the same sum score but different items right get different estimates, ordered by \(\sum_i a_i x_i\).






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL, its Go deeper callout: under the 3PL the weight of each correct answer depends on \(\theta\), so no simple statistic is sufficient. There an estimate depends on the whole pattern, not on a weighted sum.





Code
quiz({
  q: "Under a 2PL, two respondents each answer 5 of 10 items correctly, and one gets a higher EAP than the other. What can you say about their responses?",
  options: [
    {text: "The one with the higher EAP answered items with larger total slope correctly", correct: true, why: "Under the 2PL the posterior depends on the pattern only through $\\sum_i a_i x_i$, and the EAP increases with it. Same sum score, different weighted score."},
    {text: "The one with the higher EAP answered harder items correctly", correct: false, why: "Difficulty enters the likelihood only in a term without $\\theta$, which cancels in the posterior. What matters is the slopes of the items answered correctly."},
    {text: "Nothing: EAPs contain random error", correct: false, why: "An EAP is a fixed function of the pattern, the item parameters and the prior. Two patterns with the same weighted score get the same EAP."}
  ]
})

title: Estimating abilities: MLE and EAP
text:
Simulate
Which estimator lands closest to the truth? The code below simulates Rasch responses to ten items (\(b\) from −2 to 2) from 5,000 respondents in two groups whose means differ by 1 (overall mean 0, SD 1), estimates every \(\theta\) four ways with the difficulties known and a normal(0, 1) prior, and reports bias and root mean squared error (RMSE) by true \(\theta\), the SD of the estimates and the group difference. It is base R and runs in a second.
With the seed as written, 112 of the 5,000 respondents (2.2%) have no finite MLE, and optimize() on a perfect score returns 10, its upper bound. The MLE and WLE are close to unbiased across the middle; the EAP and MAP are pulled toward 0, by about 0.16 within one SD of the mean, 0.5 one to two SDs out, and 1 beyond. In return the EAP’s RMSE is 0.52 in the middle, against 0.78 to 0.80 for the MLE, and 0.61 overall against 0.79 (without the 112). At the ends the order reverses. The SDs are 1.26 (MLE) and 0.80 (EAP) against a true 1, and the group difference is 0.98 (MLE), 1.03 (WLE) and 0.65 (EAP). With length.out at 20 or 40, the EAP’s group difference rises to 0.80 and 0.89.

title: Estimating abilities: MLE and EAP
text:
With real data
Our main example is c19prc_uk_mcbride_2021_wordsum: the Wordsum vocabulary test as answered by 2,058 UK adults in the sixth wave of the COVID-19 Psychological Research Consortium study (Bentall et al., 2022; the study’s design is described by McBride et al., 2021). Wordsum is the ten-item vocabulary test of the US General Social Survey, drawn from Thorndike (1942) and analysed with item response theory by Cor, Haertel, Krosnick and Malhotra (2012): for each target word, choose the closest in meaning from five words, or “don’t know”. Its job here is to be a short test on which many respondents reach the floor or the ceiling. A response is 1 for the right word and 0 otherwise, “don’t know” included. Download the code to run every chunk yourself; it needs mirt (Chalmers, 2012).


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with a
# CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
ws_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_4:v7_0.c19prc_uk_mcbride_2021_wordsum/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(ws_url)
table(df$wave)   # one wave (6), so one response per respondent and item

20580

# resp is 1 when the respondent chose the listed word closest in meaning to the target
# word, and 0 for any other choice, including "don't know".
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
wide <- as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
c(respondents = nrow(wide), items = ncol(wide), complete = sum(complete.cases(wide)))

# The Rasch model. mirt fixes every slope at 1 and the mean ability at 0, and

m <- mirt(wide, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)

# Four estimators. Under the Rasch model each is a function of the sum score alone,
# so one row per score says everything (the last line checks it).
meth <- c("ML", "WLE", "MAP", "EAP")
est <- lapply(meth, function(k) fscores(m, method = k, full.scores.SE = TRUE))

Each estimator gives one value per sum score (the largest spread within a score is 0). In the middle they nearly agree: a score of 5 gives −0.57 (MLE), −0.60 (WLE), −0.48 (MAP) and −0.47 (EAP). They part at the ends. A score of 9 gives 2.55, 2.26, 1.95 and 2.07, and a score of 10 gives \(+\infty\), 3.59, 2.83 and 3.03. The MLE’s standard error is 0.79 at a score of 4 and 1.13 at 9; the posterior SDs are smaller everywhere.


Code
# The ML standard error is 1 / sqrt(test information) at the estimate.
fin <- is.finite(ml[, "F1"])
all.equal(unname(ml[fin, "SE_F1"]), 1 / sqrt(testinfo(m, ml[fin, "F1", drop = FALSE])),
          tolerance = 1e-4)


[1] TRUE


mirt’s MLE standard errors are \(1/\sqrt{I(\hat\theta)}\), the test information evaluated at each estimate (all.equal returns TRUE).


Code
# EAPs are pulled toward the mean: their SD is below the model's SD of ability.
# The posterior variances make up the difference.
eap <- est$EAP
sd_model <- sqrt(coef(m)$GroupPars[, "COV_11"])
round(c(sd_model = sd_model, sd_eap = sd(eap[, "F1"]), sd_wle = sd(est$WLE[, "F1"])), 2)

# The 2PL. Now the weighted score sum(a * x) carries the information about theta,
# so respondents with the same sum score can get different estimates.
m2 <- mirt(wide, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
c(BIC_Rasch = round(extract.mirt(m, "BIC")), BIC_2PL = round(extract.mirt(m2, "BIC")))

  patterns = nrow(unique(wide[five, ])),
  weighted_scores = length(unique(round(w[five], 6))),
  EAPs = length(unique(round(eap2[five], 6))),

BIC (Schwarz, 1978) prefers the 2PL to the Rasch model (19,398 against 19,887), and the slopes run from 1.09 to 5.20. The 282 respondents with a score of 5 gave 40 different response patterns, which have 40 different weighted scores and get 40 different EAPs, from −1.05 to −0.04, in exactly the order of their weighted scores (rank correlation 1). Under the Rasch model all 282 shared one EAP, −0.47: a full logit of difference among respondents with the same number right comes from the choice of model.

Which estimate to report
The choice rests on what we’ll assume and on what the numbers are for.

The MLE and WLE assume nothing about the population: the estimate comes from the respondent’s own responses, which suits comparisons across populations. The price is noise: on Wordsum the MLE’s standard errors run from 0.79 to 1.13, and 12% of respondents have no MLE.
The EAP and MAP assume the respondent comes from the population the prior describes. If so, they are closer to the truth on average (in the simulation, an RMSE of 0.61 against 0.79). The price is shrinkage toward that population’s mean, largest at the ends and on short tests, which carries into spreads and group differences.

When I report a score to an individual from a test like this one, I report the EAP with its posterior SD, and I say that it is pulled toward the mean of the population the prior describes. It always exists, it is the most accurate on average for the people the test was given to, and its standard error grows where the items run out. What I don’t do is average EAPs to compare groups: the simulation’s group difference of 1 came back as 0.65. The MLEs and WLEs came closer, but they vary too much for spreads and correlations. If a prior is unwelcome, say because respondents come from different populations, I’d use the WLE rather than the MLE, which loses everyone at the floor and the ceiling. For group questions I’d put the groups into the model, or use plausible values. And if the Rasch model fits and everyone took the same items, The Rasch model has already argued for the sum score: every estimator in the table above is a relabelling of it.

title: Estimating abilities: MLE and EAP
text:
Problems

Three items by hand. For Rasch items with \(b = -1, 0, 1.5\), plot the likelihood of 1-1-0. At what \(\theta\) does 1-1-0 become more likely than 1-0-0, and why is that a difficulty? (PS4#1)
The Rasch score equation. Show that the Rasch MLE solves \(\sum_i P_i(\theta) = r\). Then use the factorization from the Rasch lesson’s Go deeper callout to show that the EAP depends on the pattern only through \(r\) too.
Change the prior. Rescore Wordsum by EAP with a prior SD of 1 instead of 1.88 (fscores(m, method = "EAP", mean = 0, cov = 1)). Which respondents move most? What happens to the SD of the EAPs, and why?
Classroom averages. A school compares classroom means of students’ EAPs from a 15-item test, with one normal prior for everyone. What goes wrong, in which direction, and what would you report instead?
Does EAP reduce error? Extend the simulation: 1,000 respondents at each true \(\theta\) from −3 to 3 in steps of 0.5. Where does the EAP’s RMSE beat the MLE’s, and where not? Then score normal(0, 1) respondents with a prior of mean 1. What changes? (PS5#2)
Challenge (open): the floor and the ceiling. A survey analyst wants Wordsum as a predictor of, say, trust in science. What should they do with the 251 respondents at 0 or 10: drop them, use WLEs, EAPs or plausible values, or fit the regression inside the item response model? Does it depend on the question? I don’t think there is a single answer; make the case for yours.
