Going further

Bock, R. D., & Mislevy, R. J. (1982). Adaptive EAP estimation of ability in a microcomputer environment. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 431–444. https://doi.org/10.1177/014662168200600405. The EAP estimate on a grid of nodes, and its posterior SD as a standard error.
Warm, T. A. (1989). Weighted likelihood estimation of ability in item response theory. Psychometrika, 54(3), 427–450. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02294627. The WLE, compared with the MLE and Bayes modal estimates.
Magis, D., & Verhelst, N. (2017). On the finiteness of the weighted likelihood estimator of ability. Psychometrika, 82(3), 637–647. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9518-9. The WLE is finite for every pattern under the 1PL to 4PL and many polytomous models.
Magis, D., & Raîche, G. (2012). On the relationships between Jeffreys modal and weighted likelihood estimation of ability under logistic IRT models. Psychometrika, 77(1), 163–169. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-011-9233-5. Where the WLE and the Jeffreys-prior mode coincide, and where they part.
Firth, D. (1993). Bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimates. Biometrika, 80(1), 27–38. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/80.1.27. The general form of Warm’s correction.
Heinze, G., & Schemper, M. (2002). A solution to the problem of separation in logistic regression. Statistics in Medicine, 21(16), 2409–2419. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.1047. Firth’s correction as a fix for separation, the logistic-regression version of perfect patterns.
Kim, J. K., & Nicewander, W. A. (1993). Ability estimation for conventional tests. Psychometrika, 58(4), 587–599. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02294829. Five estimators compared for bias, standard error and reliability.
Lord, F. M. (1983). Unbiased estimators of ability parameters, of their variance, and of their parallel-forms reliability. Psychometrika, 48(2), 233–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294018. The bias of the MLE, and estimators without it.
Mislevy, R. J. (1986). Bayes modal estimation in item response models. Psychometrika, 51(2), 177–195. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02293979. Priors in item response models.
Mislevy, R. J. (1991). Randomization-based inference about latent variables from complex samples. Psychometrika, 56(2), 177–196. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02294457. Plausible values as multiple imputation, with NAEP data.
Mislevy, R. J., Beaton, A. E., Kaplan, B., & Sheehan, K. M. (1992). Estimating population characteristics from sparse matrix samples of item responses. Journal of Educational Measurement, 29(2), 133–161. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1992.tb00371.x. Plausible values, from the concepts to NAEP.
Wu, M. (2005). The role of plausible values in large-scale surveys. Studies in Educational Evaluation, 31(2–3), 114–128. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stueduc.2005.05.005. Plausible values and individual estimates, side by side.
Baker, F. B., & Kim, S.-H. (2004). Item response theory: Parameter estimation techniques (2nd ed.). Marcel Dekker. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781482276725. Newton–Raphson for abilities, and the rest of the machinery, step by step.

Albert, A., & Anderson, J. A. (1984). On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models. Biometrika, 71(1), 1–10. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/71.1.1. Separation, of which perfect patterns are an instance.
Andersen, E. B. (1977). Sufficient statistics and latent trait models. Psychometrika, 42(1), 69–81. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293746. Why only the Rasch model makes the sum score sufficient.

Social Science Research, 41(5), 1003–1016. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssresearch.2012.05.007. Wordsum analysed with item response theory.
Thorndike, R. L. (1942). Two screening tests of verbal intelligence. Journal of Applied Psychology, 26(2), 128–135. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0060053. Where the Wordsum items come from.

International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research, 30(1), e1861. https://doi.org/10.1002/mpr.1861. The study that gave Wordsum to these respondents.

title: Psychometrics with the IRW: course map
text:
Why psychometrics?
Much of what we want to know about people hinges on attributes we cannot observe directly: how a child’s executive functioning changes with age, whether an intervention reduces anxiety, how reading develops across school. What we observe instead are responses to items: a tap on the correct arrow, “most days” on a survey, a wrong answer to question 7. Psychometrics is the discipline that turns those responses into measurements and tells us how far to trust them.
Consider a ruler. It measures a child’s height regardless of that child’s background; a different ruler gives a reading with the same meaning; and a well-chosen ruler measures quickly across the whole range of heights we care about. Psychological measures rarely do all of this, but the ruler suggests what to aim for (Domingue, 2026):

Measurements should be insensitive to differences in attributes other than the one being measured.
Measurements from different instruments should be comparable.
Measurement should deliver precise information about the attribute as quickly as possible.

None of these comes for free. Suppose we measure executive functioning with a tablet task. Children with less tablet experience may look worse for reasons that have nothing to do with executive functioning. The task that suits a four-year-old is not the one that suits a ten-year-old, yet we want to talk about growth across those ages. And time with a child is short, so every item has to earn its place. Psychometrics has tools for each problem: checking whether items work the same way across groups (Differential item functioning), putting scores from different forms on a common scale (Linking and equating), and choosing items to fit the respondent (Item banks and adaptive testing).
The common thread is a probabilistic model for how people respond to items. Such a model can be falsified, so we can interrogate whether it works in a given setting; when it does, it gives a compact description of how an instrument functions, one that can be reused with new people, new forms and new ages.
Psychological measurement is hard, and whether it deserves the name “measurement” at all has been argued over for most of a century (What is measurement?). Interval scales do not come easily (Scale properties). But the limits of our measures are limits on what we can learn about the attributes themselves. Psychometrics is how we find out where those limits are, and how we push them back.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
What this is for
The Rasch model gives every item the same slope, and the chess data have already turned up an item that doesn’t go along: problem Y15, about as hard as Y29, whose success barely moves with skill. What happens when each item gets its own slope, and then its own floor and ceiling? This lesson builds that family, from the 1PL to the 4PL, asks what each new parameter costs and what the data can say about it, and fits all four to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test. For that test my choice is the 2PL, and most of the lesson is the case for it.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Core ideas

One family of curves
One formula covers every model here. For person \(j\) and item \(i\), \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = c_i + (u_i - c_i)\,\frac{\exp\big(a_i(\theta_j - b_i)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a_i(\theta_j - b_i)\big)}.\]

\(b_i\) is the item’s difficulty, its location on the \(\theta\) scale.
\(a_i\) is its slope or discrimination: how quickly the probability rises as \(\theta\) passes \(b_i\).
\(c_i\) is the lower asymptote, the probability of success at very low ability; on multiple-choice items it is called the guessing parameter.
\(u_i\) is the upper asymptote; below 1, even the strongest respondents sometimes miss (a “slip”).

“PL” stands for “parameter logistic”, and the number counts the free item parameters. The Rasch model, a 1PL, frees only \(b\) (\(a = 1\), \(c = 0\), \(u = 1\)). The 2PL frees \(a\) and the 3PL frees \(c\) as well, both from Birnbaum’s chapters in Lord & Novick (1968). The 4PL frees \(u\) too (Barton & Lord, 1981; Loken & Rulison, 2010).

Try it: four parameters


Code
viewof f_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof f_a = Inputs.range([0.1, 4], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a"})
viewof f_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "Lower asymptote c"})
viewof f_u = Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "Upper asymptote u"})
































Code
f_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, f_b, 1), curve: "Rasch (a = 1, c = 0, u = 1)"},
  {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, f_b, f_a, f_c, f_u), curve: "This item"}])
f_mid = (f_c + f_u) / 2
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Rasch (a = 1, c = 0, u = 1)", "This item"], range: [palette.light, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([f_c, f_u], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([f_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(f_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: f_b, p: f_mid}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})

























Code
md`At θ = b = ${f_b.toFixed(1)} this item's probability is **${f_mid.toFixed(2)}**, halfway between the two asymptotes (dashed). ${f_c === 0 && f_u === 1 ? "With c = 0 and u = 1 that is 0.5, as in the Rasch model." : "It is no longer 0.5."}`







Move \(a\) and the curve pivots around \(b\); near zero it is almost flat. Raising \(c\) lifts the floor, and lowering \(u\) (the last slider) drops the ceiling. The point at \(\theta = b\) always sits halfway between the asymptotes, so once \(c > 0\) or \(u < 1\), difficulty no longer means “the ability at which the probability is 0.5”.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A 3PL item has $c = 0.2$ (and $u = 1$). What is the probability of a correct response for a person with $\\theta = b$?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.6", correct: true, why: "At $\\theta = b$ the logistic part is 0.5, so the probability is $c + (1 - c)(0.5) = 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6$, halfway between 0.2 and 1."},
    {text: "0.5", correct: false, why: "That holds when $c = 0$ and $u = 1$. With a floor at 0.2, the midpoint of the curve moves up to $(0.2 + 1)/2$."},
    {text: "0.7", correct: false, why: "That would be $c + 0.5$. The logistic part is scaled by $(1 - c)$ before it is added to $c$."}
  ]
})







Four items, with different values of all four parameters:


Code
vq_items = [
  {item: "A", a: 1.0, b: -1.0, c: 0.00, u: 1.00, lx: -1.0, off: 0.07},
  {item: "B", a: 2.0, b: 0.5, c: 0.25, u: 1.00, lx: -3.3, off: 0.05},
  {item: "C", a: 1.5, b: -0.5, c: 0.00, u: 0.75, lx: 2.6, off: -0.07},
  {item: "D", a: 0.7, b: 0.0, c: 0.00, u: 1.00, lx: 3.6, off: -0.07}]
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["A", "B", "C", "D"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink, palette.guide]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0, 1], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(vq_items.flatMap(d => grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, p: p4pl(t, d.b, d.a, d.c, d.u), item: d.item}))),
      {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.text(vq_items, {x: "lx", y: d => p4pl(d.lx, d.b, d.a, d.c, d.u) + d.off, text: "item", fill: "item", fontWeight: "bold", fontSize: 14})
  ]
})


















Code
quiz({
  q: "Which item has an upper asymptote $u$ below 1: one that even the strongest respondents sometimes miss?",
  options: [
    {text: "B", correct: false, why: "B's peculiarity is at the other end: its curve never falls below about 0.25 on the left, a lower asymptote $c > 0$. On the right it reaches 1."},
    {text: "D", correct: false, why: "D rises slowly (a small slope $a$), but it is still climbing at θ = 4 and heads for 1. A slow curve is not a low ceiling."},
    {text: "C", correct: true, why: "Its curve flattens out near 0.75 at the right of the plot, while the others keep heading for 1: $u \\approx 0.75$."},
    {text: "A", correct: false, why: "A is an ordinary Rasch-like curve: it runs from 0 to 1, rising at an average rate."}
  ]
})










What slopes cost: sufficiency and crossing curves






Recall from The Rasch model: under the Rasch model the sum score \(r\) is sufficient for \(\theta\): patterns with the same sum score share an ability estimate. That lesson’s widget broke this by switching to a 2PL.



What takes the sum score’s place under the 2PL? Write out one person’s likelihood, as the Rasch lesson’s Go deeper callout did: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_i \frac{\exp\big(x_i a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)} = \frac{\exp\big(\theta \sum_i a_i x_i\big)\,\exp\big(-\sum_i a_i b_i x_i\big)}{\prod_i \big(1 + \exp(a_i(\theta - b_i))\big)}.\] The data meet \(\theta\) only through the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\), so under the 2PL it is sufficient (Birnbaum, 1968). A correct answer counts in proportion to its item’s slope. The weights are estimated item parameters, though; Andersen (1977) showed that a sufficient statistic free of the item parameters exists only under the Rasch model. Under the 3PL the lower asymptote spoils the factorization, and no simple statistic is sufficient.

Try it: which patterns share an estimate?
Five items (\(b\) from −1.5 to 1.5; slopes 1, 2, 1, 1, 2). Pick a pattern; the table lists every pattern with the same sum score or weighted score, and each one’s maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\theta\) under the model you choose (in the 3PL, every \(c = 0.2\)).


Code
ws_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
ws_a = [1, 2, 1, 1, 2]
ws_labels = ws_b.map((b, i) => `Item ${i + 1} (b = ${b}, a = ${ws_a[i]})`.replace("-", "−"))
viewof ws_x = Inputs.checkbox(ws_labels, {label: "Correct on", value: [ws_labels[1]]})
viewof ws_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch", "2PL", "3PL (c = 0.2)"], {value: "2PL", label: "Model"})







































Code
ws_pattern = ws_labels.map(l => ws_x.includes(l) ? 1 : 0)
ws_w = x => x.reduce((s, v, i) => s + v * ws_a[i], 0)
ws_est = x => ws_model === "Rasch" ? mle4(x, ws_b) :
  ws_model === "2PL" ? mle4(x, ws_b, ws_a) : mle4(x, ws_b, ws_a, ws_b.map(() => 0.2))
ws_sum = ws_pattern.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0)
ws_rows = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].flatMap(s => patternsWithSum(5, s))
  .filter(x => x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) === ws_sum || ws_w(x) === ws_w(ws_pattern))
  .map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), "sum score": x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0), "weighted score": ws_w(x), mle: ws_est(x)}))
  .sort((p, q) => p["weighted score"] - q["weighted score"] || q["sum score"] - p["sum score"])
Inputs.table(ws_rows.map(d => ({...d, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞"),
  "": d.pattern === ws_pattern.join("") ? "← yours" : ""})), {columns: ["pattern", "sum score", "weighted score", "MLE of θ", ""], layout: "auto", rows: 14})












































With the default pattern (only item 2 right) and the 2PL, five patterns have a weighted score of 2: 01000, 00001 and the three pairs of slope-1 items, such as 10100. All five share an estimate, −0.75, whether their sum score is 1 or 2, while 10000, with the same sum score as yours, sits at −1.55. Switch to Rasch and the grouping goes back to the sum score. Switch to the 3PL and neither score is enough: the five patterns now spread from −1.09 down to −∞, since a lone correct answer is best explained as a lucky guess.






Recall from The Rasch model: specific objectivity asks that comparisons between items not depend on who takes them. With equal slopes, curves never cross, so one item is easier than another for everyone.



Give two items different slopes and their curves cross where \(a_1(\theta - b_1) = a_2(\theta - b_2)\): below that point one item is easier, above it the other. The 2PL buys its better description of items by giving up specific objectivity, and the chess data below show a crossing where most players sit.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under a 2PL, respondent A answers only one item correctly, with slope $a = 2$. Respondent B answers two items correctly, each with slope $a = 1$. Both took the same items and answered all of them. How do their ability estimates compare?",
  options: [
    {text: "They are equal", correct: true, why: "Both have a weighted score $\\sum_i a_i x_i = 2$, and under the 2PL the weighted score is sufficient. Which items they got right, and how many, doesn't matter beyond that."},
    {text: "B's is higher: B got more items right", correct: false, why: "That's the Rasch model's answer, where the sum score is sufficient. Under the 2PL each correct answer is weighted by its item's slope."},
    {text: "It depends on the items' difficulties", correct: false, why: "The difficulties enter the likelihood, but only in a term that doesn't involve $\\theta$. The estimate depends on the pattern only through the weighted score."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: the weighted score under the 2PL, and why the 3PL has none





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the item parameters are known. Write \(L_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(a_i(\theta - b_i))\).
2PL. The factorization in the main text puts \(\theta\) and the data together only in \(\exp(\theta \sum_i a_i x_i)\), so by the factorization theorem \(t = \sum_i a_i x_i\) is sufficient. The score equation says the same thing: differentiating the log likelihood, \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\,(x_i - L_i) = t - \sum_i a_i L_i,\] so the MLE solves \(\sum_i a_i L_i(\theta) = t\), which involves the data only through \(t\). Conditioning on \(t\) removes \(\theta\), just as conditioning on \(r\) did for the Rasch model. It buys little here: with slopes that are real numbers, nearly every pattern has its own weighted score, so the conditional distribution given \(t\) usually has one pattern in it and nothing to estimate from.
3PL. Now \(P_i = c_i + (1 - c_i) L_i\), and \(\partial P_i/\partial\theta = a_i (P_i - c_i)(1 - P_i)/(1 - c_i)\). The same calculation gives \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\,(x_i - P_i)\,\frac{P_i - c_i}{P_i\,(1 - c_i)}.\] With \(c_i = 0\) the last fraction is 1 and we’re back to the 2PL. With \(c_i > 0\) it is a weight that depends on \(\theta\): near 1 for a person well above the item, near 0 for a person well below it, where a correct answer is mostly chance. Each correct answer’s weight therefore changes with the ability at which it is evaluated, and no single function of the pattern carries all the information about \(\theta\). That is the widget’s 3PL result: a lone correct answer can leave the estimate at the bottom of the scale.






Reading mirt, and what fixes the scale
mirt (Chalmers, 2012) writes these models with an intercept, \(\Pr(x = 1) = g + (u - g)\,\text{logit}^{-1}(a\theta + d)\); its g is our \(c\) and its u is our \(u\). Matching \(a\theta + d\) with \(a(\theta - b)\) gives \(b = -d/a\), the conversion every chunk below uses. When \(a\) is near 0, that ratio can be enormous, as the chess data will show.
What fixes the unit of \(\theta\)? The model only sees \(a(\theta - b)\), so multiplying every \(\theta\) and \(b\) by \(k\) and dividing every \(a\) by \(k\) changes no probability. The unit is a convention the software sets, as the origin was (The Rasch model): the Rasch fit fixes the slopes at 1 and estimates the SD of \(\theta\); the 2PL fixes that SD at 1. A Rasch fit and a 1PL with one common, estimated slope are then the same model reporting different \(a\) and \(b\). That matters when reading output or comparing numbers across fits, the problem Linking and equating takes up, but it says nothing about the data.


What the lower asymptote needs
The lower asymptote describes people far below an item’s difficulty. If few respondents are down there, the data say little about it, and a 2PL, with a lower slope and a shifted difficulty, can imitate a 3PL where the respondents are.

Try it: can a 2PL stand in for a 3PL?


Code
viewof la_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "The 3PL's lower asymptote c"})
viewof la_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability, relative to the item (b = 0)"})


















Code
la_th = grid(la_mu - 3.5, la_mu + 3.5, 141)
la_w = la_th.map(t => dnorm(t, la_mu, 1))
la_fit = closest2pl(t => p4pl(t, 0, 1.2, la_c), la_th, la_w)
la_dens = la_th.map((t, k) => ({theta: t, d: la_w[k] / dnorm(0) * 0.35}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["3PL (a = 1.2, b = 0)", "Closest 2PL"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(la_dens.filter(d => d.theta >= -5 && d.theta <= 5), {x: "theta", y: "d", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.line(grid(-5, 5).flatMap(t => [
      {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, 0, 1.2, la_c), curve: "3PL (a = 1.2, b = 0)"},
      {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, la_fit.b, la_fit.a), curve: "Closest 2PL"}]), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Closest 2PL, weighting by where respondents are (shaded): a = ${la_fit.a.toFixed(2)}, b = ${la_fit.b.toFixed(2)}. Over the middle 95% of respondents the two curves never differ by more than **${la_fit.maxDiff.toFixed(3)}**.`







As the widget loads, mean ability is 1.5, so the item is easy for most respondents. The curves differ by at most about 0.01 where respondents are, parting only to the left, where almost nobody is. Slide the mean ability down to −2 and the largest difference grows eight-fold, to 0.08: now many respondents sit near the floor, and the floor matters.
Domingue et al. (2024) looked at this through prediction. They simulated data from the 3PL and asked how much better a fitted 3PL predicted new responses than a fitted 2PL, using the IMV, a measure of predictive gain that Model fit and out-of-sample prediction teaches. The average gain never exceeded 0.001, even with pronounced guessing in the generating model, and across 89 IRW datasets it averaged 0.00016. They connect this to the difficulty of identifying the 3PL’s parameters (Maris & Bechger, 2009; Haberman, 2005; von Davier, 2009), noting that 3PL estimates may still flag items with guessing problems. A 3PL is a reasonable choice when the items are multiple choice, when a good share of respondents sits near chance, when the sample is large, or when \(c\) is fixed or given a prior, as in Guessing and priors.



The upper asymptote: ceilings and slips
What does \(u < 1\) mean? That respondents far above an item’s difficulty still sometimes miss it: through carelessness, a slip, or an item harder than it looks for experts. Barton and Lord (1981) added the upper asymptote to the 3PL in an ETS report; Loken and Rulison (2010) estimated the 4PL with Bayesian methods and applied it to a delinquency scale.
The ceiling mirrors the floor: estimating \(u\) needs many respondents far above the item, missing it now and then. Most data have few, so \(u\) is weakly identified. On the RMET, the 4PL had not converged when EM stopped at its 500-cycle limit (below).
The same two asymptotes return, without a curve between them, in cognitive diagnosis. In the DINA model (Junker & Sijtsma, 2001), a respondent who has every attribute an item requires answers correctly with probability \(1 - s\), where \(s\) is the item’s slip parameter, and a respondent who lacks any of them with probability \(g\), its guess. Cognitive diagnostic models, an extension lesson, takes this up.


Two philosophies
The choice between these models is also a choice between two traditions, which Andrich (2004) describes as incompatible paradigms in Kuhn’s sense. What does each assume?

The model comes first. The Rasch tradition starts from what measurement should mean: a sufficient sum score, and comparisons that don’t depend on which items or people were used (Rasch, 1960; Wright, 1997). It assumes items can be revised until they fit, and treats misfit as information about the items. It suits building an instrument you can still change.
The data come first. The tradition that runs from Birnbaum through Lord (1980) takes the items as given and adds parameters until the curves describe them, accepting weighted scores and crossing curves. It suits analysing a test you can’t change.

Some of the disagreement is about values, which data can’t settle; some is empirical, and the RMET tests it below.


Beyond four: asymmetric curves
All four models give point-symmetric curves. Samejima (2000) proposed the logistic positive exponent family, which raises a logistic curve to a positive power so that it can rise slowly and then steeply, or the reverse. Lee and Bolt (2018) study what asymmetry can say about item complexity, and the IRW’s asymmetric models vignette fits such models across its tables.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates 1,000 respondents answering 20 items from a 3PL with \(c = 0.25\) on every item, then fits the Rasch model, the 2PL and the 3PL. It runs in your browser; the first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, and the fits a little longer.
With the seed as written, the estimates of \(c\) have a median of 0.25, right on the truth, but range from 0 to 0.48. BIC prefers the Rasch model (25,347, against 25,362 for the 2PL and 25,464 for the 3PL), although the 3PL generated the data. The three models’ abilities correlate 0.97 to 0.99 with each other.
Now change np. At 300, the median estimate of \(c\) drops to 0.06. At 10,000 (run that in your own R session), the estimates range from 0.07 to 0.42, BIC finally prefers the 3PL, and the abilities still correlate 0.99 or above. The lower asymptote needs a lot of data to settle; the abilities hardly notice it either way.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
With real data
Our main example is wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022, responses to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), a measure of reading mental states from the eye region of a face. Each of its 36 items offers four words, one of them correct. The data are the normative sample Kim et al. (2024) released with their Multiracial RMET (the landing page describes the newer test; this table holds the original). Its job is to be a test where the lower asymptote has an obvious prediction: with four options, chance is 0.25. A response is 1 when the respondent chose the correct word. Download the code to run every chunk yourself.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
rmet_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v22_0.wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(rmet_url)
# resp is 1 when the respondent chose the correct word of the four; resp_raw is the
# word they chose. Every respondent answered every item once, and there are no waves.
head(df[, c("id", "item", "resp", "resp_raw")], 3)

item
resp

Code
c(respondents = length(unique(df$id)), items = length(unique(df$item)),
  responses_per_respondent = unique(as.vector(table(df$id))),
  words_offered_per_item = unique(as.vector(tapply(df$resp_raw, df$item, function(x) length(unique(x))))))


             respondents                    items responses_per_respondent 
                   17680                       36                       36 
  words_offered_per_item 
                       4 


Code
# IRW tables are long (one row per response); mirt wants wide (one row per respondent).
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
}
resp <- long2wide(df)
p <- colMeans(resp)
round(range(p), 2)     # proportion correct: the easiest and hardest items


[1] 0.56 0.86


All 17,680 respondents answered all 36 items. The items are easy for this sample: 56% to 86% chose the correct word.


Code
# Four models, from the Rasch model to the 4PL. To keep the fits to a minute or two
# we use a random 5,000 of the 17,680 respondents.
set.seed(252)
rs <- resp[sample(nrow(resp), 5000), ]
models <- c("Rasch", "2PL", "3PL", "4PL")
fits <- lapply(setNames(models, models), function(m) mirt(rs, 1, itemtype = m, verbose = FALSE))
data.frame(parameters = sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "nest"),
           BIC = round(sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "BIC")),
           converged = sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "converged"))

BIC

BIC (Schwarz, 1978) adds a penalty for each parameter to minus twice the log likelihood; smaller is better. It prefers the 2PL (204,337) to the Rasch model (205,192, or 855 higher), the 3PL (204,617) and the 4PL (204,707). The 4PL hadn’t converged at EM’s 500-cycle limit, itself a sign that the data say little about four parameters per item. BIC says whether a model is preferred, not how much it improves predictions of new responses; that is for Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.


Code
# The 4PL's upper asymptotes (mirt's u, our u), and how many respondents are up
# where a ceiling would show: 34 or more of 36 correct.
u_hat <- coef(fits$`4PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "u"]
round(quantile(u_hat, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)), 2)


  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
0.71 0.85 0.96 0.99 1.00 


Code
c(at_or_above_34 = sum(rowSums(resp) >= 34), share = round(mean(rowSums(resp) >= 34), 3))


at_or_above_34          share 
        352.00           0.02 


The 4PL’s ceilings run from 0.71 to 1.00 (median 0.96), yet only 2% of respondents answered 34 or more items correctly: like the floors, they rest on few respondents.


Code
# mirt writes the 2PL as a*theta + d. In our notation the difficulty is b = -d/a.
cf2 <- coef(fits$`2PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items
a <- cf2[, "a1"]
b <- -cf2[, "d"] / a
round(c(min_a = min(a), median_a = median(a), max_a = max(a)), 2)


   min_a median_a    max_a 
    0.19     0.67     1.13 


Code
round(c(min_b = min(b), max_b = max(b)), 2)


min_b max_b 
-3.23 -0.39 


Code
# The spread of the slopes on the log scale (0 under the Rasch model), and the ratio
# of the 90th to the 10th percentile. "Across the IRW" puts these in context.
round(c(sd_log_a = sd(log(a)), ratio_90_10 = unname(quantile(a, 0.9) / quantile(a, 0.1))), 2)


   sd_log_a ratio_90_10 
       0.42        2.81 


The slopes run from 0.19 to 1.13, a ratio of about 6 (\(1.13/0.19 \approx 5.9\)). Every difficulty is negative (−3.23 to −0.39): each item is easy for an average respondent. On the log scale the slopes have an SD of 0.42, which Across the IRW compares with the rest of the warehouse.


Code
predict({
  q: "Each RMET item offers four words, so a respondent who knows nothing picks the right one a quarter of the time. What lower asymptotes will the 3PL estimate?",
  choices: ["Near 0.25, as chance predicts", "Above 0.25", "Mostly near 0", "Scattered evenly between 0 and 0.5"],
  answer: "Mostly near 0",
  reveal: "Mostly near 0: the median estimate is 0.01, and three quarters of the items are at 0.16 or below. The data have almost nobody near chance, so they can't locate the floor. Check the output below."
})









Code
# mirt calls the lower asymptote g; it is our c.
c_hat <- coef(fits$`3PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"]
round(quantile(c_hat, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)), 2)


  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
0.00 0.00 0.01 0.16 0.57 


Code
# How many respondents are down where the lower asymptote lives? Chance on 36
# four-option items is 9 correct.
r <- rowSums(resp)
c(at_or_below_9 = sum(r <= 9), share = round(mean(r <= 9), 4), median_sum_score = median(r))


   at_or_below_9            share median_sum_score 
         84.0000           0.0048          26.0000 


The median estimate of \(c\) is 0.01. Why so far from 0.25? Only 84 of the 17,680 respondents (0.48%) answered 9 or fewer items correctly, the score expected from picking words at random; the median respondent answered 26. The lower asymptote describes people almost absent from these data. This says not that RMET respondents never guess, but that these data can’t tell how often. Which wrong words they chose is a question for Nominal response and multiple-choice models, with the same data.


Code
# Ability estimates (EAP) from the four models, for the same 5,000 respondents.
theta <- sapply(fits, function(m) fscores(m)[, 1])
round(cor(theta), 3)


      Rasch   2PL   3PL   4PL
Rasch 1.000 0.983 0.982 0.972
2PL   0.983 1.000 0.999 0.987
3PL   0.982 0.999 1.000 0.990
4PL   0.972 0.987 0.990 1.000


The four models’ abilities correlate from 0.972 to 0.999, and the three with free slopes at 0.987 or above. The choice matters little for ranking respondents, more for what we say about items.
So which model would I fit to a test like the RMET? The 2PL. The slopes differ six-fold, BIC prefers it to the Rasch model by 855 points, the lower asymptote can’t be estimated from a sample with almost no one near chance, and the richer models’ abilities correlate with the 2PL’s at 0.987 or above. If the RMET were being revised, the Rasch tradition’s question (which items to rewrite so that one slope fits them all) would be a fair one; for the test as it stands, the 2PL describes it.

Chess, again






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression and The Rasch model: chess problem Y15 is about as hard as Y29 (8% and 7% of players solve them), but success on Y15 barely moved with Elo, and under the Rasch model it had the largest outfit of all 40 items with mirt’s default abilities, 2.2.



Our contrast table is chess_lnirt, the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005), used again on purpose to show what the 2PL makes of Y15 (three players with no responses dropped, as before).


Code
chess_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.chess_lnirt/rows?format=csv"
chess <- long2wide(read.csv(chess_url))
chess <- chess[rowSums(!is.na(chess)) > 0, ]   # three players have no responses
dim(chess)


[1] 256  40




Code
m_r <- mirt(chess, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
m_2 <- mirt(chess, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
cc <- coef(m_2, simplify = TRUE)$items
a_ch <- cc[, "a1"]
b_ch <- -cc[, "d"] / a_ch                     # b = -d/a
round(sort(a_ch)[c(1:3, 38:40)], 2)          # the flattest and steepest items


 Y15  Y27  Y36   Y9  Y26  Y29 
0.02 0.35 0.47 2.91 3.19 3.79 


Code
round(rbind(a = a_ch, b = b_ch)[, c("Y15", "Y29")], 2)


     Y15  Y29
a   0.02 3.79
b 136.52 1.56


Code
round(c(BIC_Rasch = extract.mirt(m_r, "BIC"), BIC_2PL = extract.mirt(m_2, "BIC")))


BIC_Rasch   BIC_2PL 
     8960      8906 


The 2PL slopes run from 0.02 (Y15) to 3.79 (Y29), and BIC prefers the 2PL to the Rasch model (8,906 against 8,960). Y15’s curve is nearly flat: a player’s ability tells us almost nothing about whether they solve it. Its difficulty of 136.52 comes from dividing by a slope near zero; for an item this flat, \(b\) has no useful meaning.


Code
# The 2PL curves for Y15 and Y29, with the proportion solving each item among
# players grouped by their sum score on the other 38 items (thirds).
rest <- rowSums(chess[, setdiff(names(chess), c("Y15", "Y29"))], na.rm = TRUE)
grp <- cut(rest, quantile(rest, 0:3 / 3), include.lowest = TRUE,
           labels = c("bottom third", "middle third", "top third"))
obs <- sapply(chess[, c("Y15", "Y29")], function(x) tapply(x, grp, mean, na.rm = TRUE))
cbind(players = table(grp), round(obs, 2))

bottom third      89 0.09 0.00
middle third      83 0.05 0.02
top third         84 0.10 0.19

th_grp <- tapply(fscores(m_2)[, 1], grp, mean)   # mean 2PL ability in each group
th <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200)
icc <- function(i) plogis(a_ch[i] * (th - b_ch[i]))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(th, icc("Y29"), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2780e3", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Ability (2PL scale)", ylab = "P(solved)")
lines(th, icc("Y15"), lwd = 2, col = "#c2410c")
points(th_grp, obs[, "Y29"], pch = 19, col = "#2780e3")
points(th_grp, obs[, "Y15"], pch = 17, col = "#c2410c")
legend("topleft", c("Y29", "Y15"), col = c("#2780e3", "#c2410c"), lwd = 2, pch = c(19, 17), bty = "n")

# Where the two curves cross: a29 (theta - b29) = a15 (theta - b15).
cross <- (a_ch["Y29"] * b_ch["Y29"] - a_ch["Y15"] * b_ch["Y15"]) / (a_ch["Y29"] - a_ch["Y15"])
round(c(crossing_theta = unname(cross), share_of_players_below = mean(fscores(m_2)[, 1] < cross)), 2)


        crossing_theta share_of_players_below 
                  0.91                   0.82 


The curves cross at \(\theta = 0.91\); for the 82% of players below it Y15 is the easier problem, and for the strongest, Y29. The grouped proportions (points) agree without the model: in the bottom third of players (by score on the other 38 problems) 9% solved Y15 and none Y29; in the top third, 10% and 19%. “Y15 is easier than Y29” is true for some players and false for others: specific objectivity given up, in data.

# Under the Rasch model, players with the same sum score get the same ability
# estimate. Under the 2PL, the weighted score sum(a_i x_i) takes its place.
th_r <- fscores(m_r)[, 1]

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Problems

Weighted scores. Show that under the 2PL, \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) is sufficient for \(\theta\). Then, for the 3PL, find two patterns on three items of your choosing with the same \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) but different maximum-likelihood estimates.
What \(b\) means now. For the 3PL, show that at \(\theta = b\) the probability is \((1 + c)/2\). At what \(\theta\) is the probability 0.5? What does \(b\) describe, in words, once \(c > 0\)? And for the 4PL?
Where the floor is. Fit the 2PL and the 3PL to the RMET using only the respondents in the bottom quarter of sum scores. Do the estimated lower asymptotes change? Explain what you see, and why selecting on the same items’ sum score might itself cause trouble.
Reading \(c\). A colleague wants to report the RMET’s 3PL lower asymptotes as “the rate at which people guess on each item”. What would you tell them, using this lesson’s output?
Crossing curves. In the chess data, find two problems other than Y15 whose 2PL curves cross where most players sit. For which players is each the easier one? Check against grouped proportions, as the lesson did for Y15 and Y29.
Challenge: when does the model matter? The four models’ RMET abilities correlate at 0.97 or above. When would the choice still matter for a decision about one person? Think about the ends of the scale, cut scores and unusual patterns; Loken & Rulison (2010) is one place to start. This one is open: I don’t know of a general answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Across the IRW
How much do slopes vary in real data? For each dichotomous IRW table with at least 250 respondents, 5 to 200 items and a nearly complete response matrix, compute.R fits the Rasch model and the 2PL and summarises the slopes’ spread by the SD of \(\log a\), which rescaling \(\theta\) leaves alone. It is 0 under the Rasch model, and 0.42 for the RMET above (0.43 in the corpus run’s own sample).


Code
dd_path <- file.path("..", "deepdives", "1pl-to-4pl", "results.rds")
dd <- if (file.exists(dd_path)) readRDS(dd_path) else NULL
if (!is.null(dd)) {
  s <- dd$summary[order(dd$summary$sd_log_a), ]
  print(data.frame(table = s$table, items = s$n_items, respondents = s$n_resp,
                   sd_log_a = round(s$sd_log_a, 2), ratio_90_10 = round(s$ratio_90_10, 1),
                   BIC_prefers_2PL = s$prefers_2pl, converged = s$converged), row.names = FALSE)
  op <- par(mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
  known <- s$table %in% c("chess_lnirt", "wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022")
  plot(s$sd_log_a, rep(0, nrow(s)), pch = 19, cex = 1.3, yaxt = "n", ylab = "", bty = "n",
       col = ifelse(known, "#c2410c", "#2780e3"), xlim = c(0, max(1.5, s$sd_log_a, na.rm = TRUE)),
       xlab = "SD of log slope within a table (0 = Rasch)")
  abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "#999")
  par(op)
}

       taylorabdulai_2025_incentives     7         377     1.26        10.4
  chuemchit_2024_nonpartner_violence     5         494     1.42        14.3
 BIC_prefers_2PL converged

WarningPartial run: 6 of 316 tables



This is a pilot run of compute.R, on the lesson’s two tables and 4 others drawn at random, to check the pipeline. The full run replaces it.


Run on 24 September 2026: 6 tables fitted, 0 failed. In 5 of the 6, BIC prefers the 2PL to the Rasch model. The SD of log slopes runs from 0.28 to 1.42 (median 0.65); chess and the RMET are marked in orange.
This answers the Rasch lesson’s question: are equal slopes plausible? The nearer a table’s SD of \(\log a\) is to 0, the more so. The IRW’s 2PL discrimination vignette takes the question to its cognitive tables, slope by slope. Whether the extra parameters improve predictions of new responses is the other half, reported in Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Going further

Lord, F. M., & Novick, M. R. (1968). Statistical theories of mental test scores (with contributions by A. Birnbaum). Addison-Wesley. https://openlibrary.org/works/OL6568286W. Birnbaum’s chapters 17–20 introduce the logistic 2PL and 3PL.
Lord, F. M. (1980). Applications of item response theory to practical testing problems. Erlbaum. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203056615. The 3PL at work on real tests.
Barton, M. A., & Lord, F. M. (1981). An upper asymptote for the three-parameter logistic item-response model. ETS Research Report Series, 1981(1). https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.1981.tb01255.x. Where the fourth parameter starts.
Loken, E., & Rulison, K. L. (2010). Estimation of a four-parameter item response theory model. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 63(3), 509–525. https://doi.org/10.1348/000711009x474502. A Bayesian 4PL, and what simpler models miss at the ends of the scale.
Andersen, E. B. (1977). Sufficient statistics and latent trait models. Psychometrika, 42(1), 69–81. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293746. Why only the Rasch model has a sufficient statistic free of item parameters.
Domingue, B. W., Kanopka, K., Kapoor, R., Pohl, S., Chalmers, R. P., Rahal, C., & Rhemtulla, M. (2024). The InterModel Vigorish as a lens for understanding (and quantifying) the value of item response models for dichotomously coded items. Psychometrika, 89(3), 1034–1054. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-024-09977-2. How much the 2PL and 3PL add to prediction, in simulation and across IRW datasets.
Maris, G., & Bechger, T. (2009). On interpreting the model parameters for the three parameter logistic model. Measurement: Interdisciplinary Research and Perspectives, 7(2), 75–88. https://doi.org/10.1080/15366360903070385. What the 3PL’s parameters can and can’t be read as.
von Davier, M. (2009). Is there need for the 3PL model? Guess what? Measurement: Interdisciplinary Research and Perspectives, 7(2), 110–114. https://doi.org/10.1080/15366360903117079. A commentary in the same issue.
Haberman, S. J. (2005). Identifiability of parameters in item response models with unconstrained ability distributions. ETS Research Report Series, 2005(2), i–22. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2005.tb02001.x. The identification question in general form.
Andrich, D. (2004). Controversy and the Rasch model: A characteristic of incompatible paradigms? Medical Care, 42(1 Suppl.), I-7–I-16. https://doi.org/10.1097/01.mlr.0000103528.48582.7c. The two traditions, set out side by side.
Wright, B. D. (1997). A history of social science measurement. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 16(4), 33–45. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3992.1997.tb00606.x. The case for choosing items that fit the Rasch model.
Samejima, F. (2000). Logistic positive exponent family of models: Virtue of asymmetric item characteristic curves. Psychometrika, 65(3), 319–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02296149. Curves that aren’t symmetric.
Lee, S., & Bolt, D. M. (2018). Asymmetric item characteristic curves and item complexity: Insights from simulation and real data analyses. Psychometrika, 83(2), 453–475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-017-9586-5. What asymmetry might say about items.
Schwarz, G. (1978). Estimating the dimension of a model. The Annals of Statistics, 6(2), 461–464. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176344136. The BIC.
Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory package for the R environment. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(6). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06. The package, including its intercept parameterization.
Baron-Cohen, S., Wheelwright, S., Hill, J., Raste, Y., & Plumb, I. (2001). The “Reading the Mind in the Eyes” Test revised version: A study with normal adults, and adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 42(2), 241–251. https://doi.org/10.1111/1469-7610.00715. The source of the RMET.
Kim, H. A., Kaduthodil, J., Strong, R. W., Germine, L. T., Cohan, S., & Wilmer, J. B. (2024). Multiracial Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (MRMET): An inclusive version of an influential measure. Behavior Research Methods, 56(6), 5900–5917. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-023-02323-x. The source of the RMET data.
van der Maas, H. L. J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2005). A psychometric analysis of chess expertise. American Journal of Psychology, 118(1), 29–60. https://doi.org/10.2307/30039042. The source of the chess data.
From the IRW: the 2PL discrimination vignette (slopes across its cognitive tables) and the asymmetric models vignette.
van der Linden, W. J. (2016). Unidimensional logistic response models. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 1. Models (pp. 13–30). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315374512. A handbook chapter on the one-, two- and three-parameter logistic models.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Data sources
Data from the Item Response Warehouse (each table name links to its IRW page); references from IRW biblio.

The slide 61 simulation is the Simulate section.

title: AI and psychometrics
text:
What this is for
Language models now score essays, write items, predict item difficulty, and answer questionnaires in place of people. Each is a claim about measurement that the tools of this course can check. The lesson starts from the question What is an item? handed on: that lesson explained difficulty with features that people coded, so can an item’s text alone predict it? My answer depends on the yardstick. I judge a difficulty prediction by how many respondents it is worth, and on the general-knowledge items below the best text features are worth about three.

title: AI and psychometrics
AI and psychometrics
text:
Core ideas

Two intersections
AI and psychometrics meet in two directions. One uses AI to measure people. The other uses psychometrics to measure AI: a benchmark is a set of items and a model is a respondent, and Martínez-Plumed, Prudêncio, Martínez-Usó and Hernández-Orallo (2019) fit item response models to machine-learning classifiers, one item per test instance. The IRW holds no table of models answering questions yet, so that direction gets problem 6; the rest of the lesson is about the first.


Automated scoring is an agreement problem
An essay-scoring engine is trained to reproduce the scores human raters give; e-rater is a long-running example (Attali & Burstein, 2006). How do we know it works? The first evidence is agreement with human raters, read from the table that crosses the engine’s scores with a human’s. Three statistics summarize that table:

exact agreement, the share of responses on the diagonal;
Cohen’s kappa, exact agreement corrected for the agreement two raters would reach by chance with the same margins, \(\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)\);
quadratic weighted kappa (QWK; Cohen, 1968), which charges each disagreement by its squared distance: with weights \(w_{ik} = (i - k)^2\), observed counts \(O_{ik}\) and the counts \(E_{ik}\) expected from the margins, \[\text{QWK} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i,k} w_{ik} O_{ik}}{\sum_{i,k} w_{ik} E_{ik}}.\]

Agreement with what? The baseline is the agreement of two human raters scoring the same responses. Williamson, Xi and Breyer (2012) make human–machine agreement one strand of the evidence for an engine, beside its fit to the purpose, its relations with independent measures, its generalizability across tasks and forms, and its consequences for subgroups.

Try it: agreement by hand
Five hundred essays have a true quality. Two human raters score it on a scale from 1 to 4 with the same noise; an engine adds noise of its own, may shift, and may compress its scores toward the middle.


Code
viewof sc_noise = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.2], {value: 0.55, step: 0.05, label: "Engine's noise (humans: 0.55)"})
viewof sc_shift = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Engine's shift (score points)"})
viewof sc_comp = Inputs.range([0.3, 1.2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Engine's use of the scale (1 = like the humans)"})

























Code
sc = scoringWorld({machineNoise: sc_noise, shift: sc_shift, compress: sc_comp})
sc_cells = sc.machine.table.flatMap((row, i) => row.map((n, k) => ({human: i + 1, engine: k + 1, n})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 380, height: 320, padding: 0.05, x: {label: "Engine's score", domain: [1, 2, 3, 4]}, y: {label: "Human 1's score", domain: [4, 3, 2, 1]},
  color: {range: [palette.white, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(sc_cells, {x: "engine", y: "human", fill: "n", stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.text(sc_cells, {x: "engine", y: "human", text: "n", fill: d => d.n > 60 ? palette.white : palette.ink, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})

























Code
md`| | Exact agreement | Kappa | QWK | Mean score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Human 1 with human 2 | ${sc.human.exact.toFixed(2)} | ${sc.human.kappa.toFixed(2)} | ${sc.human.qwk.toFixed(2)} | ${sc.human.meanY.toFixed(2)} |
| Human 1 with the engine | ${sc.machine.exact.toFixed(2)} | ${sc.machine.kappa.toFixed(2)} | **${sc.machine.qwk.toFixed(2)}** | ${sc.machine.meanY.toFixed(2)} |`







As the widget loads, the engine agrees with human 1 about as well as human 2 does (QWK 0.70 against 0.65; the gap is sampling noise). Shift it up half a point: exact agreement falls from 0.54 to 0.47, QWK only to 0.65. Compress its scale to 0.6 and QWK drops to 0.55. Then cut its noise to 0.3 with the scale at 0.7: it matches the human baseline (0.66) while still hugging the middle. The same QWK can come from quite different engines.
QWK depends on the margins of the table and the length of the scale (Lewis & Casabianca, 2026). The proportional reduction in mean squared error (PRMSE) judges an engine against the human raters’ true scores, allowing for their unreliability, and can reach a different conclusion from QWK on the same data (McCaffrey, Casabianca & Johnson, 2025). And agreement says nothing about what the engine responds to: in 240,000 admission essays, content and style correlated more strongly with household income than SAT scores did (Alvero et al., 2021). An engine could agree with human raters and carry that signal too; Williamson et al.’s subgroup evidence is how you would find out.






If you’ve done Rater models: an engine is one more rater, with a severity of its own. Casabianca, Donoghue, Shin, Chao and Choi (2023) found that two human ratings connected raters better than one human rating plus an engine’s, and that engine scores alone did not connect raters adequately.





Code
quiz({
  q: "An engine gives every essay exactly one point more than rater A does (A never uses the top score). What are the exact agreement and the QWK?",
  options: [
    {text: "Exact agreement 0; QWK well above 0", correct: true, why: "No essay gets the same score, so exact agreement is 0. But the two sets of scores move together perfectly, and QWK charges a one-point gap only $1^2 = 1$ against the larger squared gaps chance would produce. With A's scores spread with variance 1, QWK is $2/(2 + 1) \\approx 0.67$ (Go deeper below)."},
    {text: "Both 0", correct: false, why: "Kappa-type statistics compare the observed disagreement with what chance would give. Chance pairs essays scored far apart; this engine is never more than a point away."},
    {text: "Exact agreement 0; QWK 1", correct: false, why: "QWK is 1 only when every essay gets the same score from both. The constant gap is charged: that is what separates agreement from correlation, which would be 1 here."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: QWK is a correlation that charges for differences in mean and spread





Assumptions: two raters score the same \(n\) responses on an integer scale; \(p_{ik}\) is the observed share with scores \((i, k)\); the expected shares are the products of the margins, \(p_{i\cdot}\,p_{\cdot k}\); weights are \((i - k)^2\); means, variances and the covariance are computed with divisor \(n\).
The numerator of the fraction in QWK is the mean squared difference between the two scores, \(\sum_{i,k} (i-k)^2 p_{ik} = E[(X - Y)^2]\). The denominator is the same expectation for two independent raters with the same margins. Expanding the square, \[E[(X-Y)^2] = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 - 2\sigma_{XY} + (\mu_X - \mu_Y)^2,\] and under independence the covariance term is 0. So \[\text{QWK} = 1 - \frac{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 - 2\sigma_{XY} + (\mu_X - \mu_Y)^2}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 + (\mu_X - \mu_Y)^2} = \frac{2\sigma_{XY}}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 + (\mu_X - \mu_Y)^2}.\] This is exact, and it is Lin’s (1989) concordance correlation coefficient. Three things follow. With equal means and variances, QWK is the Pearson correlation. A difference in means lowers it (the widget’s shift), and so does a difference in spread even when the correlation is 1 (the widget’s compression). And Fleiss and Cohen (1973) showed that weighted kappa with these weights is, apart from terms of order \(1/n\), the intraclass correlation that counts rater differences as error: the absolute-agreement coefficient of Many sources of error, if you’ve done it.






Can the text of an item predict its difficulty?






Recall from What is an item?: the LLTM writes each item’s easiness as a weighted sum of its features, and an item residual with SD \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) gives a size to what the features leave out. For the verbal aggression items, features coded from the design explained 89% of the variance in easiness, and the residual SD was 0.34.



Where do the features come from? Some are counts from the text, such as word count and sentence length, the stuff of readability measures like the Lexile framework (Stenner, Burdick, Sanford & Burdick, 2006). Some are coded by experts from a model of how items are solved: for paragraph-comprehension items from the GRE, variables describing the decision among options accounted for difficulty and those describing the text did not (Gorin & Embretson, 2006). And some are representations of the text from a language model (Benedetto et al., 2023, survey the methods). Kapoor, Truong, Haber, Ruiz-Primo and Domingue (2025) predicted the difficulty of state reading items from annotated linguistic, test and context features: a correlation of 0.77 with the true difficulties, and a root mean squared error of 0.59 against 0.92 for predicting the mean. Embeddings from language models improved the prediction only marginally, and either kind of feature alone did about as well.
Is a correlation of 0.77 good? Two yardsticks assume different uses. Accuracy (a correlation, an RMSE) assumes the prediction is the product, as when sorting a bank. Respondents assumes the point is to calibrate items with fewer people. A calibration on \(n\) respondents estimates \(b\) with a standard error of about \(1/\sqrt{n\,E[p(1-p)]}\), since each respondent adds \(p(1-p)\) to the information about the item’s location (the curvature of The likelihood and logistic regression). A prediction whose errors have SD \(\sigma\) is therefore as precise as a calibration on \[n^* = \frac{1}{\sigma^2\,E[p(1-p)]}\] respondents.
I use the second yardstick. The prize in predicting difficulty is skipping or shrinking the field test, so I want to know how many respondents a prediction is worth; accuracy statistics don’t say.

Try it: what a prediction is worth


Code
viewof wp_r = Inputs.range([0, 0.995], {value: 0.77, step: 0.005, label: "Correlation of predicted and true difficulty"})
viewof wp_sdb = Inputs.range([0.3, 2], {value: 0.92, step: 0.01, label: "SD of the items' difficulties"})
viewof wp_sdt = Inputs.range([0.3, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "SD of respondents' θ"})

























Code
wp = worthInRespondents({r: wp_r, sdB: wp_sdb, sdTheta: wp_sdt})
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {type: "log", label: "Respondents in the field test", domain: [5, 1000]},
  y: {label: "Standard error of the calibrated difficulty", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(wp.curve, {x: "n", y: "se", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([wp.sigma], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.dot(Number.isFinite(wp.nStar) && wp.nStar >= 5 && wp.nStar <= 1000 ? [{n: wp.nStar, se: wp.sigma}] : [], {x: "n", y: "se", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})


















Code
md`Prediction error SD: **${wp.sigma.toFixed(2)}** logits (dashed). It is worth a field test of about **${Number.isFinite(wp.nStar) ? Math.round(wp.nStar) : "∞"}** respondents.`







With Kapoor et al.’s correlation and spread of difficulties, the prediction is worth about 14 respondents, if their difficulties are logits on a scale where \(\theta\) has SD 1 (an assumption here). A correlation of 0.9 is worth 30; 0.95 is worth 59; matching a 200-person field test needs about 0.986. Liu, Bhandari and Pardos (2025) report their result on this yardstick: the item parameters from their language-model respondents were about as good as those from 50 undergraduates.






If you’ve done Model fit and out-of-sample prediction: the IMV put a predictive gain on a scale that compares across datasets. Respondents do the same job here, in the unit a test developer pays for.





Code
quiz({
  q: "A new text model halves the SD of the prediction errors. How many more respondents is its prediction worth?",
  options: [
    {text: "Four times as many", correct: true, why: "$n^* = 1/(\\sigma^2 E[p(1-p)])$ depends on $\\sigma^2$, so halving $\\sigma$ multiplies $n^*$ by 4."},
    {text: "Twice as many", correct: false, why: "Standard errors shrink with the square root of $n$, so halving an error takes four times the respondents."},
    {text: "It depends on the correlation, not the error SD", correct: false, why: "The correlation matters only through the error SD it implies, $\\sigma = \\text{SD}(b)\\sqrt{1 - r^2}$."}
  ]
})










Language models as simulated respondents
Argyle et al. (2023) conditioned GPT-3 on the backgrounds of real survey participants and found that it reproduced the response patterns of many subgroups. For items, Liu et al. (2025) had six models answer college algebra items: each model’s abilities were narrowly spread, an ensemble of models came closer to students, and the item parameters correlated above 0.8 with those from students for GPT-3.5. Zhou, Liu, Tang and Wilson (2026), a preprint, address that narrow spread by telling the model which student to be: each prompt describes a profile of fraction-subtraction skills from a cognitive diagnosis model. With profiles, the models’ scores spread more like students’, and the item difficulties from their answers came closer to the students’ (in the strongest case, a rank correlation of about 0.9 against 0.24 without profiles; see Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis). Scarlatos, Fernandez, Ormerod, Lottridge and Lan (2025) train a model so that simulated students at an instructed ability answer as an item response model says they should, and use the simulated answers to predict the difficulty of open-ended items.
Does simulation beat the simpler route of the last section? A simulator is a difficulty predictor, so it answers to the same yardstick, and it has to get each item right: a model may find an item easy or hard for reasons of its own.

Try it: simulated respondents
Thirty items with known difficulties, answered by a model playing simulated students.


Code
viewof sr_n = Inputs.range([20, 2000], {value: 200, step: 10, label: "Simulated respondents"})
viewof sr_spread = Inputs.range([0.1, 1.5], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of their abilities (people: 1)"})
viewof sr_bias = Inputs.range([0, 1.5], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Item-specific bias (SD, logits)"})

























Code
sr = simulatedRespondents({nSim: sr_n, spread: sr_spread, itemBias: sr_bias})
sr_worth = worthInRespondents({sigma: sr.rmse})
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "True difficulty", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {label: "Difficulty implied by the simulation", domain: [-3.5, 3.5]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[-3, -3], [3, 3]], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.dot(sr.items, {x: "truth", y: "implied", r: 5, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})

























Code
md`Correlation with the truth: **${sr.r.toFixed(2)}**; RMSE ${sr.rmse.toFixed(2)} logits, worth about **${Math.round(sr_worth.nStar)}** real respondents.`







At the defaults the correlation is 0.91 and the simulation is worth about 30 respondents. Raise the simulated respondents to 2,000 and the correlation stays at 0.91. Set the bias to 0 instead and it rises to 0.98, worth about 144 respondents. More simulated respondents remove sampling noise, not the model’s own view of the items. (The widget rescales implied difficulties to the truth’s spread, so the narrow spread matters little here.)



Automatic item generation, and checking what it makes
Items have been generated by rule for decades. A cognitive design system builds in the features that make an item hard and calibrates the design principles rather than each item (Embretson, 1999); item models are templates with slots filled by rule (Gierl & Haladyna, 2012; for medical multiple-choice items, Gierl, Lai & Turner, 2012). Language models write items without a template. AI-GENIE generates a pool with a language model and prunes it with network psychometrics before anyone answers (Russell-Lasalandra, Christensen & Golino, 2024).
Whoever writes the items, the questions are the same: does each measure its construct, how hard is it, do the wrong options draw anyone? Distractors that draw almost nobody are common in human-written tests too: Haladyna and Downing (1993) found that items seldom had more than three options that performed acceptably, and a meta-analysis of 80 years of studies supports three options (Rodriguez, 2005).

Try it: distractors that work, and dead ones
A four-option item. The key’s pull rises with \(\theta\); each distractor has a fixed pull of its own.


Code
viewof dd_key = Inputs.range([-1, 4], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Key: how easy"})
viewof dd_a = Inputs.range([-4, 1], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Distractor A's pull"})
viewof dd_b = Inputs.range([-4, 1], {value: -2.5, step: 0.1, label: "Distractor B's pull"})
viewof dd_c = Inputs.range([-4, 1], {value: -2.5, step: 0.1, label: "Distractor C's pull"})
































Code
dd_pulls = [dd_a, dd_b, dd_c]
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(choosing the option)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Key", "Distractor A", "Distractor B", "Distractor C"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.light, palette.guide]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.25], {stroke: palette.rule, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.line(optionCurves(dd_pulls, dd_key, grid(-4, 4)), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "option", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})


















Code
dd_sh = optionShares(dd_pulls, dd_key)
md`In a group with θ ~ N(0, 1): ${dd_sh.map(d => `${d.option} **${(100 * d.share).toFixed(0)}%**`).join(", ")}. Distractors chosen by fewer than 5%: **${dd_sh.slice(1).filter(d => d.share < 0.05).length}** of 3.`
















At the defaults distractor A draws 38% of the group and B and C draw 3% each: two dead distractors. Respondents far below the item choose A, so the key’s curve falls below chance (dashed). Make the key easier (2.5) and even A falls to 13%. On an easy item, dead distractors alone don’t show that they were badly written.






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL: with four options, chance is 0.25, yet the 3PL’s lower asymptotes for the RMET were mostly near 0, because almost nobody sat near chance. A working distractor is one more reason the floor needn’t be at chance.





Code
quiz({
  q: "A language model writes a four-option item. Of 190 students, 93% choose the key and the distractors draw 3%, 2% and 2%. What does this show?",
  options: [
    {text: "The item is easy for this group, and these data say little about its distractors", correct: true, why: "With only 7% choosing any distractor, there are too few wrong answers to tell a dead distractor from a working one. In a weaker group the same distractors might draw many."},
    {text: "The distractors are badly written", correct: false, why: "They may be, but an easy item leaves little for any distractor to draw, as the widget's easy key showed. Try the item on a group for whom it is harder, or look at who chooses each option."},
    {text: "The key is ambiguous", correct: false, why: "An ambiguous key would split strong respondents between the key and a distractor. Here nearly everyone agrees on the key."}
  ]
})

title: AI and psychometrics
text:
Simulate
The code simulates 200 items whose difficulties follow two text features plus a residual with SD sd_resid, fits the feature model on 150, predicts the other 50, converts the error to respondents, and compares a field test of the 50 with n_field respondents. Base R; a second.
With the seed as written, the prediction correlates 0.68 with the new difficulties (RMSE 0.57), worth about 16 respondents; a 25-person field test does better (RMSE 0.43). Set n_field <- 16 and the field test’s RMSE is 0.58, matching the prediction. Try sd_resid <- 0.2 (worth about 142) and sd_resid <- 1 (about 6).

title: AI and psychometrics
text:
With real data
Our main example is himmelstein-impossible_question-2025: its job is the deep dive in miniature, testing whether item text predicts difficulty. The two contrasts are items written by language models: gpt4mcq_young_2025, multiple-choice items written by GPT-4, and genpsych_russell_2024_gpt4o, personality items written by GPT-4o. Both are openly licensed, so their items are shown in full (citing the authors and naming the model). Download the code; it needs lme4, mirt and haven.

Impossible questions: does the text predict difficulty?
The Forecasting Proficiency Test (Himmelstein et al., 2025; materials and data at forecastingresearch/fpt) includes an impossible-question task adapted from Bennett and Steyvers (2022). Each question offers two answers and an opt-out. Most have a right answer; some ask about things that don’t exist, and the right response is to opt out. Two examples from the study’s data file are “Not all metals are attracted to magnets” (true or false) and “What’s the habitat of a Rojixon bird?” (deserts or tropical rainforests). Keying: 1 is the keyed answer, or an opt-out on an impossible question. A gentle note from the IRW’s item-text notes: the instructions said opt-outs weren’t scored, but on answerable questions they count as wrong.


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(lme4))
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with a
# CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
iq_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v24_0.himmelstein-impossible_question-2025/rows?format=csv"
iq <- read.csv(iq_url)
c(respondents = length(unique(iq$id)), items = length(unique(iq$item)),
  max_per_person_item = max(table(iq$id, iq$item)))

# item was on: the anchor form, which every respondent took, or one of two forms

Code
# Two text features, as in the IRW vignette on item language and difficulty: word
# count, and mean word length in characters with punctuation removed.
text_features <- function(txt) {
  words <- strsplit(trimws(gsub("[[:punct:]]", " ", txt)), "\\s+")
  words <- lapply(words, function(w) w[nchar(w) > 0])
  data.frame(word_count = lengths(strsplit(trimws(txt), "\\s+")),
             mean_word_length = vapply(words, function(w) if (length(w)) mean(nchar(w)) else NA_real_, 0))
}

items$impossible <- as.integer(items$question_type == "IQ")

Now the LLTM with an item residual, the text features as item predictors:


Code
# The LLTM with an item residual (from "What is an item?"), with text features as the
# item predictors: logit P(correct) = theta_j + beta_0 + features + epsilon_i. The item
# residual's variance, with and without the features, says how much of the variation
# in difficulty they explain. nAGQ = 0 keeps each fit to seconds.
d <- merge(iq, items[, c("item", "word_count", "impossible")], by = "item")
d$words_z <- (d$word_count - mean(items$word_count)) / sd(items$word_count)

m1 <- glmer(resp ~ words_z + (1 | id) + (1 | item), family = binomial, data = d, nAGQ = 0)
m2 <- glmer(resp ~ words_z + impossible + (1 | id) + (1 | item), family = binomial, data = d, nAGQ = 0)

  v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m)); setNames(v$sdcor, v$grp)[c("item", "id")] })

Items differ far more than respondents (SD 1.71 against 0.47 for \(\theta\)). Word count explains 1.4% of the item variance; adding the impossible flag, 31%, leaving a residual SD of 1.42. What is that worth?


Code
# What is each prediction worth, in respondents? One respondent carries E[p(1 - p)]
# units of information about an item's location (Rasch model, theta ~ N(0, sd_theta));
# a prediction with error SD sigma is as good as a calibration on
# n* = 1 / (sigma^2 * E[p(1 - p)]) respondents. E[p(1 - p)] is averaged over items at
# the locations each model predicts.
epq <- function(loc, sd_theta) integrate(function(t)
  plogis(loc + t) * (1 - plogis(loc + t)) * dnorm(t, 0, sd_theta), -Inf, Inf)$value
worth <- function(m) {
  v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m)); sigma <- v$sdcor[v$grp == "item"]; sd_theta <- v$sdcor[v$grp == "id"]
  loc <- unique(model.matrix(m) %*% fixef(m))
  info <- mean(sapply(loc, epq, sd_theta = sd_theta))
  c(sigma = sigma, info_per_respondent = info, respondents_worth = 1 / (sigma^2 * info))
}

Knowing only that an item belongs to this test is worth about 1.7 respondents: that is the prior. Word count adds nothing; with the impossible flag, the prediction is worth 2.7. title: AI and psychometrics
text:
Problems

QWK from a table. Show that QWK \(= 1 - \sum w_{ik}O_{ik}/\sum w_{ik}E_{ik}\) with weights \((i-k)^2\) equals \(2\sigma_{XY}/(\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 + (\mu_X - \mu_Y)^2)\). With two categories, show that it equals Cohen’s kappa.
Without the impossible questions. Drop the 18 impossible questions and refit the LLTM with word count and mean word length. What do they explain, and what is the prediction worth? Code a feature of your own from the text (true–false or not, say) and test it.
A 2PL for GPT-4’s items. Plot the 2PL test information for gpt4mcq_young_2025. Where is it informative? Which three items would you ask the writer to make harder, and how?
Judgment. A vendor’s engine agrees with human raters at QWK 0.80 on your essays; two humans agree at 0.72. What else do you need before it replaces the second rater?
Design. Design a study of whether difficulties predicted by a language model could replace a state’s field test of new reading items. What result would convince you?
Challenge (open): models as respondents. A hundred language models answer a thousand benchmark questions. What would “ability” mean for a model, and which assumption is likeliest to fail: local independence (models trained on overlapping data), one dimension, or something else? I don’t know the answer.

title: AI and psychometrics
text:
Across the IRW
Can item text predict difficulty across the IRW? compute.R takes each English dichotomous cognitive table with at least 200 respondents and item text in the IRW, and correlates word count and mean word length with the logit of proportion correct within the table. Pooling items across tables would confound an item’s length with the test it came from. No feature from a language model is used yet.






Recall from Constructs and construct maps: of the nine number-series items, NS_2 was solved by 84% of those who answered it and NS_6, whose key accepts 165 where tripling the steps gives 120, by 1.5%. The corpus run includes that table to check its own pipeline.





Code
dd_path <- file.path("..", "deepdives", "ai-psychometrics", "results.rds")
dd <- if (file.exists(dd_path)) readRDS(dd_path) else NULL
if (!is.null(dd)) {
  ns <- dd$items[dd$items$table == "himmelstein-number_series-2025", ]
  print(round(setNames(ns$p, ns$item)[c("NS_2", "NS_6")], 3))   # the pipeline check
  s <- dd$summary[order(dd$summary$r_word_count), ]
  print(data.frame(table = s$table, items = s$n_items, median_p = round(s$median_p, 2),
                   r_word_count = round(s$r_word_count, 2), r_word_length = round(s$r_word_length, 2)),
        row.names = FALSE)
}

WarningPartial run: 5 of 33 tables



This is a pilot run of compute.R, on three tables whose answers are known (the number series, this lesson’s impossible questions, and preschool_sel_box, the IRW vignette’s strongest case) and 3 drawn at random, to check the pipeline. The full run replaces it.


Run on 25 September 2026: 5 tables summarised, 1 failed (polca_cheating: fewer than 5 items with both responses and text). Within-table correlations of word count with logit proportion correct run from -0.62 to 0.07 (median -0.14).
The pipeline reproduces the number-series proportions. In this pilot the correlations for word count are small, except for the preschool task at −0.62; the full run will show how they spread across all the candidate tables. The IRW’s item language and difficulty vignette runs the same analysis with a plot for each table.
