       0.94        0.80        0.87 


Two correlated dimensions, one per wording, fit far better than one (AIC 17,460 against 16,960), and correlate 0.68. A model with a method factor for the incremental-worded items, uncorrelated with a general mindset dimension, says the same thing another way: those four items load 0.51 to 0.68 on the method factor, and it fits a little better than the two correlated dimensions (AIC 16,943 against 16,960), which is the bifactor model’s flexibility at work as much as evidence for either story. Omega hierarchical is 0.80, the share of the mindset score’s variance that the general dimension accounts for, against an omega total of 0.94. Alpha, 0.87, sits between them, as it did in the testlet widget. (A rough comparison: alpha is on the item scores, omega on the latent response scale.)
So, one score or two? Two assumptions sit under the answer. One grit-and-mindset score assumes a single construct; the two correlate 0.26, and a second dimension predicts held-out responses about as much better as a 2PL does over the Rasch model. Two mindset scores assume the entity and incremental items tap different beliefs, rather than one belief seen through two wordings; they correlate 0.68, and the general factor carries most of the score. I would report two scores, one for grit and one for mindset, and I would not split the mindset score by wording. The wording factor is real, but it is a fact about how the items are written, and it merits a note in the report rather than a score of its own. Every extra dimension fits; the question is which earn a score.

title: Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT
text:
Problems

Reductions. Show that a compensatory two-dimensional item with \(a_2 = 0\) is a 2PL in \(\theta_1\) with difficulty \(b\). Then show that rotating the slopes and the abilities by the same orthogonal matrix leaves every response probability unchanged, and that with uncorrelated standard normal abilities it leaves the marginal likelihood unchanged too. Where does the argument need the abilities to be uncorrelated?
qgrit11. Refit the confirmatory model with qgrit11 reversed, then dropped. What changes? Argue for a keying, or for dropping it, for respondents of this age. Would your answer be the same for the adults in Factor analysis II? (PS6#1.)
One mindset score or two? AIC prefers two correlated wording dimensions for the mindset items. Compute the IMV of that model over one dimension by five-fold cross-validation on the dichotomized items, and look at the fold-to-fold spread and at the slopes. Would you report one mindset score or two? What would change your mind?
Design. Items sharing a reading passage may be locally dependent. Design a check (statistic, comparison, threshold) and a remedy. How would you tell a passage effect from a second ability, such as vocabulary?
When does a second dimension pay? Using the simulation, find the correlation at which the IMV of the second dimension falls below 0.005 with 500 respondents, then with 2,000, and then with 10 items per dimension. Is there a correlation above which a second score is never worth reporting?
Challenge (open). In the compensatory model, suppose some items have \(a_1 = 0\) and the others \(a_2 = 0\), so that each dimension has its own set of items, as grit and mindset do here. What changes, compared with items that draw on both abilities, in identification and in whether separate scores are justified? The EDUC 252 slides flag this as a big question, and I don’t know of a general answer.

title: Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT
text:
Across the IRW
How often does one dimension hold? The IRW’s dimensionality vignette answers with parallel analysis, and Factor analysis I quoted it: one factor in only 3% of 810 tables. That criterion, like AIC, says whether. compute.R asks how much, with this lesson’s tool. For IRW tables with 6 to 40 items and at least 500 respondents (at most 1,000 sampled per table), it splits each item near its median, fits one- and two-dimensional (exploratory) 2PL models in five-fold cross-validation, and records the IMV of the second dimension, with the ratio of the first two eigenvalues of the item correlations as the vignette’s index for comparison.


Code
dd_path <- file.path("..", "deepdives", "dimensionality", "results.rds")
dd <- if (file.exists(dd_path)) readRDS(dd_path) else NULL
if (!is.null(dd)) {
  s <- dd$summary[order(dd$summary$imv_2d), ]
  print(data.frame(table = s$table, items = s$n_items, respondents = s$n_resp,
                   eigen_ratio = round(s$eig_ratio, 2), IMV_2D = round(s$imv_2d, 4),
                   fold_sd = round(s$imv_2d_sd, 4)), row.names = FALSE)
  op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
  plot(s$eig_ratio, s$imv_2d, pch = 19, col = "#2780e3", las = 1, log = "x",
       xlab = "First / second eigenvalue", ylab = "IMV of 2D over 1D")
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "#999")
  par(op)
}

              psychtools_bfi    25        1000        1.80  0.0321  0.0050















WarningPartial run: 5 of 1101 tables



This is a pilot run of compute.R, on two tables whose answers are known (psychtools_bfi, built for five traits, and gilbert_meta_2, a reading test) and 3 others drawn at random, to check the pipeline. The full run replaces it.


Run on 25 September 2026: 5 tables fitted, 0 failed. The IMV of a second dimension has median -0.0149 (range -0.1167 to 0.0321).
The pilot checks the pipeline. psychtools_bfi, built for five traits, gains 0.032 from a second dimension, and the reading test loses a little, as it should when there is nothing for a second dimension to find. The three random tables lose more, down to −0.117 for a seven-item anxiety scale with 544 respondents, where an unconstrained second dimension adds seven slopes to estimate from little data. A negative IMV here is a fact about fitting an exploratory model to a small table, not about the scale. The full run will say how often a second dimension pays across the warehouse, and whether the eigenvalue ratio predicts when.

For instructors

Changed from 252: the slides compared one and two dimensions on ENEM booklet 175 and found an IMV of −0.002 for the second dimension; the course doesn’t use ENEM (no tokenless CSV), and the grit and mindset data of PS6#1 carry the comparison instead. PS6#1’s two models (exploratory and confirmatory, fitted there with priors on the slopes) are fitted here without priors, as graded models for the structure and as dichotomized 2PL models for the IMV. The partially compensatory model and the frame mismatch in fscores() are new.
Held back: testlet models in their own right (the bifactor model gets a subsection and one real-data fit); multidimensional adaptive testing (Item banks and adaptive testing); local dependence from repeated trials, which Explanatory item response models models with random effects.
Data: one grit item is quoted, from the IRW’s item text, which carries no licence to reproduce an instrument. The IRW notes that its item text’s alignment with item ids isn’t guaranteed; the correlations agree with the entity/incremental split and the grit facets, with qgrit11 the one item that doesn’t follow its facet.

title: What is an item? Explanatory item response models
text:
What this is for
The Rasch model gives every item a difficulty and stops there. It says that shouting at a bus driver is harder to endorse than cursing, not why. Yet items are usually built from a design: a situation, a behaviour, a grammatical construct, a stimulus shown after another stimulus. If the design explains the difficulties, we have learned something about the construct and can say how hard an item will be before anyone answers it. This lesson writes the Rasch model as a regression, so that explaining becomes a change of formula: item features in place of item difficulties, respondent covariates, items as draws from a family. Along the way it asks what, exactly, an item is.

title: What is an item? Explanatory item response models
What is an item? Explanatory item response models
text:
Core ideas

An item response model is a regression






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: stacked long, the chess responses went into a logistic regression with one intercept per problem and Elo as the predictor, and the lesson ended by asking what would happen if each player got an unknown parameter of their own instead of Elo.



Each row of a long IRW table is one response \(x_{ij}\), and the Rasch model is \[\text{logit}\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \theta_j + \beta_i, \qquad \theta_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\theta),\] where \(\beta_i = -b_i\) is item \(i\)’s easiness. The items are fixed effects, one indicator each; the respondents are a random intercept. That is a generalized linear mixed model (Rijmen, Tuerlinckx, De Boeck & Kuppens, 2003), and lme4 (Bates, Mächler, Bolker & Walker, 2015) fits it in one line (Doran, Bates, Bliese & Dowling, 2007; De Boeck et al., 2011):
glmer(resp ~ 0 + item + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = long_table)
The 0 + gives each item its own intercept; (1 | id) is \(\theta\). Why not stay with mirt? Because everything in this lesson is a change to that formula. The two programs’ Rasch estimates agree to about a thousandth of a logit here (second Go deeper callout).

Try it: build the formula
Tick the terms you want for the 24 verbal aggression items of Item response data and the IRW. (Trait anger is a respondent covariate in lme4’s copy of these data, not the IRW’s.)


Code
viewof fb_terms = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["Item effects (one per item)", "Item features (behaviour, situation, want/do)", "Item residual", "A respondent covariate (trait anger)"],
  {value: ["Item effects (one per item)"], label: "Terms"})









Code
fb = formulaFor({
  itemEffects: fb_terms.includes("Item effects (one per item)"),
  design: fb_terms.includes("Item features (behaviour, situation, want/do)"),
  residual: fb_terms.includes("Item residual"),
  personCov: fb_terms.includes("A respondent covariate (trait anger)")
})
md`\`${fb.formula}\`

**Parameters:** ${fb.params} (including the SD of θ). **Fixed-effect columns:** ${fb.columns.join(", ")}.

${fb.note ? `*${fb.note}*` : ""}`
















The Rasch model needs 25 parameters; swap the item effects for the three item features and it needs 6. Tick both and the model is not identified. An item residual adds one parameter, however many items there are.


Code
quiz({
  q: "In `glmer(resp ~ 0 + item + (1 | id), family = binomial)`, what plays the part of the Rasch model's $\\theta_j$?",
  options: [
    {text: "The random intercept for each `id`", correct: true, why: "Each respondent gets a deviation from zero, drawn from a normal distribution whose SD the model estimates. That is $\\theta_j$ with its mean fixed at 0."},
    {text: "The coefficient on each `item`", correct: false, why: "Those are the items' easinesses, $\\beta_i = -b_i$. They are fixed effects, one per item."},
    {text: "The residual", correct: false, why: "A logistic regression has no separate residual term: the randomness is in the Bernoulli draw of each response given its probability."}
  ]
})










Descriptive and explanatory models
A model with a parameter per item describes the items; one that replaces those parameters with predictors explains them (Wilson & De Boeck, 2004). Likewise for respondents.






Recall from Item response data and the IRW: each verbal aggression item crosses a situation (someone else to blame, or yourself) with a behaviour (curse, scold, shout) and a mode (would you want to, would you do it). Wanting was reported more than doing for every behaviour, most of all for shouting.



The linear logistic test model (Fischer, 1973) writes each item’s easiness as a weighted sum of its features, \[\beta_i = \sum_k q_{ik}\,\eta_k,\] where \(q_{ik}\) is 1 if item \(i\) has feature \(k\) and \(\eta_k\) is that feature’s effect on easiness. For the verbal aggression items: an intercept, scold, shout, self to blame and want, five parameters in place of 24:
glmer(resp ~ behav + situ + mode + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = long_table)
The LLTM is a Rasch model with a constraint on the difficulties, so it keeps the Rasch model’s properties (first Go deeper callout). And a feature means something that 24 difficulties don’t: if want adds 0.7 logits whatever the situation or behaviour, that is a testable claim about how people report aggression. Written the other way round, with items built from the features, it becomes a tool for designing tests (Embretson, 1998).






If you’ve done Differential item functioning: DIF flags items one at a time. A group × feature interaction asks whether the flagged items share a feature.





Code
quiz({
  q: "An LLTM for the 24 verbal aggression items has an intercept and four feature effects. The Rasch model has 24 item easinesses. Both have the SD of $\\theta$. How many degrees of freedom does the likelihood-ratio test of the LLTM against the Rasch model have?",
  options: [
    {text: "19", correct: true, why: "The Rasch model has 25 parameters and the LLTM 6. The LLTM is nested in the Rasch model (it confines the 24 easinesses to a five-dimensional subspace), so the test has $25 - 6 = 19$ df."},
    {text: "20", correct: false, why: "That compares 24 easinesses with four feature effects and forgets the LLTM's intercept."},
    {text: "The models aren't nested, so there is no likelihood-ratio test", correct: false, why: "They are nested: any set of LLTM parameters gives 24 easinesses the Rasch model could also have."}
  ]
})









Explaining difficulty is not fitting it
How good is an LLTM? Two questions get mixed up. How much of the variation in difficulty do the features account for (the squared correlation of the LLTM’s easinesses with the Rasch model’s)? And do they account for all of it, which is what the likelihood-ratio test asks? With a few hundred respondents each easiness is estimated to within a tenth of a logit or so, so the test notices departures that barely dent the correlation.

Try it: explained, and still rejected
Each dot is an item on the verbal aggression design: its easiness is the design’s prediction plus a residual whose SD the slider sets.


Code
viewof lw_sd = Inputs.range([0, 0.6], {value: 0.3, step: 0.02, label: "SD of the item residual"})
viewof lw_np = Inputs.range([50, 2000], {value: 316, step: 1, label: "Respondents"})


















Code
lw = lltmWorld(lw_sd, lw_np)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "Easiness predicted by the features"}, y: {label: "Item's easiness"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["do", "want"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[-2.2, -2.2], [2.2, 2.2]], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.dot(lw.items, {x: "pred", y: "easy", r: 5, fill: "mode", title: "name"})
  ]
})


















Code
md`The features explain **${(100 * lw.r2).toFixed(0)}%** of the variance in easiness. With ${lw_np} respondents, the likelihood-ratio test of the LLTM against the Rasch model would give a χ² of about **${lw.chisq.toFixed(0)}** on ${lw.df} df (p ≈ ${pchisqUpper(lw.chisq, lw.df).toPrecision(2)}).`







At an SD of 0 the dots sit on the line and the expected χ² equals its 19 df. At 0.3 the features still explain more than nine tenths of the variance, and with 316 respondents the test rejects the LLTM overwhelmingly. More respondents raise the χ² and leave the share explained alone: the test weighs the distance from the line against the precision of each estimate. (The widget’s χ² is its expected value: the df plus the squared residuals weighted by each item’s information.)
So what should we conclude when the features explain nearly everything and the test says no? That items differ in ways the features don’t capture, as items written by people almost always will. Rather than set those differences to zero, a model can give them a variance: \[\beta_i = \sum_k q_{ik}\,\eta_k + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon).\] This is the LLTM with an item residual (Janssen, Schepers & Peres, 2004): the items are now random effects around the design’s prediction, and \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) says how much the features leave unexplained. In glmer it is one more term, (1 | item). Items and respondents are then both random, and crossed, since every respondent meets every item (Van den Noortgate, De Boeck & Meulders, 2003).






NoteGo deeper: the LLTM keeps the sum score sufficient





Assumptions: respondents \(j = 1, \dots, J\) answer dichotomous items \(i = 1, \dots, I\); the Rasch model holds with easiness \(\beta_i = \sum_{k=1}^K q_{ik}\eta_k\) for a known \(I \times K\) matrix \(Q\) of full column rank, \(K < I\); responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); \(\eta\) and the \(\theta_j\) are fixed.
Write \(r_j = \sum_i x_{ij}\) for respondent \(j\)’s sum score and \(s_i = \sum_j x_{ij}\) for item \(i\)’s total. The probability of the whole data matrix is \[\Pr(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_{j,i} \frac{e^{x_{ij}(\theta_j + \beta_i)}}{1 + e^{\theta_j + \beta_i}} = \frac{\exp\big(\sum_j r_j \theta_j + \sum_i s_i \beta_i\big)}{\prod_{j,i}\big(1 + e^{\theta_j + \beta_i}\big)}.\] Substitute the constraint: \(\sum_i s_i \beta_i = \sum_i s_i \sum_k q_{ik}\eta_k = \sum_k \eta_k t_k\), with \(t_k = \sum_i q_{ik} s_i\) the number of 1s given to items with feature \(k\). So \[\Pr(\mathbf{X}) = \frac{\exp\big(\sum_j r_j \theta_j + \sum_k t_k \eta_k\big)}{\prod_{j,i}\big(1 + e^{\theta_j + \beta_i}\big)}.\] Two things follow. The data meet \(\theta_j\) only through \(r_j\), so the sum score is still sufficient for \(\theta\), and conditioning on it removes \(\theta\) exactly as in The Rasch model; conditional maximum likelihood for the \(\eta_k\) follows (Fischer, 1973). And the data meet the design effects only through the \(K\) feature totals \(t_k\): the LLTM uses the item totals only through their sums over the items that share a feature. That is the sense in which it is a Rasch model with a linear constraint, and why the likelihood-ratio test against the unconstrained Rasch model loses one degree of freedom for each item parameter the constraint removes (\(I - K\) with this lesson’s marginal fits, which estimate \(\sigma_\theta\) in both models).
Adding an item residual changes the second part and not the first. For the items actually drawn the model is still a Rasch model, so \(r_j\) remains sufficient for \(\theta_j\); but the \(\varepsilon_i\) are random and integrated out of the likelihood, and the \(t_k\) are no longer sufficient for \(\eta\).





Try it: items in families
Items often come in families: four items per grammatical construct, or clones from one template (Glas & van der Linden, 2003). Fixed or random? It depends on the question (De Boeck, 2008): fixed if we care about these items, random if they stand for items that could have been written and a new form will draw new ones. Then what matters is how much variation lies between families and how much within.


Code
viewof fm_between = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 2.4, step: 0.05, label: "SD of difficulty between families"})
viewof fm_within = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.5], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "SD of difficulty within a family"})


















Code
fm_new = Math.sqrt(fm_between ** 2 + fm_within ** 2)
fm_data = grid(-7, 7, 281).flatMap(b => [
  {b, density: dnorm(b, 0, fm_within), which: "New item, known family"},
  {b, density: dnorm(b, 0, fm_new), which: "New item, new family"}])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Difficulty of the next item written (logits, from its family's or the test's average)"}, y: {label: "Density"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["New item, known family", "New item, new family"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(fm_data, {x: "b", y: "density", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})

























Code
md`Share of item variance between families: **${(100 * fm_between ** 2 / (fm_between ** 2 + fm_within ** 2)).toFixed(0)}%**. A new item from a known family has a 95% range of ±${(1.96 * fm_within).toFixed(2)} logits around its family's difficulty; from a new family, ±${(1.96 * fm_new).toFixed(2)} around the test's average.`







The defaults are close to the TROG grammar test below. Most of the variation is between families, so an item’s family pins down its difficulty, and a new family is a far larger gamble. Set the between-family SD to 0 and the two curves meet.


Code
quiz({
  q: "An LLTM explains 89% of the variance in 24 item easinesses, yet the likelihood-ratio test against the Rasch model gives $p < 10^{-20}$. What is the best reading?",
  options: [
    {text: "The features capture most of what makes items differ, but not all, and the data are precise enough to see the rest", correct: true, why: "Each easiness is estimated precisely, so small departures from the design add up to a large χ². An item residual puts a size on what is left."},
    {text: "The features are unrelated to difficulty", correct: false, why: "89% is most of the variance. The test rejects the claim that the features explain *all* of it."},
    {text: "The Rasch model doesn't fit", correct: false, why: "The test compares the LLTM with the Rasch model; it says nothing about whether the Rasch model itself fits."}
  ]
})










Person predictors
Add a respondent covariate and the random intercept becomes a residual around a regression: \[\theta_j = \sum_m \gamma_m z_{jm} + \delta_j, \qquad \delta_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\delta).\] The \(\gamma_m\) are differences in \(\theta\), estimated inside the measurement model rather than by scoring everyone and then regressing the scores, which carries each score’s error into the regression (a reasonable shortcut when scores are precise, as on a long test). This is latent regression (Mislevy, 1987; Zwinderman, 1991); in glmer, resp ~ 0 + item + grade + (1 | id).


What is an item? Trials and local dependence
In a cognitive task, what counts as an item is less clear. In the hearts and flowers task (Davidson, Amso, Anderson & Diamond, 2006), a child presses a key on the same side as a heart, or the side opposite a flower. The obvious items are shape × side, four of them, each met dozens of times. But a flower right after a heart means switching rules, which carries a cost (Monsell, 2003). Is it the same item as a flower after a flower?

Try it: the switch cost


Code
viewof sw_cost = Inputs.range([0, 1.5], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Switch cost (logits)"})
viewof sw_theta = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "A child's θ"})


















Code
sw_b = -1.8
sw_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, sw_b), trial: "Flower after flower"},
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, sw_b + sw_cost), trial: "Flower after heart"}])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Flower after flower", "Flower after heart"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleX([sw_theta], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
          Plot.line(sw_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "trial", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})

























Code
md`At θ = ${sw_theta.toFixed(1)}: P(correct) is **${p2pl(sw_theta, sw_b).toFixed(2)}** after a flower and **${p2pl(sw_theta, sw_b + sw_cost).toFixed(2)}** after a heart, a gap of ${(p2pl(sw_theta, sw_b) - p2pl(sw_theta, sw_b + sw_cost)).toFixed(2)}.`







A switch cost shifts the curve to the right. The gap in probability shrinks toward the ceiling, where most children below sit, so a cost constant in logits looks smaller in proportions correct. A trial covariate such as switch is an item predictor that redefines the item as the stimulus in its context; an item late in a booklet may likewise not be the item it was elsewhere.






If you’ve done Linking and equating: TIMSS items were 0.077 logits harder in a booklet’s second block. In an explanatory model, position is one more item predictor.









Recall from The Rasch model: responses are assumed locally independent given \(\theta\). Two items that share a reading passage were the example of how this can fail.



Random effects give local dependence a model. A respondent may do better on one family than their \(\theta\) predicts, and all its items move together. A random effect for each respondent × family, (1 | id:family), captures the shift: given \(\theta\) alone a family’s items are dependent; given \(\theta\) and the family effect, independent again. This is the testlet model (Bradlow, Wainer & Wang, 1999) in a Rasch form, and its SD against the SD of \(\theta\) says how much of a respondent’s standing is specific to a family.






If you’ve done Generalizability theory: each facet and interaction was a random intercept in lme4. With a logit link the same formulas give the models here; id:family plays the part of person × task.









NoteGo deeper: crossed random effects and the marginal likelihood





Assumptions: the Rasch model as a mixed model, \(\text{logit}\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \theta_j + \beta_i\), with \(\theta_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\theta)\) independent across respondents, and (for random items) \(\beta_i = \mu + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\) independent of \(\theta\).
Fixed items. The random effects are integrated out, which leaves the marginal likelihood of the fixed parameters, \[L(\beta, \sigma_\theta) = \prod_j \int \prod_i \Pr(x_{ij} \mid \theta, \beta_i)\, \phi(\theta; 0, \sigma^2_\theta)\, d\theta.\] It factors into one-dimensional integrals, one per respondent. mirt evaluates each by quadrature inside the EM algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). glmer instead uses the Laplace approximation: find the peak of each integrand and replace the integrand by a normal curve with the same peak and curvature (the curvature is the information of The likelihood and logistic regression). With 24 responses per respondent the integrand is close to normal and the approximation is good. On the verbal aggression data the two routes agree closely:
The easinesses differ by at most 0.001, and the SDs of \(\theta\) are 1.385 (mirt) and 1.378 (glmer).
Random items. Now the integral is over all the \(\theta_j\) and all the \(\varepsilon_i\) at once, \(J + I\) dimensions, and it does not factor, because every response involves one of each. Quadrature over hundreds of dimensions is out of reach; the Laplace approximation, applied to the whole vector of random effects, is what makes crossed models practical (Tuerlinckx, Rijmen, Verbeke & De Boeck, 2006). glmer offers adaptive quadrature (its nAGQ argument) only for models with a single scalar random effect (lme4 documentation). The Laplace approximation is least accurate for binary data with few observations per random effect, where it can understate variances (Joe, 2008). Here each respondent has 24 responses and each item 316, which is comfortable. A child × block effect in TROG rests on four responses each, so its SD is the estimate to hold most loosely.

title: What is an item? Explanatory item response models
text:
Simulate
The code simulates the verbal aggression design with 300 respondents, easinesses following the LLTM plus a residual with SD sd_item, and fits the Rasch model, the LLTM and the LLTM with an item residual. The first run takes 30 to 45 seconds, most of it loading lme4; nAGQ = 0 keeps the fits to seconds (delete it in your own R session for the full fit).
With the seed as written (sd_item <- 0.3), the features explain 88% of the Rasch easiness variance, the test gives χ² = 157 on 19 df, and the estimated residual SD is 0.33. Set sd_item <- 0: χ² falls to 13 (p = 0.82). At sd_item <- 0.15 the features explain 96% and the test still rejects (χ² = 57, p ≈ 10⁻⁵). Then keep 0.15 and set np <- 1000: the share explained barely changes and the χ² grows.

title: What is an item? Explanatory item response models
text:
With real data
verbagg is the main example: items built from a design, to be explained. trog_brinchmann_2019 is the contrast: items in families, for random items and local dependence. imps2025_hf is the case where the obvious definition of an item leaves something out, with a respondent covariate. Download the code; it needs lme4.

Verbal aggression: explaining the items
The verbal aggression data come from De Boeck and Wilson (2004), who use them throughout their book on explanatory models. As in Item response data and the IRW, 1 means the reaction was reported (“perhaps” or “yes”), and one item is stored as S4wantCurse, so the code lower-cases the names, which carry the design.


Code
library(lme4)
options(digits = 7)  # R's default, in case a .Rprofile changes it
# nloptwrap is much quicker than glmer's default optimizer when a model has many
# fixed effects, as the Rasch model (one per item) does. The other models have few
# fixed effects and use the default.
ctl <- glmerControl(optimizer = "nloptwrap")
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v60_0.verbagg/rows?format=csv"
va <- read.csv(url)
va$item <- tolower(va$item)   # one item is stored as S4wantCurse
# The item name carries the design: situation 1-4, want or do, and a behaviour.
va$behav <- factor(sub(".*(curse|scold|shout)$", "\\1", va$item))
va$mode  <- factor(ifelse(grepl("want", va$item), "want", "do"), levels = c("do", "want"))
va$situ  <- factor(ifelse(grepl("^s[12]", va$item), "other", "self"))  # who is to blame
items <- unique(va[, c("item", "situ", "mode", "behav")])
items <- items[order(items$item), ]
rownames(items) <- NULL
c(respondents = length(unique(va$id)), items = nrow(items), responses = nrow(va))

        316          24        7584

# Sanity check: the same data ship with lme4 (VerbAgg, with r2 = "Y" when the
# answer was perhaps or yes). If the item proportions agree, the models below
# can be checked against De Boeck et al. (2011), who fit them to VerbAgg.
p_irw <- tapply(va$resp, va$item, mean)

all.equal(p_irw, p_lme4[names(p_irw)], check.attributes = FALSE)


[1] TRUE


They do, item for item. Now the Rasch model, as a regression:


Code
# The Rasch model as a mixed logistic regression: a fixed intercept for each item
# (its easiness, so b = -coefficient) and a random intercept for each respondent
# (theta, with mean 0 and an SD to estimate).
rasch <- glmer(resp ~ 0 + item + (1 | id), data = va, family = binomial, control = ctl)
easy <- fixef(rasch)
names(easy) <- sub("^item", "", names(easy))
round(head(sort(easy), 3), 2)   # the hardest items: all three about shouting

The hardest items to endorse are about shouting, most of all doing it when you are to blame, and the easiest are about cursing. The SD of \(\theta\) is 1.38. Now the LLTM:


Code
# The LLTM: 24 easinesses replaced by an intercept and four design effects.
lltm <- glmer(resp ~ behav + situ + mode + (1 | id), data = va, family = binomial)
round(fixef(lltm), 2)

Each feature does what the descriptive look suggested: against cursing, scolding costs 1.06 logits and shouting 2.04; being to blame yourself costs 1.03; want adds 0.67 over do. How well do five parameters do in place of 24?


Code
predict({
  q: "The five LLTM parameters reproduce the 24 Rasch easinesses with a correlation of 0.94, so they explain 89% of their variance. Will the likelihood-ratio test of the LLTM against the Rasch model accept it?",
  choices: ["Yes, comfortably (p > 0.5)", "Borderline (p near 0.05)", "No, decisively"],
  answer: "No, decisively",
  reveal: "χ² = 159 on 19 df: the LLTM is rejected. With 316 respondents each easiness is estimated precisely enough that the 11% left over is far more than chance. The test comes first below, then the explained share."

Code
# The LLTM with an item residual: items scatter around the design's prediction
# with an SD to estimate.
lltm_r <- glmer(resp ~ behav + situ + mode + (1 | id) + (1 | item), data = va,
                family = binomial)

The residual SD is 0.34, against 1.37 for \(\theta\): items scatter around the design’s prediction by about a quarter of the spread of respondents. The feature effects barely move, and the AIC (8,164, with 7 parameters) falls between the LLTM’s and the Rasch model’s.
So which would I fit? It turns on one assumption: that the features are all there is to an item, which holds only when items were generated from the features by rule. Otherwise I’d fit the LLTM with an item residual, not without it: real items always leave something over, and the residual SD says how much. The Rasch model describes these 24 items best; the LLTM with a residual says what makes them differ, and how far that account falls short.






NoteWanting, doing and inhibition: an interaction

The want–do gap for shouting is 0.69 logits larger than for cursing (SE 0.33); scolding matches cursing (−0.06). Smits, De Boeck and Vansteelandt (2004) study this gap as the inhibition of verbal aggression, and on that reading shouting is held back most. The evidence is modest: with the item residual in the model, the test of the two interaction terms gives p = 0.059, since four items per cell leave little to test with once items may differ.





TROG: items in families
The Test for Reception of Grammar (Bishop, 1979) tests the understanding of grammar in blocks of four items, one block per grammatical construct: the child hears a sentence and picks the matching picture. These are 210 Norwegian children at the first assessment of a longitudinal study (Brinchmann, Braeken & Lyster, 2019), distributed with the mokken R package (van der Ark, 2007). The test is copyrighted, so we refer to blocks by their letters, a to t. Keying: 1 is correct.

url_trog <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v24_0.trog_brinchmann_2019/rows?format=csv"

# item_family numbers the 20 blocks of four items; the item names (a1 to t4) use letters.

Hearts and flowers: what is an item?
Obradović, Sulik, Finch and Tirado-Strayer (2018) validated a tablet version of hearts and flowers for classrooms; the IRW table also holds preschool data from DeJoseph, Merculief, Sulik and Obradović (2025). What came before moves the probability more than shape or side does: the item is the stimulus in its context. Trials as items takes this further.
Features coded by people are one way to explain difficulty. Could an item’s text alone predict it? That is deep dive #25, which AI and psychometrics takes across the IRW, with this lesson’s LLTM as the human-coded baseline.

title: What is an item? Explanatory item response models
text:
Problems

The LLTM as a constrained Rasch model. Write the verbal aggression LLTM as \(b_i = -\sum_k q_{ik}\eta_k\), give the \(24 \times 5\) matrix \(Q\), and count both models’ parameters. Why can’t glmer(resp ~ 0 + item + mode + (1 | id)) estimate an effect of mode?
Inhibition by situation. Is the want–do gap larger when someone else is to blame? Fit mode * situ with the item residual and say what the interaction means for inhibition. Can two items per cell support the three-way interaction?
Fixed or random? For TROG, argue for fixed items if the goal is these 210 children’s scores on this form, and for random items if a new form will draw new items from the same 20 constructs. What changes in what you report? What if the new form uses new constructs?
Design a bank. For 60 arithmetic word problems for grades 3 to 5, choose three to five features you expect to drive difficulty and say how you would code them. What model would you fit after piloting, and how would you judge whether the features predict new items’ difficulty well enough to skip piloting them?
The time limit. In the grades 3–5 data the time limit was 0.75 s in the fall and 1.25 s in the spring (time_limit). Does the switch cost depend on it? Why is this not a clean experiment on the time limit?
Challenge (open). When is a trial “the same item” twice? A flower after two hearts may differ from a flower after one, and the fortieth trial from the fifth. Propose a criterion and test it on these data (say, items defined by shape × side, by shape × switch, and by shape × switch × run length). What would convince you that you had the right definition?







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: What is an item? Explanatory item response models
text:
Going further

De Boeck, P., & Wilson, M. (Eds.). (2004). Explanatory item response models: A generalized linear and nonlinear approach. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-3990-9. The book this lesson follows. Its chapters by Wilson & De Boeck and Janssen, Schepers & Peres cover descriptive vs. explanatory models and item predictors with a residual.

Journal of Statistical Software, 39(12). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v039.i12. The lme4 formulas for the models here, fit to the same verbal aggression data.
Rijmen, F., Tuerlinckx, F., De Boeck, P., & Kuppens, P. (2003). A nonlinear mixed model framework for item response theory. Psychological Methods, 8(2), 185–205. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.8.2.185. Item response models as mixed models, in general.
Fischer, G. H. (1973). The linear logistic test model as an instrument in educational research. Acta Psychologica, 37(6), 359–374. https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-6918(73)90003-6. The LLTM and its conditional estimation.
De Boeck, P. (2008). Random item IRT models. Psychometrika, 73(4), 533–559. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-008-9092-x. When and why to treat items as random.
Van den Noortgate, W., De Boeck, P., & Meulders, M. (2003). Cross-classification multilevel logistic models in psychometrics. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 28(4), 369–386. https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986028004369. Respondents and items as crossed random effects.
Embretson, S. E. (1998). A cognitive design system approach to generating valid tests: Application to abstract reasoning. Psychological Methods, 3(3), 380–396. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.3.3.380. Item features as a tool for writing items, not only for explaining them.
Bradlow, E. T., Wainer, H., & Wang, X. (1999). A Bayesian random effects model for testlets. Psychometrika, 64(2), 153–168. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294533. The testlet model for items that share a context.

British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 59(2), 225–255. https://doi.org/10.1348/000711005X79857. How the marginal likelihood is approximated, and what each approximation costs.
Janssen, R. (2016). Linear logistic models. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 1. Models (pp. 211–224). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315374512. A handbook chapter on the linear logistic test model and related models.
De Boeck, P., & Wilson, M. R. (2016). Explanatory response models. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 1. Models (pp. 565–580). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315374512. A handbook chapter on explanatory item response models.
Rabe-Hesketh, S., & Skrondal, A. (2016). Generalized linear latent and mixed modeling. In W. J. van der Linden (Ed.), Handbook of item response theory: Vol. 1. Models (pp. 503–526). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315374512. A handbook chapter on item response models as generalized linear latent and mixed models.

title: Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
text:
What this is for
How many things does a set of items measure? Classical test theory mostly assumes the answer is one, and a high alpha doesn’t check that assumption. Many instruments are built to measure several things at once: a personality inventory with five domains, a quality-of-life scale with physical and emotional subscales. And an instrument meant to measure one thing may not, as the reverse-worded items in the instrument-building lesson showed. Factor analysis is the family of tools for asking what, and how many, underlying dimensions account for the correlations among a set of items. It is one of the oldest ideas in psychometrics. Spearman (1904) proposed it to explain why children who did well in one school subject tended to do well in others, and it remains the workhorse for studying the internal structure of a scale.






Recall from From construct map to items: reverse-worded items guard against acquiescence, but respondents don’t always read them as plain opposites of the forward items. In the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale the items fell, with one exception, into two blocks by the direction they were worded in (average correlations of 0.71 and 0.61 within the blocks, 0.23 across), with a second eigenvalue of 2.32. Wording direction acted as a second dimension, and alpha didn’t reveal it.



This lesson is about the exploratory version: we let the data suggest a structure. Factor analysis II takes up the confirmatory version, where we state a structure in advance and test it, and shows that factor analysis and item response theory are closer relatives than they first appear.

title: Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
text:
Simulate
The code below builds a questionnaire with a known structure (by default, two correlated factors with five items each), runs parallel analysis, fits an oblique exploratory factor analysis, and prints the loadings for comparison with the truth. It uses the psych package (Revelle, 2026), with rotations from GPArotation (Bernaards & Jennrich, 2005), and estimates by minimum residuals (Harman & Jones, 1966). It runs in your browser; the first run takes a little while as psych loads.
Things to try: set loading to 0.4 or np to 100 and see whether parallel analysis still finds the right number of factors; set phi to 0.7 and ask whether two factors are still worth distinguishing; set n_factors to 3.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

With the seed as written, the estimated factor correlation comes out at 0.18 against a true 0.3. That is sampling variability with 400 people, and a reminder that factor correlations are estimated with less precision than loadings. Download this code.

title: Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
text:
With real data
We use bfi2_zhang_2025, our main example: responses from 1,335 university students to the 60-item Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2; Soto & John, 2017), which measures five broad domains of personality with 12 items each. The data come from Zhang, Huang, Sun and Savalei (2025), who randomly assigned students to one of four response formats; we pool across formats here and return to that design in problem 4. Download the code.


Code
library(psych)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v21_0.bfi2_zhang_2025/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(url)
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
num <- as.integer(sub("self_BFI_", "", colnames(wide)))
resp <- as.data.frame(wide[, order(num)])
c(respondents = nrow(resp), items = ncol(resp))


respondents       items 
       1335          60 


Code
resp <- resp[complete.cases(resp), ]
nrow(resp)   # respondents who answered all 60 items


[1] 1199


A few responses are missing, scattered across items and respondents; we keep the 1,199 students who answered all 60.


Code
# The BFI-2 cycles through its five domains: item 1 is Extraversion, item 2
# Agreeableness, item 3 Conscientiousness, item 4 Negative Emotionality, item 5
# Open-Mindedness, item 6 Extraversion again, and so on (Soto & John, 2017).
domain <- c("Extraversion", "Agreeableness", "Conscientiousness",
            "Negative Emotionality", "Open-Mindedness")[(seq_len(60) - 1) %% 5 + 1]
table(domain)


domain
        Agreeableness     Conscientiousness          Extraversion 
                   12                    12                    12 
Negative Emotionality       Open-Mindedness 
                   12                    12 


Responses run from 1 to 5, and they arrive keyed: the BFI-2’s reverse-worded items have already been reversed, so a higher response always means more of the item’s domain (for Negative Emotionality, more negative emotion). Neither the table’s metadata nor its processing code says so, and the data can only suggest it. If the reverse-worded items were still raw, many pairs of items from the same domain would correlate negatively. The lowest of these correlations is essentially zero:


Code
# Are the reverse-worded items already reversed? If they weren't, many pairs of
# items from the same domain would correlate clearly negatively.
r <- cor(resp)
same <- outer(domain, domain, "==") & lower.tri(r)
round(range(r[same]), 3)   # Pearson correlations between items of the same domain


[1] -0.005  0.764








Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: the Mach IV arrives unkeyed, and there the data couldn’t tell us which items to reverse; we had to read them. Here the check is reassuring, but the published key (Soto & John, 2017) is what settles it.




The correlation matrix
Before fitting anything, look at the correlations with the items sorted by the domain they were written for.


Code
# Polychoric correlations treat each 1-5 response as a coarsened continuous one.
R <- polychoric(resp)$rho
by_domain <- order(domain)
image(1:60, 1:60, R[by_domain, rev(by_domain)], zlim = c(-1, 1), axes = FALSE,
      col = hcl.colors(41, "Blue-Red 3"), xlab = "Items, grouped by domain", ylab = "",
      main = "Polychoric correlations, BFI-2 items sorted by domain")
abline(v = seq(12.5, 48.5, 12), h = seq(12.5, 48.5, 12), col = "white", lwd = 2)









Code
off <- lower.tri(R)
round(c(within_domain = median(R[off & outer(domain, domain, "==")]),
        between_domains = median(R[off & outer(domain, domain, "!=")])), 2)


  within_domain between_domains 
           0.35            0.04 


Five blocks along the diagonal, and pale regions between them: the median correlation is 0.35 between two items of the same domain and 0.04 between items of different domains. The one band of blue belongs to Negative Emotionality (the fourth block, since the domains are sorted alphabetically), whose items correlate weakly and negatively with many of the others.
Do the BFI-2’s items also split by wording, as the Rosenberg items did? Half of each domain’s items are worded in reverse (the scoring key of Soto & John, 2017), so we can compare pairs of items worded in the same direction with pairs worded in opposite directions.


Code
# Reverse-worded items, from the BFI-2 scoring key (Soto & John, 2017). They arrive
# already reversed; here we only ask whether items worded in the same direction
# correlate more than items worded in opposite directions.
reversed <- seq_len(60) %in% c(3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 16, 17, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28,
                               29, 30, 31, 36, 37, 42, 44, 45, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 55, 58)
same_dom <- outer(domain, domain, "==")
same_dir <- outer(reversed, reversed, "==")
round(c(same_domain_same_direction = median(R[off & same_dom & same_dir]),
        same_domain_opposite       = median(R[off & same_dom & !same_dir]),
        other_domain_same_direction = median(R[off & !same_dom & same_dir]),
        other_domain_opposite       = median(R[off & !same_dom & !same_dir])), 2)


 same_domain_same_direction        same_domain_opposite 
                       0.35                        0.35 
other_domain_same_direction       other_domain_opposite 
                       0.05                        0.02 


Within a domain the two kinds of pair correlate equally, with a median of 0.35 each. Between domains, pairs worded the same way correlate 0.05 and pairs worded oppositely 0.02. By this measure wording direction leaves at most a trace in the BFI-2, far from the Rosenberg scale’s blocks.


How many factors?


Code
predict({
  q: "The BFI-2 was designed around five domains, each with three facets. How many factors do you think parallel analysis will suggest for these 60 items?",
  choices: ["5", "9", "12", "15"],
  answer: "9",
  reveal: "Parallel analysis suggests 9, and the eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule suggests 12. With about 1,200 respondents, the data have enough power to pick up some of the finer facet structure within domains. Neither answer is 'wrong': how many factors depends on the level of detail you care about."
})









Code
set.seed(252)
pa <- fa.parallel(R, n.obs = nrow(resp), fa = "fa", n.iter = 20, plot = TRUE,
                  main = "Parallel analysis: BFI-2")









Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  9  and the number of components =  NA 


Code
ev <- eigen(R)$values
c(parallel = pa$nfact,
  kaiser = sum(ev > 1))           # the "eigenvalue greater than one" rule, for comparison


parallel   kaiser 
       9       12 


Code
round(ev[1] / ev[2], 2)           # ratio of the first to the second eigenvalue


[1] 1.67


Code
# The same parallel analysis on Pearson correlations, for comparison:
set.seed(252)
fa.parallel(r, n.obs = nrow(resp), fa = "fa", n.iter = 20, plot = FALSE)$nfact


Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  9  and the number of components =  NA 


[1] 9


Parallel analysis says 9, the Kaiser rule 12, against a design of five domains and 15 facets. Is that unusual? Across the IRW it is the norm. The IRW’s dimensionality vignette ran parallel analysis on 810 tables and found exactly one factor in only 3% of them; for the older 25-item Big Five Inventory in psychtools_bfi, built for five traits, it suggests six. Nor is it an artifact of the polychoric correlations, which Garrido, Abad and Ponsoda (2013) recommend for parallel analysis with ordinal items: on Pearson correlations the answer is 9 again. The formal criteria find more structure than the design names, because each domain is itself made of related facets.
The same vignette gives a baseline for how multidimensional the BFI-2 is. The ratio of the first to the second eigenvalue, 1.7 here, is a rough index of how far a scale is from a single dimension (larger means closer to one). The vignette’s 57 personality tables have a median ratio of 3.26, and the 25-item BFI’s is 1.91. The vignette’s tables have at most 40 items, so the comparison is rough, but by the IRW’s standard the BFI-2 is clearly multidimensional, as it was built to be.
The five-domain structure is still the one the instrument is built to score, so that is what we fit. The choice is ours; the data inform it but do not make it.


Five factors


Code
# Five factors, minimum-residual estimation, oblique (oblimin) rotation.
f5 <- fa(R, nfactors = 5, n.obs = nrow(resp), rotate = "oblimin", fm = "minres")
L <- unclass(f5$loadings)
top <- apply(abs(L), 1, which.max)
# Name each factor after the domain whose items load on it most often.
names_f <- tapply(domain, factor(top, levels = 1:5), function(d) names(which.max(table(d))))
short <- c(Extraversion = "E", Agreeableness = "A", Conscientiousness = "C",
           "Negative Emotionality" = "N", "Open-Mindedness" = "O")[names_f]
colnames(L) <- dimnames(f5$Phi)[[1]] <- dimnames(f5$Phi)[[2]] <- short
table(domain, factor = short[top])

That is clean by the standard of the design: the median item’s loading on its own factor is 0.57, and its largest loading on any other factor is 0.16. The factor correlations sit fairly close to zero; the largest in size is −0.22, between Negative Emotionality and Conscientiousness (students higher in negative emotionality describe themselves as a little less organized and dependable).

Finally, the rotation point from above, on real data:


Code
# The same five factors with an orthogonal rotation: identical fit, different loadings.
f5v <- fa(R, nfactors = 5, n.obs = nrow(resp), rotate = "varimax", fm = "minres")
round(c(oblimin_rmsr = f5$rms, varimax_rmsr = f5v$rms), 4)


oblimin_rmsr varimax_rmsr

Identical root-mean-square residuals: the orthogonal and oblique solutions fit exactly as well, because they are the same model described in two frames. Rotation is a choice about how to read the factors, never about how well they fit.

title: Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
text:
Problems

One factor. Show that under a one-factor model with standardized items and factor, \(\text{cor}(x_i, x_j) = \lambda_i\lambda_j\) for \(i \ne j\). Then show that, for any four items, \(\text{cor}(x_1,x_3)\,\text{cor}(x_2,x_4) = \text{cor}(x_1,x_4)\,\text{cor}(x_2,x_3)\). (These “tetrad” constraints were Spearman’s test for a single factor; Spearman & Holzinger, 1924.)
Reliability, revisited. In a one-factor model, what is the correlation between the sum of the items and the factor? Use your answer to explain why items with low loadings contribute little to reliability, and connect it to the proof that alpha is a lower bound in the reliability lesson. What does tau-equivalence mean in terms of loadings?
Planning a pilot. You are piloting a new 15-item scale written for three factors, and you expect loadings of about 0.5 and factor correlations of about 0.3. Using the simulation, find the smallest sample (to the nearest 50) at which parallel analysis finds three factors in at least 9 of 10 seeds. How does your answer change if the loadings are 0.4? What does this suggest about relying on one rule in a small pilot?
Formats. The BFI-2 data come from four randomly assigned response formats (itemcov_format: Likert L, Expanded E, and two item-specific versions, ISF and ISL). Fit the five-factor model separately in each format. Do the same items load on the same factors? Are the loadings noticeably stronger in any format? What would a difference tell you about the formats, and why does random assignment matter for that inference? (Zhang et al., 2025, is the place to compare notes; Measurement invariance gives the formal test of whether a structure holds across groups.)
A weak item. Find the three BFI-2 items with the lowest communalities in the five-factor solution. Look them up in Soto and John (2017), where the item wording is published. Would you drop them? What might they be measuring instead?
Challenge: PCA versus FA. Run principal() (PCA) and fa() with five components or factors on the BFI-2. Compare the loadings. Which are systematically larger, and why? Is there a number of items per domain at which the difference stops mattering?







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

Going further

title: Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
text:
What this is for
The Rasch model left open how far from 1 an outfit statistic can stray, and From the 1PL to the 4PL noted that BIC says whether one model beats another, not by how much. Most fit statistics answer yes or no, and with thousands of respondents the answer is nearly always that the model misfits. The more useful question is how much a richer model helps. We answer it by predicting responses the model never saw, and scoring those predictions with the InterModel Vigorish (IMV), a measure of predictive gain built to be compared across datasets.

title: Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
text:
Core ideas

How far from 1 is too far?






Recall from The Rasch model: outfit and infit are mean squared standardized residuals, near 1 if the model is right. Below 1 an item overfits (it is more predictable than the model expects, typically because it discriminates better than average); above 1 it underfits. Chess problem Y15 underfit, with outfit 2.2.



The standardized residual is \(z_{ij} = (x_{ij} - p_{ij})/\sqrt{p_{ij}(1 - p_{ij})}\), with \(p_{ij}\) the model’s probability of a correct response. Outfit is the mean of \(z_{ij}^2\) over an item’s \(n\) respondents; infit weights each by \(p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})\), so respondents far from the item count for less (Wright & Masters, 1982). If the model is true, each \(z_{ij}^2\) has mean 1. How closely does outfit hover around 1? Treating each \(z^2\) as \(\chi^2_1\), with variance 2, gives the rule of thumb that its SD is about \(\sqrt{2/n}\). Wu and Adams (2013) work through how these statistics depend on sample size, and show that for dichotomous items they measure the slope of the empirical item curve relative to the model’s.

Try it: outfit when the model is true
300 simulated items at one difficulty, each answered by \(n\) respondents, with outfit computed from the true parameters. The solid line marks 1, the model’s expectation; the dashed lines mark 0.8–1.2, the range Wright and Linacre (1994) suggest for high-stakes multiple-choice items.


Code
viewof on_n = Inputs.radio([50, 200, 1000, 5000], {value: 200, label: "Respondents (n)"})
viewof on_b = Inputs.range([-2.5, 2.5], {value: 0, step: 0.5, label: "Item difficulty (ability: mean 0, SD 1)"})


















Code
on_sims = Array.from({length: 10}, (_, k) => outfitNull(on_n, Array(30).fill(on_b), 100 + k))
on_vals = on_sims.flatMap(s => s.outfit)
on_exact = on_sims[0].exactSD[0]
on_sd = Math.sqrt(on_vals.reduce((s, v) => s + (v - 1) ** 2, 0) / on_vals.length)
on_out = on_vals.filter(v => v < 0.8 || v > 1.2).length / on_vals.length
// The x range always shows 0.75-1.25 and stretches to cover the data (up to 3), with
// 50 bins across it, so the bars stay visible however narrow the spread.
on_lo = Math.min(0.75, Math.min(...on_vals))
on_hi = Math.max(1.25, Math.min(Math.max(...on_vals), 3))
on_bins = {
  const w = (on_hi - on_lo) / 50, c = Array(50).fill(0);
  for (const v of on_vals) c[Math.min(49, Math.max(0, Math.floor((v - on_lo) / w)))]++;
  return c.map((n, k) => ({x1: on_lo + k * w, x2: on_lo + (k + 1) * w, n}));
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Outfit", domain: [on_lo, on_hi]}, y: {label: "Items"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(on_bins, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y: "n", fill: palette.light, insetLeft: 0.5, insetRight: 0.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0.8, 1.2], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([1], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})



































































Code
md`Across ${on_vals.length} simulated items the SD of outfit is **${on_sd.toFixed(3)}**; the model-based SD for this item is ${on_exact.toFixed(3)}, and the rule √(2/n) gives ${Math.sqrt(2 / on_n).toFixed(3)}. ${(100 * on_out).toFixed(0)}% of items fall outside 0.8–1.2. An outfit of 1.08 here would be ${(0.08 / on_exact).toFixed(1)} SDs above 1.`







With 50 respondents, a fifth of the outfits fall outside 0.8–1.2 although the model is right; with 5,000, 1.08 sits several SDs out. Move the difficulty away from 0 and the spread grows (a strong respondent missing an easy item gives a huge \(z^2\)), so \(\sqrt{2/n}\) is only a rough anchor. A fixed band says little about chance in small samples, and a \(z\) says little about size in large ones. I read both: the \(z\) says whether a misfit could be chance, the size whether it is worth anyone’s time.


Code
quiz({
  q: "An item has outfit 1.08 in a sample of 2,000 respondents, and its $z$ is 2.7. A colleague says the item misfits badly. What would you say?",
  options: [
    {text: "The misfit is real but small: about 8% more noise than the model expects", correct: true, why: "With $n = 2000$, $\\sqrt{2/n} \\approx 0.03$, so 1.08 is unlikely under the model, but it is well inside the ranges used for acceptable items. Size and significance are separate questions."},
    {text: "It fits: 1.08 is inside 0.8–1.2", correct: false, why: "The band ignores sample size. At this $n$ an outfit of 1.08 is unlikely to be chance; the question is whether an 8% excess matters."},
    {text: "It misfits badly: $z > 2$", correct: false, why: "The $z$ says the deviation is unlikely under the model, not that it is large. With enough respondents, a small misfit gives a large $z$."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: the null distribution of outfit





Assumptions: the Rasch model holds; abilities and difficulties are known (not estimated); responses are independent.
One squared residual. For one response with probability \(p\) (and \(q = 1 - p\)), \(z^2\) equals \(q/p\) when \(x = 1\) and \(p/q\) when \(x = 0\). So \(E(z^2) = p \cdot q/p + q \cdot p/q = 1\), and \[E(z^4) = p\,\frac{q^2}{p^2} + q\,\frac{p^2}{q^2} = \frac{q^3 + p^3}{pq} = \frac{1 - 3pq}{pq}, \qquad \text{Var}(z^2) = \frac{1}{pq} - 4.\] At \(p = 0.5\) the variance is 0 (every response gives \(z^2 = 1\)); it grows without bound as \(p\) nears 0 or 1.
Outfit. Outfit is the mean of \(n\) independent \(z^2\)s, so \[\text{SD}(\text{outfit}_i) = \frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}\Big(\frac{1}{p_{ij}q_{ij}} - 4\Big)}.\] For \(\theta \sim N(0, 1)\) and an item at difficulty \(b\), \(1/(pq) = 2 + e^{\theta - b} + e^{b - \theta}\), whose mean is \(2 + 2e^{1/2}\cosh b\). The variance of one \(z^2\) therefore averages \(2e^{1/2}\cosh b - 2\): 1.30 for an item at the centre, 2 (the \(\chi^2_1\) value behind \(\sqrt{2/n}\)) at \(|b| \approx 0.64\), and 10.4 at \(|b| = 2\). The widget’s “model-based SD” is this formula. Items far from the respondents have the widest null distributions.
Estimated parameters. In practice \(p_{ij}\) comes from estimates fitted to the same responses, which pulls outfit toward the data and narrows its spread. How abilities are estimated matters too, as Simulate shows. mirt’s \(z\) statistic uses a version of this variance with the estimates plugged in.






Does the model fit? Tests and criteria
For a whole model there are four tools. The likelihood-ratio test compares nested models: twice the difference in log likelihoods is referred to a \(\chi^2\) with the extra parameters as degrees of freedom. AIC (Akaike, 1974) and BIC (Schwarz, 1978) charge a penalty per parameter against the log likelihood and work for non-nested models too. \(M_2\) (Maydeu-Olivares & Joe, 2005, 2006) compares observed and model proportions correct for each item and each pair of items, which stays usable when most of the \(2^I\) response patterns never occur; it comes with an RMSEA, a misfit per degree of freedom.






Recall from The Rasch model: conditioning on the sum score removes \(\theta\) from the Rasch likelihood, which gives conditional maximum likelihood; CML estimates of the difficulties from high and low scorers should agree, and Andersen (1973) turned that into a likelihood-ratio test.



Andersen’s test splits respondents by sum score, estimates the difficulties by conditional ML within each group, and compares with one set of difficulties for everyone, with no assumption about how \(\theta\) is distributed.
Each asks whether the data are consistent with a model (or with the smaller of two) up to sampling error. For that question the tests are the right tool, and the criteria a reasonable way to choose among models in modest samples. But sampling error shrinks as \(n\) grows while a model’s small departures from the data don’t, so with thousands of respondents every test rejects, and none says how much better the preferred model predicts.


Code
quiz({
  q: "The same test is given to 500 and to 50,000 respondents, and the 2PL describes both samples equally well. What happens to the BIC difference between the Rasch model and the 2PL?",
  options: [
    {text: "It grows roughly in proportion to the sample size", correct: true, why: "The log-likelihood gain from the 2PL is summed over respondents, so it grows with $n$, while the penalty grows only with $\\log n$. The difference says ever more confidently *that* the 2PL is preferred, not *how much* it helps."},
    {text: "It stays about the same, because the models fit equally well", correct: false, why: "The gain per response stays the same, but BIC sums over responses. Its differences are on a scale that depends on $n$."},
    {text: "It shrinks, because BIC's penalty grows with $\\log n$", correct: false, why: "The penalty does grow, but only with $\\log n$; the likelihood gain grows with $n$ and outpaces it."}
  ]
})









Predict what you didn’t fit
A model with more parameters fits its own data at least as well as the model it extends, partly by fitting noise. To tell them apart, judge a model by responses it wasn’t fitted to (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017). With item responses, hold out responses, not respondents: assign each response at random to one of \(k\) folds, fit the model to all but one fold, and predict the held-out responses from the fitted abilities and item parameters. Every respondent and item keeps most of its responses, so every held-out response can be predicted (Stenhaug & Domingue, 2022).

Try it: more parameters, better in-sample
The widget simulates one item whose true curve is a 2PL with the slope you choose, answered by respondents whose \(\theta\) we know (as Elo was known in The likelihood and logistic regression). It fits seven models for that item, labelled by how many parameters they have: 1, one probability for everyone (the item’s proportion correct); 2, a logistic curve in \(\theta\), the true form; 3 to 7, a logistic curve whose exponent is a polynomial in \(\theta\), so the curve can bend and wiggle. Each is fitted to the training respondents only. The upper plot scores each by mean log likelihood per response (closer to 0 is better; −0.69 is a coin flip) on the training respondents (in-sample) and on 5,000 new ones (out-of-sample). The lower plot shows the training responses and the curves from the 2- and 7-parameter models.


Code
viewof of_n = Inputs.radio([30, 100, 300, 1000], {value: 100, label: "Training respondents"})
viewof of_a = Inputs.range([0.3, 2.5], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "True slope of the item"})


















Code
of_data = {
  const r = rng(11), draw = m => Array.from({length: m}, () => r.norm());
  const xtr = draw(1000), xte = draw(5000);
  const u = Array.from({length: 6000}, () => r.unif());
  const y = (x, off) => x.map((t, i) => u[off + i] < logistic(of_a * (t - 0.3)) ? 1 : 0);
  return {xtr: xtr.slice(0, of_n), ytr: y(xtr, 0).slice(0, of_n), xte, yte: y(xte, 1000)};
}
of_clip = p => Math.min(Math.max(p, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4)
of_fits = Array.from({length: 7}, (_, d) => polyLogitFit(of_data.xtr, of_data.ytr, d))
of_rows = of_fits.map((beta, d) => ({k: d + 1,
  train: meanLogLik(of_data.ytr, of_data.xtr.map(x => of_clip(polyLogitPredict(beta, x)))),
  test: meanLogLik(of_data.yte, of_data.xte.map(x => of_clip(polyLogitPredict(beta, x))))}))
of_best = of_rows.reduce((u, v) => v.test > u.test ? v : u)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Number of parameters in the item's model", ticks: 7, tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {label: "Mean log likelihood per response (higher is better)"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["In-sample (training respondents)", "Out-of-sample (new respondents)"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(of_rows.flatMap(d => [{k: d.k, v: d.train, s: "In-sample (training respondents)"}, {k: d.k, v: d.test, s: "Out-of-sample (new respondents)"}]),
      {x: "k", y: "v", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 2.5, marker: "circle"})
  ]
})














































Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 220, marginLeft: 60, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [-0.05, 1.05]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["True curve", "2 parameters", "7 parameters"], range: [palette.guide, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(of_data.xtr.map((t, i) => ({t, y: of_data.ytr[i]})).filter(d => Math.abs(d.t) < 3), {x: "t", y: "y", r: 2, fill: palette.light}),
    Plot.line(grid(-3, 3, 121).flatMap(t => [
      {t, p: logistic(of_a * (t - 0.3)), c: "True curve"},
      {t, p: polyLogitPredict(of_fits[1], t), c: "2 parameters"},
      {t, p: polyLogitPredict(of_fits[6], t), c: "7 parameters"}]), {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})









Code
md`In-sample, the fit improves from ${of_rows[1].train.toFixed(3)} with 2 parameters to ${of_rows[6].train.toFixed(3)} with 7. Out-of-sample, the best model has **${of_best.k}** parameters (${of_best.test.toFixed(3)}), and the one with 7 scores ${of_rows[6].test.toFixed(3)}.`







What should you have seen? The in-sample line only rises: each added parameter lets the curve bend toward the training responses, noise included. The out-of-sample line rises from 1 parameter to 2, because the item really does depend on \(\theta\), and then flattens or falls. With 30 or 100 training respondents the 7-parameter curve in the lower plot wiggles to follow a few responses, and the wiggles are wrong for new respondents; with 1,000 the extra terms stay near zero and both lines are flat after 2 parameters. The gap between the lines is in-sample advantage that doesn’t carry over. Held-out responses measure what does; the next section puts it on a scale comparable across tests.



The IMV: how much better, on a portable scale
Held-out log likelihoods say which model predicts better, but their size depends on how predictable the responses were anyway. The InterModel Vigorish (Domingue et al., 2025; for item response models, Domingue et al., 2024) puts predictive gains on a common scale in three steps.

A coin for each set of predictions. From a model’s mean log likelihood on held-out responses, \(\bar\ell\), find the weight \(w \ge 0.5\) of a coin with the same expected log likelihood per toss: \(w\log w + (1-w)\log(1-w) = \bar\ell\). Guessing gives \(w = 0.5\); confident, correct predictions give \(w\) near 1.
A bet. You are offered fair odds on heads for the baseline’s coin, \(w_0\), but the coin is really the better model’s, \(w_1\).
The expected return per unit staked is the IMV, \[\text{IMV} = \frac{w_1 - w_0}{w_0}.\]


Try it: two predictions, two coins
The worked example of Domingue et al. (2025, §2.3.1): 20 tosses of a fair coin (14 heads), then 20 of a coin with weight 0.95 (19 heads). The baseline predicts one probability for every toss; the enhanced prediction can treat the halves differently.


Code
viewof co_p0 = Inputs.range([0.5, 0.95], {value: 0.55, step: 0.01, label: "Baseline: P(heads), every toss"})
viewof co_p1a = Inputs.range([0.3, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "Enhanced: P(heads), tosses 1–20"})
viewof co_p1b = Inputs.range([0.3, 0.99], {value: 0.9, step: 0.01, label: "Enhanced: P(heads), tosses 21–40"})

























Code
co_y = [...Array(14).fill(1), ...Array(6).fill(0), ...Array(19).fill(1), 0]
co_pb = co_y.map(() => co_p0)
co_pe = co_y.map((_, i) => i < 20 ? co_p1a : co_p1b)
co_res = imv(co_y, co_pb, co_pe)
co_pts = [{A: Math.exp(meanLogLik(co_y, co_pb)), w: co_res.w0, s: "Baseline"},
          {A: Math.exp(meanLogLik(co_y, co_pe)), w: co_res.w1, s: "Enhanced"}]
co_curve = grid(0.5, 0.9999, 300).map(w => ({w, A: Math.exp(w * Math.log(w) + (1 - w) * Math.log(1 - w))}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Likelihood per toss (geometric mean)", domain: [0.4, 1]}, y: {label: "Coin weight w", domain: [0.5, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Baseline", "Enhanced"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(co_curve, {x: "A", y: "w", stroke: palette.guide, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.dot(co_pts, {x: "A", y: "w", fill: "s", r: 7})
  ]
})





















































Code
md`Baseline coin w0 = ${co_res.w0.toFixed(2)}; enhanced coin w1 = ${co_res.w1.toFixed(2)}. **IMV = ${co_res.imv.toFixed(3)}**: with the enhanced predictions you would expect to win about ${Math.round(100 * co_res.imv)} cents for every dollar bet against someone holding the baseline.`







With the paper’s values the coins are 0.67 and 0.83 and the IMV is 0.24, as in the paper. Push the second enhanced prediction to 0.99 and the IMV falls: the one tail in those 20 tosses is now punished hard. Set both enhanced values to the baseline’s and the IMV is 0.
The IMV always compares two sets of predictions (for an absolute statement, use a simple baseline such as item proportions). In-sample it favours the more complex model, so it is computed on held-out responses (Domingue et al., 2024, §2.1). As an expected return on a fair bet, it compares across datasets, which makes it a reasonable choice whenever the question is how much. Benchmarks from simulations with 50 items and 1,000 respondents (Domingue et al., 2024, Table 1): 0.1 for the Rasch model over item proportions, 0.01 for the 2PL over the Rasch model when slopes vary substantially (log slopes with SD 0.5), and 0.0005 for the 3PL over the 2PL even when a 3PL generated the data.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Model B's IMV over model A is 0.012 on one test and 0.006 on another. What can you say?",
  options: [
    {text: "B's predictive gain over A is about twice as large on the first test", correct: true, why: "IMVs are expected returns on a fair bet, so they compare across datasets: 0.012 is twice 0.006."},
    {text: "Nothing: IMVs from different datasets can't be compared", correct: false, why: "That is true of differences in AIC or BIC, whose scale depends on sample size. Comparability across datasets is what the IMV is built for."},
    {text: "B fits the first test and misfits the second", correct: false, why: "Both IMVs are positive, so B predicts better than A on both. The IMV measures how much better, not whether either model fits."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: from a likelihood to a coin





Assumptions: binary outcomes \(y_1, \dots, y_n\) with predictions \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) from some model, evaluated on data the model wasn’t fitted to.
The likelihood per outcome. The likelihood of the outcomes is \(\prod_k p_k^{y_k}(1-p_k)^{1-y_k}\). Its \(n\)th root, \(A = \exp(\bar\ell)\) with \(\bar\ell\) the mean log likelihood, is the likelihood per outcome, comparable across datasets of different sizes. The log likelihood is also a strictly proper scoring rule: a forecaster maximizes their expected score by reporting the probabilities they believe (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007).
The equivalent coin. Predicting \(w\) for every toss of a coin of weight \(w\) has expected log likelihood \(w\log w + (1-w)\log(1-w)\), which is minus the coin’s entropy. It rises from \(\log 0.5 \approx -0.693\) at \(w = 0.5\) to 0 at \(w = 1\), so each \(\bar\ell\) in that range picks out one \(w \ge 0.5\) (the curve in the widget). The coin is exactly as uncertain as the predictions.
The bet. Fair odds on heads for a coin of weight \(w_0\) pay \((1 - w_0)/w_0\) per unit staked. If the coin is really \(w_1\), the expected profit is \(w_1 (1-w_0)/w_0 - (1 - w_1) = (w_1 - w_0)/w_0\), the IMV. It isn’t symmetric: swapping the roles gives \((w_0 - w_1)/w_1\).






Misspecification you can’t see






Recall from The Rasch model: a logistic curve with slope about 1.7 nearly matches the normal CDF, which is where the scaling constant \(D \approx 1.7\) comes from (Camilli, 1994).



Every model here assumes a logistic curve. What if responses follow another: the normal ogive, a heavy-tailed curve, or an asymmetric one such as the skewed curves of Bazán, Bolfarine and Branco (2006)? How far is the closest logistic curve from the true one, where the respondents are?

Try it: other curves, the closest logistic


Code
viewof lk_name = Inputs.radio(Object.keys(links).slice(1), {value: "Normal ogive (probit)", label: "True item curve"})
viewof lk_b = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Item location (ability: mean 0, SD 1)"})


















Code
lk_th = grid(-3.5, 3.5, 141)
lk_w = lk_th.map(t => dnorm(t))
lk_f = t => links[lk_name](t - lk_b)
lk_fit = closest2pl(lk_f, lk_th, lk_w)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-3.5, 3.5]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["True curve", "Closest 2PL"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(lk_th.map((t, k) => ({t, d: lk_w[k] / dnorm(0) * 0.3})), {x: "t", y: "d", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.line(lk_th.flatMap(t => [{t, p: lk_f(t), c: "True curve"}, {t, p: logistic(lk_fit.a * (t - lk_fit.b)), c: "Closest 2PL"}]),
      {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Closest 2PL: a = ${lk_fit.a.toFixed(2)}, b = ${lk_fit.b.toFixed(2)}. Over the middle 95% of respondents (shaded) the curves differ by at most **${lk_fit.maxDiff.toFixed(3)}**. For scale, a proportion estimated from 200 respondents near 0.5 has a standard error of ${Math.sqrt(0.25 / 200).toFixed(3)}.`







The normal ogive is matched almost exactly (slope near 1.7); the others leave gaps of a few hundredths where respondents are, about the sampling error of a proportion from 200 respondents. Slope and location absorb most of the misspecification, and residual-based fit statistics see only what is left over.

title: Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates Rasch data for 20 items at three sample sizes, fits the Rasch model with mirt (Chalmers, 2012), and summarizes the outfits, computed from mirt’s default (EAP) abilities and from maximum-likelihood ones. Then it generates data from the normal ogive and fits the logistic Rasch model anyway. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, and the fits a minute or so more.
With the seed as written, the maximum-likelihood outfits average 0.97 to 0.99, with SDs of 0.114 at 100 respondents and 0.043 at 1,600 (against 0.141 and 0.035 from \(\sqrt{2/n}\)). The EAP outfits average 0.90 at every sample size, although the model is true. EAP pulls abilities toward the mean, so the residuals come out smaller than the model expects. Outfit assumes each ability comes from the respondent’s own responses; with 20 items and EAP abilities, “near 1” means near 0.9. In the probit part, the estimated difficulties are 1.7 times the true ones (the constant \(D\) again), while the outfits run from 0.72 to about 1.1 and no \(|z|\) exceeds 1.9: the fit statistics don’t notice that the curve has the wrong shape.
