title: Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
text:
With real data
Our main example is gilbert_meta_2, a 20-item reading comprehension test taken by 2,174 students in a randomized trial of a content literacy intervention that ran from first to second grade (Kim et al., 2023). Its job is to be a mid-sized test on which every fit statistic can be compared. A response is 1 when correct; every student answered every item, and there are no waves. Download the code; the cross-validation takes a few minutes.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with
# a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
gm2_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.gilbert_meta_2/rows?format=csv"
df2 <- read.csv(gm2_url)
# resp is 1 for a correct answer. One response per student per item; no waves.
c(responses = nrow(df2), students = length(unique(df2$id)), items = length(unique(df2$item)),
  missing = sum(is.na(df2$resp)))


responses  students     items   missing 
    43480      2174        20         0 


Code
# IRW tables are long (one row per response); mirt wants wide (one row per respondent).
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  ord <- order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))), colnames(wide))
  as.data.frame(wide[, ord])
}
resp2 <- long2wide(df2)
names(resp2) <- paste0("item", names(resp2))
round(range(colMeans(resp2)), 2)   # proportion correct: hardest and easiest items


[1] 0.31 0.83



Item fit, read by size

set.seed(252)
rasch2 <- mirt(resp2, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
fit2 <- itemfit(rasch2, fit_stats = "infit")   # outfit and infit, with z statistics
# How much would outfit vary if the Rasch model were true? For one response,
# z^2 = (x - p)^2 / (p(1 - p)) has variance 1/(p(1 - p)) - 4 (see the Go deeper
# callout), so an item's outfit, the mean of n of them, has the SD below. We plug in
# the fitted model's probabilities. sqrt(2/n) is the familiar rough version.
theta <- fscores(rasch2)[, 1]

out <- data.frame(item = fit2$item, p = round(colMeans(resp2), 2), outfit = round(fit2$outfit, 2),

AIC prefers the 3PL (52,520 against 52,605), BIC the 2PL (52,832 against 52,861), and the 3PL hadn’t converged when EM stopped at 500 cycles.


Code
# Andersen's (1973) likelihood-ratio test, from conditional maximum likelihood.
# esf() gives the elementary symmetric functions gamma_0, ..., gamma_I of the item
# easinesses exp(-b); cml() maximizes the conditional likelihood of the patterns
# given the sum scores (difficulties sum to 0), dropping sum scores of 0 and I,
# which carry no information about the items.
esf <- function(eps) {
  g <- 1
  for (e in eps) g <- c(g, 0) + c(0, g) * e
  g
}
cml <- function(X) {
  X <- as.matrix(X); I <- ncol(X); r <- rowSums(X)
  X <- X[r > 0 & r < I, , drop = FALSE]; r <- rowSums(X)
  s <- colSums(X); n_r <- tabulate(r, I - 1)
  negll <- function(par) {
    b <- c(par, -sum(par))
    sum(s * b) + sum(n_r * log(esf(exp(-b))[2:I]))
  }
  o <- optim(rep(0, I - 1), negll, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 1000, reltol = 1e-12))
  list(b = c(o$par, -sum(o$par)), loglik = -o$value, n = nrow(X))
}
# Split respondents at the median sum score, estimate the difficulties separately in
# each half, and compare with one set of difficulties for everyone.
r2 <- rowSums(resp2)
high <- r2 > median(r2)
full <- cml(resp2); lo <- cml(resp2[!high, ]); hi <- cml(resp2[high, ])
LR <- 2 * (lo$loglik + hi$loglik - full$loglik)
df_LR <- ncol(resp2) - 1
c(LR = round(LR, 1), df = df_LR, p = signif(pchisq(LR, df_LR, lower.tail = FALSE), 2))

Relative to the other items, items 15 and 8 are about 1.25 logits easier among students above the median sum score than below it, and item 2 is 0.66 harder: a steep item looks easy to the strong and hard to the weak. These are the overfitting items again. The tests agree that the Rasch model misfits; they leave open how much the 2PL, or the 3PL, helps.


Out of sample






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL: the data say little about the lower asymptote when few respondents sit near chance, and a 2PL can imitate a 3PL where the respondents are. There, Domingue et al. (2024) reported that the 3PL’s gain in prediction over the 2PL never exceeded 0.001 on average in simulation.





Code
# The IMV (Domingue et al., 2024, 2025). coin() turns a mean log likelihood into the
# weight w >= 0.5 of a coin with the same expected log likelihood per toss;
# imv() is the expected return, (w1 - w0) / w0, on a bet placed with the better coin.
coin <- function(ll) {
  if (ll <= log(0.5)) return(0.5)
  uniroot(function(w) w * log(w) + (1 - w) * log(1 - w) - ll, c(0.5, 1 - 1e-12), tol = 1e-12)$root
}
mean_ll <- function(y, p) mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
imv <- function(y, p0, p1) {
  w0 <- coin(mean_ll(y, p0)); w1 <- coin(mean_ll(y, p1))
  (w1 - w0) / w0
}
# Predicted probabilities for the cells cells[, 1:2] (row, column) from a fitted model:
# mirt's form g + (u - g) * logistic(a * theta + d), with EAP abilities.
predict_cells <- function(m, cells) {
  th <- fscores(m)[, 1]
  # A respondent whose every response was held out has no ability estimate; the
  # prior mean, 0, is what EAP gives with no data.
  th[is.na(th)] <- 0
  cf <- coef(m, simplify = TRUE)$items
  i <- cells[, 2]
  cf[i, "g"] + (cf[i, "u"] - cf[i, "g"]) * plogis(cf[i, "a1"] * th[cells[, 1]] + cf[i, "d"])
}
# k-fold cross-validation over responses: each response goes into one of k folds.
# For each fold, blank out its responses, fit every model to the rest, and predict
# the blanked-out responses. Each respondent and item keeps most of its responses,
# so every held-out response has an ability and an item to be predicted from.
cv_predict <- function(resp, models, k = 5, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X <- as.matrix(resp)
  cells <- which(!is.na(X), arr.ind = TRUE)
  fold <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(cells)))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:k, function(f) {
    test <- cells[fold == f, , drop = FALSE]
    train <- X; train[test] <- NA
    preds <- sapply(models, function(m)
      predict_cells(mirt(as.data.frame(train), 1, itemtype = m, verbose = FALSE), test))
    data.frame(fold = f, item = test[, 2], y = X[test],
               p_value = colMeans(train, na.rm = TRUE)[test[, 2]], preds, check.names = FALSE)
  }))
}
# The IMV of each model over the one before it, fold by fold, then averaged.
imv_table <- function(pred, models) {
  base <- c("p_value", models)
  res <- sapply(split(pred, pred$fold), function(d)
    sapply(2:length(base), function(j) imv(d$y, d[[base[j - 1]]], d[[base[j]]])))
  res <- matrix(res, nrow = length(base) - 1)
  data.frame(comparison = paste(base[-length(base)], "->", base[-1]), IMV = round(rowMeans(res), 4))
}




Code
models <- c("Rasch", "2PL", "3PL")
pred2 <- cv_predict(resp2, models)
imv_table(pred2, models)

Out of sample, the Rasch model’s IMV over item proportions is 0.125, a little above the 0.1 benchmark; the 2PL’s over the Rasch model is 0.012, near the 0.01 benchmark for substantial slope variation; the 3PL’s over the 2PL is 0.0001. The RMSE moves from 0.454 to 0.451, a change with no obvious scale; the IMV says the 2PL’s gain is about a tenth of the gain from modelling abilities at all.

A second test
For contrast, gilbert_meta_14 is a mathematics test from the evaluation of Partnership Schools for Liberia (Romero, Sandefur & Sandholtz, 2020). Its job is to show that the size of a predictive gain depends on the data as well as the model. Its two waves share item codes but not always items (IRW item-text check), so we keep the baseline. # Where is there anything left to predict? The IMV of the 2PL over the Rasch model
# among held-out responses to items most students miss, and to the rest.
hard <- p14[pred14$item] < 0.1
round(c(items_below_0.1 = imv(pred14$y[hard], pred14$Rasch[hard], pred14$`2PL`[hard]),
        other_items = imv(pred14$y[!hard], pred14$Rasch[!hard], pred14$`2PL`[!hard])), 4)


items_below_0.1     other_items 
         0.0015          0.0154 


The 2PL’s IMV is 0.0088, smaller than in gilbert_meta_2 despite the wider slopes: 0.0015 on items with fewer than 10% correct, 0.0154 on the rest. So “for which test does the 2PL help more?” depends on which responses we ask about. The IMV puts both gains on one scale, but no scale makes a test’s items less extreme.
So which model would I fit to a test like gilbert_meta_2? The 2PL. The tests said the Rasch model misfits, which at this sample size they would say of almost any test. What decides it for me is that the 2PL’s out-of-sample gain, 0.012, is the size the benchmarks associate with substantial slope variation, while the 3PL’s shrank to almost nothing on new responses. I’d spend a parameter per item for a gain of 0.01; I wouldn’t for 0.0001.

title: Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
text:
Problems

Where \(\sqrt{2/n}\) comes from. Show that \(E(z^2) = 1\) and \(\text{Var}(z^2) = 1/(pq) - 4\) for one Bernoulli response. For \(\theta \sim N(0,1)\), at what difficulty does \(\text{Var}(z^2)\) average 2? Why is \(\sqrt{2/n}\) a rough rule rather than a result?
Does the architecture of difficulties matter? With 40 items and 1,000 respondents, compare the SD of outfit (maximum-likelihood abilities) for difficulties drawn from a standard normal, a uniform on \([-3, 3]\), and a bimodal distribution (half near ±1.5). Does the Go deeper formula predict what you see? (PS3#3; open in EDUC 252.)
Two tables, one comparison. Rerun the cross-validation for both tables with \(k = 4\) and \(k = 10\) and three seeds. How much do the IMVs move? For which table does the 2PL help more, and what makes the question hard? (PS4#2.)
Perfect predictions. Simulate Rasch data with 2,000 respondents and 20 items and compute the RMSE between the responses and the true probabilities. Compare it with the Rasch model’s 0.454 on gilbert_meta_2. Why is it so far from 0? (PS4#2a.)
Keep or drop? Item 2 in gilbert_meta_2 has outfit 1.08 and \(z = 2.7\) from mirt’s defaults, and 1.25 with maximum-likelihood abilities. Would you drop it? What would you check first, and what would change your mind?
Challenge: why the logistic? Generate data from the complementary log-log, a Cauchy and a skewed curve, fit the Rasch model and the 2PL, and describe what goes wrong: difficulties, slopes, fit statistics, and the IMV of the true probabilities over the fitted ones on new data. Can any fit statistic detect the wrong curve at 1,000 respondents? At 20,000? (PS3#4; open. I don’t know of a general answer.)

title: Model fit and out-of-sample prediction
text:
Across the IRW
Does the 2PL, or the 3PL, help out of sample across the warehouse? For the dichotomous tables of Across the IRW in From the 1PL to the 4PL, compute.R runs this lesson’s five-fold cross-validation (at most 2,000 respondents per table) and records the same three IMVs. Domingue et al. (2024, §4) did this for 89 IRW datasets, with four folds and priors on the slopes and lower asymptotes, and found averages of 0.075, 0.006 and 0.00016.

title: Guessing and priors
text:
What this is for
On the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, where chance is one in four, the 3PL’s median lower asymptote was 0.01. Yet respondents do guess. So what should we do about it? On tests like the ones in this lesson, I wouldn’t estimate \(c\) from the data alone. Where the chance rate is known, I’d fix it; where it isn’t, I’d fit the 2PL; either way I’d let held-out responses decide whether the choice earned its place. This lesson makes the case on a two-button reading task and a vocabulary test.

title: Guessing and priors
Guessing and priors
text:
Core ideas

What does the lower asymptote learn from?






Recall from From the 1PL to the 4PL: the lower asymptote \(c\) describes respondents far below an item. On the RMET only 84 of 17,680 respondents (0.48%) scored at or below chance, and the 3PL’s median \(c\) was 0.01 although chance is 0.25.



Why so little? A response carries information about \(c\) only where the logistic part of the curve is near zero; a respondent well above an item answers it correctly whatever \(c\) is. So the precision of \(\hat c\) is set by how many respondents find the item too hard, not by how many there are.

Try it: where the lower asymptote is learned
One 3PL item (\(a = 1.2\), \(b = 0\)), answered by \(n\) respondents whose abilities are normal around a mean you choose, relative to the item. The curve is the standard error of the estimated \(c\), from the Fisher information for \((a, b, c)\) with the abilities known. With estimated abilities it would be larger.


Code
viewof lc_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability, relative to the item"})
viewof lc_n = Inputs.range([100, 20000], {value: 1000, step: 100, label: "Respondents (n)"})
viewof lc_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "True lower asymptote c"})

























Code
lc_curve = grid(-2, 2, 81).map(mu => ({mu, se: se3pl(1.2, 0, lc_c, mu, lc_n).c}))
lc_now = se3pl(1.2, 0, lc_c, lc_mu, lc_n)
lc_share = shareNearFloor(1.2, 0, lc_mu)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300,
  x: {label: "Mean ability, relative to the item"},
  y: {label: "Standard error of ĉ", domain: [0, Math.min(1, Math.max(0.3, ...lc_curve.map(d => d.se)))]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(lc_curve, {x: "mu", y: "se", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{mu: lc_mu, se: lc_now.c}], {x: "mu", y: "se", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})
































Code
md`${(100 * lc_share).toFixed(1)}% of respondents sit where the item's logistic part is below 0.1, so that their correct answers are mostly chance. The standard error of ĉ is **${lc_now.c.toFixed(3)}**, so a 95% interval runs from ${Math.max(0, lc_c - 1.96 * lc_now.c).toFixed(2)} to ${Math.min(1, lc_c + 1.96 * lc_now.c).toFixed(2)}. For comparison, the slope's standard error is ${lc_now.a.toFixed(2)}.`







The opening setting, 1.5, is an easy test like the RMET: almost nobody is near the floor, and with 1,000 respondents the standard error of \(\hat c\) is 0.27. At −1 the test is hard for its takers, like the two hardest ENEM forms in the IRW’s guessing vignette, where about two-fifths of the items are answered correctly less often than chance; a fifth of the respondents are near the floor and the standard error falls to 0.05. Back at 1.5, even 20,000 respondents leave it at 0.06.






Recall from Model fit and out-of-sample prediction: the IMV turns two sets of predictions of held-out responses into the expected return on a fair bet, which makes predictive gains comparable across datasets. On a reading comprehension test, the 3PL’s IMV over the 2PL was 0.0001 out of sample and 0.0035 in-sample.



Domingue et al. (2024, §3) asked the question by simulation. With data generated from a 3PL whose lower asymptotes ran up to 0.3, the average IMV of the 3PL over the 2PL on held-out responses never exceeded 0.001, while the 2PL gained 0.01 or more over the 1PL when slopes varied substantially. They relate this to difficulties in identifying the 3PL (Maris & Bechger, 2009; Haberman, 2005; von Davier, 2009). The widget suggests why: a curve that differs from a 2PL only where few respondents are changes few predictions. The 3PL remains a reasonable choice when many respondents sit near chance, and in large calibration samples.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two samples take the same 40-item test. Sample A has 5,000 respondents, nearly all well above most items' difficulty. Sample B has 800 respondents, a third of whom find most items too hard. From which sample are the lower asymptotes better estimated?",
  options: [
    {text: "Sample B", correct: true, why: "Information about $c$ comes from respondents for whom the item is too hard. B has hundreds of them on most items; A has almost none, however large it is."},
    {text: "Sample A, because it is six times larger", correct: false, why: "Size helps only through the respondents near the floor. In the widget, a thousand respondents 1.5 above the item leave $c$ almost undetermined."},
    {text: "Neither: $c$ is set by the number of options, not the data", correct: false, why: "That is a choice we can make (the next section), but a fitted 3PL estimates $c$ from the responses, and how well depends on who gave them."}
  ]
})










Fix guessing from the item’s structure
If we know where the floor should be, why not put it there? With \(k\) equally attractive options, random choice is right with probability \(1/k\), and the simplest model with guessing fixes every lower asymptote there: \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \frac{1}{k} + \Big(1 - \frac{1}{k}\Big)\frac{\exp(\theta_j - b_i)}{1 + \exp(\theta_j - b_i)}.\] It is the Rasch model with a fixed floor, the first of three ways to add guessing that San Martín, del Pino and De Boeck (2006) list (the others estimate one floor for all items, or one per item). Han (2012) reports that fixing \(c = 1/k\) gave more stable item estimates than a free 3PL without a loss of fit, on simulated and real multiple-choice data.
What does fixing the floor assume? That a respondent who doesn’t know the answer picks at random. That doesn’t hold if some wrong options attract more than others, if respondents can rule some out (San Martín et al. let the chance of a correct guess rise with ability), or if not knowing pushes respondents toward one answer.

Try it: what a correct answer is worth
The same item (\(b = 0\)) under the Rasch model and with its floor fixed at chance. Choose the chance rate (four options for a typical multiple-choice test, two for the lexical decision task below) and how far below the item a respondent sits.


Code
viewof fg_c = Inputs.radio(new Map([["0.25 (four options)", 0.25], ["0.5 (two options)", 0.5]]), {value: 0.5, label: "Fixed lower asymptote"})
viewof fg_gap = Inputs.range([0.5, 4], {value: 3, step: 0.1, label: "Respondent's distance below the item"})


















Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ (item at 0)"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Rasch", "Rasch, c fixed"], range: [palette.light, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([fg_c], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0, -fg_gap], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(grid(-5, 5).flatMap(t => [
      {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, 0), curve: "Rasch"},
      {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, 0, 1, fg_c), curve: "Rasch, c fixed"}]), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})









Code
fg_r0 = p4pl(0, 0) / p4pl(-fg_gap, 0)
fg_r1 = p4pl(0, 0, 1, fg_c) / p4pl(-fg_gap, 0, 1, fg_c)
md`A correct answer is **${fg_r0.toFixed(1)}** times as likely at θ = 0 as at θ = −${fg_gap.toFixed(1)} under the Rasch model, but only **${fg_r1.toFixed(2)}** times as likely with the floor at ${fg_c}. That likelihood ratio is how strongly one correct answer favours the higher ability.`























With two options and a gap of 3, one correct answer favours the higher ability by a factor of 10.5 under the Rasch model and by 1.43 with the floor at 0.5. With a floor of 0.25 its worth falls less (a factor of 2.2). Wrong answers lose nothing: the floor multiplies their probability by the same \(1 - c\) at every ability (problem 1).


Code
quiz({
  q: "With the lower asymptote fixed at 0.5, an item that 55% of respondents answer correctly is, compared with its Rasch difficulty,",
  options: [
    {text: "much harder: 55% is barely above what random pressing gives", correct: true, why: "Under the fixed floor the logistic part only has to explain the 5 points above 0.5, so the item sits well above most respondents. The real data below show this in the extreme."},
    {text: "about as hard: fixing $c$ doesn't touch difficulties", correct: false, why: "It does. The difficulty is where the logistic part crosses one half, and with a floor at 0.5 the whole curve is squeezed between 0.5 and 1."},
    {text: "easier, because some of the correct answers are guesses", correct: false, why: "Guesses explain some of the correct answers, which leaves fewer to be explained by ability, so the item looks harder, not easier."}
  ]
})










Guessing may belong to respondents
The 3PL and the fixed floor both give guessing to items. But a respondent who has stopped trying, or is racing a clock, may answer items they could solve, quickly and at chance. Response times can find them: Schnipke and Scrams (1997) modelled times as a mixture of rapid guesses and slower solution behaviour, Wise and Kong (2005) measured engagement by the share of responses too fast to reflect reading, and Wise (2017) reviews the methods.






Recall from Item response data and the IRW: when a table records response times, they sit in an rt column, in seconds, beside resp.



If guessing belongs to respondents, an item’s lower asymptote spreads a few respondents’ behaviour over everyone. Response time and the speed-accuracy tradeoff models times and responses together.
Two models put guessing with respondents without response times. In the ability-based guessing model (1PL-AG) of San Martín, del Pino and De Boeck (2006), a respondent who doesn’t know the answer guesses right with a probability that rises with ability, as if stronger respondents rule out more options: \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = P_{ij} + (1 - P_{ij})\,\frac{\exp(\alpha\theta_j + \gamma_i)}{1 + \exp(\alpha\theta_j + \gamma_i)}, \qquad P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(\theta_j - b_i)}{1 + \exp(\theta_j - b_i)}.\] In a two-class mixture, each respondent either follows the Rasch model, with probability \(\pi\), or answers every item correctly with the chance probability \(c\). For a respondent whose class we don’t know, and if the classes don’t differ in ability, the probability of a correct answer is \(\pi P_{ij} + (1 - \pi)c\).

Try it: four ways to add guessing
One item with difficulty \(b\). The widget sets \(\gamma_i\) so that a respondent at \(\theta = 0\) who doesn’t know the answer guesses right with probability \(c\), as under the fixed floor.


Code
viewof gc_b = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Item difficulty b"})
viewof gc_c = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.5], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "Chance rate c"})
viewof gc_alpha = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "1PL-AG: α, how guessing rises with ability"})
viewof gc_pi = Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 0.85, step: 0.01, label: "Mixture: π, share of engaged respondents"})
































Code
gc = guessCurves({b: gc_b, c: gc_c, alpha: gc_alpha, pi: gc_pi})
gc_names = ["Rasch", "Fixed floor", "1PL-AG", "Mixture"]
gc_long = gc.curves.flatMap((d) => [
  {theta: d.theta, p: d.rasch, model: "Rasch"}, {theta: d.theta, p: d.floor, model: "Fixed floor"},
  {theta: d.theta, p: d.ag, model: "1PL-AG"}, {theta: d.theta, p: d.mix, model: "Mixture"}])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 340, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "Probability correct", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: gc_names,
          range: [palette.guide, palette.main, d3.interpolateRgb(palette.main, palette.contrast)(0.5), palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([gc_c], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.ruleY([gc.ceiling], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4 3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.line(gc_long, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "model", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})
































Code
gc_lo = gc.at(gc_b - 3)
gc_hi = gc.at(gc_b + 3)
md`Three logits below the item: fixed floor **${gc_lo.floor.toFixed(2)}**, 1PL-AG **${gc_lo.ag.toFixed(2)}**, mixture **${gc_lo.mix.toFixed(2)}** (Rasch ${gc_lo.rasch.toFixed(2)}). Three logits above: fixed floor **${gc_hi.floor.toFixed(2)}**, 1PL-AG **${gc_hi.ag.toFixed(2)}**, mixture **${gc_hi.mix.toFixed(2)}** (Rasch ${gc_hi.rasch.toFixed(2)}). The mixture's ceiling (dashed) is π + (1 − π)c = **${gc.ceiling.toFixed(3)}**.`























The curves part company at the two ends. At the bottom, the fixed floor lifts every respondent to \(c\), while the mixture lifts them only to \((1 - \pi)c\), 0.04 at the defaults, because only the guessing class guesses. At the top, the mixture never reaches 1: a guesser misses easy items too, so its ceiling is \(\pi + (1 - \pi)c\), 0.89 at the defaults. The 1PL-AG has no fixed floor at all: guessing fades for weak respondents and helps strong ones. Set \(\alpha\) to 0 and it becomes the fixed floor; set \(\pi\) to 1 and the mixture becomes the Rasch model.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under the two-class mixture, why does a very able respondent's probability of a correct answer stay below 1?",
  options: [
    {text: "We don't know their class, and a respondent in the guessing class answers even easy items only at chance", correct: true, why: "The curve averages the two classes: $\\pi$ times a probability near 1, plus $1 - \\pi$ times $c$. Knowing a respondent's class, from their responses or response times, would move them to one curve or the other."},
    {text: "The mixture adds an upper asymptote to each item, as in the 4PL", correct: false, why: "The ceiling comes from respondents, not items: it is the same for every item, and it is set by $\\pi$ and $c$."},
    {text: "Able respondents are more likely to guess", correct: false, why: "In this mixture the classes have the same abilities; that is the ability-based guessing model's idea, and there guessing helps able respondents."}
  ]
})










Priors keep item estimates in bounds






Recall from Estimating abilities: with a prior \(g(\theta)\), the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. The EAP estimate, the posterior mean, is pulled toward the prior’s mean (shrinkage), most where the likelihood is flattest: at the ends of the scale and on short tests.



Nothing in that argument needs \(\theta\) to be an ability. An item parameter can have a prior too, and its posterior is again likelihood times prior (Mislevy, 1986; Swaminathan & Gifford, 1986; Harwell & Baker, 1991). A slope is positive, so \(\log a\) gets a normal prior (a lognormal on \(a\)); a lower asymptote lies between 0 and 1, so it gets a beta prior; beta(\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) has mean \(\alpha/(\alpha + \beta)\), mode \((\alpha - 1)/(\alpha + \beta - 2)\), and counts for roughly \(\alpha + \beta\) responses, so beta(2, 18) says “about 0.1, worth about 20 responses”. Since mirt finds the posterior mode, a lower asymptote the data say little about settles near the prior’s mode, 0.056 for beta(2, 18). Where data are thin, which for \(c\) is nearly always, the estimate sits near the prior; priors are a reasonable choice whenever a sample is small for the number of item parameters. A full Bayesian treatment is in Johnson and Sinharay (2017).

Try it: prior × likelihood = posterior for a slope
One item (\(b = 0\), no floor), answered by \(n\) respondents with known abilities, from a fixed sample of 2,000. Twenty respondents is a small pilot; 300 is the size of the vocabulary subsamples below. The prior on \(\log a\) is normal with mean 0 and the SD you choose.


Code
viewof sp_n = Inputs.range([5, 500], {value: 20, step: 5, label: "Respondents (n)"})
viewof sp_a = Inputs.range([0.5, 3], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "True slope a"})
viewof sp_sd = Inputs.range([0.25, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Prior SD of log a"})

























Code
sp = slopePosterior(sp_n, sp_a, sp_sd)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Slope a", domain: [0, 6]}, y: {label: "Scaled to a peak of 1", domain: [0, 1.05]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Likelihood", "Prior", "Posterior"], range: [palette.light, palette.guide, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([sp_a], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(sp.as.flatMap((a, k) => a > 6 ? [] : [
      {a, y: sp.L[k], curve: "Likelihood"}, {a, y: sp.prior[k], curve: "Prior"}, {a, y: sp.post[k], curve: "Posterior"}]),
      {x: "a", y: "y", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})


















Code
md`With ${sp_n} respondents: MLE **${Number.isFinite(sp.mle) ? sp.mle.toFixed(2) : "none (the likelihood keeps rising)"}**, posterior mode ${sp.map.toFixed(2)}, posterior mean **${sp.eap.toFixed(2)}**; the true slope is ${sp_a.toFixed(1)} (grey line).`







With 20 respondents the maximum-likelihood slope is 3.17, more than twice the truth, and the posterior mode is 2.16, pulled back toward 1. With 300 they agree within a few hundredths. Tighten the prior’s SD to 0.25 and at 20 respondents the prior wins: the mode is 1.15, now below the truth. This is shrinkage again, now for items, and a tight prior in the wrong place pulls every estimate toward the wrong place.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A 3PL is fitted with a beta(2, 18) prior on every lower asymptote to a test on which nearly every respondent is far above every item. What will the estimated $c$s look like?",
  options: [
    {text: "Close to one another and to the prior, whatever the respondents did", correct: true, why: "The likelihood is nearly flat in $c$ when no one is near the floor, so the posterior is nearly the prior. The vocabulary test below shows this."},
    {text: "Close to 0, because nobody guessed", correct: false, why: "The data can't tell whether anybody guessed: nobody is where guessing would show. Without a prior, estimates often do land near 0; with one, they land near the prior."},
    {text: "Scattered from 0 to 0.5, as without a prior", correct: false, why: "Scatter is what a flat likelihood can give without a prior. The prior is what removes it."}
  ]
})










Judge it by prediction
Fixing \(c\) and adding priors are both assumptions, which the model’s own fit statistics take for granted. The check that doesn’t is the one from Model fit and out-of-sample prediction: fit with and without the assumption, and compute the IMV on held-out responses.

title: Guessing and priors
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates a five-option test from the 3PL (20 items, every \(c = 0.2\)) for 300 respondents, then fits the 2PL, the 3PL without priors, and the 3PL with a lognormal(0, 1) prior on the slopes and a beta(4, 16) prior on the lower asymptotes (mean 0.2, the chance rate; mode 0.17). The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, and the fits up to a minute more.
With the seed as written, the 3PL without priors has a slope as large as 6.8 (the true slopes are around 1), a slope error of 1.74 and a median \(c\) of 0.29. With the priors, the slope error is 0.31, the difficulty error falls from 1.04 to 0.51, and the median \(c\) is 0.17. All three give abilities that correlate 0.76 to 0.78 with the truth. With np <- 3000 (in your own R session) the 3PL’s slope error falls to 0.32 on its own and the priors still help (0.22). Try expbeta, 2, 18 (mean 0.1) to see what a prior in the wrong place costs.

title: Guessing and priors
text:
With real data

A two-button reading task
Our main example is roar_lexical, from the lexical decision task of the Rapid Online Assessment of Reading (Yeatman et al., 2021): children and adolescents saw a string of letters and pressed one of two buttons to say whether it was a real word, under a time limit. Its job is to be a test whose chance rate is known exactly: 0.5. Every response has a time. Download the code to run every chunk yourself; it needs mirt (Chalmers, 2012).


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with
# a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
roar_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v60_0.roar_lexical/rows?format=csv"
roar <- read.csv(roar_url)
# One row per response. resp is 1 when the respondent classified the string
# correctly (real word or made-up word); rt is the response time in seconds;
# realpseudo says which kind of string it was. One response per respondent per
# item, and no waves.
c(responses = nrow(roar), respondents = length(unique(roar$id)),
  items = length(unique(roar$item)), missing = sum(is.na(roar$resp)))


  responses respondents       items     missing 
      61500         123         500           0 


Code
table(roar$realpseudo)

round(c(accuracy = mean(roar$resp), tapply(roar$resp, roar$realpseudo, mean)), 2)


accuracy   pseudo     real

Code
# IRW tables are long (one row per response); mirt wants wide (one row per respondent).
long2wide <- function(df) as.data.frame(tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1]))
resp_roar <- long2wide(roar)
round(quantile(colMeans(resp_roar), c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1)), 2)   # proportion correct by item


  0%  10%  50% 100% 
0.14 0.64 0.84 0.96 


There are 123 respondents, each classifying the same 500 strings (half real words), with no missing responses and one wave. Overall accuracy is 0.80.


Code
predict({
  q: "Chance on this task is 0.5. If we fix every lower asymptote at 0.5 instead of 0, the number of parameters stays the same. How closely will the two models' ability estimates agree?",
  choices: ["Correlation near 1: they rank respondents almost identically", "Correlation around 0.7", "Correlation near 0: fixing chance reorders respondents"],
  answer: "Correlation near 1: they rank respondents almost identically",
  reveal: "The abilities correlate 0.97. What changes is the items: the SD of the difficulties rises from 0.8 to 2.0, and the log likelihood improves by about 200 with no extra parameters. Check the output below."
})









Code
# The Rasch model, and the Rasch model with every lower asymptote fixed at 0.5
# (two choices, so chance is one in two). guess = 0.5 fixes mirt's g, our c; it is
# not estimated, so both models have the same number of parameters.
set.seed(252)
rasch <- mirt(resp_roar, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
fixed <- mirt(resp_roar, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", guess = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
b_rasch <- -coef(rasch, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]   # mirt's d is an easiness: b = -d
b_fixed <- -coef(fixed, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
th_rasch <- fscores(rasch)[, 1]
th_fixed <- fscores(fixed)[, 1]
data.frame(parameters = c(extract.mirt(rasch, "nest"), extract.mirt(fixed, "nest")),
           logLik = round(c(extract.mirt(rasch, "logLik"), extract.mirt(fixed, "logLik"))),
           sd_ability = round(sqrt(c(coef(rasch)$GroupPars[2], coef(fixed)$GroupPars[2])), 2),
           sd_difficulty = round(c(sd(b_rasch), sd(b_fixed)), 2),
           row.names = c("Rasch", "Rasch, c = 0.5"))

The two models rank respondents almost identically (the abilities correlate 0.97), and the fixed floor fits better, with a log likelihood of −25,380 against −25,579 for the same number of parameters. The scale spreads out: the SD of ability goes from 0.92 to 1.67, and of difficulty from 0.8 to 2.0.

# Where do the two models disagree about an item? Difficulty against proportion
# correct: with c = 0.5, an item that 60% get right is only just above chance.
p_roar <- colMeans(resp_roar)
plot(p_roar, b_rasch, pch = 19, col = "#93c5fd", ylim = range(c(b_rasch, b_fixed)),

The hardest items show where the spread comes from. Seventeen strings, 11 real words and 6 made-up ones, are classified correctly by fewer than half the respondents, below what random pressing would give; the real word napery by 14%. A respondent who doesn’t know a word says it isn’t one, and a word-like made-up string gets called a word. A floor at 0.5 can’t describe an item below chance, so the fixed floor sends the five hardest to difficulties of 5.4 to 14.4: its assumption, that not knowing means choosing at random, doesn’t hold for these items.


Code
# Does fixing c help on responses the models never saw? Five-fold cross-validation
# over responses, scored by the IMV (as in the lesson "Model fit and out-of-sample
# prediction").
coin <- function(ll) {
  if (ll <= log(0.5)) return(0.5)
  uniroot(function(w) w * log(w) + (1 - w) * log(1 - w) - ll, c(0.5, 1 - 1e-12), tol = 1e-12)$root
}
mean_ll <- function(y, p) mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
imv <- function(y, p0, p1) {
  w0 <- coin(mean_ll(y, p0)); w1 <- coin(mean_ll(y, p1))
  (w1 - w0) / w0
}
# Predicted probabilities for cells (row, column) from a fitted model, in mirt's
# form g + (u - g) * logistic(a * theta + d), with EAP abilities.
predict_cells <- function(m, cells) {
  th <- fscores(m)[, 1]
  cf <- coef(m, simplify = TRUE)$items
  i <- cells[, 2]
  cf[i, "g"] + (cf[i, "u"] - cf[i, "g"]) * plogis(cf[i, "a1"] * th[cells[, 1]] + cf[i, "d"])
}
set.seed(1)
X <- as.matrix(resp_roar)
cells <- which(!is.na(X), arr.ind = TRUE)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(cells)))
cv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(f) {
  test <- cells[fold == f, , drop = FALSE]
  train <- X; train[test] <- NA; train <- as.data.frame(train)
  data.frame(fold = f, row = test[, 1], col = test[, 2], y = X[test],
             rasch = predict_cells(mirt(train, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE), test),
             fixed = predict_cells(mirt(train, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", guess = 0.5, verbose = FALSE), test))
}))
imv_folds <- sapply(split(cv, cv$fold), function(d) imv(d$y, d$rasch, d$fixed))
round(c(imv_folds, mean = mean(imv_folds)), 4)


     1      2      3      4      5   mean 
0.0027 0.0024 0.0023 0.0028 0.0011 0.0023 


Code
# Where does the gain come from? The same IMV among held-out responses from the
# quarter of respondents with the lowest accuracy, and from everyone else.
acc <- rowMeans(X)
low <- acc[cv$row] <= quantile(acc, 0.25)
round(c(lowest_quarter = imv(cv$y[low], cv$rasch[low], cv$fixed[low]),
        other_three_quarters = imv(cv$y[!low], cv$rasch[!low], cv$fixed[!low])), 4)


      lowest_quarter other_three_quarters 
              0.0574              -0.0017 


Out of sample, the fixed floor beats the Rasch model in all five folds, by an IMV of 0.0023 on average: a fifth of the 0.01 benchmark for the 2PL over the Rasch model, with no extra parameters. Among held-out responses from the quarter of respondents with the lowest accuracy, the IMV is 0.057; among everyone else it is slightly negative (−0.0017).


Code
# Response times. A response faster than 0.3 seconds leaves little time to read
# the string; how many are there, and how accurate are they?
fast <- roar$rt < 0.3
round(c(share_under_0.3s = mean(fast), accuracy_under_0.3s = mean(roar$resp[fast]),
        accuracy_otherwise = mean(roar$resp[!fast])), 3)


   share_under_0.3s accuracy_under_0.3s  accuracy_otherwise 
              0.031               0.508               0.806

# Rapid responses by respondent: are they spread thinly, or concentrated?

The response times say who those respondents are. Of all responses, 3.1% came in under 0.3 seconds, at an accuracy of 0.51 against 0.81 for the rest. Eleven of the 123 respondents gave more than 10% of their responses that fast; the four with the most gave 40–47%, at overall accuracies of 0.50 to 0.55. On this task, guessing looks more like something a handful of respondents did than something every item invites.
Can the responses alone find those respondents? Xiao, Ulitzsch, Zhang, Frank and Domingue (2026) study the two-class mixture of Guessing may belong to respondents. As \(\hat\pi\) approaches 1 it becomes the Rasch model, the “safety valve” of their title. They leave two-option tasks out of scope, since at a chance rate of 0.5 a guessing class is hard to tell from engaged respondents on hard items. The code below fits it anyway, from responses alone.


Code
# Guessing as a property of respondents: a two-class mixture (Xiao et al., 2026).
# Engaged respondents follow the Rasch model, theta ~ normal(0, sd^2); guessing
# respondents answer every item correctly with probability g = 0.5. pi is the
# share of engaged respondents. mirt has no ready-made version, so we fit it by EM
# on a grid of abilities: the E step gives each respondent's posterior over
# (class, ability); the M step updates the difficulties (Newton steps), the SD
# and pi. Takes a few seconds.
fit_mixture <- function(X, g = 0.5, Q = 41, maxit = 1000, tol = 1e-6) {
  pl <- function(x) pmin(pmax(plogis(x), 1e-10), 1 - 1e-10)
  z <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = Q); wz <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
  b <- -qlogis(pmin(pmax(colMeans(X), 0.01), 0.99)); s <- 1; pi <- 0.9
  ll_guess <- rowSums(X) * log(g) + rowSums(1 - X) * log(1 - g)
  old <- -Inf
  for (it in 1:maxit) {
    P <- pl(outer(s * z, b, "-"))                                    # nodes x items
    a <- X %*% t(log(P)) + (1 - X) %*% t(log(1 - P)) + rep(log(wz), each = nrow(X))
    m <- apply(a, 1, max); ll_engaged <- m + log(rowSums(exp(a - m)))
    both <- cbind(log(pi) + ll_engaged, log(1 - pi) + ll_guess)
    mm <- apply(both, 1, max); ll_i <- mm + log(rowSums(exp(both - mm)))
    ll <- sum(ll_i)
    p_engaged <- exp(log(pi) + ll_engaged - ll_i)
    W <- exp(a - ll_engaged) * p_engaged                            # respondents x nodes
    nq <- colSums(W); r <- t(W) %*% X
    pi <- mean(p_engaged)
    for (k in 1:5) {
      P <- pl(outer(s * z, b, "-"))
      step <- colSums(nq * P - r) / colSums(nq * P * (1 - P))
      b <- b + pmax(pmin(step, 1), -1)
    }
    s <- exp(optimize(function(ls) {
      P <- pl(outer(exp(ls) * z, b, "-")); -sum(r * log(P) + (nq - r) * log(1 - P))
    }, c(-2, 1.5))$minimum)
    if (abs(ll - old) < tol) break
    old <- ll
  }
  list(b = b, sd = s, pi = pi, loglik = ll, p_guess = 1 - p_engaged)
}
mix <- fit_mixture(X)

On roar_lexical the classes separate: \(\hat\pi\) is 0.87, 9 of the 11 heavy rapid responders land in the guessing class, and the 16 respondents there have accuracies of 0.49 to 0.63. The mixture’s log likelihood is 298 above the Rasch model’s, against 199 for the fixed floor, for one extra parameter. That is in-sample; the wide spread of difficulties here may be what lets the classes come apart.
So for a test like this one, with a known chance rate, I’d fix the floor rather than estimate it: it costs no parameters and predicts new responses better. But I’d read it as a rough description of a few respondents, fit the mixture beside it, and look at response times before trusting either. Problem 6 asks whether the mixture holds up on held-out responses.


Priors when the sample is small
Our contrast table is vocabulary_iq, the Vocabulary IQ Test from Open Psychometrics (Open Psychometrics, 2018). Each of its 45 items lists five words, and the respondent picks the two with the same meaning, so a random pair is right one time in ten. Its codebook says respondents were told not to guess, that a wrong answer cost 0.35 points, and that they could answer “don’t know”. Its job is to show what priors do for a 3PL fitted to a small sample. We drop items 46–75, a personality survey, and keep the respondents who never chose “don’t know” (missing in the table).

viqt_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v60_0.vocabulary_iq/rows?format=csv"

# the same). Items 46-75 are an optional personality survey bundled into the same

viqt <- viqt[viqt$item <= 45, ]

0.52 0.84 0.92 0.97 0.99 


Of the 12,173 respondents, 2,802 never chose “don’t know”. Of these, 48 score 0 of 45 and 30 more score 1 to 4, where choosing pairs at random would average 4.5. The source file records a question left unanswered as 0, apart from “don’t know”, and the IRW table scores it as a wrong pair: 36 of the 48 zeros left every item blank, and 74 of the 78 low scorers left at least one. These scores mostly record questions not answered, so we set the 78 aside, as the guessing vignette does for scored absences on ENEM. For the 2,724 who remain the items are easy: the median item is answered correctly by 92%.


Code
# The 3PL on everyone kept, as a reference, without priors and with them; and,
# for comparison, without priors on the sample that still includes the low scorers.
# Priors in mirt's syntax: log a ~ normal(0, 1), and c ~ beta(2, 18). mirt stores
# c (its g) on the logit scale, and "expbeta" puts the beta prior on plogis() of
# that value, the probability. mirt maximizes the posterior, so with little
# information c settles near the prior's mode, (2 - 1)/(2 + 18 - 2) = 0.056
# (its mean is 0.1, the chance rate).
ni <- ncol(resp_viqt)
spec <- mirt.model(paste0("F = 1-", ni, "\n",
  "PRIOR = (1-", ni, ", a1, lnorm, 0, 1), (1-", ni, ", g, expbeta, 2, 18)"))
set.seed(252)
ref <- mirt(resp_viqt, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE, technical = list(NCYCLES = 5000))
ref_prior <- mirt(resp_viqt, spec, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE, technical = list(NCYCLES = 5000))
ref_with_low <- mirt(resp_cc, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE, technical = list(NCYCLES = 5000))
cf_ref <- coef(ref, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items         # a, b, g (our c)
cf_ref_prior <- coef(ref_prior, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items
cf_with_low <- coef(ref_with_low, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items
round(rbind(c_with_low_scorers = quantile(cf_with_low[, "g"], c(0, 0.5, 1)),
            c_no_prior = quantile(cf_ref[, "g"], c(0, 0.5, 1)),
            c_with_prior = quantile(cf_ref_prior[, "g"], c(0, 0.5, 1)),
            a_with_low_scorers = quantile(cf_with_low[, "a"], c(0, 0.5, 1)),
            a_no_prior = quantile(cf_ref[, "a"], c(0, 0.5, 1))), 3)


                      0%   50%  100%
c_with_low_scorers 0.000 0.000 0.093
c_no_prior         0.001 0.036 0.466
c_with_prior       0.052 0.055 0.076
a_with_low_scorers 0.438 2.614 4.744
a_no_prior         0.278 1.849 4.164


Fitted to the 2,724, the 3PL puts the lower asymptotes between 0.001 and 0.47 (median 0.036). With the 78 left in, all were between 0 and 0.09 (median 0.000), and the median slope was 2.61 rather than 1.85: respondents who answered nothing look to the model like the bottom of the ability range, never lucky. With the priors (lognormal(0, 1) on the slopes, beta(2, 18) on \(c\)), every \(c\) lands between 0.052 and 0.076, around the prior’s mode: on an easy test that discouraged guessing, few respondents are where a floor would show.


Code
# A trap: "beta" in place of "expbeta" puts the beta prior on the logit of c
# itself. Logits below 0 have zero prior density, so every logit is pushed into
# (0, 1) and every c to at least 0.5.
spec_beta <- mirt.model(paste0("F = 1-", ni, "\n",
  "PRIOR = (1-", ni, ", a1, lnorm, 0, 1), (1-", ni, ", g, beta, 2, 18)"))
wrong <- mirt(resp_viqt, spec_beta, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE, technical = list(NCYCLES = 5000))
round(quantile(coef(wrong, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items[, "g"], c(0, 0.5, 1)), 3)


   0%   50%  100% 
0.501 0.508 0.514 


A warning about syntax: mirt estimates \(c\) on the logit scale, and expbeta applies the beta prior to the probability. A plain beta applies it to the logit, which it then confines between 0 and 1, so every \(c\) is pushed to at least 0.5: here, 0.50 to 0.51.


Code
# Now pretend we had only 300 respondents. Fit the 3PL to a random 300, without
# and with the priors, and compare each with the full-sample reference.
rmse <- function(x, y) sqrt(mean((x - y)^2))
compare <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  # Redraw if some item has no wrong answers in the subsample (it can't be fitted).
  repeat {
    sub <- resp_viqt[sample(nrow(resp_viqt), 300), ]
    if (all(colMeans(sub) < 1)) break
  }
  # Without priors, EM may still be crawling after 2,000 cycles (a warning says
  # so); that slow drift of slopes toward large values is part of the finding.
  none <- coef(mirt(sub, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE, technical = list(NCYCLES = 2000)),
               simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items
  prior <- coef(mirt(sub, spec, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE, technical = list(NCYCLES = 2000)),
                simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items
  list(none = none, prior = prior,
       summary = c(sd_a_none = sd(none[, "a"]), sd_a_prior = sd(prior[, "a"]),
                   a_over_5_none = sum(none[, "a"] > 5), a_over_5_prior = sum(prior[, "a"] > 5),
                   rmse_a_none = rmse(none[, "a"], cf_ref[, "a"]), rmse_a_prior = rmse(prior[, "a"], cf_ref[, "a"]),
                   rmse_b_none = rmse(none[, "b"], cf_ref[, "b"]), rmse_b_prior = rmse(prior[, "b"], cf_ref[, "b"])))
}
one <- compare(1)
round(one$summary, 2)


     sd_a_none     sd_a_prior  a_over_5_none a_over_5_prior    rmse_a_none 
          4.15           0.75           4.00           0.00           3.98 
  rmse_a_prior    rmse_b_none   rmse_b_prior 
          0.61           0.80           1.12 


Code
plot(cf_ref[, "a"], one$none[, "a"], pch = 19, col = "#c2410c", log = "xy",
     ylim = range(c(one$none[, "a"], one$prior[, "a"])),
     xlab = "Slope from the full sample", ylab = "Slope from 300")
points(cf_ref[, "a"], one$prior[, "a"], pch = 19, col = "#2780e3")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("No priors", "Priors"), pch = 19, col = c("#c2410c", "#2780e3"), bty = "n")









Fitted to 300 respondents without priors, the slopes have an SD of 4.15 and four exceed 5, while the full-sample slopes run from 0.28 to 4.16. With the priors, the SD is 0.75 and none exceeds 5, and the slopes’ error against the full-sample 3PL drops from 3.98 to 0.61. In this subsample the difficulties go the other way (0.80 to 1.12).


Code
# One subsample could be lucky. Five more, summarized by the median across them.
many <- sapply(2:6, function(s) compare(s)$summary)
round(apply(many, 1, median), 2)


     sd_a_none     sd_a_prior  a_over_5_none a_over_5_prior    rmse_a_none 
          2.30           0.77           3.00           0.00           2.11 
  rmse_a_prior    rmse_b_none   rmse_b_prior 
          0.76           5.62           2.84 


Over five more subsamples (medians above) the priors again tame the slopes (error 2.11 against 0.76), and the difficulties improve too (5.62 against 2.84; on items nearly everyone gets right, a difficulty from 300 respondents can land almost anywhere). “Error” here is distance from the full-sample 3PL, not from the truth.

title: Guessing and priors
text:
Problems

What an answer is worth. With \(c\) fixed at \(1/k\), differentiate the log likelihood for \(\theta\) from one correct and from one incorrect response. Show that the first is smaller than under the Rasch model at every \(\theta\) and the second unchanged. What does that mean for a respondent who gets most items wrong?
Real data with a twist. In roar_lexical, set responses faster than 0.3 seconds to missing and refit the Rasch model and the fixed-floor model. How does the out-of-sample IMV change?
Real data: the items below chance. Refit both models without the 17 roar_lexical items answered correctly by fewer than half the respondents. What would a lower asymptote below 0.5 mean for those items? (PS4#3.)
Judgment (a live case). Fitted to all 2,802 vocabulary_iq respondents who never chose “don’t know”, the 78 low scorers included, the 3PL puts every lower asymptote between 0.000 and 0.093, with a median of 0.000 (the output above). A colleague concludes that nobody guesses on this test. What would you check before agreeing?
Design. You must fit a 3PL to 200 respondents on a 30-item, four-option test. Choose priors, defend them, and check them by simulation. How would you know if your prior on \(c\) were in the wrong place? (PS4#4.)
Challenge (open): guessing as a respondent trait. Compare the Rasch model, the fixed floor and the mixture on held-out roar_lexical responses, by the IMV. Does the mixture’s in-sample gain survive? What would response times add? I don’t know of a single answer; Response time and the speed-accuracy tradeoff and Nominal response and multiple-choice models have pieces of one.

text:
For instructors

Source: EDUC 252 class 4 (slides c4, 33 and 60–61), problem set 4 (#3 and #4), and the code in ben-domingue/252: ps4/guessing.R, ps4/priors.R.
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 50 minutes; the real-data section works as a 30-minute lab. Locally, the roar_lexical cross-validation takes a few minutes and the vocabulary_iq subsamples several more; start them first.
Changed from 252: PS4#3 fixes guessing on the LEVANTE vocabulary task, which isn’t a tokenless IRW table; this lesson uses roar_lexical, the alternative PS4#3’s code names, and adds the out-of-sample comparison (the PS4#3 bonus), the items below chance and the response times. PS4#4 puts priors on a 3PL for gilbert_meta_2; here they go on vocabulary_iq at 300 respondents, where they have more to do, and the design half of PS4#4 is problem 5.
Held back: response times modelled jointly with accuracy (Response time and the speed-accuracy tradeoff, which reuses roar_lexical); skipped and “don’t know” responses as information (IRTree models); the wrong options (Nominal response and multiple-choice models); EM with priors on item parameters (Estimating item parameters). title: From construct map to items: building an instrument
text:
What this is for
Most of the work of building an instrument happens before anyone answers it. Constructs and construct maps ended with a map or a blueprint; Classical test theory and reliability gave us tools for judging items once there are responses. This lesson sits between the two. It walks through the steps from a map to a pilot, gives the item-writing rules that carry the most weight, and spends most of its time on one design choice that looks harmless and isn’t: writing some items in the reverse direction. The worked example is the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, answered by 1,238 medical students in China, where the reversed items form a second cluster and one of them appears to have been read the other way.

title: From construct map to items: building an instrument
From construct map to items: building an instrument
text:
Core ideas

From a map to a pilot






Recall from What is measurement?: a probe is anything we present to a respondent to draw out a response that bears on the construct (a question, a task, a statement to agree or disagree with), and an item is a probe whose response is scored. Probes are standardized: the same items, given and scored the same way for everyone.



That lesson took probes as given. Where do they come from? Wilson (2005) describes instrument building as a cycle, and the Standards treat much the same sequence as the core of test development (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014, ch. 4). In outline:

Construct map or blueprint. What the instrument is for, and what a score should mean (Constructs and construct maps).
Items. Written to the map’s levels, or to the blueprint’s cells.
Review. Content experts check that each item belongs where it was written; others look for wording that some groups would find harder for reasons unrelated to the construct.
Cognitive interviews. A handful of respondents answer the items aloud, saying what they took each to ask and how they arrived at an answer (Willis, 2005).
Pilot. A larger sample answers the draft instrument, and we run an item analysis.
Revise, and go round again.

Only steps 5 and 6 produce data, and every later lesson works on their output. Why bother with the rest? Tourangeau, Rips and Rasinski (2000) break answering a question into understanding the item, recalling what is relevant, forming a judgment, and fitting it to the response options. A pilot sees only the result. If everyone misreads an item in the same way, it can correlate well with the rest and still ask something we didn’t mean; a cognitive interview is where that shows up. And the blueprint fixes something no pilot can change: how many items each part of the domain gets.

Try it: a blueprint and its cells
A fractions test has three content areas and two kinds of task (recall, and applying to a new problem). Set its length and weights. Given the reliability of one item (last slider), the Spearman–Brown formula from Classical test theory and reliability gives the reliability of the whole test and of a score on each cell.


Code
viewof bp_len = Inputs.range([10, 60], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "Items on the test"})
viewof bp_w1 = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 40, step: 5, label: "Weight: comparing fractions"})
viewof bp_w2 = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 40, step: 5, label: "Weight: adding fractions"})
viewof bp_w3 = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 20, step: 5, label: "Weight: fractions on a number line"})
viewof bp_apply = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 50, step: 10, label: "Share of items that ask to apply (%)"})
viewof bp_rel1 = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.4], {value: 0.15, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability of one item"})














































Code
bp_cells = {
  const areas = ["Comparing", "Adding", "Number line"], w = [bp_w1, bp_w2, bp_w3];
  const tot = w.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) || 1;
  const want = [];
  areas.forEach((a, i) => ["Recall", "Apply"].forEach(p => {
    const share = (w[i] / tot) * (p === "Apply" ? bp_apply / 100 : 1 - bp_apply / 100);
    want.push({area: a, task: p, exact: share * bp_len});
  }));
  // Round to whole items, keeping the total (the largest remainders get the spare items).
  want.forEach(d => d.n = Math.floor(d.exact));
  const spare = bp_len - want.reduce((u, d) => u + d.n, 0);
  [...want].sort((a, b) => (b.exact - b.n) - (a.exact - a.n)).slice(0, spare).forEach(d => d.n += 1);
  return want.map(d => ({...d, rel: d.n > 0 ? spearmanBrown(bp_rel1, d.n) : null}));
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 520, height: 200, marginLeft: 90,
  x: {domain: ["Recall", "Apply"], label: null, axis: "top"}, y: {domain: ["Comparing", "Adding", "Number line"], label: null},
  color: {domain: [0, 1], range: [palette.white, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(bp_cells, {x: "task", y: "area", fill: d => d.rel ?? 0, stroke: palette.rule, inset: 1}),
    Plot.text(bp_cells, {x: "task", y: "area", text: d => d.n > 0 ? `${d.n} items, reliability ${d.rel.toFixed(2)}` : "no items", fill: d => (d.rel ?? 0) > 0.6 ? palette.white : palette.ink, fontSize: 11})
  ]
})


















Code
bp_filled = bp_cells.filter(d => d.n > 0)
bp_min = bp_filled.reduce((a, b) => (b.rel < a.rel ? b : a))
md`Whole test: ${bp_len} items, reliability **${spearmanBrown(bp_rel1, bp_len).toFixed(2)}**. The least reliable cell score is ${bp_min.area.toLowerCase()} × ${bp_min.task.toLowerCase()}, with ${bp_min.n} item${bp_min.n === 1 ? "" : "s"} and reliability **${bp_min.rel.toFixed(2)}**.${bp_cells.some(d => d.n === 0) ? " Some cells have no items at all, so the test can say nothing about them." : ""}`























At the starting values the whole test reaches 0.84 while the three-item cells sit at 0.35. A blueprint can guarantee coverage without supporting a score for each cell; a subscore needs enough items in its cell, and that is settled before any item is written.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A team has drafted 40 items and plans to pilot them on 2,000 respondents next week, skipping cognitive interviews because 'the item analysis will flag any bad items'. What could the pilot miss?",
  options: [
    {text: "An item that every respondent reads in the same unintended way", correct: true, why: "If the misreading is shared, the item can still correlate with the rest, so its item-rest correlation looks fine. Only asking respondents what they understood reveals it."},
    {text: "An item that nobody endorses", correct: false, why: "The pilot catches that directly: the item's mean sits at the floor."},
    {text: "An item keyed in the wrong direction", correct: false, why: "A negative or near-zero item-rest correlation usually flags that, as with the Mach IV. The pilot's statistics do this well; the harder case is a misreading that leaves the correlations intact."}
  ]
})










Formats: selected and constructed responses
What form should the response take? In a selected-response item the respondent picks from a list: multiple-choice options, or the steps of a Likert scale from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”. In a constructed-response item the respondent produces the answer: a typed number (the number-series items in Constructs and construct maps), a short answer, an essay.
Every model in this course needs each response to fall in exactly one of a fixed set of categories, usually ordered. A selected response arrives that way; a constructed response has to be put there by scoring, with a key or with a rubric and a rater. Scoring is where constructed responses get expensive, and the rater is a new source of error; Many sources of error treats raters as a facet of measurement. Selected response is a reasonable choice when recognition or judgment reaches the construct and many items are needed cheaply. Constructed response is a reasonable choice when producing the answer is the construct: writing, explaining a proof, carrying out a procedure.


Writing items
Guidance on writing items fills whole books, and it mostly agrees. Haladyna, Downing and Rodriguez (2002) distilled 31 guidelines for multiple-choice items from 27 measurement textbooks and 27 research studies and reviews; Haladyna and Rodriguez (2013) cover item development at book length; and Clark and Watson (2019) do the same for rating-scale instruments. A few rules do most of the work:

One idea per item. An item that asks about two things (a double-barrelled item) leaves a respondent who agrees with one and not the other nowhere to go (Clark & Watson, 2019).
No negatives stacked on negatives. A “not” in the stem makes the respondent do extra work; two of them invite errors that have nothing to do with the construct. Haladyna et al. (2002) advise wording the stem positively and, where a negative is needed, making it stand out.
Options that fit the question. Response labels should cover the range the construct needs, in an order and spacing respondents can read. If most labels sit on one side of neutral, the middle option isn’t neutral.
Plausible distractors. A multiple-choice distractor that nobody would choose adds only reading time. Distractors built from specific errors earn their place (Haladyna et al., 2002), and Nominal response and multiple-choice models shows that which distractor a respondent picks carries information of its own.


Try it: fix this item
Each item below breaks one rule. Decide what is wrong before you reveal the diagnosis and a rewrite. (The items are invented for this lesson.)


Code
fx_items = ({
  "I enjoy reading novels and writing poetry.": {
    fault: "Two ideas in one item. A respondent who reads novels but never writes poetry has no accurate answer.",
    fix: "Two items: \"I enjoy reading novels.\" and \"I enjoy writing poetry.\""},
  "It is not true that I never feel nervous before a test.": {
    fault: "A double negative. To agree, the respondent has to unpack \"not true that ... never\", which is a reading task, not a question about nerves.",
    fix: "\"I feel nervous before a test.\""},
  "How would you rate your teacher's feedback? (Poor / Good / Very good / Excellent / Outstanding)": {
    fault: "Unbalanced options. Four of the five labels are positive, so the middle option, \"Very good\", is not neutral. That can be deliberate when nearly everyone rates highly and the aim is to separate the top, but then it should be a stated choice.",
    fix: "(Very poor / Poor / Fair / Good / Very good), or keep the positive skew on purpose and say so in the scoring guide."},
  "What is 1/2 + 1/3?  (a) 5/6  (b) 2/5  (c) 1/6  (d) A triangle": {
    fault: "An implausible distractor. Nobody who reads the question chooses (d), so the item is in effect a three-option item. Options (b) (adding tops and bottoms) and (c) (multiplying) each come from a specific error.",
    fix: "Replace (d) with another answer produced by an error, such as 2/6 (adding the numerators over the product of the denominators)."}
})
viewof fx_which = Inputs.radio(Object.keys(fx_items), {value: Object.keys(fx_items)[0], label: "Item"})
viewof fx_show = Inputs.toggle({label: "Reveal", value: false})

























Code
md`${fx_show ? `**What's wrong:** ${fx_items[fx_which].fault}

**A rewrite:** ${fx_items[fx_which].fix}` : "*Decide what is wrong, then reveal.*"}`







Each fault puts something between the respondent and the construct, and none need show in an item analysis: a double-barrelled item can correlate well with the rest, because respondents who like one of its two things tend to like the other.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A job-satisfaction scale includes \"My manager is supportive and I am paid fairly.\" In the pilot its item-rest correlation is 0.55, in line with the others. Keep it as is?",
  options: [
    {text: "No: split it into two items, even though the statistics look fine", correct: true, why: "The item is double-barrelled. A respondent with a supportive manager and low pay can't answer it cleanly, and the score can't say which half they were answering. Good statistics don't repair the item's meaning."},
    {text: "Yes: an item-rest correlation of 0.55 shows the item works", correct: false, why: "It shows the item goes along with the total. Support and pay are both parts of job satisfaction, so the item correlates with the rest whichever half a respondent answers."},
    {text: "Drop it: double-barrelled items always have low item-rest correlations", correct: false, why: "They needn't. This one doesn't, which is why the fault has to be caught by reading the item."}
  ]
})










Reverse-worded items






Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: half the Mach IV’s items are worded so that agreeing is the less Machiavellian answer, and they must be reverse-keyed before sums, alpha or item-rest correlations mean anything. Keying had to be checked: automated keying found all ten published reversals and added m19, the one item the data couldn’t settle.



Here we write reversed items on purpose. Why? The usual answer is acquiescence, a respondent’s tendency to agree with statements whatever they say (Paulhus, 1991; Baumgartner & Steenkamp, 2001). If every item is worded so that agreeing means more of the construct, a respondent who agrees easily gets a higher score for reasons unrelated to the construct. If half the items are reversed, the extra agreement raises the forward items and, once keyed, lowers the reversed ones, and the two cancel in the sum.

Try it: agreeing with everything
Six hundred simulated respondents answer ten four-point items, each loading 0.6 on the trait. Each respondent also has a tendency to agree, added to their raw agreement with every item; the slider sets how much it varies between respondents. The two designs are an all-forward scale and a balanced one with five items reversed (and then keyed).


Code
viewof aq_sd = Inputs.range([0, 1.5], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Spread of acquiescence (SD)"})









Code
aq = simAcquiescence({seed: 7, n: 600, acq: aq_sd})
aq_rows = [
  {design: "All forward", what: "Alpha", v: aq.forward.alpha}, {design: "All forward", what: "Trait's share of the sum score", v: aq.forward.r2},
  {design: "Balanced", what: "Alpha", v: aq.balanced.alpha}, {design: "Balanced", what: "Trait's share of the sum score", v: aq.balanced.r2}
]
Plot.plot({
  width: 620, height: 220, marginLeft: 100, marginRight: 40,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: null, grid: true}, y: {label: null, axis: null}, fy: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Alpha", "Trait's share of the sum score"], range: [palette.contrast, palette.main]},
  marks: [Plot.barX(aq_rows, {x: "v", y: "what", fy: "design", fill: "what"}),
          Plot.text(aq_rows, {x: "v", y: "what", fy: "design", text: d => d.v.toFixed(2), dx: 16})]
})

























Code
md`All forward: alpha **${aq.forward.alpha.toFixed(2)}**, trait's share of the sum score's variance **${aq.forward.r2.toFixed(2)}**. Balanced: alpha **${aq.balanced.alpha.toFixed(2)}**, trait's share **${aq.balanced.r2.toFixed(2)}**.`







With no acquiescence the designs are alike (alpha 0.80 and 0.82). As the slider moves right, the all-forward scale’s alpha rises, because acquiescence is shared by every item and alpha counts anything shared as signal, while the trait’s share of the sum score falls, to 0.44 at the starting value. The balanced scale keeps the trait’s share near 0.8 and its alpha falls instead. The simulation assumes respondents read a reversed item as exactly the opposite of a forward one.
Do they? Not always. Marsh (1996), analysing the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale in a large US longitudinal study of school students, found that the negatively worded items shared a method effect beyond the general factor, and later studies modelled such effects for the same scale and others (Tomás & Oliver, 1999; DiStefano & Motl, 2006). Weijters, Baumgartner and Schillewaert (2013) model three mechanisms that can produce one: acquiescence, careless responding, and confirmation bias (reading a reversed item in the light of the items before it). Swain, Weathers and Niedrich (2008) found about a fifth of responses to reversed items landing on the same side of the scale as the forward items, and trace it to the extra work of checking a reversed statement against one’s belief. Whatever the mechanism, reversed items correlate more with each other than their content predicts, and wording direction becomes a second dimension.


Try it: a wording factor
The same ten items, keyed. Each loads 0.6 on the trait; the reversed items (R1–R5) also load on a wording factor unrelated to the trait, and a second slider gives the forward items (F1–F5) a wording factor of their own. The heat map is the correlation matrix for 600 simulated respondents.


Code
viewof wf_g = Inputs.range([0, 0.7], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Reversed items' wording loading"})
viewof wf_gf = Inputs.range([0, 0.7], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Forward items' wording loading"})


















Code
wf = simWording({seed: 56, n: 600, lambda: 0.6, gamma: wf_g, gammaF: wf_gf})
wf_lab = ["F1", "F2", "F3", "F4", "F5", "R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5"]
wf_cells = wf.R.flatMap((row, i) => row.map((v, j) => ({i: wf_lab[i], j: wf_lab[j], v: i === j ? null : v})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 420, height: 420, marginLeft: 40, x: {domain: wf_lab, label: null, axis: "top"}, y: {domain: wf_lab, label: null},
  color: {domain: [0, 1], range: [palette.white, palette.main], legend: true, label: "Correlation"},
  marks: [Plot.cell(wf_cells, {x: "j", y: "i", fill: d => d.v ?? 1, stroke: palette.rule}),
          Plot.text(wf_cells.filter(d => d.v !== null), {x: "j", y: "i", text: d => d.v.toFixed(2), fontSize: 9, fill: d => d.v > 0.55 ? palette.white : palette.ink})]
})
































Code
md`Average correlation among forward items **${wf.withinF.toFixed(2)}**, among reversed items **${wf.withinR.toFixed(2)}**, across the two **${wf.across.toFixed(2)}**. Alpha **${wf.alpha.toFixed(2)}**. The trait's share of the sum score's variance **${wf.r2.toFixed(2)}**. Largest eigenvalues of the correlation matrix: ${wf.eig.slice(0, 3).map(v => v.toFixed(2)).join(", ")}.`







At a reversed loading of 0 the matrix is one even block, with alpha 0.83 and the trait accounting for 0.83 of the sum score’s variance. At 0.6 the reversed items form their own block (0.65 among themselves, 0.32 with the forward items), alpha rises to 0.87, and the trait’s share falls to 0.69. Give the forward items a wording factor too and there are two blocks, alpha 0.90 and the trait’s share 0.59. The wording factor acts like the correlated errors that Classical test theory and reliability warned can push alpha above reliability. The second eigenvalue passing 1 is a first hint of the extra dimension; Factor analysis I explains eigenvalues and how to count dimensions with them.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A ten-item scale with five reversed items has alpha 0.90. A colleague concludes that wording effects can't be a concern, since they would have lowered alpha. What does the widget say?",
  options: [
    {text: "That doesn't follow: a wording factor shared by the reversed items can raise alpha", correct: true, why: "In the widget alpha went from 0.83 to 0.87 as the reversed items' wording loading rose from 0 to 0.6, while the trait's share of the sum score fell from 0.83 to 0.69. Alpha counts shared wording variance as if it were signal."},
    {text: "It's right: wording effects always lower alpha", correct: false, why: "Only when they work against the trait. A shared wording factor adds covariance within the reversed block, and alpha goes up."},
    {text: "It's right only if the scale is balanced", correct: false, why: "The widget's scale is balanced (five and five), and alpha still rose with the wording loading."}
  ]
})







Should a scale include reversed items, then? Including them assumes acquiescence is a large enough source of variance, for this population and format, to guard against; the first widget shows its cost. Treating them as plain opposites of the forward items assumes respondents read them that way; the second widget shows what happens when they don’t. Suárez-Álvarez et al. (2018), giving a self-efficacy test in forward, reversed and mixed forms, found lower reliability and extra variance in the mixed form. Weijters and Baumgartner (2012) review both sides, distinguish items reversed in meaning from items reversed by a negation, and recommend using reversed items with care. My own practice is this: I include reversed items when acquiescence is a real risk, as with agree–disagree formats and respondents who may answer quickly; I write them as opposites in meaning (“I am often bored”) rather than negations (“I am not often interested”); and I plan the analysis expecting a wording factor rather than hoping it away.



The pilot, and reading the items
The pilot’s item analysis uses the tools of Classical test theory and reliability: item means, item-rest correlations, alpha with each item removed. What this lesson adds is the reading. A weak item may be keyed backwards, measure something else, or be read in a sense we didn’t intend, and those call for different decisions: rekey, drop, rewrite. The number flags the item; the text and the cognitive interviews decide.
Two later lessons carry this further. Content review is the first kind of validity evidence in Gathering validity evidence, which picks up where steps 1 to 4 leave off. And an item can work well on average but differently for groups of respondents at the same level of the construct; Differential item functioning shows how to find such items.

title: From construct map to items: building an instrument
text:
Simulate
The code below generates ten four-point items from one trait, with a wording factor on the five reversed items, and prints the correlation matrix, alpha, the block averages, the largest eigenvalues, and the trait’s share of the sum score’s variance. It is base R and runs in a second.
With the seed as written (gamma <- 0.6), alpha is 0.87, the reversed items correlate 0.66 on average with each other and 0.33 with the forward items, the second eigenvalue is 1.17, and the trait accounts for 0.72 of the sum score’s variance. Set gamma <- 0 and alpha falls to 0.83 while the trait’s share rises to 0.82. Then set gamma <- 0.6 and gamma_f <- 0.6: alpha reaches 0.90, the second eigenvalue 1.95, and the trait’s share falls to 0.63. Keep that last setting in mind for the real data. Then try n <- 100: how noisy are the block averages in a small pilot?

title: From construct map to items: building an instrument
text:
With real data
Our table is song_2023_rses: the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (Rosenberg, 1965) as answered by 1,238 medical students in China, in a study of anxiety about writing in English (Song et al., 2023; data CC BY 4.0). Its job is to be our pilot: five items worded for self-esteem and five against, so we can see what reverse wording does. Responses run from 1 to 4, and every respondent answered all ten items. Download the code; it needs only base R.


Code
# The IRW table, from the CSV link on its landing page (pinned to one version).
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_3:v7_0.song_2023_rses/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(url)
x <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(v) v[1])
x <- x[, paste0("RSES", 1:10)]         # items in the order of the published scale
c(respondents = nrow(x), complete = sum(complete.cases(x)))


respondents    complete 
       1238        1238 


Code
table(df$resp)                         # 1 to 4



   1    2    3    4 
 355 2412 6592 3021 


Code
# Rosenberg's wording: items 3, 5, 8, 9 and 10 are worded against self-esteem.
neg <- paste0("RSES", c(3, 5, 8, 9, 10))


Rosenberg wrote items 3, 5, 8, 9 and 10 against self-esteem. Item 3, for example, is “All in all, I am inclined to feel that I am a failure” (wording from the scale as published by the University of Maryland Department of Sociology, which states that the scale is in the public domain). The respondents answered a Chinese version, so the English wording is the original the translation starts from, not what they read. Song et al. say the negatively worded items were reverse-scored. Are the stored responses already keyed?


Code
alpha <- function(m) { k <- ncol(m); k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(m, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(m))) }
# Summed as stored, the table gives the mean, SD and alpha Song et al. report
# (29.92, 4.79 and 0.863), so what we have are the authors' scored responses.
s <- rowSums(x)
sprintf("mean %.2f, SD %.2f, alpha %.3f", mean(s), sd(s), alpha(x))


[1] "mean 29.92, SD 4.79, alpha 0.863"


Code
# If items 3, 5, 9 and 10 had *not* been reversed, alpha would be far lower:
flip <- function(m, items) { m[, items] <- 5 - m[, items]; m }
sprintf("alpha with items 3, 5, 9 and 10 un-reversed: %.3f", alpha(flip(x, paste0("RSES", c(3, 5, 9, 10)))))


[1] "alpha with items 3, 5, 9 and 10 un-reversed: 0.658"


Summed as stored, the table reproduces the mean, SD and alpha Song et al. report (29.92, 4.79 and 0.863), and un-reversing items 3, 5, 9 and 10 drops alpha to 0.658. So the table holds the authors’ scored responses, and on those four items higher means more self-esteem. Item 8 we come back to.


Code
item_rest <- sapply(colnames(x), function(i) cor(x[, i], rowSums(x[, colnames(x) != i])))
data.frame(mean = round(colMeans(x), 2), item_rest = round(item_rest, 2),
           worded = ifelse(colnames(x) %in% neg, "against", "for"))

Every item-rest correlation is between 0.41 and 0.69. By the standard of Classical test theory and reliability, where 24 of the 30 reading items reached 0.40, the scale hangs together, and an item analysis would stop here. But as one set, or as two?


Code
predict({
  q: "Keyed, the five positively worded items correlate 0.71 on average with each other, and four of the negatively worded items (3, 5, 9, 10) correlate 0.61 with each other. What is the average correlation between a positively worded item and one of those four?",
  choices: ["About 0.65: they measure the same thing", "About 0.45", "About 0.2"],
  answer: "About 0.2",
  reveal: "0.23, with all 20 cross-correlations between 0.11 and 0.33. Items correlate about three times as strongly with items worded in their own direction as with items worded the other way."
})









Code
r <- cor(x)
pos  <- paste0("RSES", c(1, 2, 4, 6, 7))
neg4 <- paste0("RSES", c(3, 5, 9, 10))     # the negatively worded items other than 8
mean_r <- function(a, b) { v <- r[a, b]; if (identical(a, b)) mean(v[upper.tri(v)]) else mean(v) }
round(c(within_positive = mean_r(pos, pos), within_negative = mean_r(neg4, neg4),
        across = mean_r(pos, neg4)), 2)


within_positive within_negative          across 
           0.71            0.61            0.23

[1] 0.11 0.33

image(1:10, 1:10, r[ord, rev(ord)], zlim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
      col = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#2780e3"))(50),
