New developments in Mokken scale analysis in R. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(5). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i05. The package.
Holland, P. W., & Rosenbaum, P. R. (1986). Conditional association and unidimensionality in monotone latent variable models. Annals of Statistics, 14(4), 1523–1543. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176350174. What monotone curves imply for the observable data.

In M. von Davier & Y.-S. Lee (Eds.), Handbook of diagnostic classification models (pp. 21–45). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-05584-4_2. title: Nonparametric IRT: Mokken scaling
text:
For instructors

Source: new; no EDUC 252 slides cover Mokken scaling. Built from the outline in outlines/nonparametric-irt.md (#153).
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 60 minutes; the two real-data analyses work as a 30-minute lab.
Sanity check: before the lesson’s analyses, the pipeline was run on transreas_mokken, whose IRW rows equal mokken::transreas; its two pseudo-transitivity tasks have negative \(H_i\) (−0.03 and −0.14), as their design predicts. The hand-written kernel smoother reproduces KernSmoothIRT::ksIRT() with its defaults on mcmi_mokken to within \(10^{-14}\).
Held back: polytomous Mokken scaling (item-step curves) gets a sentence; two-level scalability is problem 4; a formal test of the parametric curve against the kernel curve is the open problem 6.

Solutions: held back in solutions/nonparametric-irt.qmd (not published). Problem 6 is open.

title: Person fit: does a respondent’s pattern fit the model?
text:
What this is for
A licensure program suspects 46 of its 1,636 respondents of inappropriate behaviour. Their scores look like everyone else’s. Can the responses themselves say which patterns the model doesn’t describe? Every fit statistic so far has asked whether an item behaves as the model says, over all its respondents. Person fit asks it of one respondent, over all their items. This lesson builds the two families of person-fit statistics, group-based and IRT-based, shows that estimating \(\theta\) from the same responses changes what “unlikely” means, and then asks the licensure data, a personality inventory and a matrix reasoning test what a flag can and can’t tell us.

title: Person fit: does a respondent’s pattern fit the model?
Person fit: does a respondent’s pattern fit the model?
text:
Core ideas






Recall from The Rasch model: under the Rasch model the sum score is sufficient, so two students who get 3 of 5 items right have the same ability estimate, whether they got the three easiest or the three hardest. That lesson’s quiz added that the second pattern is less likely, which is a question of person fit.



Person-fit statistics come in two families (Meijer & Sijtsma, 2001). Group-based (nonparametric) statistics use only the data: an ordering of the items by how many respondents got each right and, for some, the other respondents’ patterns. They need no model and no \(\theta\), but have no reference distribution of their own. IRT-based statistics compare a pattern with the probabilities a model gives at the respondent’s \(\theta\). They need item parameters and, in practice, \(\hat\theta\); in return, the model says how the statistic is distributed if it holds.

Group-based statistics: Guttman errors and \(H^T\)
Order the items from easiest to hardest by the share of respondents who got each right. If responses were perfectly consistent, a respondent with \(r\) correct would get the \(r\) easiest right and the rest wrong: a Guttman pattern (Guttman, 1944). Every pair in which an easier item is wrong and a harder one right is a Guttman error. A respondent can make at most \(r(n - r)\) of them, so the normalized count \[G^* = \frac{\text{Guttman errors}}{r(n - r)}\] runs from 0 (a Guttman pattern) to 1 (the reverse). It needs no model, only an ordering of the items. Counts like these are a reasonable choice before any model has been chosen, or when there are too few respondents to fit one.

Try it: Guttman errors
Ten items, easiest first: the share of a population answering each correctly runs from 0.89 to 0.11. Choose which ones the respondent gets right.


Code
gt_labels = propCorrect(gtB).map((p, i) => `${i + 1} (${p.toFixed(2)} correct)`)
viewof gt_pick = Inputs.checkbox(gt_labels, {label: "Correct on", value: [0, 1, 3, 4, 6].map(i => gt_labels[i])})


















Code
gt_x = gt_labels.map(l => gt_pick.includes(l) ? 1 : 0)
gt_r = gt_x.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0)
gt_g = guttman(gt_x)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 110, marginLeft: 20, x: {label: "Item (easiest to hardest)", domain: gt_x.map((_, i) => i + 1)}, y: {axis: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Right", "Wrong"], range: [palette.main, palette.light]},
  marks: [Plot.cell(gt_x.map((v, i) => ({item: i + 1, v: v ? "Right" : "Wrong"})), {x: "item", fill: "v", inset: 2})]
})
































Code
md`Sum score **${gt_r}** of 10. ${gt_r > 0 && gt_r < 10 ?
  `Guttman errors: **${gt_g.errors}** of a possible ${gt_r * (10 - gt_r)}, so G<sup>∗</sup> = **${gt_g.gstar.toFixed(2)}**.` :
  "With every item right or every item wrong there is only one pattern, and nothing for it to disagree with."}`







The default pattern (items 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7) has 4 Guttman errors of a possible 25. Tick items 1 to 5 and the count is 0; tick 6 to 10 instead and it is 25, with the same sum score. Whether 4 is many for this score needs a reference: a model, or the other respondents.


Code
quiz({
  q: "On a 20-item test ordered by difficulty, two respondents each have 12 items right. One has 10 Guttman errors, the other 40. What is $G^*$ for each?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.10 and 0.42", correct: true, why: "The most errors possible is $r(n - r) = 12 \\times 8 = 96$, so $G^* = 10/96 \\approx 0.10$ and $40/96 \\approx 0.42$."},
    {text: "0.50 and 2.00", correct: false, why: "That divides by the number of items, 20. $G^*$ divides by the number of (right, wrong) pairs, $r(n - r) = 96$, so it can't exceed 1."},
    {text: "It depends on the items' proportions correct", correct: false, why: "The proportions correct set the order of the items, and so which pairs count as errors, but once the errors are counted $G^*$ is the count over $r(n - r)$."}
  ]
})













If you’ve done Nonparametric IRT: Mokken scaling: Loevinger’s \(H\) compares the Guttman errors between two items with the number expected if they were unrelated, and \(H^T\) was an \(H\) computed with the roles of respondents and items swapped, to say how accurately the items’ order can be read off. The person-fit \(H^T\) below is that coefficient’s version for one respondent, as \(H_i\) is \(H\)’s for one item.



\(G^*\) compares a pattern with an ordering of the items. \(H^T\) (Sijtsma, 1986; Sijtsma & Meijer, 1992) compares it with the other respondents’ patterns. It is Loevinger’s \(H\) for one respondent of the transposed data: the covariance, across items, between their responses and everyone else’s summed responses, over the largest it could be given everyone’s proportions correct. Write \(\pi_j = r_j/n\) for the share of items respondent \(j\) got right and \(\pi_{jk}\) for the share that both \(j\) and \(k\) got right. Then \[H^T_j = \frac{\sum_{k \ne j} (\pi_{jk} - \pi_j\pi_k)}{\sum_{k \ne j} \big[\min(\pi_j, \pi_k) - \pi_j\pi_k\big]}.\] Each term in the numerator is the covariance of two respondents’ responses across the items; the matching term below is the largest that covariance can be, reached when the one with the lower score got right only items the other also got right. \(H^T\) is 1 when no one with a lower score got right an item this respondent got wrong, and no one with a higher score got wrong an item they got right. Low or negative values signal misfit. In Karabatsos’s (2003) comparison of 36 statistics, \(H^T\) was among the best at detecting aberrant patterns. Sinharay (2017) reran those simulations, computing power in a way that treated the statistics alike; \(H^T\) still did well, about as well as \(l_z\) and U3 (see also Tendeiro & Meijer, 2014). Like \(G^*\), it depends on the sample.



IRT-based statistics: person outfit, infit and \(l_z\)






Recall from Model fit and out-of-sample prediction: with \(z_{ij} = (x_{ij} - p_{ij})/\sqrt{p_{ij}(1 - p_{ij})}\), an item’s outfit is the mean of \(z_{ij}^2\) over its respondents, and infit weights each by \(p_{ij}(1 - p_{ij})\). From The Rasch model: below 1 is overfit (more predictable than the model expects), above 1 underfit.



Average the same squared residuals over one respondent’s items instead of one item’s respondents and you have person outfit and person infit (Wright & Masters, 1982). A strong respondent who misses an easy item gets a large \(z^2\) from it, just as an item does from a strong respondent who misses it.
Outfit and infit are Rasch statistics. They were built for the Rasch model, and their usual reading, a mean square near 1 with fixed limits such as 0.7 to 1.3, comes from that tradition. The formulas take any model’s \(P_{ij}\), and mirt’s personfit() computes them for a 2PL too, as the widgets below do; but outside the Rasch model they are borrowed. Even under it, fixed limits have a catch: the spread of a mean square under the model depends on how many residuals it averages, so one pair of limits is too strict for a short test and too lax for a long one (Smith, Schumacker & Bush, 1998, for items and sample size).






Recall from Estimating abilities: with the item parameters known, the likelihood of a respondent’s pattern at \(\theta\) is \(\prod_i P_i^{x_i}(1 - P_i)^{1 - x_i}\); its first widget drew it for every pattern of three items.



The other route starts from that likelihood. Let \(l_0\) be the log likelihood of the pattern at \(\theta\), \[l_0 = \sum_i \big[x_i \log P_i + (1 - x_i)\log(1 - P_i)\big].\] If the model holds, \(l_0\) has a mean and variance we can write down, item by item: \[E(l_0) = \sum_i \big[P_i \log P_i + (1 - P_i)\log(1 - P_i)\big], \qquad \text{Var}(l_0) = \sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)\Big[\log\frac{P_i}{1 - P_i}\Big]^2.\] Standardizing gives \(l_z = \big(l_0 - E(l_0)\big)/\sqrt{\text{Var}(l_0)}\) (Levine & Rubin, 1979; Drasgow, Levine & Williams, 1985). Below 0 the pattern is less likely than the model expects (underfit); above 0 it is more predictable (overfit). mirt’s personfit() reports it as Zh (Chalmers, 2012). Since \(l_0 - E(l_0) = \sum_i (x_i - P_i)\log\frac{P_i}{1 - P_i}\), \(l_z\) is a weighted sum of residuals, and a correct answer on an item far above the respondent (small \(P_i\), a large negative weight) counts most against the pattern.

Try it: same score, different likelihoods
The pattern from the widget above, among every pattern with the same sum score. Each is scored by maximum likelihood, and \(l_z\) is computed at that estimate. Under the Rasch model every pattern with the same score has the same \(\hat\theta\); the 2PL gives the items slopes from 0.5 to 2.0.


Code
viewof gl_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch", "2PL"], {value: "Rasch", label: "Model"})









Code
gl_a = gl_model === "Rasch" ? gtB.map(() => 1) : gtA
gl_all = (gt_r > 0 && gt_r < 10) ? patterns(10, gt_r).map(x => {
  const th = mle(x, gl_a, gtB), s = fitStats(x, gl_a, gtB, th);
  return {errors: guttman(x).errors, lz: s.lz, mine: x.join("") === gt_x.join("")};
}) : []
gl_me = (gt_r > 0 && gt_r < 10) ? fitStats(gt_x, gl_a, gtB, mle(gt_x, gl_a, gtB)) : null
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Guttman errors"}, y: {label: "l_z at the ML estimate"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([-1.645], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot(gl_all.filter(d => !d.mine), {x: "errors", y: "lz", r: 3, fill: palette.light}),
    Plot.dot(gl_all.filter(d => d.mine), {x: "errors", y: "lz", r: 7, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})
































Code
md`${gl_me ? `Your pattern (orange): θ̂ = **${(mle(gt_x, gl_a, gtB) + 0).toFixed(2).replace("-0.00", "0.00")}**, log likelihood ${gl_me.l0.toFixed(2)} against an expected ${gl_me.El.toFixed(2)} (SD ${Math.sqrt(gl_me.Vl).toFixed(2)}), so l<sub>z</sub> = **${gl_me.lz.toFixed(2)}**. Person outfit ${gl_me.outfit.toFixed(2)}, infit ${gl_me.infit.toFixed(2)}. The ${gl_all.length} patterns with this score run from l<sub>z</sub> = ${Math.min(...gl_all.map(d => d.lz)).toFixed(2)} to ${Math.max(...gl_all.map(d => d.lz)).toFixed(2)}.` : "Choose a sum score between 1 and 9."}`







Under the Rasch model the points fall close to a line: more Guttman errors, lower \(l_z\). They don’t fall exactly on it, because \(l_z\) weighs an error by how far apart the two items are, while \(G^*\) counts every error alike. Switch to the 2PL and the cloud spreads: an error on a steep item costs more. The Guttman pattern sits at the top, with \(l_z\) above 0: overfit, more orderly than the model expects.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A respondent's $l_z$ is +2.1 and their person outfit is 0.55. What does that say about their pattern?",
  options: [
    {text: "It is more predictable than the model expects: close to a Guttman pattern", correct: true, why: "Positive $l_z$ and outfit below 1 both mean overfit: the easy items right and the hard ones wrong, more consistently than the item curves allow."},
    {text: "It is less likely than the model expects, so the respondent may have been careless", correct: false, why: "That is underfit, which shows as negative $l_z$ and outfit above 1."},
    {text: "Nothing, since only negative $l_z$ is informative", correct: false, why: "Overfit is a finding too. It can mean that the item parameters don't describe this respondent, as the licensure data below suggest for some groups."}
  ]
})










Estimating \(\theta\) narrows the null distribution






Recall from Model fit and out-of-sample prediction, its Simulate section: with 20 items and the Rasch model true, item outfits computed from mirt’s EAP abilities averaged 0.90, and from maximum-likelihood abilities 0.97 to 0.99. Estimates fitted to the same responses pull a fit statistic toward the data.









Recall from Estimating abilities: the EAP is pulled toward the mean of the prior (shrinkage), most at the ends of the scale and on short tests. The MLE solves the score equation \(\sum_i a_i(x_i - P_i) = 0\); the WLE (Warm, 1989) adds a term that removes the MLE’s first-order bias.



\(l_z\) is standard normal (for long tests) only at the respondent’s true \(\theta\). In practice \(\hat\theta\) comes from the same responses, and a pattern looks at least as likely at its own maximum-likelihood estimate as at the truth. What does that do to the flag rate at −1.645, the 5% point of the standard normal?


Code
predict({
  q: "With 20 items and the 2PL true, what share of respondents will have $l_z$ below −1.645 when $l_z$ is computed at their maximum-likelihood $\\hat\\theta$?",
  choices: ["About 1%", "About 3%", "About 5%", "About 8%"],
  answer: "About 3%",
  reveal: "About 3% (2.9% in the widget below): the estimate absorbs part of each pattern's departure from the model, and the statistic's SD falls to about 0.8. With 170 items it is still about 0.8. Check it below."
})








Try it: \(l_z\) at the true \(\theta\) and at \(\hat\theta\)
2,000 simulated respondents answer 2PL items (slopes around 1, difficulties standard normal) whose parameters are known; only \(\theta\) is estimated, by maximum likelihood. Each line is the distribution of one version of the statistic; the dashed curve is the standard normal. Outfit and infit are standardized (see below), so that for them, too, 0 is the centre and the flag is at 1.645, on the right.


Code
viewof nl_n = Inputs.radio([10, 20, 40, 170], {value: 20, label: "Number of items"})
viewof nl_stat = Inputs.radio(new Map([["l_z", "lz"], ["Person outfit", "outfit"], ["Person infit", "infit"]]), {value: "lz", label: "Statistic"})


















Code
nl = simNull(nl_n)
nl_nm = ({lz: "l_z", outfit: "outfit", infit: "infit"})[nl_stat]
nl_cut = nl_stat === "lz" ? -1.645 : 1.645
nl_versions = [["true", `${nl_nm} at the true θ`], ["hat", `${nl_nm} at the ML estimate`], ["star", `${nl_nm}, corrected, at the ML estimate`]]
nl_series = nl_versions.map(([k, name]) => [name, nl.rows.map(d => d[nl_stat][k])])
nl_dens = nl_series.flatMap(([name, v]) => {
  const w = 0.25, c = Array(36).fill(0);
  for (const z of v) { const k = Math.floor((z + 5) / w); if (k >= 0 && k < 36) c[k]++; }
  return c.map((n, k) => ({z: -5 + (k + 0.5) * w, d: n / (v.length * w), s: name}));
})
nl_norm = Array.from({length: 101}, (_, k) => { const z = -5 + 0.09 * k; return {z, d: Math.exp(-z * z / 2) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)}; })
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Statistic", domain: [-5, 4]}, y: {label: "Density"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: nl_series.map(d => d[0]), range: [palette.light, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(nl_norm, {x: "z", y: "d", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([nl_cut], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(nl_dens, {x: "z", y: "d", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})




























































Code
nl_sd = v => { const m = v.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) / v.length; return Math.sqrt(v.reduce((s, x) => s + (x - m) ** 2, 0) / (v.length - 1)); }
nl_low = v => v.filter(x => nl_stat === "lz" ? x < -1.645 : x > 1.645).length / v.length
nl_side = nl_stat === "lz" ? "below −1.645" : "above +1.645"
md`With ${nl_n} items (${nl.dropped} respondents with a perfect or zero score set aside): ${nl_nm} at the true θ has SD **${nl_sd(nl_series[0][1]).toFixed(2)}**, with ${(100 * nl_low(nl_series[0][1])).toFixed(1)}% ${nl_side}; at the ML estimate, SD **${nl_sd(nl_series[1][1]).toFixed(2)}** and ${(100 * nl_low(nl_series[1][1])).toFixed(1)}%; corrected, SD **${nl_sd(nl_series[2][1]).toFixed(2)}** and ${(100 * nl_low(nl_series[2][1])).toFixed(1)}%.`






























At the true \(\theta\) the SD is about 1, but short tests give a skewed distribution, and 6–7% fall below −1.645 with 10 to 40 items (Molenaar & Hoijtink, 1990). At the estimate the SD drops to about 0.8 and the flag rate to 2–4%, at every length: a longer test doesn’t remove the shrinkage (Nering, 1995). Snijders (2001) derived the null distribution of any statistic that is a weighted sum of residuals, with \(\hat\theta\) in place of \(\theta\), and from it the corrected \(l_z^*\), whose SD is about 1 at every length here. Magis, Raîche and Béland (2012) set it out step by step for the logistic models and the MLE and WLE.
The correction is short. At the ML estimate, the score equation has already set \(\sum_i a_i(x_i - P_i)\) to zero, so the part of each weight \(w_i = \log\frac{P_i}{1 - P_i}\) that lies along the slopes can’t vary any more. \(l_z^*\) removes it before standardizing: \[l_z^* = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - P_i)\,\tilde w_i}{\sqrt{\sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)\,\tilde w_i^2}}, \qquad \tilde w_i = w_i - c\,a_i, \quad c = \frac{\sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)\,a_i w_i}{\sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)\,a_i^2},\] all evaluated at \(\hat\theta\). For the MLE the numerator equals that of \(l_z\); only the denominator shrinks, to match. For the WLE, Snijders adds a term for the estimator’s own correction. The WLE is worth that term: it is less biased on average than the MLE, whose estimates are pushed outward, most on short tests (Warm, 1989).
Outfit and infit are weighted sums of residuals too: for a 0/1 response, \((x_i - P_i)^2 = P_i(1 - P_i) + (1 - 2P_i)(x_i - P_i)\), so \[\text{outfit} - 1 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i - P_i)\frac{1 - 2P_i}{P_i(1 - P_i)}, \qquad \text{infit} - 1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - P_i)(1 - 2P_i)}{\sum_i P_i(1 - P_i)}.\] Standardized (positive for underfit), each shrinks at \(\hat\theta\) just as \(l_z\) does: switch the widget to outfit or infit. Magis, Béland and Raîche (2014) adapt Snijders’s correction to both under the Rasch model; the widget uses the same formula, with these weights for \(w_i\), under the 2PL. (Rasch software usually standardizes the mean squares with a cube-root transformation instead.)






Recall from Estimating abilities: all-right and all-wrong patterns have no maximum-likelihood estimate.



What of those perfect patterns? They have no person-fit statistic either, whatever the estimator. There is only one pattern with a score of 0 or \(n\), so there is nothing for it to disagree with.






NoteGo deeper: why \(\hat\theta\) shrinks \(l_z\), and where \(l_z^*\) comes from





Assumptions: dichotomous items under the 2PL with known parameters; responses independent given \(\theta\); \(\hat\theta\) the MLE; a first-order (large-test) expansion. Write \(P_i = P_i(\theta)\), \(Q_i = 1 - P_i\) and \(w_i = \log(P_i/Q_i) = a_i(\theta - b_i)\).
A weighted sum of residuals. \(W(\theta) = \sum_i (x_i - P_i)w_i\) has mean 0 and variance \(\sum_i P_iQ_iw_i^2\) at the true \(\theta\). It equals \(l_0 - E(l_0)\).
Plug in \(\hat\theta\). Since \(P_i' = a_iP_iQ_i\), expanding around \(\theta\) gives \(P_i(\hat\theta) \approx P_i + a_iP_iQ_i(\hat\theta - \theta)\), and the score equation gives \(\hat\theta - \theta \approx \sum_k a_k(x_k - P_k)/I(\theta)\), with \(I = \sum_k a_k^2P_kQ_k\). The change in \(w_i\) multiplies \((x_i - P_i)\) and is of smaller order. So \[W(\hat\theta) \approx \sum_i (x_i - P_i)w_i - (\hat\theta - \theta)\sum_i a_iP_iQ_iw_i = \sum_i (x_i - P_i)(w_i - c\,a_i), \qquad c = \frac{\sum_i a_iP_iQ_iw_i}{I}.\] The weights \(w_i - c\,a_i\) are the residuals from a weighted regression (weights \(P_iQ_i\)) of \(w_i\) on \(a_i\). Their variance, \(\sum_i P_iQ_i(w_i - c\,a_i)^2 = \sum_i P_iQ_iw_i^2 - c^2 I\), is smaller than \(\text{Var}(l_0)\) by \(c^2I\). \(l_z\) divides by the larger number, so it shrinks toward 0; \(l_z^*\) divides by the smaller one (Snijders, 2001). The loss \(c^2 I\) grows with the test (both \(c^2 I\) and \(\text{Var}(l_0)\) are sums over items), which is why more items don’t help.
Who is affected most. Under the Rasch model \(a_i = 1\) and \(w_i = \theta - b_i\), so \(c = \theta - \bar b\), with \(\bar b\) the \(P_iQ_i\)-weighted mean difficulty, and \(w_i - c = -(b_i - \bar b)\). The part removed is \((\theta - \bar b)^2 I\): nothing for a respondent in the middle of the items, a lot for one far from them. The numerator becomes \(-\sum_i (x_i - P_i)(b_i - \bar b)\), which, given \(r\), depends only on the sum of the difficulties of the items answered correctly. This is the person-side version of the point in Model fit and out-of-sample prediction that outfit from estimated abilities runs below 1.
Other estimators. The WLE solves a score equation with an added term \(r_0(\theta) = J(\theta)/2I(\theta)\); Snijders’s result then shifts the mean of \(W\) by \(-c\,r_0(\hat\theta)\), and \(l_z^*\) adds it back. Magis, Raîche and Béland (2012) give the term for each logistic model and likelihood-based estimator.





Code
quiz({
  q: "A program computes $l_z$ at maximum-likelihood abilities on a 60-item test and flags everyone below −1.645, expecting to flag 5% of respondents who fit the model. Roughly what happens?",
  options: [
    {text: "It flags fewer than 5% of them, around 2–3%", correct: true, why: "At $\\hat\\theta$ the SD of $l_z$ is about 0.8, whatever the length, so −1.645 is about two SDs out. $l_z^*$ restores the SD."},
    {text: "It flags about 5%, since 60 items is a long test", correct: false, why: "Length makes the distribution less skewed but doesn't remove the shrinkage: the variance lost to estimation grows with the test too."},
    {text: "It flags more than 5%, since estimates are noisy", correct: false, why: "The estimate is fitted to the same responses, which makes each pattern look more likely than it would at the true $\\theta$, not less."}
  ]
})










Person fit and the score
In the licensure data below, the rank correlation of \(l_z^*\) with the sum score is 0.04. Yet how a statistic behaves depends on where a respondent sits. Here is the widget’s sample split by \(\hat\theta\): the SD of each version of the statistic chosen above.


Code
nb_bands = [[-Infinity, -1.5, "below −1.5"], [-1.5, -0.5, "−1.5 to −0.5"], [-0.5, 0.5, "−0.5 to 0.5"], [0.5, 1.5, "0.5 to 1.5"], [1.5, Infinity, "above 1.5"]]
nb = nb_bands.flatMap(([lo, hi, lab]) => {
  const rows = nl.rows.filter(d => d.thetaHat >= lo && d.thetaHat < hi);
  return nl_versions.map(([k, name]) => ({band: lab, s: name, sd: nl_sd(rows.map(d => d[nl_stat][k])), n: rows.length}));
})
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "ML estimate of θ", domain: nb_bands.map(d => d[2])}, y: {label: "SD", domain: [0, 1.3]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: nl_versions.map(d => d[1]), range: [palette.light, palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(nb, {x: "band", y: "sd", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(nb, {x: "band", y: "sd", fill: "s", r: 4})
  ]
})























With 20 items, \(l_z\) at the estimate has SD 0.98 near the middle of the items and 0.4–0.5 beyond 1.5 on either side; \(l_z^*\) stays near 1 in every band. The part the estimate absorbs is nothing for a respondent among the items’ difficulties and grows with the distance from them (first Go deeper above), so one cutoff for \(l_z\) flags almost no one with an extreme score. With 10 or 20 items, corrected outfit stays narrow (SD about 0.6) below −1.5, where a single surprising answer dominates it.
Group-based statistics depend on the score too: a score near 0 or \(n\) leaves few patterns, \(\binom{n}{r}\), to tell apart. So does power: random answers from a respondent who would have scored low look much like their own. One answer is to judge a pattern only against others with the same score (second Go deeper below).


Power depends on the kind of aberrance
A global index sums over every item. What if only a few items are affected?

Try it: what the statistics can find
3,000 simulated respondents on 2PL items; about 10% of them respond aberrantly (for guessing, 10% of those below \(\theta = -0.5\)). Each statistic’s cutoff is set so that 5% of a clean simulated sample is flagged (low \(l_z^*\), high outfit, high \(G^*\), low \(H^T\)), the way PerFit sets cutoffs by simulation (Tendeiro, Meijer & Niessen, 2016).


Code
viewof ab_kind = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Random responding (1 in 4 on every item)", "random"], ["Preknowledge of the k hardest items", "preknowledge"], ["Guessing by low scorers", "guessing"], ["A different trait on k items", "shift"]]), {value: "preknowledge", label: "Kind of aberrance"})
viewof ab_n = Inputs.radio([20, 40], {value: 20, label: "Number of items"})
viewof ab_k = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 4, step: 1, label: "k, items affected (preknowledge, different trait)"})

























Code
ab = power(ab_n, ab_k, ab_kind)
ab_names = ({lzstar: "l_z*", outfit: "Person outfit", gstar: "G*", ht: "H^T"})
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, marginLeft: 190, x: {label: "Share flagged", domain: [0, 1]}, y: {label: null, domain: ab.rows.flatMap(d => [`${ab_names[d.stat]}: aberrant`, `${ab_names[d.stat]}: clean`])},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Aberrant respondents", "Clean respondents"], range: [palette.contrast, palette.light]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(ab.rows.flatMap(d => [{s: `${ab_names[d.stat]}: aberrant`, g: "Aberrant respondents", v: d.aberrant}, {s: `${ab_names[d.stat]}: clean`, g: "Clean respondents", v: d.clean}]),
      {y: "s", x: "v", fill: "g", insetTop: 2, insetBottom: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([0.05], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
})

























Code
md`Of ${ab.nBad} aberrant respondents, l<sub>z</sub><sup>∗</sup> flags **${(100 * ab.rows[0].aberrant).toFixed(0)}%**, person outfit ${(100 * ab.rows[1].aberrant).toFixed(0)}%, G<sup>∗</sup> ${(100 * ab.rows[2].aberrant).toFixed(0)}% and H<sup>T</sup> ${(100 * ab.rows[3].aberrant).toFixed(0)}%, against ${ab.rows.map(d => (100 * d.clean).toFixed(1) + "%").join(", ")} of the ${ab.nGood} clean ones.`







With preknowledge of the 4 hardest of 20 items, \(l_z^*\) flags 72% of the aberrant respondents and \(H^T\) 61%; with 2 items, 43% and 29%. Random responding is found only about half the time with 20 items, by every statistic. A different trait on a few items is barely found at all, and guessing by low scorers not much more. \(l_z^*\) is usually a little ahead, with the true model and item parameters; the group-based statistics use neither. The kind of aberrance matters more than the choice among the four.



What can misfit mean?
A low \(l_z^*\) says that the model, with these item parameters, describes this pattern poorly. It doesn’t say why. The candidates include carelessness or inattention (Meade & Craig, 2012; Niessen, Meijer & Tendeiro, 2016); preknowledge or copying (Cizek & Wollack, 2016); guessing; answering a different question from the one the scale asks, as when a respondent describes an ideal self; a trait that organizes some people’s answers less than others’ (Reise & Waller, 1993); and item parameters that are wrong for this respondent, a statement about the model, which a mixture Rasch model (Rost, 1990) turns into a model of its own. Overfit is a finding too.
The model can also be wrong for everyone. Every IRT-based statistic assumes that the fitted model is the one that generated the responses. Fit a 2PL where there is guessing, or one dimension where there are two, and the flags change. Hong, Monroe and Falk (2020) found that the share flagged across all respondents can look about right while the rate at a given \(\theta\) is far above nominal, and that respondents with extreme \(\theta\) are affected most. A flag is then partly a statement about the model, which is why checking the model’s fit (Model fit and out-of-sample prediction) comes before reading person fit.






Recall from The Rasch model, its Go deeper callout: given the sum score, a pattern’s probability is \(\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r) = \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}/\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)\), with \(\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}\), free of \(\theta\). Conditioning on \(r\) removes \(\theta\), which gave conditional maximum likelihood.









NoteGo deeper: exact person fit under the Rasch model





Assumptions: the Rasch model holds with known difficulties \(b_i\); responses are independent given \(\theta\).
A null with no estimate in it. By the Recall above, every quantity person fit needs is known once we condition on \(r\). Among the \(\binom{n}{r}\) patterns with score \(r\), the probability of each is proportional to \(\exp(-\sum_i x_ib_i)\): getting harder items right makes a pattern less probable, whatever the respondent’s ability. A pattern’s exact \(p\)-value is the total conditional probability of the patterns with score \(r\) that are at most as probable as it is. Nothing is estimated for the respondent, so the shrinkage of the previous section never arises.
The statistic. Ordering patterns by \(\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r)\) is ordering them by \(\sum_i x_ib_i\), and that is what \(l_z^*\)’s numerator reduces to under the Rasch model (previous Go deeper). Molenaar and Hoijtink (1990) compare three ways of setting the null (plug in \(\hat\theta\), integrate over the population, condition on \(r\)) and recommend conditioning on the total score. Under the 2PL the weighted score plays the part of \(r\), but its weights are item parameters, and the conditional null is no longer free of what has to be estimated.

title: Person fit: does a respondent’s pattern fit the model?
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates 1,000 respondents on 20 2PL items, makes 5% of them aberrant, fits the 2PL with mirt, scores everyone by maximum likelihood, and computes \(l_z\) (checked against mirt’s Zh) and \(l_z^*\) by hand. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load; the fit then takes a few seconds.
Unlike the widgets, this estimates the item parameters too. With the seed as written and kind <- "random", \(l_z\) has SD 0.75 among clean respondents and flags 1.7% of them; \(l_z^*\) has SD 1.01 and flags 5.4%, and it finds 36% of the random responders (\(l_z\): 16%). With "preknowledge" \(l_z^*\) finds 78%; with "guessing", 12%. Try n_items <- 40, or share <- 0.2, where the item parameters are fitted partly to the aberrant respondents.

title: Person fit: does a respondent’s pattern fit the model?
text:
With real data
Every analysis below uses the same few functions: \(l_z\), \(l_z^*\) and corrected outfit by hand, \(G^*\), \(H^T\), and a wrapper that fits a 2PL with mirt, scores respondents by maximum likelihood and collects the statistics. Download the code; it ends by checking the hand-computed statistics against PerFit (Tendeiro, Meijer & Niessen, 2016).


Code
library(mirt)
options(digits = 7)  # R's default, in case a .Rprofile changes it

# l_z and Snijders's l_z* for the 2PL, from a response matrix X, item slopes a
# and difficulties b, and each respondent's maximum-likelihood theta.
# l_0 - E(l_0) is the sum over items of (x - P) * w, with w = log(P / (1 - P)).
# l_z* replaces w by its residual after taking out the part along the slopes
# (the direction the ML score equation has already set to zero). Outfit - 1 is
# also a weighted sum of residuals, with w = (1 - 2P) / (P (1 - P)), since for 0/1
# responses (x - P)^2 = P (1 - P) + (1 - 2P) (x - P); zout and zout_star are its
# standardized and corrected versions (positive = underfit).
lz_stats <- function(X, a, b, theta) {
  P <- plogis(sweep(outer(theta, b, "-"), 2, a, "*"))
  Q <- 1 - P
  A <- matrix(a, nrow(X), length(a), byrow = TRUE)
  wsum <- function(w) {
    cn <- rowSums(P * Q * w * A) / rowSums(P * Q * A^2)
    wt <- w - cn * A
    num <- rowSums((X - P) * w)
    cbind(num / sqrt(rowSums(P * Q * w^2)), num / sqrt(rowSums(P * Q * wt^2)))
  }
  L <- wsum(log(P / Q)); O <- wsum((1 - 2 * P) / (P * Q))
  data.frame(lz = L[, 1], lzstar = L[, 2], zout = O[, 1], zout_star = O[, 2])
}

# Normalized Guttman errors G*: order the items from easiest to hardest by
# proportion correct, count the pairs in which the easier item is wrong and the
# harder one right, and divide by the most there could be, r * (n - r).
gstar <- function(X) {
  X <- X[, order(-colMeans(X))]
  n <- ncol(X); r <- rowSums(X)
  errors <- apply(X, 1, function(x) sum(x * c(0, head(cumsum(1 - x), -1))))
  errors / (r * (n - r))
}

# Sijtsma's H^T: Loevinger's H with respondents in place of items. For each
# respondent, the covariance over items between their responses and everyone
# else's summed responses, over the most it could be given the respondents'
# proportions correct p: the sum over the others of min(p_n, p_m) - p_n p_m.
# For rows that are neither all 0 nor all 1.
ht <- function(X) {
  p <- rowMeans(X)
  others <- sweep(-X, 2, colSums(X), "+")
  num <- rowMeans((X - p) * (others - rowMeans(others)))
  ps <- sort(p)
  below <- findInterval(p, ps, left.open = TRUE)   # respondents with a lower p
  sum_min <- c(0, cumsum(ps))[below + 1] + p * (length(p) - below - 1)
  num / (sum_min - p * (sum(p) - p))
}

# Fit a 2PL, score every respondent with a sum score strictly between 0 and n by
# maximum likelihood, and compute every person-fit statistic in the lesson.
person_fit <- function(X) {
  set.seed(1)
  m <- mirt(X, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
  ip <- coef(m, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items
  ok <- rowSums(X) > 0 & rowSums(X) < ncol(X)
  th <- fscores(m, method = "ML", max_theta = 10)[, 1]
  pf <- personfit(m, Theta = matrix(th))   # mirt's outfit, infit and Zh (= l_z)
  s <- lz_stats(X[ok, ], ip[, "a"], ip[, "b"], th[ok])
  list(model = m, ip = ip, ok = ok,
       res = data.frame(r = rowSums(X)[ok], theta = th[ok], s,
                        outfit = pf$outfit[ok], infit = pf$infit[ok], zh = pf$Zh[ok],
                        G = gstar(X[ok, ]), Ht = ht(X[ok, ])))
}
share_below <- function(z) round(mean(z < -1.645), 3)



A licensure exam






If you’ve done Response time and the speed-accuracy tradeoff: this was its main example, a 170-item licensure exam whose response times were modelled with a lognormal model, and its problem 3 asked about the flagged respondents. Here we use only the responses.



Our main example is credentialform_lnirt, one form of a licensure exam from the Handbook of Quantitative Methods for Detecting Cheating on Tests (Cizek & Wollack, 2016), distributed with the R package LNIRT. Its job: it is the one IRW table that marks respondents the vendor suspected of inappropriate behaviour (Flagged). A response is 1 when correct. We keep the 170 scored items; the pilot slots that follow them hold different items for different respondents.


Code
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v64_0.credentialform_lnirt/rows?format=csv"
cf <- read.csv(url)
# Items iraw.1-170 are the scored items. iraw.171-200 hold pilot items, and which
# pilot item sits under a name depends on the respondent's pilot set, so we keep
# the scored items only.
cf <- cf[cf$item %in% paste0("iraw.", 1:170), ]
X_cf <- xtabs(resp ~ id + item, cf)
X_cf <- unclass(X_cf)[, paste0("iraw.", 1:170)]
people_cf <- cf[!duplicated(cf$id), c("id", "Flagged", "Attempt", "Country")]
people_cf <- people_cf[match(rownames(X_cf), people_cf$id), ]
c(respondents = nrow(X_cf), items = ncol(X_cf), missing = sum(is.na(cf$resp)),
  flagged = sum(people_cf$Flagged), perfect_or_zero = sum(rowSums(X_cf) %in% c(0, 170)))

           1636             170               0              46               0 


Every respondent answered all 170 items, and no one scored 0 or 170.

pf_cf <- person_fit(X_cf)
res_cf <- pf_cf$res
# l_z by hand matches mirt's Zh
all.equal(res_cf$lz, res_cf$zh)


[1] TRUE

round(c(sd_lz = sd(res_cf$lz), below_lz = share_below(res_cf$lz),
        sd_lzstar = sd(res_cf$lzstar), below_lzstar = share_below(res_cf$lzstar),
        above_lzstar = round(mean(res_cf$lzstar > 1.645), 3)), 3)

       0.762        0.020        1.139        0.078        0.076 


At the maximum-likelihood \(\hat\theta\), \(l_z\) has SD 0.76 and flags 2.0% below −1.645: the shrinkage from the widget, on 170 real items. \(l_z^*\) has SD 1.14 and flags 7.8%, with 7.6% above +1.645. Both tails hold more respondents than a standard normal would put there.

     1.00      0.99     -0.96     -0.80     -0.86     -0.61      0.70      0.04 


The IRT-based statistics largely agree: the rank correlation of \(l_z^*\) with \(l_z\) is 0.99, with person infit −0.96, and with outfit −0.80 (−0.86 once corrected). The group-based ones agree less: −0.61 with \(G^*\) and 0.70 with \(H^T\). With the sum score it is 0.04. Split by score, though:

# The statistics by sum-score band (fifths of the respondents): the SD of l_z and
# l_z*, the share of each below -1.645, and the mean of G* and H^T.
band5 <- cut(res_cf$r, quantile(res_cf$r, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE)

About a fifth of the respondents educated in India (19.9%) or the Philippines (19.0%) have \(l_z^*\) above +1.645, against 4.8% of the 1,243 educated in the USA; repeat takers show the same, less strongly (13.6% against 5.1%). These groups score lower, but within each score band the gap remains (12–26% against about 5%). One possibility, which the patterns alone can’t settle, is that some items work differently in these groups, so that parameters from a calibration dominated by USA-educated respondents don’t describe them (problem 5).






If you’ve done Differential item functioning: an item functions differently when respondents from two groups with the same ability have different chances of answering it correctly. Group-specific slopes are one form of it.





A personality inventory
For contrast, psychtools_epi holds the Eysenck Personality Inventory (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1968, as distributed in the R package psychTools). Its job is to show misfit next to a measure of one possible cause: besides neuroticism and extraversion, the inventory has a Lie scale, nine items on which one answer describes an implausibly virtuous self. We analyse the 24 neuroticism items. In the IRW table 1 means “no” (the processing script subtracts 1 from psychTools’ 1 = yes, 2 = no); we reverse it once, so that 1 is yes, the neurotic answer for every item.


Code
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v64_0.psychtools_epi/rows?format=csv"
epi <- read.csv(url)
X_epi <- xtabs(resp ~ id + item, epi, addNA = TRUE, na.action = na.pass)
X_epi <- unclass(X_epi)
X_epi[unclass(xtabs(is.na(resp) ~ id + item, epi)) > 0] <- NA
# psychTools codes 1 = yes and 2 = no; the IRW table subtracts 1, so there 1 means
# "no". We turn it around once, here: from now on 1 = yes.
X_epi <- 1 - X_epi
# Scoring keys from psychTools (epi.keys). Every neuroticism item is keyed the same
# way; the Lie scale has three items keyed yes and six keyed no.
N_items <- paste0("V", c(2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 19, 21, 23, 26, 28, 31, 33, 35, 38,
                         40, 43, 45, 47, 50, 52, 55, 57))
L_yes <- paste0("V", c(6, 24, 36)); L_no <- paste0("V", c(12, 18, 30, 42, 48, 54))
lie <- rowSums(X_epi[, L_yes]) + rowSums(1 - X_epi[, L_no])
XN <- X_epi[, N_items]
complete <- rowSums(is.na(XN)) == 0 & !is.na(lie)
c(respondents = nrow(XN), complete = sum(complete), missing_responses = sum(is.na(epi$resp)))

res_epi <- pf_epi$res
res_epi$lie <- lie[pf_epi$ok]

        sd_lzstar = sd(res_epi$lzstar), below_lzstar = share_below(res_epi$lzstar)), 3)

Of the 3,232 respondents who answered every neuroticism and Lie item, 3,216 have a score strictly between 0 and 24. \(l_z^*\) flags 8.8% of them below −1.645, again more than 5%.

A matrix reasoning test
Our failure case is test_taking_much_2025_mr: 20 matrix reasoning items from the Open Matrices Item Bank (Koch, Spinath, Greiff & Becker, 2022), answered online by 1,244 respondents (Much, Mutak, Pohl & Ranger, 2025; data at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9J6HM). Among the 924 respondents with a statistic, the 58 who reported not understanding the task, fully or partly, have a higher mean \(l_z^*\) (0.39) than those who reported no issues (0.13), and fewer are flagged (3.4% against 7.7%). Attention checks make little difference either. A respondent who hasn’t understood the task gets items wrong in a way that looks like low ability, and person fit, which asks only whether a pattern is consistent with some \(\theta\), finds nothing to flag.
So what should a program do with a person-fit statistic? Each option rests on assumptions. \(l_z^*\) assumes the item parameters are right for everyone and corrects for \(\theta\) being estimated from the same responses; \(G^*\) and \(H^T\) assume only an ordering of the items and the other respondents’ patterns, but they have no reference distribution without a model or a simulation, and a value means something only within its sample. Neither sees disengagement that looks like low ability, or a problem confined to a few items. In the case that the question is whether a respondent’s pattern is consistent with the model, \(l_z^*\) at a maximum-likelihood or WLE \(\hat\theta\), read alongside a group-based statistic such as \(H^T\), may be sufficient for some purposes as a first screen. A flag is a reason to look at the pattern, not a finding about the respondent.

title: Person fit: does a respondent’s pattern fit the model?
text:
Problems

Derivation. Show that \(E(l_0)\) and \(\text{Var}(l_0)\) at a known \(\theta\) are as given in the core ideas, and that \(l_0 - E(l_0) = \sum_i (x_i - P_i)\log\frac{P_i}{1 - P_i}\). Then, following the Go deeper callout, show that for the Rasch model at the ML \(\hat\theta\) the variance lost is \((\hat\theta - \bar b)^2 I(\hat\theta)\). Whose \(l_z\) is least affected?
Real data with a twist. Repeat the EPI analysis on the extraversion scale, whose items are keyed in both directions (psychTools epi.keys), remembering that the IRW table codes 1 as “no”. Does the Lie gradient hold? What happens to \(l_z^*\) if you forget to reverse the negatively keyed items?
Judgment. A licensure program proposes to review everyone with \(l_z^* < -1.645\): 7.8% of 1,636, about 128 people. What should a review look for, what would a flag not justify, and what would you tell a respondent who asks why they were reviewed?
Design. Suppose preknowledge of 20 of the 170 licensure items. Why is a global index weak? Design a statistic on a suspected subset (for example, performance on the subset given a \(\hat\theta\) from the other items), and simulate its power against \(l_z^*\) (Cizek & Wollack, 2016).
Real data: the overfit tail. In credentialform_lnirt, fit the 2PL separately to the USA-educated respondents and to the rest, and recompute \(l_z^*\) in each group with its own item parameters. Does the tail above +1.645 shrink? What else could make patterns more predictable than the model expects?
Challenge (open): across the IRW. Across many IRW tables, how often does \(l_z^*\) fall below −1.645 more often than 5%, and is the excess about respondents or about the model? What would tell the two apart? (I don’t know the answer. One start: compare the excess under a 2PL, a 3PL and a two-class mixture.)

title: The Rasch model
text:
What this is for
Sum scores treat every item as interchangeable: a correct answer is worth one point no matter which item it came from. Yet items differ, and the chance of getting any one of them right does not rise in a straight line with the sum score (Where CTT breaks). What is the simplest model that takes items seriously? The Rasch model (Rasch, 1960), with one parameter per person and one per item, on the same scale. That parsimony buys some unusual properties, chief among them that the sum score is all the model needs to know about a person, and it makes demands of the data. This lesson is about both.






Recall from Where CTT breaks: against the sum score, the proportion correct on each item of a mathematics test rose in an S-shape, at its own place and rate, and a logistic regression on the sum score described each curve. But the sum score is an observed stand-in: it contains the item, and it depends on which items were taken.

title: The Rasch model
The Rasch model
text:
Core ideas

From logistic regression to the Rasch model






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: we regressed 40 chess problems on the players’ Elo ratings, \(\Pr(y = 1) = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)/(1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x))\). Giving each problem its own intercept raised the Elo slope from 0.50 to 0.83. Problem Y15 stood out: about as hard as Y29, but success on it barely moved with Elo. That lesson ended on a question: what if each player had an unknown parameter of their own instead of an observed Elo rating?



The Rasch model answers it, and takes the step Where CTT breaks pointed to. It keeps the shape of the logistic regression, but everything on the right-hand side is unknown. For person \(j\) and item \(i\), \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \frac{\exp(\theta_j - b_i)}{1 + \exp(\theta_j - b_i)}.\]

\(\theta_j\) is the person’s ability, an idealized version of the sum score. It, and it alone, determines how a person performs on the items. It takes the place of \(\beta_1 \times \text{Elo}\), or of the sum score in the item curves.
\(b_i\) is the item’s difficulty, the item intercept with its sign flipped. When \(\theta = b\), the odds of a correct response are even.

Plotting the probability of a correct response against \(\theta\) for a single item gives the item characteristic curve (ICC): the item curve of Where CTT breaks, with \(\theta\) where the sum score was. Move the difficulty around and watch what happens.

Try it: an item characteristic curve


Code
viewof icc_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof icc_a = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a (Rasch: a = 1)"})
viewof icc_norm = Inputs.toggle({label: "Overlay the normal CDF", value: false})

























Code
icc_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, icc_b, icc_a), curve: "This item"},
  ...(icc_norm ? [{theta: t, p: pnorm(t - icc_b), curve: "Normal CDF"}] : [])
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: icc_norm, domain: ["This item", "Normal CDF"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: palette.rule}), Plot.ruleX([icc_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(icc_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: icc_b, p: p2pl(icc_b, icc_b, icc_a)}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})
















Changing \(b\) slides the curve left and right without changing its shape: a harder item needs more ability for the same chance of success. The curve never reaches 0 or 1, so nobody is certain to get any item right or wrong. The Rasch model fixes the slope at 1 for every item; letting it vary gives the 2PL of From the 1PL to the 4PL.






NoteA challenge: the logistic and the normal curve





Especially if you know probit regression: turn on the normal CDF in the widget and find the slope that makes the two curves nearly identical. The answer is roughly 1.7: the scaling constant \(D\) that older IRT papers carry around so that logistic and normal-ogive parameters can be compared. Camilli (1994) traces where it came from.





Code
quiz({
  q: "A person's ability equals an item's difficulty ($\\theta = b$). What is the probability they get the item right under the Rasch model?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.5", correct: true, why: "At $\\theta = b$ the exponent is 0, and $e^0/(1+e^0) = 1/2$. This is what 'difficulty' means on this scale."},
    {text: "It depends on the item's slope", correct: false, why: "Under the Rasch model every slope is 1. Even in the 2PL, the probability at $\\theta = b$ is still 0.5; the slope only changes how quickly the curve rises around that point."},
    {text: "1, because the person is at the item's level", correct: false, why: "The model never gives a probability of 1. At $\\theta = b$ the person is exactly as likely to get it right as wrong."}
  ]
})










The scale has no origin
Where is zero on this scale? Nowhere in particular. Add the same constant \(C\) to every ability and every difficulty: the model only ever sees \(\theta - b\), so no predicted response changes.

Try it: shift everything


Code
viewof shiftC = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Add C to every θ and b"})









Code
shift_items = [{item: "Easy", b: -1}, {item: "Medium", b: 0.5}, {item: "Hard", b: 2}]
shift_people = [{person: "Ana", theta: -0.5}, {person: "Ben", theta: 1}]
Inputs.table(shift_people.flatMap(pp => shift_items.map(it => ({
  person: pp.person, "θ + C": (pp.theta + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  item: it.item, "b + C": (it.b + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  "P(correct)": p2pl(pp.theta + shiftC, it.b + shiftC).toFixed(3)
}))), {layout: "auto", rows: 7})























The probabilities in the last column do not move. The data say how far apart people and items are, but not where zero is: without an extra constraint the model is not identified. Software picks one for you. mirt (Chalmers, 2012) fixes the mean of the ability distribution at 0, as the chess fit below shows. Programs that use conditional maximum likelihood (see the Go deeper callout below) instead fix one item’s difficulty at 0 or make the difficulties sum to 0 (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007). The choice is arbitrary, so two programs’ results can differ by exactly such a shift.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two analysts fit the Rasch model to the same data. One reports that item 7 has $b = 1.2$; the other reports $b = 0.9$. Which is most likely?",
  options: [
    {text: "One of them made an error", correct: false, why: "Not necessarily. If one program centers abilities and the other centers difficulties, every $b$ shifts by the same constant."},
    {text: "They used different identification constraints", correct: true, why: "If every item (and every person) differs by the same 0.3, the two solutions make identical predictions. Check the other items before worrying."},
    {text: "Item 7 is misfitting", correct: false, why: "Misfit wouldn't produce a clean shift in the difficulty estimate like this; a constant offset across items points to the choice of origin."}
  ]
})










People and items on one scale: the Wright map






Recall from Where CTT breaks: the same 664 students averaged 9.6 on an easy half of a test and 5.7 on a hard half. A sum score doesn’t locate anyone until we know the items.



In the Rasch model a person’s location is \(\theta\), not a count of items, and \(\theta\) and \(b\) live on the same scale, so we can plot them together. A Wright map puts the distribution of people on one side and the item difficulties on the other, and shows at a glance whether a test is well matched to the people who took it.

Try it: build a Wright map


Code
predict({
  q: "Suppose the average person sits 1.5 logits *above* the average item. Roughly what proportion of items will a typical person get right?",
  choices: ["About 50%", "About 60%", "About 75%", "About 95%"],
  answer: "About 75%",
  reveal: "A gap of 1.5 logits puts a typical person at $e^{1.5}/(1+e^{1.5}) \\approx 0.82$ on an average item, and spreading people and items out pulls the average back toward 50%, to roughly three in four. Set the sliders below to check."
})









Code
viewof wm_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability"})
viewof wm_bmean = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean item difficulty"})
viewof wm_bsd = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Spread of item difficulties"})

























Code
wm_people = normalQuantiles(300, wm_mu, 1)
wm_items = normalQuantiles(20, wm_bmean, wm_bsd)
wm_pc = expectedPropCorrect(wm_items, wm_mu, 1)
wm_bins = grid(-5, 4.75, 40).map(lo => ({lo, hi: lo + 0.25, n: wm_people.filter(t => t >= lo && t < lo + 0.25).length}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, y: {label: "Logits", domain: [-5, 5]},
  x: {label: null, ticks: [], domain: [-45, 45]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX(wm_bins, {x1: d => -d.n, x2: 0, y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: palette.light, insetTop: 0.5}),
    Plot.dot(wm_items, {y: d => d, x: (d, i) => 6 + (i % 5) * 6, symbol: "diamond", fill: palette.contrast, r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.text(["People"], {x: -22, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13}),
    Plot.text(["Items"], {x: 18, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Expected proportion correct for this population: **${(100 * wm_pc).toFixed(0)}%**. ${
  wm_mu - wm_bmean > 1 ? "This test is easy for this group: many people sit above the hardest items, and we learn little about differences among them." :
  wm_bmean - wm_mu > 1 ? "This test is hard for this group: many people sit below the easiest items." :
  "Items and people overlap well, which is where a test measures most precisely."}`







Where people and items overlap, the test can tell people apart; where people sit beyond every item, it cannot. That precision depends on where you are on the scale is the subject of Information, precision, and short forms.



What the model assumes
Two assumptions merit emphasis (Lord, 1980). First, the formula is right: in particular, a single \(\theta\) drives every response (the model is unidimensional). Second, responses are locally independent: once we know \(\theta\), knowing how someone answered item 3 tells us nothing more about item 4. Both can fail: think of two items that share a reading passage, or a test whose last ten items measure something else. IRW vignettes look at how often each assumption holds across many IRW datasets: dimensionality and local dependence.


The sum score is sufficient
The Rasch model has a property that sets it apart from nearly every other item response model: the sum score \(r\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) (Fisher, 1922). Once you know how many items someone got right, nothing else in their responses, not even which items, changes what we can learn about their ability.






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: in a logistic regression with an intercept, the derivative of the log likelihood with respect to the intercept is \(\sum_i (y_i - p_i)\), so at the maximum the model’s predicted number of successes equals the observed number.



For one respondent, \(\theta\) plays the part of that intercept. So the maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\theta\) is the value at which the expected number correct, \(\sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), equals the observed number correct, \(r\). Which items make up \(r\) never enters the equation.
Below are five items of increasing difficulty. Pick a response pattern and look at the likelihood for \(\theta\); then look at every other pattern with the same sum score.

Try it: sufficiency


Code
suf_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
suf_a2 = [0.5, 1.8, 1.0, 0.6, 2.0]
viewof suf_x = Inputs.checkbox(["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 2 (b = −0.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)", "Item 4 (b = 0.5)", "Item 5 (b = 1.5)"],
  {label: "Correct on", value: ["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)"]})
viewof suf_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch (all slopes 1)", "2PL (slopes differ)"], {value: "Rasch (all slopes 1)", label: "Model"})
































Code
suf_pattern = suf_b.map((_, i) => suf_x.some(s => s.startsWith(`Item ${i + 1} `)) ? 1 : 0)
suf_slopes = suf_model.startsWith("Rasch") ? null : suf_a2
suf_sum = suf_pattern.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0)
suf_same = patternsWithSum(5, suf_sum).map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), mle: mle(x, suf_b, suf_slopes)}))
suf_curve = grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, ll: Math.exp(loglik(t, suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes))}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "Likelihood of this pattern"},
  marks: [Plot.line(suf_curve, {x: "theta", y: "ll", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.ruleX([mle(suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes)].filter(Number.isFinite), {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})]
})














































Code
md`Your pattern is **${suf_pattern.join("")}** (sum score ${suf_sum}). The maximum-likelihood estimate of θ for every pattern with the same sum score:`









Code
Inputs.table(suf_same.map(d => ({pattern: d.pattern, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞")})), {layout: "auto", rows: 11})







Under the Rasch model the column is constant. Switch to the 2PL and it no longer is: getting a highly discriminating item right now counts for more. The relationship between sum scores and Rasch abilities is one-to-one but not linear. On these five items the step from 3 to 4 correct moves the estimate from 0.50 to 1.67, and 5 of 5 has no finite estimate at all.
So which should you report, the sum score or \(\hat\theta\)? If the Rasch model fits and everyone took the same items, I’d report the sum score. It carries everything the model knows about the respondent, it orders people exactly as \(\hat\theta\) does, and nobody needs it explained. \(\hat\theta\) earns its keep when respondents take different items, as in Linking and equating: there the sum scores are no longer comparable and \(\theta\) is.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under the Rasch model, two students both answer 3 of 5 items correctly. Student A got the three easiest items right; student B got the three hardest right. What do their ability estimates look like?",
  options: [
    {text: "B's estimate is higher, because B solved harder items", correct: false, why: "That is the intuition the 2PL (and a lot of common sense) would support, but the Rasch model says otherwise: the sum score is sufficient."},
    {text: "They are identical", correct: true, why: "The sum score is sufficient for θ under the Rasch model. B's pattern is less *likely* (it may suggest misfit), but the estimate is the same."},
    {text: "A's estimate is higher, because A's pattern is more consistent", correct: false, why: "Consistency affects how plausible the pattern is under the model—person fit—but not the ability estimate."}
  ]
})










Specific objectivity
The Rasch tradition has a name for the property it prizes: specific objectivity (Rasch, 1977). Comparisons between people should not depend on which items we happened to use, and comparisons between items should not depend on which people happened to take them. It is a demand we place on the data, not something the data grants us for free.
If two items’ curves never cross, then everyone finds item A easier than item B, whatever their ability. If they cross, the ordering of the items depends on who you ask—and the statement “item A is easier than item B” stops meaning anything on its own.

Try it: do the curves cross?


Code
viewof so_bA = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item A difficulty"})
viewof so_bB = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item B difficulty"})
viewof so_aB = Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Item B slope (Rasch: 1)"})

























Code
so_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bA, 1), item: "Item A"},
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bB, so_aB), item: "Item B"}])
so_cross = Math.abs(so_aB - 1) < 1e-9 ? null : (so_aB * so_bB - so_bA) / (so_aB - 1)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(so_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          ...(so_cross !== null && Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? [Plot.ruleX([so_cross], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})] : [])]
})

























Code
md`${so_cross === null ? "With equal slopes the curves never cross: whoever you are, the ordering of the two items is the same." :
  Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? `The curves cross at θ ≈ ${so_cross.toFixed(2)}. Below that, one item is easier; above it, the other is. Which item is "harder" now depends on the person.` :
  "The slopes differ, so the curves cross somewhere—but outside the range plotted. Push the slope further from 1 to bring the crossing into view."}`







This is why advocates of the Rasch model hold to it so firmly: specific objectivity and sufficiency are what classical measurement in the physical sciences looks like (Wright, 1997). The catch is that the model has to fit. Consistency with the Rasch model comes from hard work—iterative item development and pruning of items that don’t behave—not from applying it to whatever data you have. Whether equal slopes are plausible for typical test data is an empirical question, and the 2PL discrimination vignette looks at it across many IRW datasets.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two items' ICCs cross at θ = 1. What does that imply?",
  options: [
    {text: "The items have different difficulties", correct: false, why: "Items with different difficulties and equal slopes never cross. Crossing requires different slopes."},
    {text: "The items have different slopes, so which item is easier depends on the person's ability", correct: true, why: "Below θ = 1 one item is easier; above it, the other is. That breaks specific objectivity."},
    {text: "The model has not converged", correct: false, why: "Crossing curves are a property of the fitted model (a 2PL or beyond), not a sign of estimation trouble."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: why the sum score is sufficient, and what follows





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; the Rasch model holds for every item; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the difficulties \(b_1, \dots, b_I\) are fixed. Write \(\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}\) (the item’s easiness) and \(r = \sum_i x_i\).
Factorize the likelihood. Using \(\Pr(x_i \mid \theta) = e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}/(1 + e^{\theta - b_i})\) for \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\), \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{I} \frac{e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}}{1 + e^{\theta - b_i}} = \frac{e^{r\theta} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}.\] The data meet \(\theta\) in one place only, \(e^{r\theta}\). The product \(\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}\) depends on which items were right but not on \(\theta\), and the denominator depends on \(\theta\) but not on the data. Taking logs and differentiating gives \(r - \sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), the score equation from the main text.
Condition on \(r\). Add up the probabilities of all the patterns with the same sum score: \[\Pr(r \mid \theta) = \frac{e^{r\theta}\,\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}, \qquad \gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}:\, \sum_i y_i = r} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{y_i},\] where \(\gamma_r\), the elementary symmetric function of order \(r\), is a sum over patterns and contains no \(\theta\). Divide: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r, \theta) = \frac{\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}.\] \(\theta\) has cancelled. Given \(r\), the pattern carries no further information about \(\theta\); that is the definition of a sufficient statistic. Three things follow.

Conditional maximum likelihood. Multiply \(\Pr(\mathbf{x}_j \mid r_j)\) over respondents and you have a likelihood for the difficulties with no \(\theta\) in it. Maximizing it is conditional maximum likelihood (CML). It needs no assumption about how \(\theta\) is distributed, and it gives consistent estimates of the \(b_i\) as the number of respondents grows (Andersen, 1970). Estimating every \(\theta_j\) jointly with the \(b_i\) does not, because the number of person parameters grows with the data (Neyman & Scott, 1948). The wirs analysis below uses \(\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid r)\) to compare the model with the data without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\).
Specific objectivity is a theorem. Take two items, \(i\) and \(k\), and condition on the respondent getting exactly one of them right. The same cancellation, with two items, gives \[\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid x_i + x_k = 1, \theta) = \frac{\varepsilon_i}{\varepsilon_i + \varepsilon_k} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{b_i - b_k}},\] which contains no \(\theta\). Whoever the respondents are, strong or weak, the comparison of the two items comes out the same. Swap the roles of people and items (two respondents, one item, exactly one of them right) and the comparison depends on \(\theta_j - \theta_l\) and not on \(b\). This is Rasch’s specific objectivity, derived rather than assumed. When the model fails, it fails in a checkable way: CML estimates of the difficulties from high and low scorers should agree, and Andersen (1973) turned that into a likelihood-ratio test. Problem 3 tries the two-item version on the chess data.
The converse. For dichotomous items, if some statistic is sufficient for \(\theta\) and is the same statistic whatever the item parameters, it is the sum score, and the model must be the Rasch model: logistic curves with equal slopes (Andersen, 1977). Fischer (1995) collects this and other derivations of the Rasch model. Under the 2PL, the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) plays the part of \(r\), but its weights are item parameters, which is where From the 1PL to the 4PL picks up.







A note on estimation
Nothing on the right-hand side is known, so fitting takes two steps. mirt estimates the item parameters first, integrating over the distribution of abilities with the EM algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), then estimates abilities with those item parameters treated as known. Conditional maximum likelihood (Go deeper, above) is the Rasch model’s own alternative. Estimating abilities and Estimating item parameters take these in turn.

title: The Rasch model
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates responses from the Rasch model, fits the model with mirt, and compares the estimated difficulties to the truth. It runs here in your browser; the first run takes about 20 seconds while R and mirt load.
Try changing np to 50, then to 2000, and watch the scatter around the line. With the seed as written, the root mean squared error of the estimated difficulties is 0.34 with 50 people, 0.13 with 500 and 0.04 with 2,000. Now change ni to 40: with 500 people the error barely moves (0.13), because each difficulty rests on the people who answered that item. More items sharpen the abilities instead, which is where Information, precision, and short forms picks up.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

mirt writes the Rasch model as \(\Pr(x = 1) = 1/(1 + \exp(-(\theta + d)))\), so its parameter d is an easiness. Our difficulty is \(b = -d\), which is why the code negates it.
Download this code to run it as large as you like in your own R session.

title: The Rasch model
text:
With real data
Our main example is chess_lnirt, the 40 problems of the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005), which we met in The likelihood and logistic regression; its job here is to show what the Rasch model says about a test built for a wide range of skill. A response is 1 if the player solved the problem; download the code behind every number below.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
chess_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.chess_lnirt/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(chess_url)
head(df[, c("id", "item", "resp")])

item
resp

147

We reshape to one row per player. The first rows above belong to a player with no responses; three of the 259 players are like that, and we drop them, leaving 256.


Code
# IRW tables are long: one row per person-item response. mirt wants wide: one
# row per person, one column per item.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
}
resp <- long2wide(df)
# A few players have no responses at all (resp is NA for every item; the first
# rows of the table are one of them). They carry no information, so drop them.
c(players_in_table = nrow(resp), with_no_responses = sum(rowSums(!is.na(resp)) == 0))


 players_in_table with_no_responses 
              259                 3 


Code
resp <- resp[rowSums(!is.na(resp)) > 0, ]
dim(resp)


[1] 256  40




Code
m1 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
# mirt writes the Rasch model as P(x = 1) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(theta + d))), so its
# "d" is an easiness. The difficulty in our notation is b = -d.
b <- -coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
round(head(sort(b)), 2)   # the easiest items


  Y31    Y1    Y2    Y3   Y21    Y5 
-4.87 -3.56 -3.48 -3.24 -2.99 -2.82 


Code
round(tail(sort(b)), 2)   # the hardest items


 Y36  Y18  Y19  Y15  Y29  Y30 
2.12 2.19 2.74 3.02 3.14 3.61 


The easiest problem (Y31) sits nearly five logits below zero, the mean ability, and the hardest (Y30) more than three and a half above. Is that a wide spread, and compared with what? The IRW’s difficulty pool holds Rasch difficulties for 145 IRW tables (Zhang et al., 2025), and chess is one of them.


Code
# How wide is wide? The IRW's difficulty pool (the diffsim vignette) holds
# difficulty estimates for 145 IRW tables and ships with the irw package.
round(c(sd_b = sd(b), range_b = diff(range(b))), 2)   # chess, from our fit


   sd_b range_b 
   2.13    8.48 


Code
if (requireNamespace("irw", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data("diff_long", package = "irw")
  pool_sd <- tapply(diff_long$difficulty, diff_long$dataset, sd)
  print(c(tables = length(pool_sd), round(quantile(pool_sd, c(.25, .5, .75)), 2)))
  # chess_lnirt is in the pool. Compare its entry with the rest of the pool:
  cat(sprintf("chess_lnirt in the pool: SD %.2f, wider than %.0f%% of the %d tables\n",
              pool_sd[["chess_lnirt"]], 100 * mean(pool_sd < pool_sd[["chess_lnirt"]]),
              length(pool_sd)))
  # The pool's chess SD is ours divided by the SD of ability in our fit: the pool
  # puts ability on a scale with SD 1, while mirt's Rasch fit estimates it.
  sd_theta <- sqrt(coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$cov[1, 1])
  cat(sprintf("SD of ability in our fit %.2f; our SD of b divided by it: %.2f\n",
              sd_theta, sd(b) / sd_theta))
}


tables    25%    50%    75% 
145.00   0.70   0.99   1.75 
chess_lnirt in the pool: SD 1.75, wider than 74% of the 145 tables
SD of ability in our fit 1.22; our SD of b divided by it: 1.75


The median table in the pool has a standard deviation of difficulties of 0.99; chess, at 1.75 on the pool’s scale, is more spread out than 74% of them. (The pool fixes the SD of ability at 1, while the Rasch model fixes the slopes at 1 and lets the SD of ability float, here to 1.22; dividing our 2.1 by 1.22 recovers the pool’s 1.75.) That spread is what you want from a test meant to separate novices from masters.
How do these difficulties relate to the simplest measure of item difficulty, the proportion of players who solve the problem?


Code
p <- colMeans(resp, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(p, b, xlab = "Proportion correct (p-value)", ylab = "Rasch difficulty (b)",
     pch = 19, col = "#2780e3")









Code
sprintf("%.4f", cor(p, b, method = "spearman"))   # rank correlation of p and b


[1] "-0.9998"


The rank correlation is −0.9998. That is sufficiency from the item side: with complete data an item’s total is sufficient for its difficulty (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007), and a few missing responses keep it from being exactly −1. The relationship is not linear, though: the Rasch scale stretches out the extremes, where a few percentage points correct correspond to a large difference in difficulty.


Code
theta <- fscores(m1)[, 1]
br <- seq(floor(min(c(theta, b))), ceiling(max(c(theta, b))), by = 0.25)
h <- hist(theta, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-max(h$counts), 12), ylim = range(br), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Logits", main = "Wright map: chess_lnirt")
rect(-h$counts, h$breaks[-length(h$breaks)], 0, h$breaks[-1], col = "#dbeafe", border = "white")
points(rep(1.5, length(b)) + (seq_along(b) %% 8), b, pch = 18, col = "#c2410c")
abline(v = 0)
axis(1, at = c(-max(h$counts) / 2, 5), labels = c("People", "Items"), tick = FALSE)









Code
par(op)
round(c(mean_theta = mean(theta), mean_b = mean(b)), 2)


mean_theta     mean_b 
      0.00       0.12 


Code

all.equal(plogis(outer(theta + 1, b + 1, "-")), plogis(outer(theta, b, "-")))

The mean ability is 0.00, the constraint mirt imposes, and adding 1 to every ability and difficulty leaves every probability unchanged (all.equal returns TRUE). Does the model fit? One first look is the infit and outfit statistics (Wright & Masters, 1982): mean squared standardized residuals, which should be near 1 if the model is right. Values well below 1 mean an item is more predictable than the Rasch model expects (typically an item that discriminates better than average); values well above 1 mean it is noisier. How far from 1 is too far is the subject of Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.

Four of the five worst-fitting items by \(|z|\) overfit (outfit from 0.64 to 0.73): they separate strong and weak players more sharply than a common slope allows. The exception is Y15, whose outfit of 2.2 is the largest of all 40 items under mirt’s default: by the size of its misfit, it is among the worst-fitting items on the test. It is the problem whose success barely moved with Elo in The likelihood and logistic regression. The empirical plot compares the model’s curve with the proportions solved among players grouped by ability. Those proportions barely rise: below-average players solve Y15 more often than the model expects, and the strongest group less often. Why is a question about the problem itself, which the responses alone can’t answer. These outfits come from mirt’s default EAP abilities, which pull outfit below 1 even when the model is true (Model fit and out-of-sample prediction). For contrast, a table whose job is to show a setting where one ability and equal slopes describe the data less well: wirs, six items from the 1990 Workplace Industrial Relations Survey analysed by Bartholomew (1998). Each item asks whether a kind of consultation took place about the most recent introduction of new equipment (1 = yes), from informal discussion with individual workers (item 1) through joint consultative committees (item 3) to paid union officials (wording from the ltm documentation, Rizopoulos, 2006). Because the sum score is sufficient, the Rasch model says what proportion of respondents with each sum score should say yes to each item, without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\) (the Go deeper callout gives the formula).

# Because the sum score r is sufficient, the Rasch model predicts the proportion
# endorsing item i among respondents with sum score r without reference to theta:
#   P(x_i = 1 | r) = eps_i * gamma_(r-1)(items other than i) / gamma_r(all items),
# with eps = exp(-b) and gamma_r the elementary symmetric functions (see the
# Go deeper callout in the lesson).
esf <- function(eps) {               # gamma_0, gamma_1, ..., gamma_n
  g <- 1
  for (e in eps) g <- c(g, 0) + c(0, g) * e
  g
}
p_given_r <- function(b, i) {        # P(x_i = 1 | r) for r = 0, ..., n
  eps <- exp(-b); g <- esf(eps); g_i <- esf(eps[-i]); r <- seq_along(b)
  c(0, eps[i] * g_i[r] / g[r + 1])
}

title: The Rasch model
text:
Problems

The logit. Show that \(\frac{e^x}{1+e^x} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\). Then show that under the Rasch model, \(\log\frac{\Pr(x=1)}{\Pr(x=0)} = \theta - b\). What does a one-unit increase in \(\theta\) do to the odds of a correct response, on any item?
Indeterminacy. Suppose \(\theta' = \theta + C\) and \(b' = b + C\). Show that \(\Pr(x = 1)\) is unchanged. Now suppose instead \(\theta' = k\theta\) and \(b' = kb\) for some \(k \ne 1\). Is the Rasch model still unchanged? What does your answer say about which feature of the scale the Rasch model does pin down, and how does it square with the difficulty pool’s chess SD of 1.75 against our 2.1?
Specific objectivity in the chess data. By the Go deeper callout, among players who solved exactly one of problems \(i\) and \(k\), the proportion who solved \(i\) should be \(1/(1 + e^{b_i - b_k})\) whatever their ability. Pick two problems of middling difficulty, take the players who solved exactly one, and split them at the median of their sum score on the other 38. Compare the two halves with each other and with the prediction. Repeat for a pair that includes Y15. What do you see?
Targeting. Draw the Wright map for chess_lnirt. For which players does this test give the least information, and why? Suggest the difficulty of two items you would add to the test to improve measurement for them.
Fit, two ways. Using itemfit(..., empirical.plot = i), compare several items in chess_lnirt and in wirs. Which dataset does the Rasch model describe better? Now run the simulation above with np = 2000 and ni = 50 and look at the same plots. What does “good fit” look like when you know the model is true?
Challenge: sufficiency in the data. In chess_lnirt, find two players with the same sum score but very different response patterns. Compare their estimated abilities (fscores). Then fit a 2PL (itemtype = "2PL") and compare again. Explain what you see. Then the open part: if the 2PL fits the chess data better, how much would you lose by reporting the sum score anyway, and how would you decide?
